title: FailSAE: Towards Interpretable Failure Prediction for Vision-Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have achieved strong performance across multimodal tasks by aligning visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space. As VLMs are increasingly used for high-stakes domains, failure prediction becomes critical for risk-aware deployment and human intervention. Existing failure prediction methods typically rely on confidence scores or auxiliary classifiers. Although these methods are effective on predicting VLM failures, they provide limited interpretability. In this work, we investigate the use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpretable failure prediction in VLMs. We formulate failure prediction as a classification task over sparse SAE latent activations and introduce a three-stage failure-aware training pipeline that encourages the learned latent directions to remain interpretable while becoming more informative for failure prediction. Our experiments show that the resulting framework outperforms the evaluated baselines in failure prediction. Further analysis suggests that failure-aware training encourages SAE latent directions to capture more class-specific concepts. We also use the SAE to provide a concept-level analysis of how model representations change during failures, revealing a shift from class-specific concepts toward more ambiguous or style-related concepts. Finally, we explore how the learned SAE latent directions can support runtime failure recovery.

AI.tldr: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are used for interpretable failure prediction in Vision-Language Models; a three-stage training pipeline targets interpretable latent directions to improve failure detection; SAE insights reveal failure mechanisms and enable potential runtime recovery.
AI.motivation: As VLMs like CLIP are deployed in high-stakes settings, reliable failure prediction is essential for risk-aware deployment and human intervention. Existing methods rely on confidence scores or auxiliary classifiers and lack interpretable explanations of failures.
AI.method: Formulate failure prediction as a classification task over SAE latent activations. Introduce a three-stage failure-aware training pipeline designed to preserve interpretability of latent directions while enhancing their informativeness for failure prediction.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves superior failure-prediction performance compared to evaluated baselines. SAE latent directions tend to capture more class-specific concepts under failure-aware training. Concept-level analysis shows failures involve a shift from class-specific concepts to more ambiguous or style-related concepts. The SAE directions also support potential runtime failure recovery.
AI.conclusion: SAE-based failure prediction offers interpretable insights into VLM failures and improves predictive performance, with latent directions providing meaningful, class-specific concept representations and enabling runtime recovery strategies.

title: When Seeing Overrides Knowing: Visual Dominance and Deferral-Based Method for Personalized Safety in VLMs
comment: Published as a main conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, where a response that is reasonable in general may still be unsafe for a particular user whose medical, emotional, or situational context is unknown to the model. We study this problem of personalized safety in multimodal systems and introduce MPS-Bench, a benchmark of 5,181 scenarios from 584 real-world images across 12 high-risk domains, each paired with a hidden user profile. Evaluating eight frontier VLMs, we find that they almost always respond directly (86-99%) rather than seek missing context, and none exceeds 2.6/5 on personalized safety. To understand why these failures arise, we analyze multimodal interactions and identify visual dominance: visual information enters text representations early and suppresses textual risk signals during multimodal fusion. Causal interventions reveal a two-stage mechanism in which visual affect is first transferred into the text stream in early layers and then shapes the final decision through this altered text representation, making late-stage internal remediation unreliable. Motivated by this mechanism, we propose PRISM, a lightweight input monitor that uses bidirectional cross-modal modulation to predict when a query is likely to require deferral. PRISM achieves 0.978 AUC and strictly dominates the safety-utility Pareto frontier across all tested models.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (MPS-Bench) reveals personalized safety gaps in vision-language models (VLMs) and identifies visual dominance as a key failure mechanism; a deferral-based monitor (PRISM) achieves high discrimination and improves safety-utility trade-offs.
AI.motivation: To address unsafe responses of VLMs in high-risk, user-context-unknown scenarios by evaluating personalization safety and designing mechanisms that can predict when a user query requires deferral to obtain missing context.
AI.method: 1) Construct MPS-Bench with 5,181 scenarios from 584 real-world images across 12 high-risk domains, each paired with a hidden user profile. 2) Evaluate eight frontier VLMs and analyze multimodal interactions; perform causal interventions to uncover the two-stage visual-to-text risk transfer. 3) Propose PRISM, a lightweight input monitor that uses bidirectional cross-modal modulation to predict when deferral is needed; evaluate on AUC and safety-utility Pareto frontier.
AI.result: Findings show that 86–99% of responses are direct rather than seeking context; none exceed 2.6/5 on personalized safety. Visual information enters text representations early and suppresses textual risk signals during fusion; causal interventions reveal a two-stage mechanism: visual affect is transferred to the text stream in early layers and then shapes final decisions, making late remediation unreliable. PRISM achieves 0.978 AUC and dominates the safety-utility Pareto frontier across tested models.
AI.conclusion: Personalized safety in multimodal systems is hampered by early visual-to-text influence that biases decisions against deferral. A lightweight cross-modal monitor like PRISM can reliably predict when deferral is warranted, enabling safer deployments and guiding future model design to mitigate visual dominance.

title: Step Back to Move Forward: Reflection-Aware Preference Optimization for Visual Generation
summary: Diffusion models have become the mainstream paradigm for modern visual generation and have substantially advanced multimedia content synthesis, especially in text-to-image and text-to-video tasks. To further align such generative models with human preferences, reinforcement learning (RL) has recently shown strong potential as a post-training strategy. Nevertheless, existing policy gradient-based methods often explore inefficiently, making them vulnerable to local optima that may degrade semantic faithfulness and visual realism. To address these challenges, we present Reflection-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO), a new RL-based preference alignment framework for diffusion generative models. The core idea is to improve "forward" generation by incorporating "backward" reflection during optimization. We first introduce Diffusion Reflection, which rectifies intermediate sampling trajectories by inverting the diffusion process with a weak estimator, guiding latent states toward higher-probability regions of the true data manifold. Furthermore, we introduce Counterfactual Path Synthesis to implicitly distill these rectified trajectories into the policy, enabling the model to internalize the benefits of search-based exploration without incurring inference-time overhead. Extensive experiments on T2I and T2V models demonstrate that RA-GRPO significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in mitigating reward hacking and improving generalization. The method remains architecture-agnostic and integrates seamlessly with standard pipelines, suggesting a promising direction for stable preference alignment.

AI.tldr: RA-GRPO introduces Reflection-Aware gradient-based RL for diffusion models, using diffusion reflection and counterfactual path synthesis to improve preference alignment, mitigate local optima, and enhance generalization across T2I/T2V tasks with minimal inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Address inefficiencies and local optima in policy-gradient RL for diffusion-model alignment, aiming to improve semantic faithfulness and visual realism while avoiding reward hacking.
AI.method: 1) Diffusion Reflection: invert diffusion with a weak estimator to rectify intermediate sampling trajectories, steering latent states toward higher-probability regions of the data manifold. 2) Counterfactual Path Synthesis: distill rectified trajectories into the policy to enable search-based exploration benefits without extra inference time.
AI.result: Empirical results on text-to-image and text-to-video tasks show RA-GRPO outperforms existing methods, reducing reward hacking and improving generalization; method is architecture-agnostic and integrates with standard diffusion pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a stable, architecture-agnostic approach to preference alignment for diffusion models by combining forward generation with backward reflection and implicit policy distillation, offering a promising direction for robust alignment with human preferences.

title: Approximating CDTW Distance of Piecewise Algebraic Curves
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures. Preliminary manuscript, comments welcome!
summary: Curves as input data naturally arise in a variety of fields including finance, seismology, medicine, spatio-temporal data mining, malicious activity detection, and more. A common way to analyze these data sets is to do similarity matching or clustering. The most common metrics used for measuring similarity of curves are Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) and Fréchet distance. These metrics are sensitive to sampling rate and outliers respectively, and do not yield robust outcomes. Continuous Dynamic Time Warping (CDTW) is a more robust distance metric that improves upon DTW and Fréchet distances. Existing algorithms for CDTW are either exact algorithms that focus on non-Euclidean norms and piecewise linear curves, or approximation algorithms limited to piecewise linear curves. We present an approximation algorithm for computing the CDTW distance under Euclidean norm between piecewise (higher degree) algebraic curves. That is, we present a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) of multiplicative error $\varepsilon$, with $O \left( (m+n)^{\frac{19}{6}} (\frac{1}{\varepsilon})^{\frac{10}{3}} \log \left( \frac{ (m+n) }{\varepsilon^2} \right) \right)$ complexity, where $m$ and $n$ are the number of pieces of the two input curves.

AI.tldr: An FPTAS for CDTW distance between piecewise higher-degree algebraic curves under Euclidean norm; complexity: O((m+n)^{19/6} (1/ε)^{10/3} log((m+n)/ε^2)).
AI.motivation: CDTW is a robust metric for curve similarity; existing CDTW methods are exact for non-Euclidean norms or limited to piecewise linear curves; a scalable approximation for Euclidean CDTW on algebraic curves is needed for practical applications like clustering and retrieval.
AI.method: Develop an FPTAS for CDTW under Euclidean norm by discretizing/approximating curve representations (piecewise algebraic segments) and solving a refined dynamic-programming formulation with controlled multiplicative error ε.
AI.result: Proves a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme with the stated complexity, achieving (1+ε) multiplicative accuracy for the CDTW distance between two piecewise algebraic curves with m and n pieces.
AI.conclusion: Extends CDTW applicability to higher-degree algebraic curves and provides a scalable, provable-approximation method under Euclidean norm, improving robustness for curve similarity tasks; applicability is currently limited to Euclidean norm and piecewise algebraic curves.

title: Joint Alignment and Distillation for Video Generation via Sample-Guided Distribution Matching
summary: Aligning video generative models to human preferences heavily relies on Reinforcement Learning (RL), which suffers from extensive computational overhead. Existing workflows typically treat RL and distillation as disconnected stages: applying RL before distillation incurs prohibitive computational costs, whereas applying RL after distillation frequently leads to model collapse. To overcome these limitations, we propose a unified, single-stage optimization framework grounded in Distribution Matching (DM). In the standard DM framework, distillation updates the model via a gradient direction that minimizes the gap between the real and fake models, guiding generations toward clarity and high fidelity. Building upon this, we introduce DM-Align, which derives a complementary gradient direction to guide the model toward human-preferred samples. Inspired by DPO and GRPO, our method leverages the distributional gap -- formulated from either preference pairs or intra-group exploration -- to directly construct this preference-guided gradient. By synergizing these two gradient directions, our approach eliminates the need for multi-step reward evaluation and complex ODE-SDE conversions inherent in traditional RL. Comprehensive experiments across multiple foundational video models demonstrate that this sample-guided framework robustly enhances both distillation quality and preference alignment, consistently outperforming both standalone variants and sequential two-stage pipelines.

AI.tldr: Unified single-stage distribution-matching approach (DM-Align) for video generative models that combines distillation with a human-preference gradient to align outputs with user preferences, eliminating RL overhead and ODE/SDE steps. It yields better distillation quality and alignment than two-stage or standalone methods.
AI.motivation: RL-based alignment with video models incurs high compute; two-stage pipelines suffer from inefficiency and risk collapse; need a single-stage method that preserves fidelity while incorporating human preferences.
AI.method: Extend DM framework: standard distillation gradient minimizes gap between real and fake models; derive a complementary preference-guided gradient from distributional gaps using preference pairs or intra-group exploration (inspired by DPO/GRPO). Combine both gradients to update model in one stage, avoiding RL reward evaluation and ODE-SDE conversions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across multiple foundational video models shows consistent improvements in distillation quality and human-preference alignment; outperforms both stand-alone DM or RL-based methods and sequential two-stage pipelines.
AI.conclusion: DM-Align provides a unified, efficient framework for policy-aligned video generation, reducing computational overhead while improving alignment fidelity; potential applicability beyond video to other generative domains.

title: Spectral-Target Physical Latent Structuring for JEPA-Style World Models
summary: Latent world models have become increasingly popular as a method to predict and plan in latent space rather than pixel space. Recent architectures, such as LeWorldModel (LeWM), jointly train the encoder and predictor using regularization techniques like SIGReg to prevent representation collapse. Even with such regularization preventing representation collapse, we identify a new world model failure mode of \textit{physical representation laziness}, particularly noted in highly dynamic environments. For these lazy cases, the learned latent states do not collapse but nonetheless fail to represent key physical properties, causing ubiquitous downstream planning failure. To resolve this issue, we propose training-time auxiliary supervision with a lightweight "Fourier auxiliary head", which enforces physically-informed structuring of the latent space with no additional inference-time cost and can be generalized to any environment. Experimentally, we show that the auxiliary head substantially improves planning success rates in dynamic environments where the baseline LeWM exhibits physical representation laziness. It also leads to modest improvements in other environments, even when the baseline does not exhibit physical representation laziness. We further observe superior planning performance being accompanied by higher latent space correlations with key physical properties, indicating both the ability of our method to physically structure latent states and the potential planning-side benefit to the learned representation being physically structured. We also see in low-data regimes, auxiliary supervision is particularly impactful in increasing success rate. These findings support the use of our Fourier auxiliary head method to improve both overall success rate and data efficiency, while avoiding representation laziness in latent world models.

AI.tldr: A Fourier auxiliary head provides training-time supervision to structure latent representations in latent world models, mitigating physical representation laziness in dynamic environments and boosting planning performance with no extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Latent world models like LeWorldModel (LeWM) with regularization (SIGReg) prevent representation collapse but exhibit a failure mode in dynamic environments where latent states fail to reflect key physical properties, hurting planning.
AI.method: Introduce a lightweight Fourier auxiliary head during training to enforce physically-informed structuring of the latent space. This is a training-time addition with no inference-time cost and is generalizable across environments.
AI.result: Planning success rates improve in dynamic environments where physical representation laziness appears; modest gains in other environments; higher correlations between latent states and physical properties; improved data efficiency, especially in low-data regimes.
AI.conclusion: The Fourier auxiliary head effectively enforces physical structure in latent representations, improving planning performance and data efficiency in latent world models while avoiding representation laziness; it generalizes to diverse environments.

title: FailureSpot: Label-Efficient Timestamp-Level Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but they can still fail unpredictably during long-horizon execution, making reliable failure detection essential for safe deployment. Existing methods either rely on visual models that typically detect failures only after erroneous actions have occurred, or use lightweight proactive detectors trained on VLA internal representations. However, these proactive methods are often supervised with trajectory-level labels, causing normal pre-failure behavior in unsuccessful trajectories to be incorrectly labeled as failure. This supervision mismatch introduces label noise and limits both trajectory-level detection accuracy and precise timestamp-level failure localization. In this work, we study fine-grained timestamp-level VLA failure detection while addressing the cost of dense annotation. We propose a data-efficient framework that first leverages unlabeled VLA action chunks to construct action-derived weak supervision signals, capturing abnormal patterns such as inconsistent consecutive chunks, frozen or idle actions, and aggressive random motions. We then use active learning to select only the most uncertain trajectories for timestamp-level annotation and fine-tune the detector with these informative labels. Experiments across multiple VLA policies show that our method improves both timestamp-level and trajectory-level failure detection performance.

AI.tldr: A data-efficient framework for fine-grained failure detection in vision-language-action (VLA) policies using weak supervision from unlabeled action chunks and active learning, achieving improved timestamp-level and trajectory-level failure detection with reduced annotation effort.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon VLA manipulation can fail unpredictably, and existing failure detectors either wait for errors or rely on trajectory-level labels that introduce noise and hinder precise timestamp localization.
AI.method: 1) Derive action-based weak supervision from unlabeled VLA action chunks by detecting abnormal patterns (inconsistent consecutive chunks, frozen/idle actions, aggressive random motions). 2) Train an initial timestamp-level failure detector using these weak signals. 3) Apply active learning to identify the most uncertain trajectories for timestamp-level annotation and 4) fine-tune the detector with these informative labels.
AI.result: Empirical results across multiple VLA policies show improvements in both timestamp-level and trajectory-level failure detection performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data-efficient approach enables precise, timestamp-level failure localization for VLA policies while reducing annotation costs, illustrating the value of combining weak supervision with active learning for failure detection.

title: EXAONE Forecast for Finance
summary: This technical report presents EXAONE Forecast for Finance (EXAONE Finance), a financial time series (TS) foundation model (TSFM) tailored to financial forecasting. Recent TSFMs achieve strong zero-shot performance through large-scale pretraining. However, they are primarily developed for general-domain TS and largely rely on self-attention backbones whose computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length and variate count. Moreover, they assume fully observed inputs and are pretrained on corpora that fail to capture the unique dynamics of financial markets. These limitations hinder their applicability to finance, where long, many-channel, intermittently observed panels are common. To address these challenges, EXAONE Finance adopts an attention-free architecture, replacing self-attention with two simple yet effective linear-time operators: 1) a causal 1D convolution for temporal mixing and 2) a group-aware pooling multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for variate mixing. Furthermore, a masked context augmentation exposes the model to contiguous missing spans during training, improving robustness to the missingness pervasive in financial markets. EXAONE Finance is pretrained on a large-scale financial corpus covering not only equities but also foreign exchange, commodities, crypto-assets, fixed income, and macroeconomic indicators. On FinVerse, a financial forecasting benchmark covering diverse asset classes, EXAONE Finance attains state-of-the-art performance, ranking first across all three evaluation tiers---point-forecast accuracy, cross-sectional asset ranking, and portfolio profitability.

AI.tldr: EXAONE Finance introduces an attention-free financial time series foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art forecasting on FinVerse by using causal 1D convolution for temporal mixing, a group-aware pooling MLP for cross-variate mixing, and masked context augmentation, trained on broad financial data.
AI.motivation: General-domain TSFMs are computationally expensive (quadratic in sequence length and var count) and often assume fully observed data, failing to capture finance-specific dynamics and intermittently observed panels; a finance-tailored, scalable TSFM is needed.
AI.method: Replace self-attention with two linear-time components: (1) causal 1D convolution for temporal mixing; (2) group-aware pooling MLP for variate mixing. Train with masked context augmentation to expose the model to missing spans. Pretrain on a large-scale financial corpus spanning equities, FX, commodities, crypto, fixed income, and macro indicators. Evaluate on FinVerse across point forecasts, asset rankings, and profitability.
AI.result: On FinVerse, EXAONE Finance achieves state-of-the-art performance, ranking first in all three evaluation tiers: point-forecast accuracy, cross-sectional asset ranking, and portfolio profitability.
AI.conclusion: The architecture yields a scalable, finance-tailored TSFM that overcomes attention-based limitations and demonstrates strong, multi-faceted forecasting capability across diverse financial assets.

title: The microscope is the mask: privileged views and labels from a cryo-ET forward model
summary: We explore the use of simulated data for training a model for protein annotation in crowded cryo-electron tomography volumes reconstructed from images collected at limited tilt angles and severely corrupted by the measurement operator. Firstly, we leverage the corruptions imposed by the forward model to generate domain-specific augmented paired views of the exact same scene for an invariance objective integrated into the LeJEPA self-supervised training framework. Secondly, we use additional information from the simulation pipeline such as the positions and identity of proteins in the simulated volumes to inform the architecture of the model and the loss function, so that semantic information is localised at protein positions in the resulting dense feature volume. The resulting model, CARNIVAL, is evaluated without finetuning on classification and detection tasks in real tomograms, using a benchmark dataset containing multiple protein types and two tomogram processing types. We show that CARNIVAL outperforms a state-of-the-art model trained using a contrastive objective on simulated data but without forward model-based paired views or privileged information.

AI.tldr: Simulated data with forward-model-based paired views and simulation-privileged cues enable CARNIVAL to achieve zero-shot protein annotation in crowded cryo-ET volumes, outperforming a contrastive-baseline trained on simulated data.
AI.motivation: Overcome severe forward-model corruption and tilt limitations in cryo-ET for accurate protein annotation; exploit physics-based augmentations and simulated protein metadata to improve self-supervised learning.
AI.method: LeJEPA self-supervised framework with invariance objective using forward-model-corrupted paired views; integrate privileged information (protein positions/identity) into architecture and loss to localize semantic features at protein positions; train as CARNIVAL; evaluate zero-shot on real tomograms across protein types and processing types.
AI.result: CARNIVAL outperforms a state-of-the-art contrastive-model trained on simulated data lacking forward-model paired views and privileged information in classification and detection tasks on real tomograms without finetuning.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed data augmentation and privileged simulation cues enhance zero-shot protein annotation in crowded cryo-ET, offering a pathway for robust in-silico-to-real transfer in challenging tomographic domains.

title: ProToMEx: Rapid, Interpretable Explanations via Structured Representations
summary: Existing post-hoc explainers for machine learning classifiers primarily focus on feature attribution, assigning importance scores to individual features. While valuable, this approach struggles to articulate the complex, combinatorial patterns that often drive a model's decision-making process. To overcome this limitation, we introduce ProToMEx, a new paradigm for explainability that leverages Probabilistic Topic Models (PTMs). Our model-agnostic framework learns latent ''topics'' that represent distinct, high-level reasons for a classification, moving beyond simple feature importance to reveal underlying semantic structures. ProToMEx naturally provides both global explanations of a model's overall behaviour and local explanations that can disentangle multiple co-existing reasons for a specific prediction. We demonstrate empirically that ProToMEx not only produces explanations of comparable fidelity to popular methods like SHAP and LIME but also drastically reduces the amortised computational cost of generating local explanations, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Specifically, we show that ProToMEx is ~30-40x faster than SHAP and LIME over standardised tabular datasets and synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: ProToMEx leverages probabilistic topic models to produce global and local explanations for classifiers, revealing latent high-level reasons behind predictions; it achieves comparable fidelity to SHAP/LIME with 30–40x faster local explanations, enabling real-time use.
AI.motivation: Feature attribution methods struggle to express combinatorial decision patterns and semantic reasons; need a model-agnostic approach that provides interpretable, high-level explanations.
AI.method: Unsupervised/model-agnostic application of Probabilistic Topic Models to learn latent topics representing distinct reasons for classifications; outputs both global explanations for overall model behavior and local explanations for specific predictions; claims significant speedup in local explanation amortized costs.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show comparable fidelity to SHAP/LIME; local explanations are ~30–40x faster on tabular and synthetic datasets.
AI.conclusion: ProToMEx presents a semantically meaningful, model-agnostic explanation paradigm that trades off negligible fidelity for substantial speed gains, suitable for real-time applications; future work could explore topic interpretability and scalability to different data modalities.

title: VLA-Precision: Asymmetric Co-Bootstrapping for Efficient Real-World Online RL of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models enable broad manipulation but remain unreliable in tasks demanding precision and repeatability. Applying real-world online reinforcement learning (RL) to VLA post-training enables autonomous trial-and-error improvement beyond demonstrations alone, but exposes two bottlenecks: 1) unreliable value signals can induce policy drift; 2) large-VLA overhead constrains throughput and sample efficiency. To address these challenges, we present VLA-Precision, an efficient real-world online RL framework featuring the Asymmetric Co-Bootstrapping (ACoB) algorithm and the ACoB-Stream architecture. Specifically, ACoB establishes asymmetric co-bootstrapping across timescales: early intervention-guided behavioral learning rapidly improves policy performance while enhancing online experience quality. As autonomous experience accumulates, global return propagation and local preference ranking progressively calibrate value estimates, yielding relative action advantages for reference-regularized policy improvement while suppressing drift. To enable ACoB on large VLAs, we develop ACoB-Stream, a closed-loop experience--policy architecture that establishes invariant-state decoupling and on-demand streaming as design principles, delivering up to 10.9$\times$ improvements in throughput and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on nine high-precision chemistry tasks across four categories and four robot embodiments show that VLA-Precision achieves 98.3\% mean success rate in 45.8 min/task, with 27.6 s episodes running at 1.2$\times$ and 1.8$\times$ the speeds of VLA and RL baselines. Resources are available at https://vla-precision.github.io.

AI.tldr: Presents VLA-Precision: efficient real-world online RL for vision-language-action models using Asymmetric Co-Bootstrapping (ACoB) and ACoB-Stream, delivering high precision and throughput across diverse tasks.
AI.motivation: Address two bottlenecks in real-world online RL for large vision-language-action (VLA) models: (1) unreliable value signals causing policy drift, and (2) large VLA overhead limiting throughput and sample efficiency.
AI.method: ACoB: asymmetric co-bootstrapping across timescales combining early intervention-guided learning with eventual global return propagation and local preference ranking to calibrate value estimates and suppress drift; ACoB-Stream: closed-loop experience–policy architecture with invariant-state decoupling and on-demand streaming to enable large VLA deployment.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on nine high-precision chemistry tasks across categories and robot embodiments. VLA-Precision achieves 98.3% mean success rate in 45.8 minutes per task, with 27.6 s episodes and speeds of 1.2× and 1.8× relative to VLA and RL baselines. Reports up to 10.9× throughput/computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: VLA-Precision provides a practical, scalable framework for reliable, efficient real-world online RL on large VLA systems, offering substantial improvements in success rate, latency, and throughput; resources are publicly available.

title: From Matching Models to Recruiting Agents: A Systematized Narrative Review of AI Recruitment Systems, Evaluation, and Governance
comment: 53 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables; companion literature-coding and search-log CSVs included in the source package
summary: Artificial intelligence in recruitment has shifted the object being automated from profile pairs and ranked lists to multi-stage workflows that retrieve evidence, compare candidates, and support or execute actions. This systematized narrative review traces that development from bilateral retrieval and behavioral ranking through neural person--job matching, large language model (LLM) components, and tool-using recruiting agents. Using a purposive search and coding protocol updated through 23 July 2026, plus targeted updates through 2 September 2026, we organize 40 representative works with supporting industrial and legal sources. This synthesis is not a prevalence estimate. We analyze three coupled transitions: from similarity to reciprocal suitability, from a model to a compound workflow, and from offline prediction to evidence- and productivity-aligned evaluation. Across document understanding, retrieval, ranking, assessment, interviewing, sourcing, and human handoff, we distinguish field-, pair-, list-, case-, trajectory-, and outcome-level evidence. Persistent gaps arise because behavioral labels confound exposure, preference, and qualification; private and synthetic data limit external validity; final-output scores conceal pipeline failures; and, within the coded set, privacy is not directly evaluated and no row jointly evaluates utility, fairness, privacy, and security. These observations describe the coded set rather than the field as a whole. We therefore introduce a staged mapping from evaluation evidence to the strongest defensible claim, together with an agenda for reciprocal, evidence-grounded, temporally controlled, selective, and auditable systems. Progress should be judged by whether workflows retrieve the right evidence, preserve uncertainty, support contestable decisions, and improve outcomes under explicit cost and risk constraints.

AI.tldr: Abbreviated synthesis showing evolution of AI in recruitment from bilateral retrieval/ranking to multi-stage, evidence-based workflows; highlights persistent gaps and proposes an auditable evaluation agenda.
AI.motivation: Motivated by a shift from static prediction to compound, evidence-grounded recruiting workflows; aims to clarify transitions, evaluate validity, and improve privacy and accountability.
AI.method: Systematized narrative review with purposive search and coding protocol updated through 23 July 2026 and targeted updates through 2 September 2026; analyzes 40 representative works plus industrial/legal sources; categorizes evidence across stages and levels.
AI.result: Identifies three coupled transitions: 1) similarity to reciprocal suitability; 2) model to compound workflow; 3) offline prediction to evidence-/productivity-aligned evaluation. Distinguishes evidence types across document understanding, retrieval, ranking, assessment, interviewing, sourcing, and human handoff. Notes persistent gaps: confounded behavioral labels, private/synthetic data, opaque final-output scores, and lack of joint privacy/utility/fairness evaluation. Proposes staged mapping from evaluation evidence to defensible claims and an agenda for auditable, temporally controlled systems.
AI.conclusion: Progress should be judged by retrieval of the right evidence, preservation of uncertainty, support for contestable decisions, and outcomes under explicit cost and risk constraints; recommends an evidence-grounded, reciprocal, auditable, and temporally controlled approach to system design.

title: Object Concepts Emerge from Motion
summary: Object-centric visual representations are important for physical-world perception, but existing visual pretraining methods often capture semantic categories without preserving the identity and coherence of individual instances. We present a biologically inspired framework that learns object-centric representations for single images from raw videos. Our approach uses motion boundaries as a source of object-level grouping: off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering produce pseudo-instance masks, which supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. The framework requires neither human annotations nor camera calibration. We first obtain 195 million pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving and web videos, then expand the supervision to 421 million frames with Motion-Verified Self-Training, which combines model proposals with motion evidence. We train encoders up to Swin-H and distill the learned representations into a family of Swin backbones. Across monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, the resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance relative to supervised and self-supervised pretraining baselines, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks. These results show that motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining.

AI.tldr: A motion-driven, object-centric pretraining framework creates pseudo-instance masks from optical flow to supervise single-image encoders, scaling with large video data and a Motion-Verified Self-Training variant. It distills to Swin backbones and achieves strong geometry- and instance-sensitive transfer across depth, 3D perception, and planning tasks without labeled data.
AI.motivation: To preserve instance identity in pretraining representations and avoid conflating distinct objects under semantic categories; leverage motion cues from raw videos to derive object-level supervision for single-image encoders without manual labels or calibration.
AI.method: Compute motion boundaries via off-the-shelf optical flow; cluster to produce pseudo-instance masks; supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. Scale with 195M pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving/web videos, then expand to 421M frames using Motion-Verified Self-Training, combining model proposals with motion evidence. Distill learned representations into Swin backbones (up to Swin-H).
AI.result: Encoders achieve competitive or superior performance versus supervised and self-supervised baselines on monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: Motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, offering a scalable, complementary direction for visual pretraining that does not rely on labeled data or camera calibration.

title: A Data Fusion Framework for Grounding Aerospace Surrogate Model via Experimental Wind-Tunnel Observations
summary: Aerodynamic surrogate models trained on high-fidelity CFD data reproduce numerical predictions of both scalar outputs and entire fields accurately, yet their predictive fidelity is limited by systematic discrepancies between CFD and experimental observations. We present an experimentally grounded correction framework that adapts a CFD-trained deep learning surrogate using wind-tunnel PSP measurements. A Geotransolver surrogate trained on 2,300 high-fidelity CFD simulations of the NASA CRM wing-body configuration, spanning geometric variation, Mach 0.70-0.85, and angles of attack 0 to 4 degrees, reproduces the CFD integrated aerodynamic forces and pitching moment to R2 > 0.99 but does not match the experimental data. To incorporate experimental information without retraining the surrogate, a correction network is trained on spatially registered PSP measurements at two freestream Mach numbers (0.70 and 0.85) across the same angle-of-attack range, learning the discrepancy between the surrogate-predicted and experimentally measured surface-pressure distributions. At Mach 0.85 the correction substantially improves agreement with PSP, particularly at the wing suction peak, shock location, and subsequent pressure recovery, reducing both the magnitude of the prediction error and the fraction of wetted surface on which it exceeds 0.05 in Cp, and it does so from a limited experimental dataset without modifying the pretrained surrogate parameters. On held-out angles of attack the grounded surrogate agrees with measurement to within 2.3-2.7% of the measured Cp range, and outperforms direct interpolation between the measured conditions at every state tested. Experimental measurements can therefore ground a large-scale simulation-trained surrogate by learning systematic CFD-to-experiment discrepancies while preserving its generalization capability and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: An experimentally grounded correction framework that grounds a CFD-trained deep learning surrogate to wind-tunnel PSP data, improving CFD-to-experiment fidelity without retraining the surrogate.
AI.motivation: CFD-based surrogates reproduce CFD predictions well but exhibit systematic CFD-to-experiment discrepancies; integrating experimental information is needed to close the gap without retraining large models.
AI.method: Train a Geotransformer surrogate on 2,300 high-fidelity CFD simulations of the NASA CRM wing-body across geometric variation, Mach 0.70–0.85, and AoA 0–4°, capturing integrated forces and pitching moment with high fidelity. Train a correction network on spatially registered PSP measurements at Mach 0.70 and 0.85 across the same AoA range to learn the discrepancy between surrogate-predicted and measured surface-pressure Cp distributions. Apply the correction without modifying the pretrained surrogate parameters. Evaluate on held-out AoA and compare to direct interpolation between measured conditions.
AI.result: Correction at Mach 0.85 substantially improves PSP agreement, notably at the wing suction peak, shock location, and pressure recovery. It reduces Cp prediction error magnitude and lowers the fraction of wetted surface where Cp error > 0.05. Achieved with a limited experimental dataset. On held-out AoA, the grounded surrogate matches measurements within 2.3–2.7% of the measured Cp range and outperforms direct interpolation between measured conditions.
AI.conclusion: Experimental measurements can ground large-scale CFD-trained surrogates by learning CFD-to-experiment discrepancies while preserving generalization and computational efficiency.

title: Scalable Edge-assisted Fusion and Path Prediction for Connected Autonomous Vehicles
summary:
The planning algorithms inside an Autonomous Vehicle (AV) rely on information from on-board sensors whose line of sight is limited by emerging traffic conditions and occlusions. Edge-assisted creation of a unified world model fusing information from AVs and Road Side Units (RSUs) in a geographical locale, and the prediction of AVs' future trajectories, can enhance the
  planning algorithms inside AVs to improve quality metrics, such as better traffic flow and collision prevention. AVs participating in such enhancements are called Connected Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs). However, such information generated by the edge (world model and motion predictions) must reach the planners within a tight Age of Information (AoI) time budget to be
  useful. The state of the art fuses per-CAV information: each AV fuses inputs from other actors locally, which limits both scalability with actor count and quality of results.
  We present Conductor, an edge-based solution for creating a unified world model from the perspective of a fixed anchor (e.g., an RSU) in a locale and predicting future trajectories of AVs in that locale. Our solution adheres to the AoI time budget by dynamically limiting the number of AVs that would lead to the best quality of results. Specifically, we introduce an
  occlusion-aware selector that favors information contribution by AVs that detect objects in the locale not covered by RSUs. We pair this selector with a runtime controller that adapts both the number of AV inputs to fuse and the amount of trajectory predictions in each cycle to stay within the AoI time budget. Evaluation on CAV simulation infrastructure shows our joint
  selector-controller meets the AoI safety bound across traffic scenarios with up to 31 CAVs, with fusion fidelity close to an Oracle and much better than a random selector under the same AoI constraint.

AI.tldr: Edge-based CAV world-model fusion (Conductor) with an occlusion-aware selector and runtime controller meets AoI constraints while scaling to multiple AVs, delivering near-oracle fusion fidelity much better than random selectors.
AI.motivation: Current per-AV local fusion limits scalability and fusion quality for AV planning due to limited sensor sightlines and AoI constraints. A fixed-anchor edge approach can provide a unified world model and timely trajectory predictions if the number of fused inputs and predictions adapt to the AoI budget.
AI.method: Conductor operates from a fixed anchor (e.g., an RSU) to fuse data into a unified world model and predict AV trajectories. It uses an occlusion-aware selector to prioritize AVs that detect objects not covered by RSUs, and a runtime controller that dynamically limits the number of AV inputs and the amount of trajectory predictions per cycle to stay within the AoI budget.
AI.result: Evaluation on CAV simulation shows the joint selector-controller preserves AoI safety bounds across scenarios with up to 31 CAVs. Fusion fidelity is close to an Oracle and significantly better than a random selector under the same AoI constraint.
AI.conclusion: An edge-based, selector-driven fusion framework (Conductor) can deliver timely, high-fidelity world-model data for AV planning at scale, by balancing information gain against AoI limits and adapting inputs and predictions per cycle.

title: Harbor Adapters and Harbor-Index: Infrastructure and a Curated Meta-Dataset for Large-Scale Agentic Evaluation
summary: Evaluating agents on the growing number of agentic benchmarks is challenging because they often require complex environments and agent integrations. We introduce Harbor Adapters, a unified evaluation infrastructure for agentic benchmarks. Our work makes three contributions. First, we develop benchmark adapters that port more than 80 benchmarks to evaluate arbitrary agents, and validate them through rigorous code review and parity experiments. Second, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 8 models spanning capability tiers across 54 benchmarks; every model is run with Terminus-2 and with one of 3 native harnesses. This enables a broader analysis of agent capabilities and failure modes than was previously possible. Third, we introduce Harbor-Index, a curated set of 82 difficult, diverse, and high-quality tasks spanning 29 benchmarks, refined from the adapted suite through difficulty filtering, AI and human audit, and an audit-and-fix loop. Harbor-Index preserves the challenge and breadth of large-scale agentic evaluations while being affordable to run; no evaluated model-harness configuration exceeds 30% pass rate, and the strongest (GPT-5.5 with Codex) reaches 28.0%. We release the adapters, evaluation results, in-depth analysis, and Harbor-Index as open-source artifacts to support more reliable and comprehensive evaluation of language-model agents.

AI.tldr: Harbor Adapters provide a unified, open-source evaluation stack for agentic benchmarks by porting 80+ benchmarks and introducing Harbor-Index, enabling large-scale cross-model evaluation and revealing substantial difficulty across models.
AI.motivation: Evaluating agentic benchmarks is challenging due to heterogeneous environments and integrations; a unified, scalable evaluation infrastructure is needed to enable fair, broad, and reproducible assessments.
AI.method: Develop benchmark adapters porting more than 80 benchmarks for arbitrary agents; conduct a large-scale evaluation of 8 models across 54 benchmarks using Terminus-2 and 3 native harnesses; create Harbor-Index by difficulty-filtering, audits (AI and human), and an audit-and-fix loop.
AI.result: Evaluation across 8 models and 54 benchmarks shows no model-harness configuration exceeds 30% pass rate; the strongest model (GPT-5.5 with Codex) reaches 28.0% pass; Harbor-Index comprises 82 difficult, diverse tasks refined from the adapted suite.
AI.conclusion: Harbor Adapters enable more reliable, comprehensive agentic evaluation at scale and provide an affordable, representative benchmark subset (Harbor-Index) for ongoing assessment; all artifacts are released open-source.

title: AdaptVPR: Route-Aware Hard Positive Generation for Robust Visual Place Recognition
summary: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) localizes a query image by retrieving database images of the same or nearby place, yet its robustness is often degraded by domain shifts arising from illumination, weather, seasonal changes, and dynamic occlusions. One contributing factor is the limited appearance diversity of the same place in existing training data. To address this issue, we propose AdaptVPR, a route-aware generative augmentation framework that constructs same-place hard positives for robust VPR training. AdaptVPR first uses a vision language model to parse scene attributes and estimate editing feasibility, while a rule-based scheduler determines the generation route according to editability scores and risk constraints. The generation process is decomposed into three complementary routes: the Global Appearance Route introduces global scene changes in weather, illumination, and time of day; the Local Occlusion Route inserts plausible dynamic occluders; and the Dual Route combines both types of perturbations to produce more challenging appearance shifts. Each generated candidate is evaluated using a VPR-oriented verification scheme based on geometric consistency and appearance diversity, reducing the risk of structural drift while ensuring sufficient appearance variation. Global candidates are generated once and rejected if verification fails, while Local Occlusion and Dual candidates use verification feedback for limited prompt refinement and regeneration. Using this framework, we construct AdaptCities, containing 160K verified synthetic same-place hard positives. Experiments across multiple VPR baselines and vision foundation backbones show consistent gains on standard benchmarks and substantial improvements under challenging domain shifts, with R@1 gains of up to 9.2%. The source code and data resources are publicly available at https://github.com/chenshunpeng/AdaptVPR.

AI.tldr: AdaptVPR introduces route-aware generative augmentation to create hard positive pairs for robust Visual Place Recognition (VPR).
AI.motivation: VPR robustness is hindered by domain shifts (illumination, weather, season, dynamic occlusions) and limited appearance diversity of same places in training data; need harder positives to improve generalization.
AI.method: A three-route augmentation framework guided by vision-language parsing and editability scores: Global Appearance Route (weather/illumination/time), Local Occlusion Route (dynamic occluders), and Dual Route (combined perturbations). A rule-based scheduler selects routes per editability and risk, with a VPR-oriented verification step using geometric consistency and appearance diversity. Global candidates are generated once and verified; Local Occlusion/Dual use verification feedback for refinement. Produces AdaptCities with 160K verified hard positives.
AI.result: Consistent gains across multiple VPR baselines and vision backbones; improved robustness under domain shifts with up to 9.2% relative improvement in R@1; demonstration on standard benchmarks; code and data released.
AI.conclusion: AdaptVPR effectively increases appearance diversity and hard positives for robust VPR, enabling substantial performance gains under challenging domain shifts; introduces a scalable pipeline and a large synthetic dataset (AdaptCities).

title: Quantum-Assisted Memory-Efficient Training for Parameter-Intensive Wi-Fi-Based Human Activity Recognition
summary: Wi-Fi-based human activity recognition (HAR) has become an important part of integrated sensing and communications, paving the way for a range of context-aware services. However, most existing Wi-Fi-based HAR systems rely on deep learning (DL) models that are computationally and memory intensive in both training and inference, which poses significant challenges for real-world deployment. Conventional training requires simultaneous updates of millions of parameters, leading to prohibitive memory consumption. In this paper, we propose a novel quantum-assisted memory-efficient training framework (Q-MET) designed to improve efficiency in both training and inference. Q-MET utilizes a hybrid quantum classical neural network to indirectly generate parameters for HAR models, significantly reducing the trainable parameter count compared to direct optimization. To further support the deployment on resource-constrained devices, we integrate structured pruning during the training phase. Experimental results demonstrate that Q-MET achieves a 90% to 95% reduction in trainable parameters compared with conventional backpropagation-based DL training while maintaining or even exceeding classical classification accuracy. Additionally, Q-MET supports lightweight inference through structured pruning, achieving 75% to 85% model sparsity with less than 2% loss in classification accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first quantum-assisted approach to simultaneously tackle memory inefficiencies in both the training and inference stages of HAR systems.

AI.tldr: Q-MET: a quantum-assisted, memory-efficient training framework for Wi-Fi HAR using a hybrid quantum-classical network with structured pruning, achieving large parameter reduction and sparse inference with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Mitigate memory and computation bottlenecks in DL-based Wi-Fi HAR, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices by reducing trainable parameters and enabling sparsity.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical neural network that indirectly generates HAR model parameters; integrated structured pruning during training to produce sparse models for efficient inference.
AI.result: 99ly reduced trainable parameters by 90–95% compared with conventional backpropagation-based DL training; maintained or improved classification accuracy; 75–85% model sparsity achievable at inference with <2% accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: First quantum-assisted approach to address memory inefficiency in both training and inference for HAR; demonstrates feasibility and potential for edge deployment of quantum-enhanced HAR systems.

title: AquaBEV: Monocular Underwater BEV Occupancy with 3D Sonar Supervision
summary:
Autonomous underwater robots are widely used for exploration, monitoring, and inspection, where safe navigation depends on understanding the surrounding free and occupied space. Bird's eye view (BEV) occupancy provides such a representation, but predicting it from a single underwater RGB image is difficult due to limited, unreliable geometric cues from appearance alone. 3D imaging sonar offers complementary geometric measurements to supervise this task.
  We introduce AquaBEV, a monocular underwater occupancy model that predicts local BEV occupancy from a single RGB image, using paired 3D imaging sonar as geometric supervision during training. AquaBEV maps visual features into a calibration free polar representation and applies causal decoding along the range dimension before reconstructing the prediction in Cartesian BEV coordinates. A controlled underwater occupancy benchmark was established, adapting representative occupancy methods to the same RGB to sonar task under a unified protocol. AquaBEV achieves 31.4 Visible IoU and 38.6 Observed IoU, 4.0% and 4.3% relative improvements over the strongest transferred baseline.

AI.tldr: AquaBEV predicts BEV occupancy from a single underwater RGB image by using paired 3D sonar as geometric supervision during training, mapping features to a polar BEV and decoding along range for Cartesian reconstruction, achieving notable gains on a controlled underwater occupancy benchmark.
AI.motivation: Underwater perception for safe navigation is hampered by unreliable appearance-based cues. Leveraging 3D sonar provides geometric supervision to guide monocular BEV occupancy estimation.
AI.method: Train a monocular network that maps RGB features to a calibration-free polar representation of BEV, apply causal decoding along the range dimension, and reconstruct a Cartesian BEV. Use paired 3D imaging sonar as geometric supervision during training and evaluate on a unified RGB-to-sonar protocol benchmark.
AI.result: Achieves 31.4 Visible IoU and 38.6 Observed IoU, surpassing the strongest transferred baseline by 4.0% and 4.3%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that monocular underwater BEV occupancy can be effectively supervised by sonar geometry, with a polar-to-Cartesian decoding strategy and a unified benchmark, enabling better occupancy understanding for underwater robots.

title: Data-Optimized Contingency Screening: A Machine Learning Approach to Power System Security
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 3rd EIE International Conference on Computing, Networking, Robotics and Telecommunication (EIECon), 2025. To appear in IEEE Xplore
summary: Ensuring the security of the power system is essential for stability and reliability, especially in the event of disruption. Effective classification of contingency in power systems enables proactive decision-making and mitigates large-scale breakdowns and failures. This study explores the use of machine learning algorithms to classify security levels of contingencies in power systems into safe, moderate or severe classes. For this approach, Newton-Raphson load flow method extracts system data from contingency scenarios, using Overall Performance Index (OPI) as safety measure. For data pre-processing, Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is used to address class imbalance and reduce dimensionality, respectively. K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machines (SVM) is trained and evaluated on datasets generated through N-k contingency scenarios for k equal 1, 2, and 3 on IEEE-14 and IEEE-30 bus systems using four hybrid pre-processing configurations: normalized, SMOTE-balanced, PCA-transformed, and a combined SMOTE PCA-transformed. Performance is assessed by precision, recall and F1 score, with priority given to the severe contingency classes. The RF achieved the highest F1 scores of 0.97 in IEEE-30 and 0.86 in IEEE-14, SVM benefits significantly from PCA and improves the accuracy of the classification, while KNN is best suited for SMOTE and PCA conversion. The findings show that PCA contributes more than SMOTE to the overall performance of the model. However, SMOTE improves recall but can introduce false positives and is therefore a compromise of accuracy. This study highlights machine learning as a scalable and powerful alternative to traditional contingency analysis, which improves the assessment of security in real time.

AI.tldr: Multi-class (safe/moderate/severe) contingency classification in power systems using ML. NR load flow yields Overall Performance Index (OPI) as safety label; SMOTE and PCA used for preprocessing; RF, SVM, and KNN evaluated on N-k contingencies for k=1–3 on IEEE-14/30 buses; RF performs best; PCA helps more than SMOTE; SMOTE boosts recall but may incur false positives. ML shows potential as scalable alternative to traditional contingency analysis for real-time security assessment.
AI.motivation: Enhance real-time security assessment and proactive decision-making in power systems by automating contingency classification, addressing class imbalance and high dimensionality before large-scale outages occur.
AI.method: Generate contingency data via Newton-Raphson load flow for N-k scenarios (k=1,2,3) on IEEE-14 and IEEE-30 buses; label with Overall Performance Index (OPI). Apply four preprocessing configurations: normalized; SMOTE-balanced; PCA-transformed; SMOTE+PCA-transformed. Train KNN, Random Forest, and SVM; evaluate using precision, recall, and F1 with emphasis on severe class.
AI.result: Random Forest yields the highest F1: 0.97 on IEEE-30 and 0.86 on IEEE-14. SVM benefits from PCA, improving classification accuracy. KNN performs best with SMOTE+PCA. PCA contributes more to performance than SMOTE; SMOTE improves recall but risks more false positives, requiring a trade-off. Four preprocessing configurations are explored with varying performance.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning provides a scalable, effective alternative to traditional contingency analysis for real-time security assessment in power systems, capable of facilitating proactive risk mitigation across contingency severities.

title: Where Appearance Fails, Geometry Recognizes: A CAD-Free 3D Shape Prior That Complements Vision Foundation Models
summary: Recognizing specific objects onboarded without a labeled training set recurs across manufacturing and service robotics, yet the conventional renderable prior, a computer-aided-design (CAD) model, is often unavailable. Two-dimensional capture supplies no shape prior, and frozen foundation features fail on geometrically similar, low-texture industrial parts. We ask what a short object-centric scan buys for recognition beyond the captured images themselves: each object is reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), summarized into a per-class shape prototype, and fused with frozen DINOv2 image features. First, the scan recovers the recognition value of CAD without CAD: geometry from RGB-D depth (on T-LESS), 3DGS, and CAD gives comparable recognition (tied on HOPE, within 1.6 points on T-LESS); 3DGS is only a convenient route to a point cloud. Second, the payoff is governed by how recognizable the shape is: on shape-distinctive household objects (HOPE) geometry alone reaches 0.920 versus image-only 0.832, a ceiling below which fixed-weight fusion (0.872) sits. On shape-confusable textureless industrial parts (T-LESS) the gain is modest but consistent (0.560 to 0.591 fused, above both single signals). Third, the prior is complementary, not uniformly additive: it rescues far more image failures than it breaks successes, and its benefit grows under partial occlusion. Finally, the worth lies in geometry, not rendered pixels: 3DGS renderings do not help the image side, and frozen-feature recognition is nearly lighting-invariant (within 2.5 points). The study is scoped to recognition, not the BOP pose benchmark.

AI.tldr: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based geometry from short object-centric scans can substitute CAD for recognition and complement image features, with gains depending on object shape distinctiveness; geometry drives the benefit and occlusion robustness.
AI.motivation: Enable object recognition without labeled data or CAD models by extracting a compact geometric prior from brief 3D scans and fusing it with frozen image features.
AI.method: Reconstruct each object with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to create a per-class shape prototype; fuse with frozen DINOv2 image features; compare against image-only and CAD-based baselines on HOPE and T-LESS; evaluate recognition accuracy and robustness under occlusion.
AI.result: 3DGS-based geometry yields recognition comparable to CAD (tied on HOPE; within 1.6 points on T-LESS). On HOPE, geometry alone reaches 0.920 vs image-only 0.832; fixed-weight fusion is 0.872. On T-LESS, fusion improves from 0.560 to 0.591 (modest but above single signals). The prior rescues more image failures than it breaks successes, especially under partial occlusion. 3DGS renderings do not aid the image stream; frozen-feature recognition is nearly lighting-invariant (within 2.5 points). The study targets recognition, not BOP pose benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-derived priors from short scans can match or exceed CAD-based recognition and actively complement image features, with benefits depending on object geometry; the prior is not uniformly additive and is most useful under occlusion and for shape-distinctive objects; renders do not improve the image stream, implying the value lies in geometry itself rather than rendered pixels.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Forced Outage Risk Prediction: Benefits and Comparison to Machine Learning
summary: This study examines the ability of large language models (LLMs) to predict the risk of weather-related forced outages in the distribution grid in a zero-shot framework, without labeled training data. The problem is formulated as a binary severity classification task across three forecast horizons (3h, 6h, 12h), using six years of outage records and high-resolution weather data for a utility service area in central Texas. Four zero-shot LLMs are benchmarked against two supervised classifiers across two input configurations: one using current weather observations and the other using weather forecast data. Results show that supervised models outperform LLMs on macro-F1 and precision, while newer LLM generations achieve competitive scores. Beyond accuracy, LLMs offer complementary strengths in actionable reasoning and geographic scalability, suggesting that combining them with supervised models may be the best practice.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot LLMs vs supervised models for predicting weather-related distribution-grid outages; supervised models excel on macro-F1/precision, but newer LLMs are competitive; a hybrid approach leveraging LLMs for reasoning and scalability with supervised models for accuracy is suggested.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether zero-shot large language models can predict weather-related outage risk without labeled data and to compare them with traditional supervised classifiers across forecast horizons and input configurations.
AI.method: Binary severity classification (3h, 6h, 12h) using six years of outage records and high-resolution weather data for a central Texas utility. Four zero-shot LLMs are benchmarked against two supervised classifiers across two input configurations: current weather observations and weather forecast data.
AI.result: Supervised models outperform LLMs on macro-F1 and precision; newer LLM generations achieve competitive scores. LLMs provide complementary strengths in actionable reasoning and geographic scalability.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with supervised models may yield the best practice: use LLMs for reasoning and scalability, and supervised models for accuracy and reliability.

title: Achieving Asymptotic Near-Optimality Without $δ$-Similarity
summary: Sampling-based motion planning algorithms are a popular class of trajectory planning algorithm due to their speed in complex, high-dimensional environments and ability to handle kinodynamic constraints, specifically through the use of forward dynamics propagation. Many such planners claim to achieve asymptotic near-optimality by proving the almost sure sampling of trajectories that are close to an optimal trajectory in the state space, known as $δ$-similar trajectories. This paper shows that the proof behind asymptotic $δ$-similarity relies on an unstated assumption that $δ$-similar trajectory segments will always be kept once sampled. This assumption does not hold in general. A problematic case, referred to as ``crowding out,'' is described, where locally low-cost paths prevent trajectories that are $δ$-similar to the optimal trajectory from being added to the tree. It is shown, however, that asymptotic near-optimality guarantees can still be achieved without guarantees of $δ$-similar solution trajectories when crowding out is properly accounted for. An example environment and system are provided where crowding out is shown to occur, demonstrating a scenario where inductively sampling a $δ$-similar solution trajectory is impossible.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that δ-similarity proofs for sampling-based planners rely on an unstated assumption that δ-similar segments are invariantly kept, which fails under crowding-out. It shows near-optimality can still be achieved if crowding-out is accounted for, and provides a counterexample where δ-similar sampling is impossible.
AI.motivation: To test the validity of δ-similarity-based asymptotic optimality proofs in kinodynamic, sampling-based motion planning and identify conditions (crowding-out) that violate key assumptions.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of δ-similarity proofs, identification of the crowding-out phenomenon, construction of a counterexample environment where δ-similar segments cannot be inductively maintained, and argument that asymptotic near-optimality can be achieved without δ-similarity guarantees when crowding-out is properly addressed.
AI.result: Demonstrates that asymptotic near-optimality can be preserved without guarantees of δ-similar trajectories if crowding-out is handled, and provides a concrete scenario in which δ-similar sampling is infeasible.
AI.conclusion: Conventional proofs assuming δ-similarity are incomplete due to an unstated preservation assumption; however, asymptotic near-optimality remains achievable by incorporating crowding-out considerations into the analysis and planners.

title: Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier
summary: We present Iris-mini and Iris-pro, two search agents trained at the 35B-A3B and 397B-A17B scales, together with the data pipeline and training recipe behind them. Tasks are reverse-constructed from the hyperlink structure of a web corpus: we author multi-hop chains over an entity graph distilled from a seed page and its out-links, rewrite every non-answer entity into a descriptive reference so that no clue can be resolved by string matching, and admit only questions that a reference model fails closed-book yet solves once the supporting evidence is supplied. These questions are then turned into trajectories, which are filtered at both the trajectory and the turn level before SFT. The policy is then optimized by RL against live search, with the reward judge and the observation summarizer served inside the training cluster, and with over-long rollouts interrupted at the request level and resumed from their committed prefix at the next step. We alternate the two stages in a procedure we call SFT-RL climbing, returning the hardest solved and most efficient rollouts of each RL round to the next supervised pass. Because inference-time context management is worth more on these benchmarks than most reported differences between systems, we evaluate every benchmark both with and without it, holding the tool set, the context limit, and the judge fixed. All results come from a single ReAct agent, with no sub-agents and no test-time verification. With management enabled, on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE the two models reach $82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3$ and $88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4$, the strongest overall results among open-source search agents in their respective parameter ranges. We plan to release the model weights together with the complete recipe for data construction, training, and evaluation.

AI.tldr: Iris-mini and Iris-pro are open-source search agents trained at 35B-397B scales using a novel SFT-RL climbing pipeline on a hyperlink-graph data setup; they achieve strong open-source benchmark results with and without inference-time context management and plan to release weights and training recipe.
AI.motivation: Advance open-source, high-performance search agents capable of multi-hop reasoning by constructing tasks from a web corpus, while probing the impact of inference-time context management on benchmark performance.
AI.method: Reverse-construct tasks from a hyperlink-derived entity graph: author multi-hop chains, rewrite non-answer entities as descriptive references to prevent string matching, and restrict questions to those solvable only with supporting evidence. Turn questions into trajectories, filter at trajectory and turn levels, then perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Optimize the policy via reinforcement learning against live search, with in-cluster reward judge and observation summarizer, managing long rollouts by interruption/resumption. Alternate two stages in a SFT-RL climbing loop, returning hardest, most efficient rollouts to the next supervised pass. Evaluate with and without inference-time context management; results come from a single ReAct agent (no sub-agents, no test-time verification).
AI.result: With context management enabled, on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE the two models reach 82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3 and 88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4, respectively—the strongest open-source results in their parameter ranges.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that SFT-RL climbing plus explicit context-management analysis yields strong open-source search-agent performance, with plans to release model weights and the full data/training/evaluation recipe; however, evaluation relies on a particular setup (single ReAct agent, no test-time verification) and may warrant broader validation.

title: What Moves? Localized Motion Representations for Compositional Scene Control
summary: Real-world dynamics are inherently compositional: multiple entities move simultaneously within a shared scene, each exhibiting distinct motion patterns. Yet most existing video representations encode motion globally, without explicitly capturing localized motion for individual entities. Crucially, motion is defined relative to a global reference frame, including camera motion and scene layout. However, localized embeddings are often computed from cropped images or obtained by masking features after encoding, discarding the context needed to interpret motion. To address this, we introduce a promptable localized motion representation that produces persistent embeddings for user-specified regions defined by spatial masks. Rather than cropping the input or masking features, our model processes the full video and conditions motion encoding directly on the queried region. This yields temporally consistent, region-addressable embeddings that isolate local dynamics while retaining the global context required for disambiguation. We demonstrate object-level motion transfer, enabling controlled composition of dynamic scenes. Beyond generative control, our embeddings support localized action classification in multi-actor videos. Across both tasks, our approach improves controllability and outperforms global representations localized through cropping or post-hoc masking. Project Page: https://compvis.github.io/WhatMoves

AI.tldr: Introduces a promptable, region-specific motion representation that encodes local dynamics directly on the full video without cropping, yielding persistent region embeddings that are temporally consistent and region-addressable for object-level motion transfer and localized action recognition.
AI.motivation: Real-world scenes are compositional with multiple entities moving concurrently. Global motion encodings and post-hoc masked/cropped features lack region-specific context and can misinterpret local dynamics. A region-conditioned, context-preserving representation is needed for controllable editing and localized analysis.
AI.method: Encode motion directly on the full video while conditioning the encoding on user-specified spatial masks (region prompts). Generate persistent, region-addressable embeddings that preserve global scene context and disambiguate local motion without cropping inputs or masking features post-encoding.
AI.result: Demonstrates object-level motion transfer and localized action classification in multi-actor scenes. The region-focused embeddings improve controllability and outperform global representations that are cropped or masked after encoding.
AI.conclusion: Promising approach for region-aware motion understanding that combines local dynamics with global context, enabling finer control in video generation/editing and improved regional action analysis; broad potential for scalable, prompt-driven video representations.

title: BER-PEF: Unified Human Mobility Predictability Evaluation via Bayes Error Rate Estimation
summary: Human mobility predictability concerns the best prediction performance attainable from a given target and input information, but its ground truth is not directly observable on real mobility data. We present BER-PEF, a Bayes-error-rate-based framework that converts BER estimation into mobility predictability estimation and provides a unified protocol for comparing estimators without observable ground truth. The framework maps symbolic sequences, numeric trajectories, contextual features, and learned representations into a common feature--label space, then evaluates estimator outputs along controlled perturbation curves against a shared predictability reference interval by measuring deviations below the interval, above the interval, and across the full interval. Experiments on Foursquare NYC and TKY, GeoLife, and T-Drive show that several BER-based estimators achieve lower reference discrepancy than existing predictability methods on symbolic sequences and numeric trajectories, while their estimates track changes in empirical prediction performance under perturbation. Additional analyses show that contextual inputs and multiple structured representations can be evaluated under the same protocol, and that aggregating evidence across multiple perturbation levels provides a more reliable basis for estimator selection than relying on a single unperturbed observation. BER-PEF therefore offers a unified and verifiable path for evaluating predictability estimators on heterogeneous mobility data when ground-truth predictability is unavailable.

AI.tldr: BER-PEF: Bayes error-rate-based framework to estimate mobility predictability from BER, enabling ground-truth-free evaluation across heterogeneous data via perturbation curves.
AI.motivation: Ground-truth predictability is unobservable in real mobility data; a unified, verifiable evaluation of estimators across symbolic, numeric, contextual, and learned representations is needed.
AI.method: Maps inputs into a common feature-label space; uses BER estimation; compares estimators against a shared predictability reference interval; uses controlled perturbation curves; measures deviations below/above/across interval; evaluates across datasets; aggregates evidence across perturbation levels.
