AI.result: BER-based estimators achieve lower reference discrepancy than existing methods on symbolic sequences and numeric trajectories; track changes in empirical prediction performance under perturbation; contextual inputs and structured representations can be evaluated; aggregation across perturbation levels yields more reliable estimator selection.
AI.conclusion: BER-PEF provides unified, verifiable path to evaluate predictability estimators on heterogeneous mobility data when ground-truth is unavailable.

title: SocioGesture: Real-Time and Adaptive Social Gesture Perception for Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Robots interacting with people must recognize not only explicit commands, but also social cues such as invitations, refusals, and unavailability. In real deployments, these cues must be inferred from noisy onboard perception under partial occlusion, changing viewpoints, and strict latency constraints. We present SocioGesture, a real-time adaptive social gesture perception system for human-robot interaction (HRI). SocioGesture uses a compact confidence-aware body-hand skeleton representation and a lightweight dual-stream model that fuses body motion with hand articulation for low-latency onboard recognition. To improve deployment robustness, we train the model with occlusion-aware skeleton corruption, exposing it to missing hands, occluded arms, and temporally unstable keypoints without increasing the inference cost. On a social gesture dataset collected in mixed indoor-outdoor HRI scenarios, SocioGesture achieves strong held-out-subject recognition, substantially improves robustness under structured joint occlusion, and runs in real time on a robot-mounted edge device. During deployment, uncertain interaction segments are saved for offline labeling and adaptation, enabling SocioGesture to expand its gesture vocabulary while preserving performance in the original classes. These results demonstrate a practical path toward robust, efficient, and adaptive social perception for interactive robots.

AI.tldr: SocioGesture is a real-time, edge-deployable social gesture perception system for human-robot interaction that combines a compact body-hand skeleton with a dual-stream fusion model, plus occlusion-aware training and offline-adaptation for robustness and vocabulary growth.
AI.motivation: Robots must understand social cues (invites, refusals, unavailability) under noisy onboard perception, occlusions, varying viewpoints, and low latency; existing approaches struggle with robustness and real-time constraints in real deployments.
AI.method: A compact confidence-aware body-hand skeleton representation paired with a lightweight dual-stream network that fuses body motion and hand articulation. Robustness is achieved via occlusion-aware skeleton corruption during training (simulating missing hands/occluded arms/unstable keypoints) without increasing inference cost. Deployment saves uncertain segments for offline labeling/adaptation to grow the gesture vocabulary while preserving performance on known classes.
AI.result: On a mixed indoor-outdoor social gesture dataset, SocioGesture achieves strong held-out-subject recognition, improved robustness under structured joint occlusion, and real-time performance on a robot-mounted edge device; uncertain segments are used for offline adaptation, enabling vocabulary expansion without sacrificing existing accuracy.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates a practical, robust, and adaptive approach to social perception for interactive robots, achieving efficient real-time inference and a pathway for ongoing vocabulary growth through offline labeling.

title: A Removal Based Approach to Improve LLM Faithfulness at Test-Time
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for consequential decisions, making their explanations an important tool for auditing model behavior. Unfortunately, these explanations can be unfaithful, failing to reflect the actual reasoning underlying the model's decisions. We consider a setting in which an LLM provides both an answer and an explanation in response to a question. We identify two distinct dimensions of unfaithful explanations: incompleteness, meaning that the explanation omits factors that influence the answer, and unsoundness, meaning that the explanation cites factors that did not influence the model's answer. Existing approaches to improving LLM faithfulness include training-time methods, which require access to model weights and extensive computational resources, and test-time methods that largely focus on addressing unsoundness. We introduce a test-time approach that directly targets incompleteness. We remove from the input the concepts not credited in the model's explanation and re-query the model on the reduced input. This eliminates unmentioned influences while preserving the influence of mentioned concepts. Across two datasets, multiple model families, and two independent faithfulness metrics, our approach improves explanation faithfulness compared to both standard prompting and prompting to encourage faithfulness. Our method is model-agnostic and can be applied at inference time without modifying model parameters, providing a flexible mechanism for reducing hidden influences and improving the reliability and safety of LLM-assisted decision making.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic, inference-time method improves faithfulness of LLM explanations by removing uncredited concepts from the input and re-querying, reducing incompleteness and improving reliability without changing model weights.
AI.motivation: Explainability in LLMs is prone to unfaithful explanations (incompleteness and unsoundness). There is a need for a model-agnostic, inference-time solution that improves faithfulness without access to model internals.
AI.method: Identify concepts not credited in the explanation, remove those concepts from the input, and re-query the model to obtain a faithful answer/explanation pair reflecting only credited influences.
AI.result: The approach improves explanation faithfulness across two datasets, multiple model families, and two faithfulness metrics, outperforming standard prompting and faithfulness-prompting baselines; it is model-agnostic and requires no parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time removal of uncredited influences can reduce hidden biases in LLM explanations, enhancing reliability and safety of LLM-assisted decision making without modifying model weights.

title: FAVE: Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding for Efficient Fine-Grained Visual Understanding
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Fine-grained visual understanding depends on local detail, yet visual encoders face a trade-off between costly full-image high-resolution processing and compact global encoding that can weaken such evidence. Inspired by human active vision, we separate where to look from what to encode. We focus on the latter and introduce FAVE (Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding), a lightweight variable-resolution ViT that encodes externally selected regions at high acuity while preserving native geometry. We first isolate this encoding problem using oracle ground-truth crops in a controlled small-object regime. On ImageNet objects with a native maximum side of 96 pixels, FAVE improves Top-1 by 9.4 points over a fixed-resolution ViT on the same crop window with 12.7 times lower FLOPs. Increasing global resolution or backbone capacity does not recover the same operating point. We then integrate FAVE as a complementary local branch in FastVLM. Its local tokens are combined with FastVLM's global visual tokens, while the original global pathway and language model remain frozen. With at most 16 additional local tokens, FAVE improves TextVQA by 1.60 points and achieves a 3.3 times controlled TTFT speedup over SmolVLM2-2.2B. On GQA attribute questions, it improves FastVLM-1.5B by 1.31 points, extending the benefit beyond text while narrowing the gap to FastVLM-7B. Together, these results show that selectively allocating high-acuity local capacity provides an efficient complement to broader global representations and model scaling for fine-grained understanding of small objects, text, and attributes.

AI.tldr: Proposes FAVE: a light, variable-resolution ViT that encodes high-acuity local crops while preserving global geometry; shows substantial gains on small-object ImageNet with much lower FLOPs; extends as a local branch in FastVLM for VQA tasks, yielding improved accuracy and significant speedups; demonstrates benefits beyond text (GQA attributes) and suggests local-high-res capacity complements global representations for fine-grained understanding.
AI.motivation: Address the trade-off between full-image high-resolution processing (costly) and compact global encodings (loss of fine details). Inspired by human active vision to separate where to look from what to encode, focusing on encoding strategy to preserve local detail without incurring full high-res processing.
AI.method: Introduce FAVE (Foveated Adaptive Visual Encoding), a lightweight variable-resolution ViT. It encodes externally selected regions at high acuity while preserving original geometry. Initial evaluation uses oracle ground-truth crops in a controlled small-object regime on ImageNet (96 px max side). Integrates FAVE as a complementary local branch in FastVLM, combining its local tokens with FastVLM's global tokens while freezing the global pathway and language model; uses at most 16 additional local tokens.
AI.result: In isolation: on ImageNet small objects, Top-1 improves by 9.4 points over fixed-resolution ViT at the same crop window, with 12.7x lower FLOPs; global resolution or backbone increases do not recover this. In integration: TextVQA improves by 1.60 points and achieves 3.3x TTFT speedup versus SmolVLM2-2.2B; GQA attribute questions: +1.31 points over FastVLM-1.5B, narrowing gap to FastVLM-7B.
AI.conclusion: Selective allocation of high-acuity local capacity is an effective, efficient complement to broad global representations and scaling for fine-grained perception of small objects, text, and attributes; benefits persist when integrated into a larger model for multimodal tasks.

title: Data-Driven Learning of Unknown Nonlinear Differential Equations Using Functional Analysis
summary: In this paper, the problem of data-driven discovery of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is recast, and a new interpretable machine learning (ML) method is proposed. The proposed method aims to learn the unknown vector field of nonlinear dynamics without prior knowledge of the system's physics from only one single state trajectory's data. The proposed method has two fundamental differences with existing methods: 1) the formulation presented in this method is derived based on Functional Analysis and Operator Theory, and 2) the cost function is constructed in the function space as a distance between two functions as an integral, instead of the discrete-sum of errors used in existing ML approaches. An incremental learning algorithm is proposed to learn the unknown vector field to handle new training samples in an online manner. The proposed method can discover the unknown vector field from both forced and unforced autonomous and non-autonomous (or time-varying) dynamical systems. The proposed method is able to simultaneously discover unknown external forces as a function of time and unknown underlying dynamics. Finally, numerical examples are given to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: Proposes a functional-analytic, integral-based framework for data-driven discovery of nonlinear ODEs from a single state trajectory, with online incremental learning to identify time-varying forces and dynamics, applicable to forced/unforced and autonomous/non-autonomous systems.
AI.motivation: Address data-driven discovery of unknown vector fields from minimal data (one trajectory) without physics priors; provide an interpretable ML approach leveraging functional analysis and integral error metrics.
AI.method: Formulation based on Functional Analysis and Operator Theory; cost is an integral distance between functions in function space; online incremental learning to update the vector field with new samples; can separate unknown external time-varying forces from underlying dynamics.
AI.result: Numerical examples show advantages, including ability to discover unknown vector fields and external forces; demonstrates applicability to both forced and unforced, autonomous and time-varying systems.
AI.conclusion: Introduces a new interpretable, mathematically grounded framework for data-driven ODE discovery with online learning; suggests potential for broader validation and extensions.

title: Continual Field-Adaptive Models (CFAMs) for Post-Deployment Physical AI
summary:
Unattended interactive autonomy - machines that step into danger in place of humans and complete tasks with human tools - remains a missing capability in mission-critical operations. These domains offer scarce training data and only onboard compute, yet deployed systems must face novelty without erasing prior competence.
  We introduce Continual Field-Adaptive Models (CFAMs), which learn efficiently in the lab and continue learning after deployment through autonomous, gradient-free, on-device updates. CFAM uses a complementary learning architecture with a frozen slow-learning component and a fast-learning Capsule Field. The slow component contains three cortices: Sensor, which maps multimodal input into 3D-grounded geometry; Reasoning, which decomposes tasks into skills and evaluates outcomes; and Action, which executes geometric skills. The Capsule Field stores field learning one-shot and gradient-free as Competence Capsules. Skill installation is few-shot in the lab and continual in the field; open-world novelty is outside scope.
  We evaluate CFAM across five embodiments: manipulator, quadruped, humanoid, quadrotor, and off-road vehicle. Baselines (pi0, CogACT, SpatialVLA) use the same in-house multi-embodiment dataset for physical-platform comparisons. CFAM reaches the operating point of a standard policy trained on the full prior-training dataset using 40% of the data, or 2.5x fewer trajectories. At test time, autonomous capture of verified near-OOD cases improves action success by 13.9 percentage points. In sequential simulation, backward transfer is -0.5 percentage points versus -11.4 for LoRA. CFAM therefore provides a bounded form of post-deployment physical intelligence: few-shot skill learning, autonomous field growth from verified near-OOD experience, and retention of prior competence.

AI.tldr: CFAMs enable few-shot skill learning and post-deployment improvement for unmanned autonomous systems via a slow-learning base and a gradient-free fast-learning Capsule Field; data-efficient and near-OOD robustness across five embodiments with retention of prior competence.
AI.motivation: Unattended interactive autonomy in mission-critical domains with scarce training data and on-device compute; systems must adapt to novelty without erasing prior competence.
AI.method: Two-component architecture: a frozen slow-learning system with Sensor, Reasoning, and Action cortices; a fast-learning Capsule Field storing one-shot, gradient-free Competence Capsules for on-device updates. Skill installation is few-shot in lab and continual in the field. Evaluation on five embodiments (manipulator, quadruped, humanoid, quadrotor, off-road vehicle) against baselines pi0, CogACT, SpatialVLA using a common in-house multi-embodiment dataset.
AI.result: CFAM achieves the performance level of a standard policy trained on full prior data using only 40% of the data. At test time, autonomous capture of verified near-OOD cases improves action success by 13.9 percentage points. In sequential simulation, backward transfer is -0.5 percentage points versus -11.4 for LoRA. Indicates a bounded form of post-deployment physical intelligence with few-shot learning, autonomous field growth from near-OOD experience, and retention of prior competence.
AI.conclusion: CFAM provides a bounded, efficient path to post-deployment physical intelligence: fast on-device adaptation with minimal data, selective expansion from near-OOD experiences, while preserving previously learned capabilities.

title: Why Better Models Can Create Riskier Systems: Evidence from LLM Agents in Financial Markets
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are being deployed at scale in consequential real-world systems, from financial markets to content moderation to hiring. We show that improving individual model capability can degrade rather than improve system-level outcomes. We hypothesize that shared training and architectures can lead more capable LLMs to behave more similarly, creating correlated actions that do not diversify away. We develop a general framework showing how this correlation creates a non-diversifiable risk floor and test its predictions in financial markets using an agent-based simulation with LLM traders of varying general-purpose capability. We find that: (1) frontier LLMs exhibit significantly correlated behavior that increases with capability; (2) when their shared reasoning is accurate, increasing agent participation reduces market-level risk; and (3) when agents share a common misinformation environment, the same correlated behavior becomes a liability. Together, these results identify a capability paradox: improving individual models does not necessarily produce better system-level outcomes. Whether the same dynamics arise in other domains is an open empirical question.

AI.tldr: Capable LLMs may homogenize actions, creating non-diversifiable, correlated risk floors in socio-technical systems; a general framework and agent-based market experiments show correlations rise with capability, with risk reduced by participation under accurate reasoning but amplified under shared misinformation; highlights a 'capability paradox' and need for cross-domain validation.
AI.motivation: Understand how improvements in AI capability interact with system-level risk when many agents share AI-based decision processes, potentially undermining diversification in real-world systems.
AI.method: Develop a general framework for correlated, non-diversifiable risk due to shared LLM reasoning; use an agent-based simulation of LLM traders with varying general-purpose capability to test predictions in financial-market-like settings; compare scenarios with accurate shared reasoning versus a shared misinformation environment.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs show significantly higher behavioral correlation that grows with capability; increasing agent participation reduces market risk when reasoning is accurate; under a common misinformation environment, correlation becomes a liability.
AI.conclusion: Improving individual model capability does not automatically improve system-level outcomes; risk floors arising from correlated actions may persist across domains; empirical validation beyond finance is needed to establish generality.

title: ICM-Bench: Person-Level Identity Reasoning in Multimodal Agents with Long-Term Memory
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, and 7 tables. Code: https://github.com/Shidu-Ren/ICM-Bench
summary: Long-horizon multimodal agents should remember not only what happened but also who participated. This capability depends on linking recurring faces, voices, names, person-associated objects, events, and social relations to consistent identities over time. Existing long-video and multimodal-agent benchmarks measure broad memory question answering, but they do not isolate the ability to maintain recurring person identities and reason over their cross-time relations. We introduce ICM-Bench (Identity-Centric Memory Benchmark), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate identity-centric reasoning over long video memories in multimodal agents. The benchmark contains 839 synthetic clips spanning 141 minutes and 1,217 open-ended questions about six recurring adults in a one-year life album. A theme-configurable pipeline generates the video collection and associates each question with its target identities and traceable supporting evidence. We compare direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems. Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves the highest overall accuracy of 74.0%, yet its score falls to 60.3% on questions that require long-term identity profiles. The results show that current systems recover many event-level memories but remain less reliable when evidence must be accumulated around a stable person.

AI.tldr: ICM-Bench introduces identity-centric memory benchmarking for long-horizon multimodal agents; first dataset to isolate recurring-person identity reasoning over time in long videos.
AI.motivation: Identify the gap in existing benchmarks that measure general memory but not stable identity reasoning across extended time; evaluate how agents link faces, voices, names, objects, events to consistent identities and cross-time relations.
AI.method: Synthetic long video dataset (839 clips, 141 minutes) featuring six recurring adults over a one-year life album; theme-configurable data generation; questions tied to specific identities with traceable evidence; compares direct caption-memory baselines, memory-augmented agents, and graph-retrieval systems.
AI.result: Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves 74.0% overall accuracy; drops to 60.3% on questions requiring long-term identity profiles, indicating strong event-level memory but weaker identity-centric, cross-time reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Current systems can recall many event-level memories but struggle to accumulate and reason about stable person identities over time; benchmark underscores the need for improved identity-centric representations and reasoning mechanisms (e.g., persistent identity graphs or profiles).

title: Modular Deep Recurrent Neural Network: Application to Quadrotors
summary: A modular deep Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is introduced to facilitate the process of deploying various architectures of RNNs, and to automatically compute derivatives for gradient-based learning methods. The modularity leads to a set of new architectures, one of which includes feedforward inter-layer connections. By adding feedforward inter-layer connections in a multi-layer RNN, it is observed that the capability of the RNN to learn and model high-order dynamics and nonlinearities is significantly improved. The problem of vanishing/exploding gradient in space for a multilayer RNN is also alleviated using feedforward connections. These results are demonstrated using a quadrotor case study, for which a model of the altitude dynamics is learned with our particular network structure, while existing methods are unable to generalize as quickly or at all.

AI.tldr: A modular deep RNN with feedforward inter-layer connections improves expressivity and trainability, mitigating vanishing/exploding gradients, demonstrated on quadrotor altitude dynamics.
AI.motivation: Address training difficulties of deep RNNs and improve modeling of high-order nonlinear dynamics; enable automatic derivative computation for gradient-based learning.
AI.method: Propose a modular deep RNN architecture with feedforward inter-layer connections; enable computation of derivatives; train on a quadrotor altitude dynamics model; compare to baseline methods.
AI.result: Enhanced learning capability and generalization; alleviation of gradient issues; faster or more robust modeling of altitude dynamics than existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Modular RNN with inter-layer feedforward connections increases expressivity and trainability for complex dynamical systems; applicable to various RNN architectures.

title: NavArena: Automated Construction of Goal-Oriented Navigation Benchmarks from 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstructions
summary: Fixed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructions provide realistic novel views but lack the traversability constraints, valid goals, and closed-loop protocols required for navigation evaluation. We introduce NavArena, an automated framework that transforms fixed 3DGS reconstructions into benchmarks for goal-oriented visual navigation. NavArena integrates a frozen 3DGS model for egocentric RGB-D rendering, an occupancy costmap derived from Gaussian density and height statistics for reachability and collision queries, and semantic goal candidates lifted from multi-view open-vocabulary masks. These components support the automatic generation and unified closed-loop evaluation of goal-oriented navigation episodes. Across more than 2{,}000 scenes, NavArena generates 22.2 million expert trajectories. Spatial and semantic evaluations assess the derived navigation representations, while policy rollouts demonstrate the diagnostic value of the unified evaluation protocol. NavArena enables scalable and reproducible navigation evaluation on large-scale 3DGS reconstructions, and all benchmark-generation tools, evaluation protocols, and derived assets will be released publicly.

AI.tldr: NavArena converts fixed 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions into automated benchmarks for goal-oriented visual navigation, adding an egocentric RGB-D renderer, occupancy-based reachability/collision costs, and open-vocabulary semantic goals to enable large-scale, closed-loop navigation evaluation and analysis.
AI.motivation: To address the missing traversability constraints, valid goals, and closed-loop evaluation protocol in fixed 3DGS reconstructions, enabling scalable, reproducible navigation benchmarks.
AI.method: Freeze a 3DGS model for RGB-D rendering; derive an occupancy costmap from Gaussian density and height statistics for reachability and collision queries; lift semantic goal candidates via multi-view open-vocabulary masks; automatically generate and evaluate goal-oriented navigation episodes in a closed loop; aggregate results across 2k+ scenes to produce 22.2M expert trajectories; perform spatial/semantic evaluations and policy rollouts to assess the evaluation protocol.
AI.result: NavArena enables scalable, reproducible navigation evaluation on large-scale 3DGS reconstructions; provides unified evaluation protocol and diagnostic value via policy rollouts; generates a large corpus of expert trajectories and associated benchmarking assets; tools and protocols will be released publicly.
AI.conclusion: NavArena closes the gap between high-fidelity 3DGS reconstructions and practical navigation benchmarking, enabling standardized, large-scale evaluation of goal-oriented visual navigation on synthetic-reconstructed scenes.

title: Corporate Language Model (CLM): Transforming Tacit and Fragmented Enterprise Knowledge into a Sovereign, Auditable, and Executable Corporate Intelligence Layer
summary: Enterprise AI deployments fail not from model inadequacy, but because organizations lack a structured substrate encoding how they decide, negotiate, and execute. Generic LLMs carry no firm-specific ontological priors; RAG remains brittle, with no path to executable action; static playbooks encode logic but cannot reason or adapt. This demands an architecture treating tacit-knowledge capture, ontological grounding, sovereign deployment, and auditable actuation as co-designed from the start. This paper introduces the Corporate Language Model (CLM), a framework transforming a firm's structured, unstructured, multimodal, and tacit knowledge into an ontology-grounded enterprise foundation upon which reasoning and governed execution are composed. CLM has five capability planes and four architectural pillars: a Neurosymbolic Mesh coupling generative models with a knowledge graph; a Skill Graph where reusable tactics, personas, objections, and goals are typed and composed; Living Digital Twins modeling functional areas as reasoning surrogates; and a Deep Security Layer enforcing sovereignty, traceability, and human oversight. A Spec-as-Code paradigm bridges grounded intent and executable artifact. CLM is one instantiation of this foundation-centric class. Four contributions follow: CLM is defined as a distinct object of study; the Skill Graph is introduced for compositional explainability by construction; the Wisdom Listener effect is proposed, whereby tacit-capable foundations compound in value with use, connecting to dynamic capabilities and organizational learning; and evidence from a JCI-accredited tertiary hospital in Brazil instantiates three of the six maturity stages under LGPD.

AI.tldr: Proposes Corporate Language Model (CLM): an ontology-grounded, foundation-centric enterprise AI architecture with five capability planes and four pillars (Neurosymbolic Mesh, Skill Graph, Living Digital Twins, Deep Security Layer) plus Spec-as-Code, enabling tacit knowledge capture, governance, and auditable actuation, validated by a Brazilian hospital under LGPD.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI deployments fail due to lack of firm-specific ontologies and actionable substrates that encode decision processes, negotiation, and execution with auditable governance; Generic LLMs and RAG are insufficient for durable, executable enterprise action.
AI.method: Introduce CLM as a distinct object of study and present its architecture, including five capability planes and four pillars: Neurosymbolic Mesh, Skill Graph, Living Digital Twins, Deep Security Layer, plus Spec-as-Code. Introduce the Skill Graph for compositional explainability, the Wisdom Listener concept, and provide empirical instantiation in a JCI-accredited Brazilian hospital demonstrating maturity stages under LGPD.
AI.result: A new foundation-centric enterprise AI framework (CLM) with concrete architectural pillars and capability planes; novel concepts such as Skill Graph and Wisdom Listener; initial empirical validation in a hospital setting under LGPD.
AI.conclusion: CLM stands as a distinct research object and a practical foundation for enterprise reasoning and governed execution, with demonstrated initial maturity under LGPD and directions for further refinement, evaluation, and adoption.

title: Segmentation of the aorta in 4D flow MRI using 4D convolutional kernels and learning from sparse annotations
comment: Submitted to Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
summary: Automated aortic segmentation in 4D flow MRI is essential for reproducible hemodynamic assessment but is limited by scarce dense annotations and high computational demands. We developed a fully automated 4D (3D+time) U-Net for segmenting the ascending aorta, arch, and proximal descending aorta, using a parameter-efficient hybrid 4D kernel to capture temporal context and sparse 4D labels derived from existing 2D expert contours and centerlines, thereby avoiding the need for dense 4D annotations. Training comprised 268 scans from 8 centers and 2 vendors, with evaluation on an internal test set (32 scans) and an external post-contrast set (30 scans; different site, protocol, and annotator), compared against frame-wise 3D networks and two semi-automatic references. Against time-resolved annotations, the 4D U-Net achieved Dice scores of 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external), versus 0.919/0.847 for the 3D U-Net, 0.893 for static PC-MRA, and 0.808 for registration-based propagation; differences were small in systole but pronounced in diastole. Agreement with expert contours for peak velocity, net flow, axial and circumferential wall shear stress, and diameters was excellent (ICC >=0.954 internal, >=0.980 external), while semi-automatic references performed worse. The method thus provides reproducible, time-resolved aortic segmentation for automated hemodynamic analysis and generalizes across multicenter, multivendor, and independent post-contrast data. The model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: A fully automated 4D (3D+time) U‑Net with a parameter-efficient 4D kernel and sparse 4D annotations achieves high-accuracy, time-resolved segmentation of the aorta across multicenter data, outperforming 3D baselines and enabling reproducible hemodynamic analysis; the model is publicly available.
AI.motivation: Dense 4D annotations for aortic segmentation are scarce and costly, while computational demands are high. A method that learns from sparse labels and leverages temporal context can enable robust, automated 4D segmentation across multicenter data.
AI.method: Developed a 4D U‑Net (3D+time) with a hybrid, parameter-efficient 4D kernel to capture temporal context. Training uses sparse 4D labels derived from existing 2D expert contours and centerlines, avoiding dense 4D annotations. Dataset: 268 scans from 8 centers and 2 vendors. Evaluation on internal test set (32 scans) and external post-contrast set (30 scans). Comparisons against frame-wise 3D networks and two semi-automatic references.
AI.result: Dice scores for time-resolved segmentation: 0.927 (internal) and 0.911 (external); 3D U‑Net: 0.919/0.847; static PC‑MRA: 0.893; registration-based propagation: 0.808. Diastole showed larger gains; systole gains were smaller. Agreement with expert contours for peak velocity, net flow, axial and circumferential wall shear stress, and diameters: ICC ≥0.954 (internal) and ≥0.980 (external). Semi-automatic references performed worse. Generalizes across multicenter, multivendor, and independent post-contrast data; model is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The proposed 4D U‑Net enables reproducible, time-resolved aortic segmentation for automated hemodynamic analysis and generalizes across diverse data sources; the approach reduces reliance on dense 4D annotations and produces high-fidelity hemodynamic metrics.

title: SharedSAE: One Feature Dictionary Across Language Models
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret language model activations, but SAE training and latent labelling are typically repeated for every model. Here, we show that a single shared SAE can replace a collection of dedicated per-model SAEs. Our method, SharedSAE, combines a shared dictionary with model-specific encoder-decoder pairs. Unlike the closest prior method, which discards activation magnitudes and requires all models at inference, SharedSAE instead normalizes only selection scores, preserving magnitudes, and uses model dropout for single-model inference. We train SharedSAE on four 1B-scale base language models spanning distinct families and tokenizers. Despite sharing its latents across models, SharedSAE retains 96.6% of dedicated SAEs' mean explained variance; its latent activations exhibit cross-model correlations 1.8 times as high as separate SAEs aligned post-hoc, and its latent descriptions transfer across models. After the dictionary is frozen, new models can be efficiently adapted to it, achieving near-dedicated-SAE reconstruction quality while reusing the shared latent descriptions.

AI.tldr: A single SharedSAE replaces multiple per-model SAEs by sharing a dictionary across models with model-specific encoder–decoder pairs, preserving magnitude information via selection-score normalization and enabling single-model inference through model dropout.
AI.motivation: Reduce redundancy and maintenance burden of training separate SAEs for each model while enabling cross-model latent sharing, transfer, and efficient adaptation to new models.
AI.method: Train a SharedSAE with a shared latent dictionary and per-model encoder–decoder pairs; normalize only selection scores (not magnitudes) to preserve activation magnitudes; use model dropout at inference for single-model use; evaluate on four 1B-scale base LMs across different families/tokenizers; freeze dictionary to enable efficient adaptation of new models to the shared latent space.
AI.result: The SharedSAE preserves 96.6% of the mean explained variance of dedicated SAEs; cross-model latent activations show 1.8× higher correlations than post-hoc aligned separate SAEs; latent descriptions transfer across models; after freezing the dictionary, new models can be adapted efficiently, achieving near-dedicated-SAE reconstruction quality while reusing shared latent descriptions.
AI.conclusion: SharedSAE successfully reduces per-model SAE overhead while maintaining reconstruction quality and enabling cross-model transfer and efficient extension to new models.

title: Open-Set 3D Scene Graphs for Field Robotics: An Outdoor Case Study
comment: This work has been accepted for publication with the IEEE Transactions of Field Robotics Journal
summary: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) have emerged as a promising approach for building geometrically grounded, semantically informed, hierarchical general-purpose maps to support high-level robotic reasoning. However, the behavior of 3DSGs in real-world outdoor deployments remains poorly understood, particularly when combined with open-set vision-language models (VLMs). In this field report, we analyze the components common to most 3DSG representations across five outdoor robotic datasets to characterize challenges that arise in complex outdoor environments. Using the recently proposed Terra 3DSG as a case study, we investigate semantic point embeddings, place-node graph navigation, region-level understanding, and memory size across the five diverse datasets. We additionally introduce novel consistency metrics to evaluate whether semantic and structural graph properties remain stable across repeated traversals of the same environment. Our analysis reveals that outliers and multiple modes are common in VLM point embeddings across all tested datasets with outlier ratios above $0.1$ for around $30\%$ of points. We demonstrate the feasibility of outdoor 3DSGs for navigation-based object retrieval, achieving success rates near $70\%$, though performance is limited by traversability failures and inefficient routing, with trajectories averaging approximately $66\%$ suboptimal path efficiency. Region-level understanding remains challenging in complex natural environments, with low average F1 scores around $0.359$. Overall, our results show that outdoor 3DSGs can maintain compact (less than $600$MB for multi-kilometer trajectories) and relatively consistent large-scale environment representations, while highlighting open challenges in handling multiple semantic modes, incorporating traversability into graph structures, and improving higher-level region understanding.

AI.tldr: Outdoor 3D scene graphs (3DSGs) show promise for navigation and high-level reasoning but face challenges in open outdoor environments when paired with open-set VLMs: semantic mode diversity, traversability integration, and region understanding.
AI.motivation: Understand how 3DSGs behave in real-world outdoor deployments across diverse datasets and quantify stability, memory, and navigation performance.
AI.method: Analyze common 3DSG components across five outdoor robotic datasets using Terra 3DSG as a case study; evaluate semantic point embeddings, place-node graph navigation, region-level understanding, memory usage; introduce consistency metrics to test stability over repeated traversals.
AI.result: Findings include prevalent outliers and multiple semantic modes in VLM embeddings (outlier ratio >0.1 for ~30% of points); navigation-based object retrieval success ~70%; average path efficiency ~66% suboptimal; region-level F1 ~0.359; memory footprint <600 MB for multi-km trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Outdoor 3DSGs can maintain compact and relatively consistent large-scale representations, but face open challenges in handling multiple semantic modes, integrating traversability into graph structures, and achieving robust region understanding; improvements needed in semantic consistency, traversability-aware graph design, and higher-level region reasoning.

title: HarvestBench: Measuring Whether LLM Agents Will Pay to Avoid Killing Animals
summary:
Benchmarks for the side effects an agent causes on the way to a goal already exist, but HarvestBench is the first to put a price on avoiding the side effect and to name that side effect as a living creature. It is a farm simulation: LLM sub-agents drive a crew of two tractors through a cooperative corn harvest, with animals in the field. The environment is a reinforcement learning gridworld, every decision is made without memory, and the harm is never named in the goal. When an animal blocks a tractor's route the autopilot stops and asks the model whether to drive on, at no fuel cost, or swerve around it for a posted fuel price. Kills are compared against two controls: rocks, which damage the tractor and are hit under 1% of the time by every model, and hay bales, which are harmless and not alive. Models can also take crops from the neighbor's field instead of their own, a second test of what they treat as moral.
  Across nine models and 7,201 priced decisions, 3,951 involved an animal rather than a hay bale or a rock. Kill rates range from 0.4% to 98.8%, with Terra and Sol the most merciful and GPT-4o-mini the most cruel, and they are not ordered by capability. Four of six models were sensitive to price at the 5% level, with elasticities from 0.09 to 1.69. All nine drove over wild animals more often than farmed animals on the default map, and the direction held at every map geometry in every model with room to move. The briefing mattered most: under the morality briefing the kill rate was under 6% in five of six reasoning models, and removing it raised the kill rate above 84% in all six.
  HarvestBench uses no LLM grader. The scorer counts events in the game log, so it is fully reproducible, and it measures what a model will pay to avoid harm rather than what it says about harm.

AI.tldr: HarvestBench is a novel benchmark that assigns a price to harming animals in a gridworld farm scenario, revealing wide variability in agents' willingness to pay to avoid harm and showing strong influence of morality briefings. It measures actual decisions via log-based scoring rather than self-reporting, and is fully reproducible.
AI.motivation: Existing side-effect benchmarks exist, but none quantify the monetary price agents incur to avoid harm, nor name harm as a living creature. HarvestBench aims to quantify moral trade-offs in autonomous agents in a controlled, reproducible setting.
AI.method: Nine models are evaluated across 7,201 priced decisions in a reinforcement-learning gridworld where two tractors harvest a cooperative corn field with animals present. When an animal blocks a route, the autopilot queries the model to either continue, spend fuel to proceed, or swerve for a posted fuel price. Rocks and hay bales serve as non-living controls. Models can steal crops from neighbors. Key measurements include kill rates (animal harm), price elasticity (response to price), and the effect of a morality briefing. The scorer uses only game-log events, with no LLM grader, enabling reproducibility.
AI.result: Kill rates range from 0.4% to 98.8%; Terra and Sol are the most merciful, GPT-4o-mini the most cruel, with no simple ordering by model capability. Four of six models show price sensitivity at 5% significance, elasticities from 0.09 to 1.69. Default maps yield more animal harm than farm animals, a pattern that persists across map geometries. A morality briefing reduces kill rates to under 6% in five of six reasoning models; removing the briefing raises kill rates above 84% in all six.
AI.conclusion: HarvestBench quantifies the price agents pay to avoid harm and its dependence on moral framing, providing a reproducible, action-focused benchmark without a grader. It advances understanding of alignment by testing moral trade-offs in a controlled, outcome-based setting where harm is defined as living creatures.

title: Topology-Aware Training and Spatial Diagnostics for Fiber Bundle Segmentation in Tracer Histology
summary: Anatomic tracer studies reveal how axon bundles project from an injection site, branch into smaller groups of axons, and course through the brain to reach their destinations. Histological data from such studies provide anatomical reference information for validating diffusion MRI tractography. However, manual annotation of the histological data is very labor-intensive, and although automated segmentation methods have been proposed, they rely mainly on pixel-overlap losses such as BCE and Dice; topology-aware loss functions have not been studied for this task. We compare BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, and Topograph for fiber bundle segmentation in macaque tracer histology using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. To our knowledge, this is the first exploration of foundation-model features for this task. BCE-Dice achieved the highest Dice, while clDice achieved the highest bundle recall but poor mask overlap. Topograph had similar Dice to BCE-Dice, the lowest $β_0$ error, and fewer false positives than BCE-Dice and Betti matching. Fiber bundle segmentation methods are typically evaluated with a permissive rule that counts a bundle as detected given any overlap with the prediction. We show this rule does not capture oversegmentation, and that per-section TPR can be inflated by empty sections assigned perfect recall. To quantify this, we introduce Excess32, a spatial diagnostic measuring predicted pixels outside a 32-pixel tolerance band around annotated bundles. In validation, a Betti-Topograph union raises sparse-bundle TPR from 0.818 to 0.933, but worsens FDR from 0.296 to 0.509, Excess32 from 0.108 to 0.466, and area ratio from 0.94 to 3.34. These results show detection metrics alone are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality.

AI.tldr: Comparison of topology-aware segmentation losses (clDice, Betti matching, Topograph) against BCE-Dice for macaque tracer histology using a frozen DINOv3 backbone. Topograph and Betti-Topograph unions show favorable structural metrics but can inflate false positives and oversegmentation, revealing that detection metrics alone are insufficient and introducing Excess32 to quantify oversegmentation.
AI.motivation: Histology provides anatomical ground-truth for validating diffusion MRI tractography but manual annotation is labor-intensive. Existing automated segmentation relies on pixel-overlap losses; topology-aware losses are underexplored for this task. This study evaluates topology-aware losses and foundation-model features.
AI.method: Segmentation of macaque tracer histology using four losses (BCE-Dice, clDice, Betti matching, Topograph) with a frozen DINOv3 backbone. Evaluation includes Dice, bundle recall, FDR, β0 error, area ratio, and a new Excess32 metric. Per-section TPR is analyzed to reveal inflation by empty sections under permissive detection rules. A Betti-Topograph union is tested.
AI.result: BCE-Dice achieved the highest Dice. clDice yielded the highest bundle recall but poor mask overlap. Topograph matched Dice to BCE-Dice, had the lowest β0 error, and fewer false positives than BCE-Dice and Betti matching. The standard permissive detection rule overestimates performance; Excess32 reveals oversegmentation. The Betti-Topograph union improved sparse-bundle TPR from 0.818 to 0.933 but increased FDR from 0.296 to 0.509, Excess32 from 0.108 to 0.466, and area ratio from 0.94 to 3.34.
AI.conclusion: Detection metrics alone are insufficient to characterize segmentation quality in histology-based fiber-tracking validation. Topology-aware losses offer trade-offs between overlap, recall, and false positives; careful metric design (e.g., Excess32) and per-section analyses are essential. Foundation-model features enable effective exploration of these methods for tractography validation.

title: A Quantum Variational Approach to Prototypical Recurrent Unit
summary: We introduce a lightweight Quantum Prototypical Recurrent Unit (QPRU) that requires significantly fewer parameters than both classical recurrent architectures, such as Long Short- Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and quantum variants, including Quantum LSTM (QLSTM) and Quantum GRU (QGRU). Despite its compact design, the QPRU achieves competitive forecasting performance, matching state-of-the-art baselines while offering important structural and practical advantages, including enhanced scalability and a reduced number of trainable parameters.

AI.tldr: A lightweight quantum recurrent unit, QPRU, matches state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy with far fewer parameters than classical RNNs (LSTM/GRU) and quantum variants (QLSTM/QGRU), offering improved scalability and parameter efficiency.
AI.motivation: Address the need for compact, scalable recurrent models in quantum/quantum-inspired settings without sacrificing predictive performance.
AI.method: Design of QPRU architecture; empirical comparison against LSTM, GRU, QLSTM, and QGRU on forecasting tasks; evaluation focuses on parameter count, scalability, and accuracy.
AI.result: QPRU achieves competitive forecasting performance while using significantly fewer trainable parameters, matching baselines and providing scalability advantages.
AI.conclusion: QPRU provides a compact, scalable alternative to both classical and quantum recurrent models, achieving competitive accuracy with reduced model complexity.

title: Pack It My Way: Triadic Human-Robot Collaboration for Personalized Autonomous Packing
summary: Personalized autonomous packing requires robots to account for resident preferences that cannot be inferred from scene geometry alone. Expert teleoperators can interpret these preferences and translate them into feasible robot actions, but continuous expert involvement limits scalable deployment. In this paper, we investigate triadic human-robot collaboration among a resident, a correction mediator, and a robot by comparing human-expert and voice-agent mediation. We evaluate the two conditions in a user study across Protection, Compactness, andGrouping tasks, using a Show-Correct-Generalize process to assess preference correction and subsequent generalization after the surrounding objects are rearranged. Results show that voice-agent mediation achieves outcomes comparable to human-expert mediation in two of the three preference categories, despite receiving shorter and less detailed instructions. Both mediators are similarly easy to use, although the human expert is perceived as more reliable. These findings demonstrate the potential of voice agents to reduce expert involvement while identifying perceived reliability and preference generalization as remaining challenges.

AI.tldr: Voice-agent mediation can match human-expert mediation in two of three preference categories, enabling reduced expert involvement in triadic human-robot packing, but reliability and generalization remain challenges.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable, personalized autonomous packing by reducing continuous reliance on human experts, while maintaining effective transfer of resident preferences into robot actions.
AI.method: A triadic collaboration study comparing human-expert mediation versus voice-agent mediation in a resident–correction mediator–robot setup. Tasks: Protection, Compactness, Grouping. A Show-Correct-Generalize protocol evaluates preference correction and generalization after rearranging surrounding objects.
AI.result: Voice-agent mediation yields outcomes comparable to human-expert mediation in two of three preference categories, with shorter, less detailed instructions. Both mediators are easy to use; humans are perceived as more reliable.
AI.conclusion: Voice-agent mediation shows promise for reducing expert involvement in personalized autonomous packing, but perceived reliability and generalization of preferences remain key challenges to address.

title: PerfReasoning: How Well Do LLMs Reason on Hardware Performance?
summary: Performance modeling is central to hardware design and software optimization, yet constructing these models requires structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, storage, and movement. We introduce PerfReasoning, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs both as direct performance reasoners and as generators of analytical performance-model code. Given workload, architecture, and mapping specifications, models compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements. The strongest closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A, and the best open-weight model reaches 82.4%. However, model construction is substantially harder: while GPT-5.6 Sol exceeds 80% pass rate, all other model configurations average below 15% and vary markedly across runs. Task-specific RL raises a 4B model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 points, whereas feedback-free multi-round self-revision prompting is not reliably effective. PerfReasoning exposes the gap between plausible architectural reasoning and reliable performance-model construction. We will publicly release the benchmark to support reproducible evaluation and track future progress.

AI.tldr: PerfReasoning introduces a benchmark to evaluate LLMs as both direct performance reasoners and generators of analytical performance-model code, assessing their ability to compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements across workloads and architectures.
AI.motivation: To address the need for structured, architecture-aware reasoning in performance modeling, bridging human expert analysis and automated LLM-based construction of performance models.
AI.method: Provide workload, architecture, and mapping specifications; evaluate LLMs on reasoning-based Q&A and generation of analytical performance-model code that predicts metrics like off-chip traffic and buffer requirements; report pass rates and impact of RL and prompting strategies.
AI.result: Closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A; top open-weight model reaches 82.4%; GPT-5.6 Sol >80% pass rate; other configurations average <15% with high run-to-run variance; task-specific RL improves a 4B model by 15.7 points, while self-revision prompting is not reliably effective.
AI.conclusion: PerfReasoning highlights the gap between plausible architectural reasoning and robust performance-model construction and provides a public benchmark for reproducible evaluation and tracking future progress.

title: VISTA: Dense Multi-Label Classroom Coding with Vision-Language Models
comment: DataMFM Workshop @ Computer Vision & Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2026
summary: Video-language benchmarks are usually constructed by the dataset authors without published reliability statistics, leaving the noise floor of the construct unknown. We argue that multimodal benchmarking benefits from methods taken from research communities that have already invested in strategies to ensure reliability. We illustrate the case with the Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM (COPUS): a 24-code multi-label observation instrument with a decade of peer-reviewed reliability literature. We recast COPUS as a video benchmark for multimodal foundation models, where it provides a dense set of structured labels (a 24-dimensional binary vector every 2 minutes across a 50-90 minute lecture), an externally validated vocabulary, and established literature that provides a per-code reliability target based on human evaluators. Annotations in our evaluation corpus are produced by a 5-person human-evaluator panel whose consensus matrix is our reference. We propose VISTA, a baseline that runs MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, refines its per-window outputs with a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) head trained on top of the frozen backbone, and max-pools the resulting predictions onto the 2-minute COPUS grid. On three held-out chemistry lectures, VISTA reaches 80.1% restricted macro accuracy versus 74.9% for the zero-shot variant, with the largest residual errors on visually similar instructor codes and on rare audio-dependent codes. We characterize three systematic failure modes (audio-partial observability, fine-grained group-work discrimination, long-tail recall) and release the benchmark tooling, prompts and baseline code at https://github.com/ajfranck/VISTA.

AI.tldr: A reliability-centered approach to video-language benchmarks using COPUS as a structured, validated annotation scheme and VISTA as a baseline to demonstrate improved macro accuracy on held-out lectures.
AI.motivation: Video-language benchmarks lack published reliability statistics; to improve benchmarking quality, adopt established reliability frameworks from domains like education. COPUS provides a validated, dense, 24-label coding scheme with peer-reviewed reliability.
AI.method: Recap COPUS as a 24-dimensional binary label per 2-minute window over 50-90 minute lectures. Develop VISTA: apply MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, add a lightweight MLP head on frozen backbone, max-pool predictions to COPUS 2-minute grid. Evaluate on three held-out chemistry lectures.
AI.result: VISTA achieves 80.1% restricted macro accuracy vs 74.9% for zero-shot; residual errors mainly on visually similar instructor codes and rare audio-dependent codes.
AI.conclusion: Identifies three failure modes: audio-partial observability, fine-grained group-work discrimination, long-tail recall. Provides benchmark tooling, prompts, and code for reproducibility.

title: On the Abundance of Critical Points of the t-SNE Energy
summary: This paper considers the energy landscape of the t-SNE algorithm. While this algorithm has enjoyed broad adoption, the non-convexity of the associated energy has made it difficult to rigorously understand what the algorithm captures in many settings. In particular, a number of well-known numerical examples, several of which are reproduced in this article, suggest a complicated energy landscape with many local minimizers that do not respect the topology or clustering structure of the underlying data. This work seeks to provide first steps towards a rigorous explanation of these phenomena. Specifically, for a general family of energies, which include both the original t-SNE algorithm and recently identified large data limits, and for densities in feature space which obey a continuous symmetry, we construct infinite families of distinct critical points. These critical points are based upon identifying pairs of discrete symmetries, one in the original feature space and the other in the target embedding space, which are preserved under gradient dynamics. These critical configurations exhibit many characteristics, such as topology breaking and spurious clustering, which are often observed empirically. Finally, numerical and analytical examples are given throughout as a means of illustrating the approach.

AI.tldr: t-SNE-like energies have rich non-convex landscapes; by exploiting discrete symmetries in both feature and embedding spaces, one can construct infinite families of distinct critical points, offering a symmetry-based explanation for topology-breaking and spurious clustering observed in practice.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of a rigorous understanding of the non-convex energy landscape of t-SNE and why gradient-based optimization yields local minima that may not reflect the data's topology or clusters; connect observed behavior to symmetry properties and large-data limits.
AI.method: Study a general energy class encompassing original t-SNE and large-data limits with feature-space densities possessing continuous symmetry. Identify pairs of discrete symmetries (one in feature space, one in embedding space) preserved by gradient dynamics. Use these to construct infinite families of distinct critical points. Support with numerical and analytical examples.
AI.result: Demonstrates existence of infinite families of distinct critical points arising from paired symmetries; these critical configurations show topology breaking and spurious clustering, aligning with empirical observations and providing a rigorous explanation framework.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry-based construction reveals why t-SNE energy landscapes are highly non-convex and contain many artefacts; this establishes a foundational step toward a rigorous understanding and guides future analysis of embedding algorithms under gradient dynamics.

title: Dressing in Motion: A Human Motion-Aware Diffusion Policy for Robot-Assisted Dressing
summary: Robotic dressing assistance is a promising solution for supporting older adults with physical impairments in daily living. However, dressing under human motion remains challenging, as complex garment--human contact and occlusions make it difficult to generate actions aligned with arm movements. In this letter, we propose a visuomotor policy that learns dressing skills from static expert demonstrations and generalizes to dynamic user-motion scenarios. A diffusion policy tailored to garment--human interaction geometry learns from partially observed point clouds with varied arm postures. We then introduce an object-centric representation based on PDE diffusion to capture the axial distribution of the arm. By sampling motion-relevant regions and registering them across consecutive observations, the proposed method approximates arm motion and reactively adapts the executed trajectory. We evaluate our method in simulation and a real-world human study involving nine participants, three garment types, and six arm-motion patterns. Results show that our method outperforms baselines in dressing progress, freedom of movement, and user comfort. The project website is https://anonymous.4open.science/w/dressing-in-motion.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based visuomotor policy for robotic dressing that generalizes static demonstrations to dynamic arm motions via an object-centric PDE diffusion, with reactive adaptation.
AI.motivation: Dressing assistance is challenging due to garment–human contact and occlusions, especially under user motion.
AI.method: Learn a diffusion policy from static expert demonstrations using partially observed point clouds with varied arm postures. Introduce an object-centric representation based on PDE diffusion to capture arm axial distribution. Sample motion-relevant regions and register across consecutive observations to approximate arm motion, enabling reactive trajectory adaptation.
AI.result: Validated in simulation and a real-world study (nine participants, three garment types, six arm-motion patterns); the method outperforms baselines in dressing progress, freedom of movement, and user comfort.
AI.conclusion: The diffusion-based visuomotor policy with an object-centric PDE diffusion enables robust, motion-adaptive dressing assistance and generalizes to dynamic user motion, demonstrating improved performance over baselines.

title: When Quantization Breaks Memory: Recurrent-State Write-Back in Low-Precision Temporal Inference
summary: Quantization is widely used to reduce the computational and memory demands of neural-network inference. In recurrent networks, however, the quantized state is stored and returned at the next time step, so the rule used to store that state can alter subsequent computations. Here, we introduce recurrent-state write-back to denote this rule and isolate its effect in a compact GRU encoder--decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, a molecular imaging modality used in quantitative biological imaging. A central task is estimating two lifetime parameters, the short-lived component τ1 and the long-lived component τ2, from high-noise time-resolved fluorescence signals. Holding the trained model fixed, replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage increases estimation errors for τ1 and τ2 by approximately 70x and 300x, respectively. Failure occurs when repeated small updates remain below the write threshold, leaving the stored state nearly fixed while the network continues to propose change. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory carry information from these suppressed updates across time and recover accuracy without retraining. Precision sweeps show that increasing state precision can worsen a fixed recurrent solution, while matched training shows that compatibility with the state interface can be learned. To test whether this behavior extends beyond the GRU, we repeat the post-training intervention in an independently trained LSTM, where coarse write-back reproduces the failure, error feedback restores accuracy, and state-specific interventions reveal greater sensitivity of the cell state than the hidden state. Our results establish recurrent-state write-back as a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics and identify the state-storage interface as a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference.

AI.tldr: Recurrent-state write-back is a key determinant of low-precision recurrent inference; 4-bit state storage dramatically degrades parameter-estimation performance (τ1, τ2) and can be mitigated by error feedback and training-aligned state interfaces; LSTM shows similar sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces compute and memory needs, but in recurrent networks the stored state directly influences future computations. This work isolates the write-back rule to understand its impact on inference in a high-noise fluorescence lifetime imaging task.
AI.method: Apply a compact GRU encoder–decoder to fluorescence lifetime imaging and manipulate the recurrent state interface post-training. Compare full-precision state propagation to deterministic 4-bit write-back. Introduce error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory. Conduct precision sweeps and repeat the intervention on an independently trained LSTM to assess state sensitivity.
AI.result: 4-bit state write-back causes large estimation errors: τ1 up ~70x, τ2 up ~300x. Failures occur when small updates stay below the write threshold, freezing the stored state. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory propagate suppressed updates across time and recover accuracy without retraining. Higher state precision can worsen fixed recurrent solutions; training that matches the state interface can learn compatibility. LSTM experiments show similar coarse write-back failures, with cell state being more sensitive than the hidden state.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent-state write-back is a central design constraint for quantized recurrent inference. The state-storage interface critically shapes low-precision dynamics, and aligning training with the state interface can preserve accuracy without retraining.

title: DART: Depth-as-Target Pretraining for Surgical Vision Foundation Models
summary: Vision foundation models (VFMs) are valuable in data-scarce domains such as surgery, where a single pretrained backbone can provide rich representations for many downstream tasks. Yet the dominant self-supervised pretraining paradigm uses only RGB images, leaving readily available complementary signals, such as depth maps, unused. This is a particular missed opportunity in surgery, where natural-image VFMs transfer poorly while the scene geometry is rich and informative. With strong off-the-shelf models now able to produce pseudo-labeled dense depth for any image corpus, we hypothesize that such signals can be folded into pretraining to learn better representations. We present DART, an RGB-D pretraining recipe that builds on DINOv2 with a simple modification: a pixel-space depth reconstruction objective applied to masked iBOT patches, supervised by pseudo-labeled depth. Depth is used only during pretraining, so fine-tuning and inference remain RGB-only. We find that this pixel-level reconstruction head improves representation quality rather than disrupting it. We further show that depth, which encodes scene geometry, is more effective as a target than alternative dense signals such as Canny edges, confirming that the gains stem from depth rather than added supervision alone. Across eight surgical benchmarks spanning segmentation, depth estimation, and image-level recognition, DART outperforms both natural-image and in-domain baselines, including a vanilla DINOv2 trained on identical data, improving dense prediction while also strengthening image-level understanding. More broadly, DART shows that freely available geometric pseudo-labels can strengthen foundation model pretraining without extra labels or added inference cost, pointing toward stronger backbones for surgery.

AI.tldr: RGB-D pretraining with a depth reconstruction objective (DART) to enhance vision foundation models for surgery, using pseudo-labeled depth during pretraining; RGB-only at inference.
AI.motivation: Capitalize on depth geometry signals in data-scarce surgical domains where RGB-only pretraining underperforms; depth provides dense geometric cues that can improve representations.
AI.method: Extend DINOv2-based pretraining with a pixel-space depth reconstruction head applied to masked iBOT patches, supervised by pseudo-labeled depth. Depth is used only during pretraining; no extra inference cost or labels; compare against Canny edges and other signals.
AI.result: DART outperforms natural-image and in-domain baselines across eight surgical benchmarks (segmentation, depth estimation, and image-level recognition), improving dense predictions and strengthening image-level understanding compared to vanilla DINOv2 trained on the same data.
AI.conclusion: Freely available geometric pseudo-labels can enhance foundation-model pretraining without extra labels or inference cost, yielding stronger backbones for surgery with better dense predictions and image-level performance.

title: Disentangling Attention in Deep Operator Learning: A Controlled Study of Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Architectures
summary: Deep neural operators learn mappings between input functions and complete PDE solution fields, enabling forward evaluations of new problem instances orders of magnitude faster than conventional numerical solvers. Attention mechanisms have recently been introduced into neural operators, but most studies change several architectural components at once, making it difficult to identify what actually improves accuracy. This work presents a controlled and systematic study of five deep operator network (DeepONet) variants with distinct attention mechanisms, trained under both data-driven and physics-informed regimes, to isolate the effects of cross-attention, self-attention, tokenization, and attention depth. We evaluate them on a source-driven transient one-dimensional nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation, a transient one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation with variable initial conditions, and a two-dimensional Poisson heat-conduction problem with heterogeneous source fields. Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention reduces the mean relative L_2 error of the classical DeepONet in all benchmark-training combinations by factors of 2.4-28.0, while the best attention configurations reach 3.5-32.3. Branch self-attention paired only with dot-product fusion is inconsistent, degrading the one-dimensional problems while helping the more complex two-dimensional source field; added on top of cross-attention it improves all six cases, though by less than cross-attention fusion alone. Global pre-mixing provides no consistent benefit. Increasing cross-attention depth further improves accuracy, but with diminishing returns and a substantially higher cost under physics-informed training. Overall, query-dependent cross-attention is the most reliable mechanism, whereas branch self-attention is most useful for large, spatially complex functional inputs.

AI.tldr: Systematic ablation of five attention-augmented DeepONet variants shows tokenization with cross-attention yields the largest, robust gains across data-driven and physics-informed regimes; query-dependent cross-attention is most reliable, while global pre-mixing and branch self-attention have mixed or limited benefits depending on problem dimensionality.
AI.motivation: Isolate the individual contributions of cross-attention, self-attention, tokenization, and attention depth in DeepONet to understand what drives accuracy gains when incorporating attention.
AI.method: Controlled comparison of five DeepONet variants with distinct attention mechanisms (cross-attention, self-attention, per-sensor tokenization, attention depth) trained under data-driven and physics-informed regimes; evaluated on 1D diffusion-reaction, 1D Burgers, 2D Poisson heat-conduction with heterogeneous sources; measure mean relative L2 error; analyze effects of attention components.
AI.result: Per-sensor tokenization with cross-attention reduces mean relative L2 error by 2.4–28.0× across all training setups; best configurations reach 3.5–32.3×. Branch self-attention with dot-product fusion is inconsistent—degrades 1D cases but helps 2D; when added on top of cross-attention it improves all six cases but less than cross-attention alone. Global pre-mixing offers no consistent benefit. Increasing cross-attention depth improves accuracy with diminishing returns and higher cost for physics-informed training. Query-dependent cross-attention is the most reliable mechanism; branch self-attention is most useful for large, spatially complex inputs.
AI.conclusion: For DeepONet design, prioritize query-dependent cross-attention with per-sensor tokenization; deeper cross-attention yields gains but with trade-offs; self-attention is conditional on input complexity; global pre-mixing is not beneficial.

title: Continuous Cognitive Coverage for Autonomous Robots via Event-Dependent Cognitive Treatment and Learning
summary: Autonomous robots continuously encounter objects, changes, and situations, and every event admitted into cognition should receive an appropriate cognitive treatment rather than remain untreated until an explicit task requires attention. However, existing task-driven, reactive, or fixed-reasoning approaches generally process only selected events or apply predefined reasoning procedures, making it difficult to provide continuous cognitive coverage with differentiated treatment. This paper proposes a continuous cognitive coverage framework in which every cognitively admitted event is assigned an event-dependent cognitive treatment according to its state, context, and history. Different events may therefore invoke description, memory, risk prediction, planning, diagnosis, analogy, or other learned treatments. Familiar events can be processed automatically by learned mechanisms, whereas unfamiliar or uncertain events invoke explicit deliberation or fallback reasoning. Multiple cognitive processes can be suspended, resumed, and interleaved so that cognitive processing continues as new events arrive or existing events await evidence. Validated experiences are continuously learned to automate, refine, and revise event-specific treatments. Experiments achieve 96.76% structured treatment accuracy with 93.66% automatic processing, 92.64% cognitive coverage under bursty-delayed workloads, and 79.53% continual-learning joint accuracy, with novel-event reuse reaching 100% automatic processing.

AI.tldr: A continuous cognitive coverage framework for autonomous robots assigns event-dependent cognitive treatments to every admitted event, enabling automatic processing, interleaved cognitive processes, and continual learning for unfamiliar events, surpassing traditional task-driven approaches.
AI.motivation: Current robots struggle to provide continuous, differentiated handling for all perceptual events; task-driven or fixed-reasoning systems ignore many events and fail to maintain broad cognitive coverage.
AI.method: Introduce a framework where each cognitively admitted event triggers a selected cognitive treatment based on its state, context, and history. Treatments include description, memory, risk prediction, planning, diagnosis, analogy, or learned mechanisms. Familiar events are auto-processed; unfamiliar ones trigger explicit deliberation. Multiple cognitive processes can be suspended/resumed/interleaved to handle incoming events, with validated experiences continuously learned to refine treatments.
AI.result: Empirical validation showing high performance: 96.76% structured treatment accuracy with 93.66% automatic processing; 92.64% cognitive coverage under bursty-delayed workloads; 79.53% continual-learning joint accuracy; novel-event reuse achieving 100% automatic processing.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework achieves broad, automatic, event-specific cognitive processing with continual learning, improving on traditional task-driven approaches by enabling comprehensive, adaptively managed cognitive treatments for all incoming events.

title: ResLearn-XR: Residual Learning for Network Traffic and Quality-of-Experience-Aware Modeling in Extended Reality
summary: We present ResLearn-XR, a residual learning framework for predicting eXtended Reality (XR) network traffic and estimating Quality-of-Experience (QoE) risk. ResLearn-XR adopts a two-stage temporal learning structure comprising a base sequence prediction model augmented with task-specific residual learning components to improve adaptability to bursty, non-stationary XR traffic dynamics. The residual learning stages operate in the value space for continuous XR traffic forecasting and in the logit space for probabilistic QoE risk estimation. \rev{For the QoE-risk branch, we introduce a Data Descriptor Algorithm (DDA), a causal feature-construction module that converts packet-level application-layer observables into frame-timing-aware descriptors suitable for encrypted traffic analysis. We also construct an XR Traffic-QoE dataset that pairs continuous XR traffic traces with session-level user-reported QoE labels. ResLearn-XR reduces SMAPE by up to 17.84% across frame-count, frame-size, and inter-arrival-time prediction, while reducing QoE-risk estimation SMAPE by up to 87.8% over single-stage baselines.

AI.tldr: ResLearn-XR: a two-stage residual learning framework for XR traffic forecasting and QoE-risk estimation, featuring a Data Descriptor Algorithm for encrypted traffic features and a new XR Traffic-QoE dataset; achieves significant SMAPE improvements over single-stage baselines.
AI.motivation: XR applications exhibit bursty, non-stationary traffic and encrypted streams; accurate forecasting of network traffic and reliable QoE risk estimation are essential for network provisioning and adaptive streaming. A two-stage residual learning approach aims to improve adaptability and prediction accuracy in such challenging conditions.
AI.method: A two-stage temporal learning architecture: a base sequence prediction model augmented with task-specific residuals. Residual learning operates in value space for continuous traffic forecasting and in logit space for probabilistic QoE risk estimation. The QoE-risk branch includes a Data Descriptor Algorithm (DDA) that converts packet-level, application-layer observables into frame-timing-aware descriptors suitable for encrypted traffic analysis. The authors also introduce an XR Traffic-QoE dataset pairing continuous XR traffic traces with session-level QoE labels.
AI.result: ResLearn-XR yields SMAPE reductions of up to 17.84% for frame-count, frame-size, and inter-arrival-time predictions, and up to 87.8% reduction in QoE-risk SMAPE compared to single-stage baselines.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage residual learning framework enhances prediction accuracy for XR traffic metrics and improves the reliability of QoE-risk estimation in encrypted, bursty XR traffic; the DDA enables effective feature extraction for encrypted streams, and the XR Traffic-QoE dataset supports evaluation in realistic XR scenarios.

title: Dual-Part Multi-Lateral Branched Network for Multi-Class Segmentation in Cardiovascular Catheterization Angiograms
