UCB performs refinement-mode selection, and the policy-conditioned Double DQN performs tick-level action selection from navigation variables, active policy parameters, and the LLM action prior. Each of the four configurations was evaluated over 30 rounds. In the fixed simulation, the complete configuration reached the goal in all 90 correlated robot--round records and achieved the lowest median completion time (42 ticks) and P90 (73.2 ticks); its median was 25.0--39.1\% lower than those of the other configurations. These observations provide descriptive, configuration-level evidence from the evaluated configurations.

AI.tldr: A decentralized, multi-robot navigation study shows that a fully integrated configuration combining LLM-based policy, UCB refinement, and policy-conditioned Double DQN at the action level yields best performance in NetLogo–Python simulations, achieving consistent goal attainment and the fastest medians across 90 runs.
AI.motivation: Investigate how policy reasoning (LLMs) and local controllers (UCB, Double DQN) interact under decentralized, asynchronous updates; assess whether round-level LLM inference suffices for effective navigation and whether cross-LLM communication supports coordination.
AI.method: NetLogo–Python simulation; three robots with shared motion dynamics but different LLM backends; each robot comprises an LLM policy agent, a UCB bandit, and a policy-conditioned Double DQN controller; no central LLM; LLM inference at round-level; cross-LLM communication through a shared round summary; four configurations; 30 rounds per configuration; metrics: completion status, median time, P90; fixed simulation with 90 robot-round records.
AI.result: The complete configuration achieved goal in all 90 trials; median completion time 42 ticks; P90 73.2 ticks; median times 25.0–39.1% lower than other configurations; results are descriptive at configuration level.
AI.conclusion: Shows feasibility and potential benefits of combining LLM-based policy reasoning with traditional RL and bandit components in a decentralized multi-robot setting; round-level LLM updates reduce overhead while maintaining performance; cross-LLM communication and refinement steps contribute to improved efficiency; findings are descriptive; further studies needed for statistical generalization and exploration of parameter sensitivity.

title: From Answers to Interpretations: Rethinking Ambiguity-Induced Aleatoric Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs
summary: A key challenge in reliable LLM deployment is recognizing when uncertainty reflects irreducible variability in the task rather than limitations in the model's knowledge. In language tasks, a central source of such aleatoric uncertainty is input ambiguity or underspecification, where multiple interpretations remain plausible. Existing decomposition methods estimate aleatoric uncertainty by generating multiple clarifications of the input, querying the model for an answer under each clarification, and comparing the resulting answers. We argue that answers are not necessary for identifying ambiguity: they are often redundant, add avoidable cost, and can mislead through epistemic leakage. We support this claim theoretically, and propose a clarification-only approach that estimates this ambiguity-induced component directly from the space of plausible interpretations, without answers to the clarified inputs. Using ambiguity detection as an operational evaluation across three benchmarks, this direct approach improves AUROC (63.34 vs. 60.85), reduces computational cost by 4-26x in output tokens and 2.2-3.5x in API calls, and yields estimates with substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty. Overall, our results suggest that ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is better estimated from the interpretation space than from the response space.

AI.tldr: Clarification-only approach to estimate ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty in LLMs, avoiding answers. Improves ambiguity detection AUROC, reduces cost, lowers epistemic leakage compared to answer-based methods.
AI.motivation: In language tasks, irreducible uncertainty often comes from input underspecification. Existing methods generate clarifications and compare answers, but answers can be redundant, costly, and leak epistemic information about the model. A direct, clarification-space approach targets ambiguity without producing answers.
AI.method: Propose and evaluate a clarification-only pipeline that operates on the space of plausible interpretations rather than on clarified inputs and their answers. Ambiguity is estimated from interpretation space without producing model answers, serving as an operational measure of ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty.
AI.result: Ambiguity-detection AUROC improves (63.34 vs. 60.85) across three benchmarks. Computational cost drops substantially: 4–26× fewer output tokens and 2.2–3.5× fewer API calls. The estimates exhibit substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is more accurately and efficiently estimated from the space of interpretations than from the space of model outputs (answers).

title: LookThere! Sparse Vision by Reinforced Selection
summary: Vision transformers typically treat every image token as equally important, yet for most tasks in computer vision only a fraction are needed. Adaptive computation methods accelerate inference by choosing which tokens to process, but existing methods struggle at extreme sparsity and require heuristics that may not generalize like token diversity and attention scores. We address these limitations with LookThere, achieving a new pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs through an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains a shallow input selector and a deep representation extractor. The selector learns where to look and the extractor learns what to see, together saving computation by selecting only what is worth processing for a given task without relying on auxiliary signals. We show that LookThere only selects the task-specific input, excelling at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (traffic signs, billiards), and maintaining accuracy with as little as 0.2% of the input. It generalizes across tasks and models, including global recognition (ImageNet classification), local recognition (ADE20K segmentation), zero-shot classification (by distillation), and regression (counting). Across all settings, LookThere surpasses state-of-the-art selection to provide a general and scalable framework for specialized and efficient adaptive computation.

AI.tldr: LookThere uses end-to-end RL to jointly train a shallow input selector and a deep extractor, enabling adaptive token processing in Vision Transformers and achieving a strong perf/compute Pareto frontier across tasks, with accuracy surviving on as little as 0.2% of the input.
AI.motivation: To overcome equal-token processing in Vision Transformers and the limitations of heuristic adaptive methods, especially under extreme sparsity and across diverse tasks.
AI.method: An end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that learns where to look (selector) and what to see (extractor) jointly, without relying on auxiliary signals, selecting only task-relevant input.
AI.result: Achieves a new Pareto frontier in performance-compute trade-offs; excels at sparse recognition in high-resolution settings (e.g., traffic signs, billiards); maintains accuracy with as little as 0.2% of the input; generalizes across tasks (ImageNet classification, ADE20K segmentation, zero-shot classification via distillation, and counting). It outperforms previous selection methods.
AI.conclusion: Provides a general, scalable framework for adaptive computation in vision transformers that is effective across specialized tasks and model types, reducing computation while maintaining or improving accuracy.

title: Hakken: Predicting future discoveries to fill the gaps in today's knowledge
summary: We present Hakken, a domain-agnostic prediction and explanation system performing knowledge prediction, i.e., growing scientific knowledge by establishing novel relationships, ones that are not limited to the deductive hull of previous knowledge. Hakken uses a transformer-based prediction model built on temporal sequences of knowledge graphs extracted from vast bodies of research publications, fused with an LLM's semantic knowledge, to predict the presence and define the type of as-yet undocumented relationships between scientific concepts. It then calls a model-agnostic explanation framework to provide accompanying information for each prediction that allows scientists to evaluate the suggested new relationship. While general purpose, we demonstrate Hakken's practical capabilities by applying it to the biomedical domain. There, Hakken's prediction model establishes a new benchmark for time-aware multi-label relation prediction, and we show that the model's output stays coherent and informative over extended time spans in historic data. In addition, we scored 1.5 million above-confidence-threshold hypotheses related to aging, qualitatively validated batches of these predictions with biologists and progressed three of them for empirical validation in wet-lab. Two predictions with potentially significant impact in the context of drug discovery and repurposing were confirmed, introducing previously undocumented interactions between TP53 and BAMBI, and between RAF1 and TNF, to biomedical science.

AI.tldr: Hakken is a domain-agnostic prediction and explanation system that uses temporal knowledge graphs, a transformer-based predictor, and an LLM's semantic knowledge to forecast and classify undocumented relationships between scientific concepts; demonstrated in biomedicine with validated predictions, including two confirmed interactions relevant to drug discovery.
AI.motivation: To extend scientific knowledge beyond the deductive hull of existing data by predicting novel, temporally-aware relationships and providing explanations to enable scientist evaluation; address the need for effective, explainable knowledge discovery across domains, with a strong biomedical demonstration.
AI.method: Construct temporal sequences of knowledge graphs from large corpora of research publications; apply a transformer-based prediction model that merges structured temporal signals with semantic knowledge from an LLM; predict the presence and type of as-yet undocumented relationships; deploy a model-agnostic explanation framework to generate interpretable justifications for each prediction; evaluate time-aware multi-label relation prediction and perform qualitative and wet-lab validations in biomedicine.
AI.result: Achieves a new benchmark for time-aware multi-label relation prediction in biomedicine; outputs remain coherent and informative over long time spans; scored about 1.5 million high-confidence hypotheses related to aging; qualitative validation with biologists; three hypotheses advanced to wet-lab testing; two predictions confirmed: undocumented interactions TP53–BAMBI and RAF1–TNF.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of an explainable, domain-agnostic knowledge-discovery system capable of proposing credible, novel relationships with accompanying explanations; the approach shows practical impact for drug discovery and aging research and is generalizable to other domains.

title: LIBERO-RECOVER: Beyond Task Success Towards Failure Recovery in Robotic Manipulation Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) or World Action (WAM) models have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in robotic manipulation. On LIBERO, SOTA method have achieved nearly 100\% success rates, seemingly suggesting that the models are ready for deployment in real world. However, near perfect performance on existing benchmarks can be misleading: success under ideal conditions does not imply real world robustness. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate task completion from predefined initial states, while real world interactions inevitably involve failures such as failed grasps, collisions, and unintended object movements. A robot must therefore not only execute tasks successfully, but also recognize and recover from failures to continue the task. Yet this capability remains largely unmeasured, revealing a critical gap between benchmark performance and real world reliability. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Recover Benchmark, a large scale benchmark for failure recovery in robotic manipulation. Built upon LIBERO, we collect real execution failures from SOTA embodied models and construct 1,000+ scenarios across four recovery levels: (1) Action Retry, (2) Action Adaptation, (3) Object State Recovery, and (4) Environmental Recovery. We evaluate four core capabilities: spatial understanding, object structure reasoning, interaction understanding, and topological reasoning. As the first large-scale benchmark for embodied failure recovery, LIBERO-Recover shifts evaluation from \emph{Can the robot succeed?''} to \emph{Can the robot recover after failure?''}, promoting robust and generalizable embodied agents. The project will be avaible in \textcolor{blue}{https://liulin815.github.io/LIBERO-Recovery/}.

AI.tldr: Introduces LIBERO-Recover, a large-scale benchmark for failure recovery in robotic manipulation, extending LIBERO with 1,000+ scenarios across four recovery levels to evaluate recovery capabilities.
AI.motivation: Benchmark results on LIBERO show near-perfect task success but do not assess the robot's ability to recover from real-world failures; there is a gap between benchmark performance and reliability.
AI.method: Build upon LIBERO; collect real execution failures from state-of-the-art embodied models; create 1,000+ failure-recovery scenarios across four levels: Action Retry, Action Adaptation, Object State Recovery, Environmental Recovery; evaluate capabilities: spatial understanding, object structure reasoning, interaction understanding, topological reasoning.
AI.result: First large-scale benchmark focusing on embodied failure recovery; enables evaluating recovery performance rather than only task success; public release URL.
AI.conclusion: Shifts research emphasis towards robust, generalizable embodied agents capable of recovering from failures, addressing real-world reliability concerns.

title: IPGeoAI: Transformer-Based Geolocation with LLM Semantic Fusion
summary: Accurate city-level IP Geolocation is an important enabler for the modern digital ecosystem, underpinning services ranging from local content delivery and targeting to digital rights enforcement. However, traditional heuristic and database-driven methods often struggle to resolve the complex, non-linear allocation patterns of modern network infrastructures, particularly within the exploding IPv6 address space and transient mobile networks. In this paper, we introduce IPGeoAI, a novel deep learning model architecture that reframes geolocation from a static lookup problem to a sequential modeling task. Our approach utilizes the Transformer Encoder to capture hierarchical dependencies inherent in IP subnet structures. We propose a method to resolve geographic ambiguity by integrating unstructured semantic context via a Zero-Shot LLM Feature Extraction pipeline. We utilize Large Language Models to transform raw, noisy Autonomous Systems (AS) descriptions into structured, domain-specific metadata (such as 'University' vs. 'ISP' or 'Global' vs. 'Local') via an offline pre-computation process. By fusing these semantic signals into the network via a Multi-Head Cross-Attention module, we bridge the gap between numerical network topology and real-world semantic identity. Extensive offline evaluation on a proprietary dataset spanning 200,000 cities demonstrates that IPGeoAI significantly outperforms a leading external vendor in city-level granularity. By adopting a hierarchical inference strategy that refines coarse-grained country signals, our model achieves a 6% improvement in city-level accuracy while extending coverage to 100% of the traffic. Furthermore, in large-scale online production tests, the model drove a statistically significant +0.35% improvement in our 1st-tier downstream use cases metric.

AI.tldr: IPGeoAI reframes city-level IP geolocation as a sequential problem using Transformer Encoder with semantic signals from LLMs, delivering 6% accuracy gain and 100% coverage offline, plus a +0.35% online uplift in first-tier metrics.
AI.motivation: City-level geolocation is critical for services like content delivery and rights enforcement, but traditional heuristic and database methods struggle with complex, non-linear IP allocation patterns, IPv6 scale, and transient mobile networks; semantic context is needed to resolve geographic ambiguity.
AI.method: Use Transformer Encoder to model hierarchical IP subnet dependencies. Integrate unstructured semantic context via a Zero-Shot LLM Feature Extraction pipeline. Offline, use LLMs to convert raw AS descriptions into structured metadata (e.g., University vs ISP; Global vs Local). Fuse semantic signals with topology through a Multi-Head Cross-Attention module. Employ hierarchical inference to refine coarse country signals. Evaluate offline on a proprietary dataset spanning 200k cities; validate online in production.
AI.result: Offline evaluation on 200k-city dataset shows IPGeoAI outperforms a leading external vendor in city-level granularity, achieving a 6% improvement in city-level accuracy with 100% traffic coverage. In large-scale online production tests, the model yields a statistically significant +0.35% improvement in the first-tier downstream use cases metric.
AI.conclusion: IPGeoAI demonstrates that combining Transformer-based topology modeling with structured semantic features derived from LLMs can deliver accurate, fully covering city-level geolocation and tangible online performance gains, validating the viability of semantic-augmented geolocation.

title: AngelFingerprint: A Traceable, Explainable, and White-Box Stealthy Watermark for Text-Guided Image Editing
summary: Text-guided diffusion editing raises disinformation concerns, making reliable image provenance essential. While watermarks are commonly used for this purpose, most methods carry a fixed ID that cannot explain what was changed and which prompt produced it. Furthermore, under open-source white-box access, attackers can easily locate and remove watermarks added as separate modules. Targeting this setting, we propose AngelFingerprint, a novel watermarking framework ensuring edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness. It integrates a LoRA into the diffusion model to embed the editing prompt's CLIP text embedding directly into the model's weights. An extractor then recovers this embedding from the image pixels alone. This semantic payload explains the edit, while the weight-integrated design makes it hard to detect and isolate even under full white-box access. Two techniques make this possible: a velocity-alignment anchor that preserves edit quality, and a specially designed frequency filter that keeps the watermark imperceptible yet recoverable and robust. On the MagicBrush dataset, our extractor achieves $86\%$ top-1 accuracy in a 200-way prompt retrieval, versus $20\%$ for prompt inversion.

AI.tldr: A LoRA-based watermarking framework, AngelFingerprint, embeds the editing prompt's CLIP embedding into diffusion model weights to enable explainable, white-box stealthy edit provenance, recoverable from image pixels; achieves strong prompt-retrieval performance.
AI.motivation: Text-guided diffusion editing risks disinformation and weak provenance; fixed watermarks can't explain changes or prompts and can be removed under white-box access; need semantically meaningful, robust, hard-to-remove provenance.
AI.method: Embed the CLIP embedding via a LoRA into the diffusion model weights; use a pixel-recoverable extractor; introduce velocity-alignment anchor to preserve edit quality; employ a frequency filter to maintain imperceptibility and robustness.
AI.result: On MagicBrush, extractor achieves 86% top-1 accuracy in 200-way prompt retrieval vs 20% for prompt inversion.
AI.conclusion: AngelFingerprint provides edit traceability, explainability, and white-box stealthiness; semantic payload explains edits; challenging to detect and remove under white-box access; improves image provenance for diffusion-editing.

title: An Energy-Based Conservative-Dissipative Latent Neural Evolution Operator for Magnetization Dynamics
summary: We develop an energy-based reduced-order model for micromagnetic magnetization dynamics that couples a convolutional autoencoder to a structured latent neural ordinary differential equation. Motivated by the precessional-dissipative structure of the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, the latent vector field is generated from the gradient of a learned scalar potential through an antisymmetric operator and a symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator. This potential is learned in nonunique latent coordinates and is not identified with the Gibbs free energy, but decreases monotonically along autonomous continuous-time solutions, while the antisymmetric component permits motion along its level sets. The encoder, decoder, latent energy, and operators are trained jointly on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses alone, without time-derivative supervision, physical-energy labels, or dissipation penalties. At inference, an initial state is encoded once, evolved in latent space, and decoded only at the requested output times, enabling substantially cheaper trajectory prediction than the micromagnetic solver used to generate the training data. We compare quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic latent energies on two datasets parameterized by field amplitude and generated for the two applied-field directions of the NIST $μ$MAG Standard Problem 4. Dissipative-only and antisymmetric-dissipative models achieve comparable accuracy on short training-style windows but differ substantially on uninterrupted rollouts, for which the antisymmetric-dissipative models provide markedly more accurate trajectory predictions. The deep-quadratic energy gives the best overall accuracy for both field directions and exhibits slower error growth when rollouts are extended to twice the training horizon.

AI.tldr: An energy-based latent-ODE reduced-order model (ROM) for micromagnetic dynamics uses a convolutional autoencoder and a structured latent vector field driven by the gradient of a learned potential via antisymmetric and symmetric (dissipative) operators. Training on short windows yields cheap inference with accurate long-horizon predictions; among latent energies, deep-quadratic performs best, with antisymmetric-dissipative dynamics outperforming purely dissipative models on long rollouts.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational cost of micromagnetic simulations while preserving essential precessional-dissipative structure by learning a physically structured latent dynamical system that is trained without explicit time-derivative or energy labels.
AI.method: Encode micromagnetic states to a latent space with a convolutional autoencoder. Evolve the latent state via a neural ODE where the latent vector field is the gradient of a learned scalar potential acted on by an antisymmetric operator plus a symmetric positive-semidefinite dissipative operator. Learn the potential in latent coordinates (not tied to Gibbs energy). Train encoder, decoder, latent energy, and operators jointly on short trajectory windows using latent and decoded-rollout losses, without time-derivative supervision or energy labels. At inference, encode once, roll out in latent space, and decode at requested times. Compare quadratic, deep, and additive deep-quadratic latent energies on two NIST μMAG Standard Problem 4 datasets for two field directions.
AI.result: Dissipative-only and antisymmetric-dissipative models perform similarly on short windows but antisymmetric-dissipative models deliver substantially more accurate long-rollout trajectories. The deep-quadratic latent energy yields the best overall accuracy for both field directions and shows slower error growth when rollouts extend to twice the training horizon.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating an antisymmetric component in the latent dynamics better captures precessional motion along energy level sets, improving long-horizon predictions. The choice of latent energy form impacts long-term accuracy, with deep-quadratic energy offering the strongest performance among tested variants. The approach achieves substantial computational savings by separating inference-time rollout in latent space from decoding only at requested times.

title: Morphology and actuation as inductive biases in robotic hand manipulation
summary: Robotic hands vary widely in anatomical fidelity and mechanical complexity, and these structural choices influence the coordination of joint motions and the difficulty of controlling the system. A unified framework is presented in which the kinematic and actuation stages are analysed separately and in composition, through the conditioning of the task Jacobian, the actuation matrix, and their product. It is applied to two hands representing opposing design philosophies, the Shadow Dexterous Hand and the Anatomically Correct, Biomechatronic Hand, along four morphological aspects: joint axis geometry, actuator-to-DOF ratio, coupling architecture, and authority distribution. All parameters are derived from the hands' canonical digital representations. Anatomical fidelity carries no uniform advantage: oblique axes improve thumb conditioning but leave the long fingers worse conditioned than the orthogonal-axis design, while the branching tendon network improves the effective control mapping at every long finger and worsens it significantly at the thumb, where actuator authority is concentrated on thumb opposition. Predictions derived from these metrics are evaluated against reinforcement learning experiments using PPO, DDPG+HER, and TQC+HER, across three different tasks.

AI.tldr: A unified kinematic-actuation framework analyzes robotic hand design via task Jacobian conditioning and actuation mapping; anatomical fidelity shows nonuniform effects; RL experiments validate design-dependent conditioning across tasks.
AI.motivation: To quantify how morphology and actuation influence controllability of high-DOF hands using a digital-model-based metric, enabling principled design choices.
AI.method: Separate analysis of kinematics and actuation; analyze J (task Jacobian), A (actuation matrix), and J A; apply to Shadow Dexterous Hand and Anatomically Correct, Biomechatronic Hand; evaluate across joint axis geometry, actuator-to-DOF ratio, coupling architecture, and authority distribution; parameterize from canonical digital models; validate with RL (PPO, DDPG+HER, TQC+HER) on three tasks.
AI.result: Anatomical fidelity does not confer universal advantage: oblique axes improve thumb conditioning but harm long fingers; branching tendon network improves long-finger control but worsens thumb due to concentrated actuation on thumb opposition; metric predictions align with RL outcomes across tasks.
AI.conclusion: The framework reveals nonuniform, task-dependent conditioning across hand designs; anatomical fidelity alone is not a guaranteed performance boost; digital-geometry-based metrics plus RL validation offer a robust design-and-evaluate tool.

title: Reducing Hallucinated Transcripts in Whisper via Hallucination Space Projection
summary:
Whisper is a widely used foundation model for automatic speech recognition (ASR), but its generative decoder can produce fluent hallucinated transcripts for inputs containing little or no speech. We propose a training-free, inference-time method to reduce these hallucinations using low-rank projection of decoder activations. A compact hallucination-associated subspace is estimated from non-speech calibration data, and decoder hidden states are projected away from this subspace during inference.
  We evaluate two variants: always-on, which applies projection to all inputs, and gated, which applies it only when Whisper predicts that an input is likely non-speech. Across non-speech benchmarks, always-on projection reduces average hallucination rate (HR) from 31.31% to 2.44%, a 92.21% relative reduction, while gated projection reduces HR to 3.74%, an 88.05% relative reduction, with lower false rejection of genuine speech. On LibriSpeech, gated projection increases absolute word error rate (WER) by 0.33-4.39 percentage points and yields false-rejection rates (FRR) of 0.41--9.97% across model and split settings.
  These results show that low-rank activation projection can substantially suppress Whisper hallucinations without retraining, while providing a controllable trade-off between hallucination suppression and speech recognition performance.

AI.tldr: Training-free, inference-time low-rank projection suppresses Whisper hallucinations by projecting decoder activations away from a hallucination-associated subspace. Two variants—always-on and gated—achieve substantial hallucination reduction with measurable WER/FRR trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Whisper's generative decoder can produce fluent hallucinated transcripts for inputs with little or no speech. Retraining is costly; a lightweight, inference-time method is needed to mitigate hallucinations.
AI.method: Estimate a compact hallucination-associated subspace from non-speech calibration data. Apply a low-rank projection to decoder hidden states to steer activations away from this subspace during inference. Two variants: (1) always-on — project for all inputs; (2) gated — apply projection only when Whisper estimates non-speech with high likelihood.
AI.result: On non-speech benchmarks, always-on projection reduces hallucination rate (HR) from 31.31% to 2.44% (92.21% relative reduction). Gated projection reduces HR to 3.74% (88.05% relative reduction) with lower false rejection of genuine speech. On LibriSpeech, gated projection increases absolute WER by 0.33–4.39 percentage points and yields false-rejection rates (FRR) of 0.41–9.97% across model and split settings.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank activation projection can substantially suppress Whisper hallucinations without retraining, while providing a controllable trade-off between hallucination suppression and speech recognition performance.

title: Counting Beyond Instances: A Benchmark for Group-Individual Object Counting
summary: Visual counting is commonly formulated at the instance level, aiming to estimate how many objects of a queried category appear in an image. However, real-world counting often involves higher-level semantic units formed by multiple instances, such as a bunch of grapes, a stack of plates, or a pair of shoes. This exposes a key limitation of existing counting formulations, which mainly focus on what to count, while largely overlooking at which semantic unit to count. We introduce Group-Individual Object Counting (GIC), a new setting that requires models to count both individual objects and semantic groups within a unified framework. To support this new task, we present BunchCount, a real-world benchmark with 1,330 images, 89,254 individual annotations, and 11,065 group annotations. BunchCount provides paired individual-group annotations within the same image and explicitly records containment relations between each group and its constituent individuals. Experiments on BunchCount show that current advanced counting models perform well on individual instances but fail to count semantic groups more accurately. To mitigate semantic granularity conflict, we propose a counting-unit guided relational counting framework, which exploits group-individual containment relations to regularize cross-granularity representations during training. Our method substantially improves group-level counting while better preserving individual-level counting ability, establishing a strong baseline for counting beyond instances.

AI.tldr: Introduces Group-Individual Object Counting (GIC) and the BunchCount benchmark; proposes a counting-unit guided relational counting framework; demonstrates improved group-level counting with preserved instance-level accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing instance-level counting neglects semantic units (groups) and faces cross-granularity conflicts; a unified framework is needed to count both individuals and semantic groups, supported by a real-world dataset.
AI.method: Proposes a counting-unit guided relational counting framework that utilizes group–individual containment relations to regularize cross-granularity representations during training.
AI.result: BunchCount dataset with 1,330 images, 89,254 individual annotations, 11,065 group annotations; experiments show state-of-the-art models count individuals well but struggle on groups; the proposed method substantially improves group-level counting while preserving individual counting.
AI.conclusion: Validates counting beyond instances; demonstrates a practical approach to joint counting across granularities; introduces a strong baseline for unified counting tasks and establishes a dataset and framework to study semantic-unit counting.

title: Distilled Continuous Diffusion Language Models Can Write Code in Few Steps---or One
summary: Language generation is almost universally treated as a sequential process: autoregressive models emit one token at a time, while diffusion language models replace token-level seriality with a long trajectory of iterative refinement. In this work, we introduce PlaidQ, a 0.7B continuous diffusion language model for code generation, and show that its trajectory can be aggressively distilled into only a few denoising steps---or even one, enabling efficient code generation. PlaidQ repurposes a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser over continuous token embeddings. We distill PlaidQ with distribution matching for few-step generation and paired-trajectory supervision for one-step generation. At matched model scale, PlaidQ is competitive with discrete diffusion language models on code generation. Distillation then shifts the quality--compute frontier: a 16-step student reaches 31.78 and 40.49 pass@10 on HumanEval and MBPP+, surpassing the same PlaidQ teacher sampled for 512 steps. At the extreme, paired-trajectory distillation achieves 7.07 pass@1 on HumanEval with a single denoising step, producing functionally correct programs. Together, these results establish continuous diffusion as a viable path to few-step and one-step code generation. Broadly, continuous diffusion is not merely another representation for language: it provides an interface through which language models can inherit the acceleration and distillation machinery of continuous diffusion modeling. Training and inference code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/pengzhangzhi/plaidq.

AI.tldr: PlaidQ: a 0.7B continuous diffusion model for code generation that can be distilled to few or even one denoising step, enabling efficient generation. It repurposes a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser over continuous token embeddings and uses distribution matching and paired-trajectory supervision for distillation. At scale, it rivals discrete diffusion models on code tasks, with notable performance gains when distilled to 16 steps (and especially to 1 step).
AI.motivation: Address the bottlenecks of token-by-token autoregression and long diffusion trajectories by exploring continuous diffusion as a viable, efficient alternative for code generation, leveraging distillation to achieve few-/one-step generation.
AI.method: Repurpose a pretrained autoregressive model as a bidirectional denoiser on continuous token embeddings. Train PlaidQ as a 0.7B continuous diffusion model. Distill via (1) distribution matching to enable few-step generation and (2) paired-trajectory supervision for one-step generation. Compare against a discrete diffusion teacher at 512 steps and evaluate on HumanEval and MBPP+.
AI.result: A 16-step student reaches 31.78 pass@10 on HumanEval and 40.49 pass@10 on MBPP+, surpassing the teacher's 512-step samples. A single denoising step via paired-trajectory distillation yields 7.07 pass@1 on HumanEval, indicating functionally correct programs can be produced in one step. Overall, continuous diffusion at matched scale is competitive with discrete diffusion models for code generation, with distillation expanding the efficiency frontier.
AI.conclusion: Continuous diffusion is a viable path to few-/one-step code generation, enabling speedups through distillation while preserving generation quality. The work also demonstrates how continuous diffusion can inherit acceleration and distillation benefits from the diffusion literature; code and checkpoints are released.

title: One Word, Different Action: A Real-Robot Benchmark for Language-Conditioned Embodied Reasoning
summary: Natural-language instruction changes can directly alter robot behavior. A reliable embodied system should preserve its action when the task is unchanged and update it correctly when the task itself changes. We introduce One Word, Different Action, a real-robot benchmark built on physical decision states and executable actions, using task-preserving and task-changing instruction pairs to jointly evaluate Decision Invariance and Decision Sensitivity, with further evaluation under multi-constraint reasoning and real-RGB grounding. Experiments show that modern models are near saturation on single-constraint instruction changes, yet several models degrade noticeably when multiple task constraints must be integrated into one executable decision. These results suggest that the more salient remaining challenge is no longer recognizing an isolated instruction change, but reliably composing multiple task requirements into a correct robot action decision.

AI.tldr: A real-robot benchmark, One Word, Different Action, evaluates how robots handle instruction changes by measuring decision invariance (preserving action when task unchanged) and decision sensitivity (changing action when task changes), including multi-constraint reasoning and real-RGB grounding; results show models excel on single changes but struggle with integrating multiple constraints, shifting the challenge to reliable multi-constraint composition into a correct action.
AI.motivation: Ensure robust robotic decision-making under natural-language instruction changes, addressing both preserving actions for unchanged tasks and correctly adapting when tasks change, and extending evaluation to multi-constraint and perceptual grounding scenarios.
AI.method: Introduce a real-robot benchmark built on physical decision states and executable actions; use task-preserving and task-changing instruction pairs to jointly evaluate Decision Invariance and Decision Sensitivity; extend evaluation to multi-constraint reasoning and real-RGB grounding.
AI.result: Modern models are near saturation on single-constraint instruction changes, but degrade noticeably when multiple task constraints must be integrated into one executable decision.
AI.conclusion: The main remaining challenge is not recognizing isolated instruction changes but reliably composing multiple task requirements into a correct robot action decision.

title: La Agente Óptima: Towards Agentic Self-Driving Laboratories
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) combine automated experimentation with adaptive decision-making to accelerate scientific discovery. Their operation nevertheless often depends on human specialists who translate scientific objectives into executable closed-loop campaigns. Specialists adjust them as data and operating conditions change. Here, we present La Agente Óptima, an agentic framework that constructs and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns across computational and experimental systems while maintaining a persistent optimization state. By separating large language model (LLM) reasoning from executed campaigns, Óptima runs repetitive optimization loops consistently, returns control to the agent only when progress requires interpretation or campaign revision, and keeps every decision auditable. We evaluate Óptima across ablation studies, five digital discovery tasks, and two physical platforms. Throughout, Óptima maintained executable campaigns as both the scientific problem and execution environment evolved. In a closed-loop contact angle optimization campaign, Óptima identified and corrected a mid-run measurement failure, bringing the contact angle from 71.4 to 67.8 degrees, just above the 64-66 degree range. From this result, Óptima correctly inferred that the target was likely unattainable with the available reagents and recommended changing the formulation. In a five-day multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign, Óptima increased the yield from 30% to 59% over 23 experiments. Despite substantial inference costs, it cost less and used substantially less starting material than a human-directed campaign, while selecting a more mass-efficient operating point. These results show that LLM-based agents can make rigorous, long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists without specialist setup, expanding the scope of SDLs.

AI.tldr: LLM-driven agentic framework (La Agente Óptima) for Bayesian optimization in self-driving laboratories; separates LLM reasoning from campaign execution to maintain persistent optimization state; demonstrates robustness and efficiency gains across digital and physical campaigns, including error correction and improved yields with reduced resources; suggests wider accessibility of SDLs to domain scientists.
AI.motivation: Overcome reliance on human specialists for translating objectives into executable optimization campaigns; ensure persistent state, auditability, and adaptability as problems and conditions evolve;.
AI.method: Builds an agentic framework that delegates campaign execution to Bayesian optimization loops while LLM handles high-level reasoning; maintains a persistent optimization state; separates reasoning from execution to allow repetitive optimization with minimal LLM calls; evaluates via ablations, five digital discovery tasks, two physical platforms; includes a mid-campaign fault handling and a multi-objective flow-chemistry campaign.
AI.result: Maintains executable campaigns despite evolving problems; corrected a mid-run measurement failure shifting contact angle from 71.4 to 67.8 degrees (near the target); inferred unachievability with current reagents and suggested reformulation; in a 5-day flow-chemistry campaign, yield rose from 30% to 59% over 23 experiments; reduced cost and starting material relative to human-directed campaigns; identified a mass-efficient operating point.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agents can render long-running optimization campaigns accessible to domain scientists, enabling SDLs to operate beyond specialist-driven setups; the approach provides auditable, reusable optimization states and can adapt as problems evolve; potential to broaden adoption of SDLs.

title: HiSfM: Disambiguating Structure-from-Motion via Scaffold-Anchored Hierarchical Reconstruction
summary: Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a fundamental tool for sparse 3D reconstruction with broad impact in robotics and vision, supporting mapping, localization, and large-scale scene modeling. However, conventional pipelines often fail under hard visual ambiguity caused by repeated or symmetric structures, and incur heavy computational cost due to redundant cameras and constraints. We present HiSfM, a hierarchical coarse-to-fine SfM framework that improves robustness and efficiency through scaffold construction. HiSfM first forms strong local communities using geometrical induced heuristics, then connects communities with a compact yet strong skeleton by packing edge-disjoint spanning trees (EDST) while verifying skeletal edges with a two-view disambiguator. We reconstruct a stable scaffold on this verified skeleton, serving as an anchor to capture the essence of the scene, and subsequently absorb remaining images via efficient registration and triangulation for further refinements. Experiments on ambiguity-focused benchmarks and general datasets show that HiSfM prevents ambiguity-induced failures while substantially reducing runtime compared to previous methods, and improves completeness over aggressive sparsification methods. Code is available at https://github.com/3dv-casia/HiSfM.

AI.tldr: HiSfM introduces a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine SfM framework that builds a robust scaffold for 3D reconstruction by forming strong local communities, connecting them with an edge-disjoint spanning-tree skeleton verified by a two-view disambiguator, and progressively absorbing remaining images to refine the scene with efficient registration and triangulation.
AI.motivation: Conventional SfM pipelines struggle under visual ambiguity from repeated or symmetric structures and incur high computational costs due to redundant cameras and constraints; there is a need for robustness and efficiency in large-scale 3D reconstruction.
AI.method: 1) Form strong local communities using geometrical heuristics; 2) Connect communities with a compact, strong skeleton via packing edge-disjoint spanning trees (EDST) and verify skeletal edges with a two-view disambiguator; 3) Reconstruct a stable scaffold on the verified skeleton to capture the scene essence; 4) Absorb remaining images through efficient registration and triangulation for refinement.
AI.result: On ambiguity-focused benchmarks and general datasets, HiSfM prevents ambiguity-induced failures while substantially reducing runtime compared to previous methods, and improves completeness over aggressive sparsification methods.
AI.conclusion: HiSfM provides a robust and efficient hierarchical SfM framework by constructing and leveraging a scaffold skeleton to anchor reconstruction and enable efficient integration of additional views; code is publicly available.

title: Mitra-v2 Technical Report
comment: 38 pages. Model weights, inference and fine-tuning code, and evaluation results: https://huggingface.co/autogluon/mitra-finetune
summary: We introduce Mitra-v2, a tabular foundation model that delivers state-of-the-art performance on real-world classification and regression problems, from credit-risk scoring and clinical prediction to equipment-failure detection and house-price estimation. Mitra-v2 is trained only on synthetic data, with a pretraining distribution that is much larger and more diverse than Mitra-v1's. Built on a small 2D Transformer backbone, Mitra-v2 supports longer contexts and larger feature spaces. Improved optimization lets it learn from this larger task distribution. We evaluate Mitra-v2 on the TabArena and TALENT benchmarks, comprising more than 300 real-world datasets under two evaluation protocols. On the full TabArena benchmark, Mitra-v2 delivers state-of-the-art performance at the level of the industry-scale TabFM and EXAONE Tabular models, while surpassing TabPFN-3 by a wide margin in both classification and regression. Mitra-v2 matches the 1.6B-parameter TabFM with only 5% of its size (77M parameters), delivering frontier performance at a fraction of the cost. On TALENT, Mitra-v2 remains among the leading models, clearly outperforming TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2. It also ranks first on classification tasks with more than ten classes, even though it was pretrained only on tasks with at most ten classes. These results make Mitra-v2 one of the strongest and most broadly applicable open tabular foundation models released to date. We release the model weights, the inference and fine-tuning code, and our evaluation results under the Apache-2.0 license.

AI.tldr: Mitra-v2 is a synthetic-data–trained tabular foundation model achieving state-of-the-art results on real-world benchmarks (TabArena and TALENT) with high parameter efficiency, and is released openly under Apache-2.0.
AI.motivation: To advance tabular foundation learning by leveraging diverse synthetic pretraining data to improve performance and reduce reliance on labeled real data, enabling scalable, cost-efficient models that generalize across many tabular tasks.
AI.method: A small 2D Transformer backbone is trained on a synthetic data distribution that is larger and more diverse than prior work (Mitra-v1). The model handles longer contexts and larger feature spaces, with improved optimization to learn from the expanded task distribution. Evaluation is performed on TabArena and TALENT benchmarks with two protocols.
AI.result: On TabArena, Mitra-v2 achieves state-of-the-art performance comparable to industry-scale TabFM and EXAONE, and surpasses TabPFN-3 in both classification and regression. It matches TabFM at 1.6B parameters with only 77M parameters. On TALENT, Mitra-v2 remains among the top models, clearly beating TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2, and ranks first on multi-class classification tasks (>10 classes) despite pretraining on tasks with at most ten classes.
AI.conclusion: Mitra-v2 emerges as one of the strongest and most broadly applicable open tabular foundation models to date, combining strong real-world performance with notable parameter efficiency and open accessibility (weights, code, evaluation results under Apache-2.0).

title: TacPAC: Tactile Prediction and Real-Time Action Correction in World-Action Models for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: World-action models guide action generation with predicted future observations, but vision-centric predictions miss the local contact cues that decide contact-rich manipulation. However, naively predicting future tactile observations as additional views recovers only a third of the achievable gain in our experiments. This gap reflects a timing mismatch: predictions precede execution, while tactile feedback arrives during it. We introduce TacPAC, which turns tactile prediction into real-time action correction. Once the base model has planned an action chunk, TacPAC caches the predicted contact that plan was conditioned on together with the plan's own representation, and a tactile expert reads each newly observed tactile image against that cache to correct the actions not yet executed. Feedback is thus interpreted against what the plan anticipated rather than in isolation, and one correction is a single pass over that cache, $20.7\times$ cheaper than regenerating the chunk. On five real-robot tasks spanning precision insertion, fragile-object handling, object reorientation, and long-horizon manipulation, TacPAC leads every task and raises the average from 22% for its vision-only base model to 64%. Code is available at https://github.com/LogosRoboticsGroup/TacPAC.

AI.tldr: TacPAC integrates real-time tactile correction into a vision-based action planner. By caching the plan-conditioned tactile prediction and using a tactile expert to compare new tactile observations against that cache, it yields corrective actions without re-planning, addressing timing gaps between prediction and tactile feedback. It improves average task success from 22% to 64% across five real-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Vision-centric world-action models miss local contact cues essential for contact-rich manipulation. Predicting tactile observations alone yields limited gains due to a timing mismatch between planned actions and tactile feedback during execution.
AI.method: After the base model plans an action chunk, TacPAC caches the plan-conditioned predicted tactile observation and the plan representation. A tactile expert then reads each newly observed tactile image against the cache to correct upcoming actions. This yields a single-pass correction over the cache and is 20.7x cheaper than regenerating the chunk.
AI.result: Evaluated on five real-robot tasks—precision insertion, fragile-object handling, object reorientation, and long-horizon manipulation—TacPAC achieves state-wide improvement, raising success from 22% (vision-only) to 64% on average and succeeding in all tasks.
AI.conclusion: TacPAC effectively aligns tactile feedback with planned cognition, enabling real-time corrections that significantly boost performance while reducing computation compared to full re-planning. The approach demonstrates strong practical gains in contact-rich manipulation and is accompanied by publicly available code.

title: Extremely Sparse Supervision Incentivizes Reasoning Ability
summary: Large language models demonstrate increasingly strong reasoning capabilities through effective post-training. Yet, prevailing post-training methods optimize over massive numbers of tokens, implicitly assuming that effective learning must be token-intensive. We revisit this assumption in the on-policy distillation (OPD) setting, which naturally admits dense teacher supervision at every generated token. Using the Qwen3 family, we discover a counter-intuitive phenomenon: reasoning can be effectively incentivized by an extremely small fraction of generated tokens--as few as one or two tokens per reasoning trajectory, corresponding to only 0.05% of all tokens. Surprisingly, this sparse supervision in most cases matches or surpasses full-token training in improving reasoning ability, despite excluding the vast majority of generated tokens from the training objective. This phenomenon is consistently observed across nine teacher--student configurations spanning different model scales on mathematical reasoning tasks, and is further validated on coding reasoning, Llama models and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR). Interestingly, such extremely sparse supervision may be closer to the natural learning process: rather than correcting every step word by word, one reflects on a few critical reasoning steps, updates prior understanding, and continues the trial-and-error, avoiding micro-level corrections while remaining remarkably effective. Overall, our results challenge the assumption that effective post-training must be token-intensive and point to a new direction for understanding and designing more efficient post-training algorithms.

AI.tldr: Sparse on-policy distillation (OPD) with extremely few tokens (as low as 1–2 tokens per reasoning trajectory, ~0.05% of total) can match or surpass full-token post-training in improving reasoning across multiple LLMs and tasks; challenges the token-intensive assumption of post-training.
AI.motivation: Question the prevailing belief that effective post-training requires token-intensive supervision; explore whether dense teacher guidance per token is necessary by evaluating OPD with very sparse supervision.
AI.method: Empirical study across Qwen3 family models with nine teacher–student configurations; tasks include mathematical reasoning and coding reasoning; validation on Llama models and PPO-based RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
AI.result: Extremely sparse supervision yields reasoning improvements comparable to or better than dense, full-token training in most configurations; as few as 1–2 tokens per reasoning trajectory can suffice for many settings; observed consistently across model scales and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Token-efficient post-training is plausible; high-density token supervision may be unnecessary for acquiring reasoning abilities; results motivate designing more efficient post-training algorithms and further investigation into why sparse signals are effective.

title: Bridging Modalities and Tasks: A Unified Hierarchical ViT for SAR-to-Optical Translation and Semantic Segmentation
summary: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images have all-weather, day-and-night observation capabilities. However, compared with optical images, their speckle noise and non-intuitive scattering mechanism limit the interpretability of the images. Generative models for SAR-to-optical (S2O) conversion can improve visual interpretability, but existing methods often ignore the constraints on semantic structure, which are necessary for downstream tasks, for the sake of visual effects. We propose a unified collaborative dual-task learning framework, termed BMT (Bridging Modalities and Tasks), that jointly optimizes S2O image translation and semantic segmentation through a shared hierarchical Vision Transformer. The framework integrates: (1) a LocalViTBlock that fuses global self-attention with spatial depthwise convolution through a learnable gating mechanism; (2) an enhanced output module combining multi-scale refinement processing, color correction and anti-aliasing, which calibrates channel-level color statistics through feature fusion; (3) a ControlNet-style conditional injection mechanism that encodes SAR wavelet features and segmentation labels into a multi-scale feature pyramid and injects them at each encoder layer through zero-initialized convolution; (4) a bounded Kendall uncertainty weighting scheme that prevents either task from dominating the shared representation. We evaluate the framework under both paired and unpaired translation settings, on the public WHU-OPT-SAR paired dataset and a self-constructed unpaired ship dataset built from HRSID and DIOR, respectively. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves competitive S2O translation quality and semantic segmentation performance. The dataset and source code have been publicly released at https://github.com/Lewisyuaner/BMT-S2O-main.

AI.tldr: A unified BMT framework for joint SAR-to-optical translation and semantic segmentation using a shared Vision Transformer, with LocalViTBlock, multi-scale refinement, ControlNet-style conditioning on SAR features and labels, and Kendall-based uncertainty weighting; achieves competitive results on paired/unpaired data and releases code.
AI.motivation: SAR imagery offers all-weather, day–night observation but suffers from speckle and non-intuitive scattering, limiting interpretability. Integrating semantic constraints via joint S2O translation and segmentation can improve both translation quality and downstream task performance.
AI.method: A unified dual-task architecture (BMT) built on a hierarchical Vision Transformer. Key components: (1) LocalViTBlock fusing global self-attention with spatial depthwise conv through learnable gating; (2) enhanced output module with multi-scale refinement, color correction, and anti-aliasing to calibrate channel-wise color statistics; (3) ControlNet-style conditional injection that encodes SAR wavelet features and segmentation labels into a multi-scale feature pyramid, injected at each encoder layer via zero-initialized conv; (4) bounded Kendall uncertainty weighting to balance task losses. Training under paired (WHU-OPT-SAR) and unpaired (ships from HRSID and DIOR) settings. Code and data released at the provided link.
AI.result: The approach yields competitive S2O translation quality and semantic segmentation performance in both paired and unpaired settings, demonstrating that semantic constraints can be effectively integrated into cross-modal translation. Public dataset and source code have been released.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing translation and segmentation within a shared, conditioned Vision Transformer with uncertainty balancing and modular conditioning yields robust, semantically coherent S2O results. The framework effectively leverages multi-scale features and marginalizes task dominance, with demonstrated applicability to paired and unpaired data.

title: Fast Surrogate Modeling of Excitable and Oscillatory FitzHugh-Nagumo Dynamics with Parametric Neural Operators
comment: Human Brain & AI @ International Joint Conferences on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) 2026
summary: The FitzHugh-Nagumo (FHN) system serves as a simplified model of neuronal voltage dynamics, capturing the activator-inhibitor structure behind both isolated action potentials and the rhythmic spiking seen across the brain. Exploring its 5D physiological parameter space is important for neuromodulation and mapping voltage recordings back to biophysics, yet classical finite-difference solvers make rapid parameter sweeps expensive. We train parameter-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) as fast, differentiable surrogates for the FHN voltage and recovery fields on a one-dimensional spatial domain, conditioning each Fourier layer on the parameter vector $λ= (D_u, D_v, a, b, τ)$ via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). We apply a single bifurcation analysis that delimits the two distinct regimes the model spans, oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (action-potential propagation), and we train one operator in each. In the oscillatory regime the surrogate attains sub-$0.1\%$ relative $L^2$ error on both fields, runs nearly three orders of magnitude faster than the finite-difference baseline, generalizes uniformly across the parameter space, and extrapolates to low single-digit percentage errors outside of the training bounds. In the excitable regime the same operator accurately reproduces the firing threshold and the $c \propto \sqrt{D_u}$ conduction-velocity law and replicates full traveling pulses, fully capturing the excitable bifurcation structure rather than just smoothly interpolating fields.

AI.tldr: Parameter-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators trained separately for oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (action-potential propagation) regimes of the FitzHugh–Nagumo system serve as fast, differentiable surrogates across a 5D parameter space, accurately reproducing fields, bifurcation structure, and traveling pulses with substantial speedups and good extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Reduce computational cost of parameter sweeps and enable neuromodulation applications by providing fast, differentiable surrogates that map 5D biophysical parameters to voltage and recovery fields, while preserving bifurcation structure and dynamics.
AI.method: Train two FiLM-conditioned Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) on 1D spatial domain for FHN voltage and recovery fields, conditioning on λ=(D_u, D_v, a, b, τ). Use FiLM to integrate parameters into each Fourier layer. Separate operators for oscillatory (tonic firing) and excitable (propagation) regimes, identified via a single bifurcation analysis. Evaluate on accuracy, speed, generalization across parameter space, and extrapolation to out-of-distribution values; verify dynamical features (firing threshold, c ∝ sqrt(D_u), traveling pulses).
AI.result: Oscillatory regime: relative L2 error < 0.1% on both fields; ~1000x faster than finite-difference baseline; uniform generalization across parameter space; extrapolates to low single-digit percentage errors outside training bounds. Excitable regime: accurately reproduces firing threshold and the c ∝ sqrt(D_u) conduction-velocity law; replicates full traveling pulses; captures the excitable bifurcation structure rather than mere field interpolation.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-conditioned FNO surrogates provide accurate, fast, and bifurcation-faithful representations of the FitzHugh–Nagumo system over a 5D parameter space, enabling efficient neuromodulation studies and robust inversion from recordings, with strong generalization and extrapolation capabilities.

title: Temporal Tactile Encoding and Compliance for Intent-Aware Robot-to-Human Bimanual Handover
summary: Reliable robot-to-human handover requires the robot to infer when the person is ready to receive the object, and release it safely, comfortably, and at the right time. This is challenging because visual observations alone may not disambiguate clear taking intent from accidental contact, weak grasping, wrong-direction forces, or transient interactions. In this work we treat human-robot handover as an intrinsically multimodal problem. Our approach couples a VLA model with a compliance controller that reduces interaction forces during object transfer. We finetune the VLA model with human demonstrations using RGB observation, temporally encoded tactile feedback and proprioception. We evaluate the complete system in a human-subject study against two baselines: one without tactile feedback and one using tactile feedback without compliance control. We hypothesize that combining compliance and temporal tactile encoding yields the most reliable and comfortable handovers, as compliance facilitates physical interaction while tactile history captures sustained taking intent. Performance is measured through objective metrics and an ad-hoc questionnaire. The results show that the two components provide complementary benefits and substantially outperform the baselines. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: A multimodal robot-to-human handover approach that couples a VLA model with a compliance controller and temporally encoded tactile feedback, finetuned from human demonstrations; it outperforms baselines and shows complementary benefits of compliance and tactile history.
AI.motivation: Visual observations alone may not disambiguate taking intent from accidental contact, weak grasping, wrong-direction forces, or transient interactions; reliable handover requires multimodal sensing (vision, tactile, proprioception) and safe, comfortable execution.
AI.method: Integrate a VLA model with a compliance controller. Finetune the VLA using RGB observations, temporally encoded tactile feedback, and proprioception from human demonstrations. Evaluate via a human-subject study against two baselines: no tactile feedback and tactile feedback without compliance.
AI.result: The combination of compliance and temporal tactile encoding yields the most reliable and comfortable handovers; the two components provide complementary benefits and substantially outperform the baselines; results supported by objective metrics and subjective questionnaire; code and data to be released upon acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal integration of vision, tactile history, and proprioception with compliant control improves handover reliability and comfort, indicating synergy between physical interaction and sustained taking intent signals.

title: Does the Selected Object Reach the Reader? Auditing Identity Handoffs in Grounded Language-Model Pipelines
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 23 tables. Accepted to the GroundLM Workshop (Grounding Language Models: Learning Faithfully and Efficiently) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Grounded language-model pipelines can be divided into three stages: selecting an object, retrieving passages for it, and using that evidence to answer. If the selected object must reach the reader, losing it breaks the handoff. Benchmark recall checks the dataset-linked object, which can differ. We audit 600 HybridQA questions across three selector families. On 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matches the dataset-traced passage, exact key lookup and exact title matching return the object every time. With every ranked rule given the same decoded selected title, body-only BM25 omits it on 389 records (26.6%) at cutoff five, while hybrid retrieval with reranking omits it on 14 (1.0%). The two identities differ on 329 of 1,792 resolvable records. With original-question rankings, their top-five checks disagree on 106 records (5.9%). Frozen reader comparisons associate the aligned object's presence with 28.6 to 31.0 points higher exact match. In a deliberately selected 64-item cohort, removing that passage sharply lowers exact match, while removing a similar-length comparison passage does not reproduce the drop. We release the Returned-Object Profile (ROP), an executable record of the target, returned-ID field, cutoff, membership rule, and complete expected population, with data and an offline replay.

AI.tldr: Dataset-linked objects can diverge from the selected object in grounded language-model pipelines, causing handoff failures. An empirical audit shows nontrivial recall gaps across selector methods, with object-alignment boosting exact-match scores; a reproducible evaluation artifact (ROP) is released for offline replay.
AI.motivation: To evaluate how reliably the selected object is retained across selector methods and how that object influences end-to-end accuracy in grounded LMs, highlighting object-level recall as a bottleneck in three-stage pipelines.
AI.method: Audit 600 HybridQA questions across three selector families. Analyze 1,463 resolvable records where the selected object matches the dataset-traced passage. Compare exact key lookup and exact title matching. Evaluate body-only BM25 vs hybrid retrieval with reranking. Assess agreement with original-question rankings. Use frozen-reader comparisons to relate object presence to exact-match. Create a deliberately selected 64-item cohort to test removal effects. Release Returned-Object Profile (ROP) with executable records for offline replay.
AI.result: Exact-key lookup and exact-title matching return the object for all 1,463 resolvable records. Body-only BM25 omits the object on 389 of these records (26.6%) at cutoff five; hybrid retrieval with reranking omits it on 14 records (1.0%). The two identities differ on 329 of 1,792 resolvable records. With original-question rankings, top-five checks disagree on 106 records (5.9%). Frozen-reader analysis links the aligned object to a 28.6–31.0 point increase in exact-match scores. In a 64-item cohort, removing the target passage sharply reduces exact-match, whereas removing a similar-length comparator passage does not. The work releases the Returned-Object Profile (ROP) for reproducibility, including target, returned-ID, cutoff, rules, population, and an offline replay.
AI.conclusion: Object identity preservation across selector and evidence retrieval stages is crucial for end-to-end accuracy in grounded LMs. Standard retrieval baselines can fail to retrieve the correct object, underscoring the need for objective, reproducible evaluation of returned objects (ROP) to diagnose and mitigate handoff breaks.

title: Where to Look Matters: Learning Influential Views for VLM-based 3D Visual Grounding
summary: Recent zero-shot 3D visual grounding methods leverage vision-language models (VLMs) to localize objects in 3D scenes from natural language queries. However, these methods typically rely on heuristic rules to select which camera views are provided to the VLM, often prioritizing object visibility rather than grounding relevance. We present IVSGround, a framework that learns Influential View Selection for VLM-based 3D visual grounding. Instead of using fixed heuristics, a lightweight view selector is trained to identify views that provide discriminative evidence for grounding. To obtain supervision signals, we generate training signals using feedback from a reasoning VLM through a two-stage rejection sampling process. During inference, the learned selector predicts query-conditioned influential views for each candidate object, which are then evaluated by a frozen reasoning VLM through comparative grounding. Experiments on ScanRefer and NR3D show that IVSGround consistently improves grounding accuracy over existing zero-shot pipelines, demonstrating that selecting where to look is crucial for effective 3D visual grounding. Project page: https://ivsground.github.io/

AI.tldr: IVSGround learns to select influential camera views for zero-shot 3D grounding with VLMs, using a lightweight view selector trained via supervision from a reasoning VLM with two-stage rejection sampling; at inference, it chooses query-conditioned views for each candidate object and uses a frozen VLM for comparative grounding, achieving better grounding on ScanRefer and NR3D.
AI.motivation: Current zero-shot 3D grounding relies on fixed heuristics to pick camera views, which may emphasize visibility over discriminative relevance to the query. A learnable view selection mechanism can provide targeted evidence for grounding and improve accuracy.
AI.method: Train a lightweight view selector to identify discriminative views conditioned on the query. Generate supervision signals via a two-stage rejection sampling process using feedback from a reasoning VLM. During inference, the selector outputs influential views for each candidate object, which are evaluated by a frozen reasoning VLM through comparative grounding.
AI.result: IVSGround consistently improves grounding accuracy over existing zero-shot pipelines on ScanRefer and NR3D, demonstrating that selecting where to look is crucial for effective 3D visual grounding.
AI.conclusion: Selecting informative views is crucial for effective zero-shot 3D grounding; learning this selection end-to-end with supervision from a reasoning VLM yields tangible gains on standard benchmarks.

title: Training-Free Halving of Activated Experts in Fine-Grained Mixture-of-Experts Models
summary: Modern fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a small number of experts and renormalize their router probabilities. We show that this renormalization implicitly calibrates expert output gain to the training top-$k$: reducing $k$ at inference changes not only which experts are used but also the strength of the expert branch. We separate these effects by activating the top $k_1$ experts while normalizing by the probability mass of the top $k_2$ experts, introducing one integer with no parameters, training, or measurable compute overhead. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, reducing from 8 to 4 experts causes a 4.65-point MMLU drop under standard renormalization but only 0.35 points with $k_2=16$, while halving routed-expert compute. The result replicates on the $11\times$ larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, where reducing from 10 to 5 experts loses only 0.55 points with an appropriate reference set. Removing renormalization entirely is catastrophic, showing that preserving a suitable reference mass is crucial. We further find that perplexity and downstream accuracy favor different $k_2$, cautioning against selecting MoE compression settings using unlabeled text alone. Analyses also show that expert identity matters substantially more than expert weighting, while balanced and domain-specialized routing leaves limited room for expert pruning.

AI.tldr: Proposes a simple, parameter-free knob for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) pruning by decoupling top-k token routing from renormalization: activate k1 top experts but renormalize using only the top k2 mass. This preserves a reference mass while pruning, reducing performance loss and halving compute in experiments on large Qwen models; removing renormalization is catastrophic. Perplexity and downstream tasks prefer different k2; expert identity matters more than weighting; balanced/domain routing leaves little room for pruning.
AI.motivation: MoE routing commonly renormalizes expert probabilities, which implicitly scales expert outputs. Pruning experts changes both which experts are used and their effective gain due to renormalization. The paper seeks to decouple selection from scaling to better understand and control pruning effects, and to identify a practical, lossless compression knob.
AI.method: Introduce a simple, parameter-light mechanism: activate the top-k1 experts for routing while renormalizing only the probability mass of the top-k2 experts (k1 and k2 are integers, with no learned parameters or extra compute). Evaluate on large MoE models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B), comparing standard renormalization, the k2 mass-preserving normalization, and full removal of renormalization. Use MMLU, perplexity, and downstream accuracy as metrics, and analyze the role of expert identity vs weighting and the effect of routing balance/domain specialization.
AI.result: Reducing number of routed experts from 8 to 4 causes a 4.65-point MMLU drop with standard renormalization, but only 0.35-point drop when using k2=16, while also halving routed compute. The trend replicates on a 11x larger model (10 to 5 experts), with only 0.55-point loss given a suitable reference set. Removing renormalization entirely is catastrophic. Perplexity and downstream accuracy favor different k2 values. Expert identity matters substantially more than expert weighting; balanced and domain-specialized routing leaves limited room for pruning.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining a reference mass via mass-preserving renormalization is crucial for MoE pruning. The identity of experts drives performance more than their weights; there is limited benefit from aggressive pruning under balanced/domain routing. When compressing MoE models, choose k2 with task type in mind (perplexity vs downstream accuracy) and avoid relying on unlabeled text alone for setting MoE compression.

title: Human-Human & Human-Robot Interaction Transformer (H2INT) for Robot Navigation in Dense and Uncertain Crowds
summary: Safe robot navigation in dense crowds requires reasoning about pedestrian motion and how it may change in response to a robot. However, many learning-based approaches generate pedestrian motion independently of the robot or assume uniform reciprocity, omitting an important source of interaction uncertainty. This paper presents a Human-Human & Human-Robot Interaction Transformer (H2INT), a reinforcement learning framework that retains robot-conditioned changes in pedestrian motion during policy learning while allowing responsiveness to vary across pedestrians. Responsiveness affects the crowd dynamics when the robot is visible but is not supplied as a policy input; the policy must instead infer its consequences from robot-centered relative positions. A two-stage gated Transformer progressively encodes human-human and human-robot relations, while a recurrent policy captures their temporal evolution. A curriculum gradually reduces pedestrian responsiveness to increase interaction difficulty. Simulation experiments demonstrate improved navigation safety and robustness over representative baselines across response conditions and crowd densities, and show transfer without retraining to structurally distinct crowd-flow layouts. Ablations support the hierarchical relational encoding and gated updates. Real-robot deployment further verifies that the learned policy can operate with sparse observations in a physical environment.

AI.tldr: H2INT is a reinforcement learning framework that models human–human and human–robot interactions with a two-stage gated Transformer and a recurrent policy, enabling robot-conditioned changes in pedestrian motion, variable responsiveness, curriculum-driven difficulty, and transfer to new crowd layouts, with successful real-robot deployment.
AI.motivation: Safe navigation in dense crowds requires reasoning about how pedestrians adapt to the robot and to other pedestrians. Prior work often treats pedestrian motion independently or assumes uniform reciprocity, neglecting interaction uncertainty and cross-person variability. There is a need to capture structured H-H and H-R interactions and to learn policies robust to varying responsiveness.
AI.method: A two-stage gated Transformer encodes human–human and human–robot relations; a recurrent policy captures temporal evolution. Responsiveness to the robot affects crowd dynamics when the robot is visible but is not provided as a policy input; the policy must infer consequences from robot-centered relative positions. A curriculum progressively reduces pedestrian responsiveness to increase interaction difficulty. Evaluations include simulations across densities and response conditions, transfer to different crowd-flow layouts without retraining, ablations on the relational encoding/gated updates, and real-robot deployment with sparse observations.
