AI.result: The approach yields improved safety and robustness over baselines across varying response conditions and crowd densities, with successful transfer to structurally distinct crowd layouts without retraining. Ablations support the importance of hierarchical relational encoding and gated updates. Real-robot experiments demonstrate operability with sparse observations in physical environments.
AI.conclusion: Modeling interaction uncertainty and variable responsiveness via structured H-H and H-R relations enables safer, more robust crowd navigation. The method transfers across layouts and is viable in real robots, even with limited observations.

title: $τ^τ$-Bench: An Environment for End-To-End, Realistic Agent Construction
summary: LLM agents are rapidly becoming production software, deployed to handle customer service, adjudicate disputes, and operate internal systems. Notably, the work of building them is increasingly handed to coding agents, yet existing benchmarks say little about whether an AI system can deliver one under the conditions of a real client engagement. We introduce $τ^τ$-bench (pronounced hyper-tau-bench), a benchmark that makes agent construction the task. A developer agent is given the records a business actually keeps, a client who holds requirements, a production API that operations must run through, a codebase to inherit, and limits on serving cost and models: the same starting point a real engagement provides. From these it must deliver a complete customer-service agent, scored by deploying that agent against held-out simulated users. Across 53 tasks spanning four domains, the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code, passes just 23.9% of evaluation simulations. Meanwhile, an expert-authored reference ceiling scores 82.2%. The failures mirror ones human agent developers see: models issue shallow queries in place of deep comprehension of the records, communicate almost nothing to the client, and experiment too little with agent architecture and serving spend, shipping the first design that runs. We aim for $τ^τ$-bench to turn the work of cooperative agent building into a measurable target for coding agents.

AI.tldr: τ^τ-bench evaluates whether LLM-based developer agents can build production-ready customer-service agents under realistic client constraints; current top models perform far below human ceilings (≈24% vs 82% success).
AI.motivation: To transform cooperative agent-building into a measurable, production-relevant benchmark that reflects real client engagements (records, requirements, APIs, codebase, and cost constraints) and to quantify the capability gap of coding agents.
AI.method: Provide 53 tasks across four domains; supply a developer agent with actual business records, a client with requirements, a production API, a codebase to inherit, and serving-cost/model limits; require a complete customer-service agent; evaluate by deploying against held-out simulated users; compare the best configuration (Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code) to an expert-authored ceiling.
AI.result: Strongest configuration passes 23.9% of evaluation simulations; expert ceiling scores 82.2%. Failures mirror human issues: shallow queries, minimal client communication, insufficient exploration of agent architecture and spending, and rushing to a first runnable design.
AI.conclusion: τ^τ-bench aims to make cooperative agent-building a measurable target for coding agents, highlighting a substantial gap to production-ready deployment and guiding future improvements in reasoning over records, client-facing communication, architectural exploration, and cost-aware deployment.

title: SeamFlow: Structure-Aware Flow Matching on Edge Probabilities for Artist-Like UV Unwrapping
summary: 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping are fundamental problems in computer graphics. Traditional geometric optimization methods mainly focus on reducing parameterization distortion, but they often overlook visual semantic coherence in seam layouts. Recent autoregressive generative methods improve semantic coherence, yet limited perception of mesh topology often causes inaccurate local cuts. To address these limitations, we introduce SeamFlow, a novel generative framework for 3D surface cutting. We reformulate the discrete mesh-cutting problem as continuous flow matching in a high-dimensional edge-probability space. Through continuous relaxation, SeamFlow learns a deterministic mapping from a Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution. An evolution network couples local topological tokens with global shape priors and guides smooth probability flow through Ordinary Differential Equation solving. Compared with existing autoregressive generative frameworks, SeamFlow improves topology awareness through edge tokenization while eliminating both 3D spatial projection errors and artificial sequential-order bias. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SeamFlow achieves exceptional semantic coherence and remarkably low parameterization distortion. The project page is https://meshy-dev.github.io/seamflow.

AI.tldr: SeamFlow uses continuous normalizing flow for 3D mesh cutting/UV unwrapping, modeling seam probabilities in an edge-probability space via continuous relaxation; an evolution network and ODE-based flow enable topology-aware, distortion-minimized seams, outperforming autoregressive methods and avoiding projection biases.
AI.motivation: To address semantic coherence and topological awareness in seam layouts, overcoming limitations of existing parameterization methods and autoregressive approaches that mis-handle topology and introduce sequential bias.
AI.method: Reformulate discrete mesh-cutting as continuous flow matching in a high-dimensional edge-probability space. Learn a deterministic map from Gaussian prior to a target seam-probability distribution. Use an evolution network that couples local topological tokens with global shape priors to guide smooth probability flow via ODE solving. Employ edge tokenization to enhance topology awareness and eliminate 3D projection errors and order bias.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show high semantic coherence and low parameterization distortion, with a project page provided for further details.
AI.conclusion: SeamFlow delivers topology-aware, distortion-minimizing seam generation for 3D surface cutting and UV unwrapping, surpassing autoregressive methods and mitigating projection and order biases.

title: Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis
summary: We investigate how optimizers scale across the overtraining axis and show that relative optimizer performance and optimal hyperparameters change substantially with training horizon. In particular, we study how matrix-preconditioned methods (Muon and SOAP) and a momentum-scheduled method (ADANA) scale relative to AdamW. We compare these four optimizers across models from 51M to 253M parameters and overtraining (OT) factors from 1x to 256x, sweeping the base learning rate at every setting. The preferred learning rate schedule can reverse across the overtraining axis, the best weight decay coefficient scales approximately as sqrt(OT), and longer horizons generally favor longer fixed memory. ADANA's scaling advantage over AdamW persists after tuning AdamW's fixed memory separately at each horizon. Log-time weight decay and momentum cooldown provide substantial gains for ADANA that compound as training increases. With this treatment, ADANA outscales AdamW with an exponent advantage close to that predicted by DANA theory on power-law random features. Muon and SOAP instead provide roughly constant token-efficiency advantages over AdamW across most of the measured range, although SOAP may gain further at the highest overtraining factors. ADANA begins behind both matrix-preconditioned optimizers but closes the gaps as training increases, surpassing Muon and becoming competitive with SOAP at our highest OT factors. These results establish training horizon as an essential axis for optimizer evaluation and design.

AI.tldr: Across a wide range of model sizes and training horizons, ADANA and other optimizers exhibit distinct scaling; ADANA provides the strongest gains at long horizons, Muon/SOAP offer steady token-efficiency advantages, and training horizon is a crucial axis for optimizer design.
AI.motivation: To understand how optimizer performance scales along the overtraining axis and across model scales, and how matrix-preconditioned methods (Muon, SOAP) and a momentum-scheduled method (ADANA) compare to AdamW under varying horizons and hyperparameters.
AI.method: Empirical study sweeping base learning rate across four optimizers (Muon, SOAP, ADANA, AdamW) on models from 51M to 253M parameters and overtraining (OT) factors from 1x to 256x. Systematically vary learning-rate schedules, weight decay, and memory (fixed/learned), including log-time weight decay and momentum cooldown, to assess scaling exponents and performance across horizons.
AI.result: ADANA outscales AdamW with an exponent advantage close to DANA-theory predictions on power-law random features; Muon and SOAP offer roughly constant token-efficiency gains over AdamW across most settings (SOAP potentially gains more at very high OT). ADANA begins behind the matrix-preconditioned optimizers but closes the gap with training horizon, ultimately surpassing Muon and rivaling SOAP at the highest OT. The best learning-rate schedule and weight-decay scale with OT, and longer horizons favor longer fixed memory; ADANA’s advantage persists after tuning AdamW’s fixed memory. These findings position training horizon as a key axis for optimizer evaluation and design.
AI.conclusion: Training horizon fundamentally alters optimizer effectiveness; ADANA exhibits strong horizon-dependent scaling and outperforms AdamW at longer horizons, while Muon/SOAP provide stable advantages. The results advocate horizon-aware optimization and targeted hyperparameter strategies (log-time weight decay, momentum cooldown) for scalable performance.

title: RoboSPA: Can VLA Models Go Beyond Simple Scenes and Short-Horizon Tasks?
comment: Accepted at the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising progress in language-conditioned robotic manipulation. However, existing datasets and benchmarks mainly evaluate task completion under predefined settings, offering limited insight into model reasoning under increasing spatial and procedural complexity. We introduce \textbf{RoboSPA} (\textbf{Robo}t \textbf{S}patial-\textbf{P}rocedural \textbf{A}ssessment), a large-scale robotic manipulation dataset and benchmark for diagnosing embodied reasoning in VLA models. \texttt{RoboSPA} focuses on two core dimensions, Fine-Grained Spatial Reasoning and Long-Horizon Procedural Planning, covering 10 task categories and 56 base tasks. Each task is instantiated across five difficulty levels, yielding 280 variants with increasing spatial ambiguity and procedural complexity. We collect 527K trajectories across multiple embodiments and diverse scenes. Beyond binary success rate, \texttt{RoboSPA} introduces diagnostic metrics for more detailed evaluation. Experiments on representative VLA models show that current systems still struggle with complex spatial relations, precise low-level execution, and memory-intensive planning. These results establish \texttt{RoboSPA} as a challenging diagnostic benchmark for developing more capable, reliable, and generalizable embodied agents. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/fanzhenxuan/RoboSPA.

title: Leveraging Imperfect Restoration for Data Availability Attack
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2024. Equal contribution by Yi Huang, Jeremy Styborski, Mingzhi Lyu - cite in any order
summary: The abundance of online data is at risk of unauthorized usage in training deep learning models. To counter this, various Data Availability Attacks (DAAs) have been devised to make data unlearnable for such models by subtly perturbing the training data. However, existing attacks often excel against either Supervised Learning (SL) or Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) scenarios. Among these, a model-free approach that generates a Convolution-based Unlearnable Dataset (CUDA) stands out as the most robust DAA across both SSL and SL. Nonetheless, CUDA's effectiveness against SSL is underwhelming and it faces a severe trade-off between image quality and its poisoning effect. In this paper, we conduct a theoretical analysis of CUDA, uncovering the sub-optimal gradients it introduces and elucidating the strategy it employs to induce class-wise bias for data poisoning. Building on this, we propose a novel poisoning method named Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP), aiming to preserve high image quality while achieving strong poisoning effects. Through extensive comparisons of IRP with eight baselines across SL and SSL, coupled with evaluations alongside five representative defense methods, we showcase the superiority of IRP. Code: https://github.com/lyumingzhi/IRP

AI.tldr: IRP is proposed to surpass CUDA as a robust data availability attack, maintaining image quality while achieving strong poisoning across supervised and self-supervised learning; extensive experiments show IRP's superiority over eight baselines and resilience against five defenses, with code release.
AI.motivation: Address CUDA's suboptimal gradients and class-wise bias, and its poor trade-off between image quality and poisoning effectiveness, by designing an attack that preserves visual fidelity while delivering strong unlearnability in both SL and SSL.
AI.method: The authors perform a theoretical analysis of CUDA to reveal its gradient properties and bias-inducing mechanism, then introduce Imperfect Restoration Poisoning (IRP). They conduct extensive empirical comparisons against eight baselines across SL and SSL, and evaluate against five defenses, with code provided.
AI.result: IRP achieves stronger poisoning with higher image quality than CUDA and baselines, demonstrated across SL and SSL and under defense methods; the proposed method outperforms competitors in both attack strength and visual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: IRP offers a more effective, robust data poisoning method that maintains image quality and generalizes across learning paradigms, supported by comprehensive experiments; code is released for reproducibility.

title: LUMIN: Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network for Anomaly Detection
summary: Industrial anomaly detection faces two engineering bottlenecks: memory bank construction latency and inference efficiency. Traditional sampling algorithms (Farthest Point Sampling, K-Means, etc.) rely on numerous backbone forward passes and iterative distance computations, with construction times ranging from minutes to hours; heavy computation components such as multi-scale feature extraction struggle to meet the millisecond-level real-time requirements of production lines. This paper focuses on sampling efficiency and inference optimization for industrial deployment with two core contributions: (1) PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline)---a four-stage adaptive memory bank sampling pipeline based on 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins. PSP completes all sampling with zero backbone forward passes; coarse filtering is sub-second numerical sorting, and metadata extraction is a one-time offline cost. PSP supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. (2) Two engineering optimization strategies---parallel memory bank similarity computation (reducing inference memory and latency by over 95\%) and stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (reducing computation time by 20$\times$ while keeping metrics stable). As a vehicle for validation, we introduce LUMIN (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression, systematically exploring the accuracy-efficiency frontier against strong baselines. Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost (341$\times$ faster than FPS), while inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by 20$\times$ with negligible accuracy loss.

AI.tldr: PSP introduces a four-stage, plugin-based memory bank sampling pipeline that eliminates backbone forward passes and accelerates inference; augmented by parallelized similarity computation and stratified pixel sampling, achieving substantial speedups with negligible accuracy loss across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection suffers from slow memory-bank construction and heavy inference due to iterative sampling and multi-scale feature extraction; there's a need for real-time deployment on production lines.
AI.method: PSP (Plugin Sampler Pipeline): a four-stage adaptive sampling pipeline using 18-dimensional pixel metadata and five complementary visual plugins; zero backbone forward passes; coarse filtering via sub-second numerical sorting; metadata extraction is offline; supports progressive deployment and incremental updates. Two engineering optimizations: (a) parallel memory bank similarity computation (reduces memory and latency by >95%), and (b) stratified pixel sampling for large-scale evaluation (reduces computation time by ~20x while maintaining metrics). Additionally, the LUMIN network (Lightweight Universal Manufacturing Inspection Network) with extreme segmentation-head compression is introduced to explore the accuracy-efficiency frontier.
AI.result: PSP matches state-of-the-art sampling accuracy at near-random construction cost, being 341× faster than traditional FPS-based sampling. Inference optimizations reduce evaluation time by ~20× with negligible accuracy loss. Validated on five benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The approach delivers a practical, scalable solution for real-time industrial anomaly detection by removing backbone forward passes in sampling, leveraging plugin-based metadata, and employing targeted optimization strategies. It enables progressive deployment and shows strong empirical performance across multiple benchmarks.

title: Representation Redundancy and Structural Complexity in Finite-Field Inversion
summary: The representation chosen for a mathematical operation can affect both its algebraic form and its empirical learning difficulty. We study this phenomenon for inversion over \(\mathbb F_{2^n}\), with field elements expressed in varying ordered \(\mathbb F_2\)-bases. We prove that two ordered bases induce the same coordinate inversion map if and only if they belong to the same Galois orbit. Since every orbit has size \(n\), the correspondence between ordered bases and distinct inversion maps is exactly \(n\)-to-one. We then analyze three Boolean formulations of inversion. The reference formulation has algebraic degree \(n-1\) and joint ANF leap \(1\), the mixed representation formulation has degree \(2(n-1)\) and joint ANF leap \(2\), and the complete raw formulation has degree at most \(3(n-1)\) and joint ANF leap at least \(n\). Exhaustive computations agree with the theoretical results and bounds in the cases considered. Controlled experiments with multilayer perceptrons show the same ordering in learning difficulty, while Galois orbit redundancy provides only a limited generalization benefit under the tested conditions. These results show that exact redundancy among representations can coexist with changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is exposed as part of the input.

AI.tldr: The work analyzes how choosing an ordered F2-basis for inversion in F_{2^n} shapes the algebraic form and learning difficulty. It proves that two bases yield the same coordinate inversion map iff they lie in the same Galois orbit, giving an exactly n-to-one correspondence between bases and inversion maps. It examines three Boolean formulations with distinct algebraic degree and joint ANF leap bounds, and confirms these via exhaustive computation. Multilayer perceptron experiments corroborate the theoretical ordering of learning difficulty, while Galois orbit redundancy offers only limited generalization under tested conditions. The study shows that representation redundancy can coexist with changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is part of the input.
AI.motivation: To quantify how representation choices for a mathematical operation affect the resulting algebraic form and the empirical learning difficulty, using finite-field inversion and the structure of Galois orbits.
AI.method: 1) Theoretically prove that two ordered F2-bases induce the same coordinate inversion map iff they are in the same Galois orbit, with orbit size n, yielding an n-to-one correspondence. 2) Analyze three Boolean formulations of inversion: reference (degree n−1, joint ANF leap 1), mixed representation (degree 2(n−1), joint ANF leap 2), and complete raw (degree ≤3(n−1), joint ANF leap ≥ n). 3) Do exhaustive computations for cases considered to verify bounds. 4) Conduct controlled neural network experiments (MLPs) to compare learning difficulty and assess generalization benefits from Galois orbit redundancy.
AI.result: - Equivalence: two ordered bases induce the same coordinate inversion map iff they are in the same Galois orbit; each orbit has size n, so the mapping from ordered bases to distinct inversion maps is exactly n-to-one. - Boolean formulation properties: reference degree n−1, joint ANF leap 1; mixed formulation degree 2(n−1), joint ANF leap 2; complete raw degree ≤3(n−1), joint ANF leap ≥ n. - Exhaustive computations align with these theoretical bounds. - ML experiments show the same ordering of learning difficulty across formulations; Galois orbit redundancy provides only limited generalization benefit under the tested conditions.
AI.conclusion: Exact redundancy among representations can coexist with changes in Boolean structure and learning behavior when the representation is used as input. Representation choice affects both the algebraic form and learning dynamics, and while Galois orbit redundancy exists, it yields only limited generalization in the tested scenarios.

title: FIRE-LIVWO: Robust LiDAR-Inertial-Visual-Wheel Odometry via Failure-Immune mmWave Radar Enhancement
comment: Accepted by IROS 2026.The project website is "https://kj-falloutlast.github.io/FIRE-LIVWO"
summary: Achieving robust SLAM in large-scale underground coal mines with complex structures and severe degeneracies remains highly challenging. Dense smoke and dust cause substantial loss of visual information and degrade LiDAR point-cloud features, while long, self-similar corridors induce geometric degeneration, leading to pronounced odometry drift. To address these issues, we propose FIRE-LIVWO: Failure-Immune mmWave Radar-Enhanced LiDAR-Inertial-Visual-Wheel Odometry, a tightly coupled multi-modal odometry framework based on an iterated error-state Kalman filter (IESKF). The framework fuses 4D mmWave radar, LiDAR, and visual features within a unified VoxelMap and jointly constructs LiDAR-radar point-to-plane residuals and sparse visual photometric residuals. In smoke-filled environments, we exploit the strong penetration of 4D mmWave radar and introduce pointwise Doppler velocity constraints to preserve state observability. In geometrically degenerate corridors, we tightly couple wheel odometry using non-holonomic constraints (NHC) and online lever-arm compensation to reduce drift. Our central contribution is a degeneration detection and adaptive fusion model switching strategy grounded in geometric and visual observability analysis, which quantifies observability online and dynamically adjusts modality weights. Real-world experiments in underground coal mines demonstrate that FIRE-LIVWO accurately identifies failure boundaries, enabling reliable modality switching under extreme conditions. Compared with baselines, it achieves superior accuracy and robustness (average localization error of 5.677m). We open source our code on Github to benefit the robotics community.

AI.tldr: A robust, multi-modal odometry framework (FIRE-LIVWO) fusing mmWave radar, LiDAR, visuals, and wheel data with degeneration-aware adaptive fusion to maintain SLAM in underground mines.
AI.motivation: Address severe visual/LiDAR degradation and geometric degeneracies in large-scale underground mines, where smoke, dust, and long self-similar corridors cause information loss and odometry drift.
AI.method: Tightly coupled IESKF-based fusion of 4D mmWave radar, LiDAR, and visual features within a VoxelMap. Jointly constructs LiDAR-radar point-to-plane residuals and sparse visual photometric residuals. Uses Doppler velocity constraints from radar, wheel odometry with non-holonomic constraints and online lever-arm compensation. Introduces a degeneration detection and adaptive fusion strategy that quantifies observability online and dynamically tunes modality weights for robust fusion.
AI.result: Real-world underground coal mine experiments show FIRE-LIVWO accurately identifies failure boundaries and achieves superior accuracy and robustness, with an average localization error of 5.677 m compared to baselines. Code is open-sourced on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a degeneration-aware, failure-immune multi-modal fusion framework that maintains robust odometry in challenging underground environments and enables reliable modality switching under extreme conditions.

title: SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Appendix includes full proofs, attack-family constructions, and the extended process-reward study
summary: A runtime gate for an LLM tool agent is usually cast as a filter. In a ReAct loop a rejected proposal is followed by another at the same state, so the gate is a search operator over the proposal stream whose admission criterion shapes which trajectories are reachable. We study post-violation recovery admission, where progress must be admitted while the system is still in violation, and identify the scalar projection trap: an aggregate-score gate accepts a locally improving proposal and commits the trajectory to a plateau. SiLR instead shadow-executes each proposal and admits it under a product order over the branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity). We prove that no scalar surrogate is sound for this order, so the failure is representational, not a matter of threshold tuning. On mined Gym-ANM scenarios, SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes against 0/21 for terminal and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, significant across the full 24-scenario benchmark. The terminal-versus-structured dichotomy holds across three model families and in CityLearn. Because admission rests on deterministic simulation, the LLM lies outside the trust boundary: a magnitude-redistribution attack that defeats both scalar and support-only baselines is contained only by the full per-branch predicate. With two constraint families active, every tested scalar projection admits physically unsafe actions; support-only admits the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410; product order 0). In the hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates recover only through that unsafe class. Reused as a GRPO process reward, it outperforms its count projection in every mined scenario and is the only tested reward whose ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778). Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design points; only the full product order is structurally sufficient.

AI.tldr: Scalar gates for LLM tool-usage (admission in ReAct-like loops) are representationally unsound for multi-branch violation states; a full per-branch product-order gate (SiLR) outperforms scalar projections across benchmarks, is robust to magnitude redistribution attacks, and improves downstream rewards.
AI.motivation: Understand why simple scalar gating fails in LLM tool adoption under post-violation recovery and design a gate that accounts for branch-level violation states to ensure safe, reliable progression.
AI.method: Introduce SiLR with shadow-execution and admission under a product order over branch-level violation states (including overloaded-branch support and per-branch severity); prove no scalar surrogate is sound for this order; empirical evaluation on Gym-ANM (21 multi-action episodes, 24-scenario benchmark) and CityLearn across three model families; test against magnitude-redistribution attacks; compare with terminal and scalar gates; assess use as GRPO process reward.
AI.result: SiLR recovers 21/21 multi-action episodes on Gym-ANM; scalar gates achieve 0/21 for terminal and 9/21 for best scalar gate. With two constraint families, every tested scalar projection admits unsafe actions; product order restricts such failures. Scalar projection fails to preserve violation geometry; full product order is necessary. Across hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates rely on unsafe class; GRPO-reward experiments show ungated policies outperform untrained base; scalar projection yields representational deficiency that no threshold tuning fixes.
AI.conclusion: A per-branch product-order admission is structurally sufficient to capture violation geometry and ensure safe, effective progress, while scalar projections are inherently unsound for multi-branch violation dynamics. Gate design thus must incorporate branch-level states to resist distribution attacks and improve policy performance across domains.

title: CoMLP: Cooperatively-Gated MLPs for Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Information Fusion in Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Multi-modal medical images and clinical reports provide complementary anatomical, functional, and semantic information for medical image segmentation. Effectively exploiting these heterogeneous sources requires fine-grained cross-modal information fusion that preserves subtle spatial details while capturing semantic dependencies across modalities. Existing fusion approaches frequently rely on cross-attention, whose computational burden increases rapidly with spatial resolution, making dense cross-modal interaction difficult on high-resolution feature maps, particularly for volumetric medical images. In this work, we propose CoMLP, a cooperatively-gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation. CoMLP models cross-modal dependencies through cooperative cross-gating, built upon complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions, to capture local and global cross-modal dependencies. We further develop a multi-source fusion architecture in which CoMLP performs both inter-image fusion across imaging modalities and vision-language fusion between visual features and textual reports, enabling heterogeneous information to be integrated without relying on dense cross-attention. Extensive experiments on five medical segmentation benchmarks, covering 2D/3D images, clinical reports, multiple imaging modalities, and diverse anatomical regions, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods. Ablation studies further show that fine-grained interaction at high spatial resolutions and complementary local-global fusion are critical to the performance gains. These results demonstrate the potential of MLP-based interaction as an effective alternative for fine-grained cross-modal information fusion in medical image segmentation.

AI.tldr: Introduces CoMLP, a cooperative gated MLP module for fine-grained cross-modal fusion in medical image segmentation, enabling inter-modality and vision-language fusion without dense cross-attention; shows consistent gains on 5 benchmarks (2D/3D) with ablations confirming high-resolution local-global interaction.
AI.motivation: Need for effective fusion of heterogeneous medical data (multi-modal images and clinical text) that preserves spatial detail and semantic dependencies; dense cross-attention is computationally expensive at high resolutions, especially for volumetric data.
AI.method: CoMLP uses cooperative cross-gating built on complementary regional and dilated MLP interactions to model local and global cross-modal dependencies. A multi-source fusion architecture enables inter-image fusion across modalities and vision-language fusion with textual reports, avoiding dense cross-attention.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multi-modal and language-guided segmentation methods across five medical segmentation benchmarks, including 2D/3D images and diverse anatomical regions. Ablations show high-resolution fine-grained interaction and complementary local-global fusion as critical to performance gains.
AI.conclusion: MLP-based cross-modal interaction is a viable and efficient alternative to cross-attention for fine-grained cross-modal fusion in medical image segmentation, with potential for broader heterogeneous information integration.

title: GNN-Guided Graph Coarsening and Adaptive QUBO Penalties for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows on a Quantum Annealer
summary:
Graph coarsening reduces the large Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations arising when vehicle-routing problems are solved by quantum annealing. Nearby customers with compatible time windows are merged into super-nodes, the reduced problem is solved, and the solution is expanded to the original graph. For the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (CVRPTW), existing coarsening heuristics require family-specific tuning and remain unreliable on random instances. We address these limitations on the Solomon benchmark using simulated annealing and a D-Wave Advantage2 processor.
  We first introduce adaptive penalty calibration. Uniform penalty scaling has little effect, whereas controlling the internal coefficient range substantially improves raw samples. Removing non-binding constraints, normalising binding ones, and scaling the remaining penalties reduces mean raw constraint violations from 33.0 to 0.06 at the same solver budget (p=3.7e-11, n=56). A variable-count-preserving control attributes this gain to conditioning rather than problem size.
  Second, we replace the hand-tuned merge score with a graph neural network (GNN) using one configuration across all families. At N=10, it achieves 100% feasibility across all Solomon families, including R-type (100% vs. 80% for the tuned heuristic). Across N=10,...,100, feasibility is 83% vs. 69%, with the GNN better or tied on 85/90 instance-size pairs. At N=80,100, the difference is significant (p=0.002; 25/25 pairs), while the QUBO remains approximately 5-6 times smaller.
  Finally, hardware experiments reproduce the conditioning effect at fixed logical variable count: feasible samples increase from 0.02% to 39% across 13 instances. Classical repair with local search remains a reference bound for end-to-end solution cost.

AI.tldr: Adaptive penalty calibration plus GNN-guided coarsening significantly improves feasibility and reduces QUBO size for CVRPTW in quantum-annealing contexts; hardware experiments confirm conditioning gains; classical repair remains a strong benchmark.
AI.motivation: Address unreliable, family-specific coarsening heuristics for CVRPTW QUBO formulations in quantum annealing and seek a generalizable approach that scales across problem families and instance sizes.
AI.method: 1) Adaptive penalty calibration: remove non-binding constraints, normalise binding ones, and scale remaining penalties to reduce constraint violations; assess impact at fixed logical-variable count. 2) Replace hand-tuned merge score with a graph neural network (GNN) that generalizes across families, evaluated on Solomon benchmark across varying N. 3) Hardware experiments on D-Wave Advantage2 to validate conditioning effects; compare with simulated annealing and classical repair as end-to-end solution baseline.
AI.result: Constraint violations drop from 33.0 to 0.06 at the same solver budget (p=3.7e-11, n=56), attributed to conditioning rather than problem size. GNN-based coarsening achieves 100% feasibility at N=10 across all Solomon families (vs. 80% for tuned heuristic); for N=10–100, feasibility is 83% vs. 69%, with the GNN outperforming in 85/90 instance-size pairs; at N=80,100 the improvement is significant (p=0.002; 25/25 pairs) while QUBO is 5–6x smaller. Hardware experiments show feasible samples rise from 0.02% to 39% across 13 instances; classical repair with local search remains a strong end-to-end bound.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive penalty calibration and a single-configuration GNN-based coarsening provide robust improvements for QUBO CVRPTW solving, yielding higher feasibility and smaller QUBO, with conditioning driving gains and cross-family generalization; hardware results corroborate conditioning benefits, though end-to-end performance remains bounded by classical repair methods.

title: Adaptation Needs in Robotic Systems: Assessing Behavior Trees and Their Enhancement
summary:
Robotic systems increasingly operate in dynamic, uncertain, and open-ended environments, where design-time assumptions may no longer hold, and adaptation becomes necessary to maintain effective and safe operation. Behavior Trees (BTs) are widely used in robotic control architectures due to their modularity, readability, and reactivity. This raises a central question: are BTs sufficient to meet the adaptation needs of modern robotic systems?
  This paper investigates this question through a literature-driven study complemented by empirical validation. First, we derive a classification of robotic adaptation needs from the literature, organizing them into six categories: Knowledge, Perception, Actuation, System, Mission, and Environment. Then, we analyze the capabilities and limitations of classical BTs with respect to these needs. Then, we characterize BT-based approaches for adaptation from the existing literature and organize them into four primary families, i.e., generation, extension, evolution, and refinement, including approaches that combine multiple families.
  Our analysis shows that the modularity, flexibility, and reactivity of classical BTs are insufficient for adaptation needs involving runtime restructuring, reasoning under uncertainty, mission reinterpretation, learning, or integration with external knowledge and planning mechanisms. Enhanced BT approaches address several of these limitations, but to different extents and often with limitations of their own. Our findings relate adaptation needs to both the capabilities and limitations of classical and enhanced BTs, providing guidance on when classical BTs are sufficient, when enhanced mechanisms are needed, and which challenges remain or emerge for adaptive robotic control architectures.

AI.tldr: BTs are modular and reactive but not always sufficient for runtime adaptation in open robotic systems; enhanced BTs (generation, extension, evolution, refinement) address several needs but have trade-offs; a six-category adaptation framework (Knowledge, Perception, Actuation, System, Mission, Environment) guides when classical BTs suffice versus when enhancements are required.
AI.motivation: Assess whether classical Behavior Trees (BTs) meet the adaptation demands of modern robotic systems and map adaptation needs to BT capabilities and enhancements.
AI.method: Literature-driven study that (1) derives a six-category taxonomy of adaptation needs, (2) analyzes classical BTs against these needs, (3) characterizes BT-based adaptation approaches and groups them into four families (generation, extension, evolution, refinement), including hybrids.
AI.result: Classical BTs exhibit strong modularity, reactivity, and readability but lack sufficient support for runtime restructuring, uncertainty reasoning, mission reinterpretation, learning, and external knowledge/planning integration. Enhanced BTs address several gaps with varying effectiveness and trade-offs. The study offers guidance on when classical BTs suffice and when enhanced mechanisms are warranted, as well as remaining challenges for adaptive robotic control architectures.
AI.conclusion: BTs are not universally sufficient for all adaptation needs in dynamic robotic systems. While enhanced BT approaches broaden capabilities, full adaptation—especially under uncertainty and dynamic mission reinterpretation—often requires integrating BTs with planning, learning, or probabilistic/knowledge-based components. The work provides a structured framework to decide the appropriate level of BT-based adaptation.

title: A Cost-Aware Agentic Architecture for NL-to-SQL over Nested Enterprise Schemas, with a New Benchmark
summary: Natural-language-to-SQL systems have ad- vanced rapidly on academic benchmarks, yet production enterprise schemas exhibit graph- like, semi-structured, deeply nested structure that current benchmarks do not measure. We make two complementary contributions. First, we introduce the DevRev NL2SQL bench- mark: 900 execution-verified queries with nested-type and link-graph structure, accom- panied by the Semantic Depth Score (SDS), a schema-agnostic rubric for analytical reasoning depth. Second, we present a cost-aware single- generation agentic architecture whose schema- selection, metadata-retrieval, and error-repair components are designed for the requirements this regime imposes. On the DevRev NL2SQL benchmark the system attains 91.7% answer correctness, a margin of 54.6 percentage points over the next-best baseline; on the Spider 2.0 Snowflake public dataset, it is competitive with leading systems at a single-generation operating point.

AI.tldr: Introduces DevRev NL2SQL benchmark and a cost-aware single-generation agentic NL2SQL system. Benchmark: 900 execution-verified queries with nested-link graphs and Semantic Depth Score. System achieves 91.7% accuracy on DevRev benchmark, +54.6 points over a baseline; competitive on Spider 2.0 Snowflake dataset.
AI.motivation: Enterprise schemas are graph-like, semi-structured, deeply nested; existing benchmarks fail to capture analytical reasoning and schema-structure challenges; need benchmarks and architectures tailored to production data.
AI.method: Benchmark design with 900 execution-verified queries and SDS; architecture with schema-selection, metadata retrieval, error repair in a single-generation framework; cost-aware planning.
AI.result: DevRev NL2SQL: 91.7% accuracy, +54.6 pp vs baseline. Spider 2.0 Snowflake: competitive at single-generation point.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates value of schema-aware, cost-aware single-generation NL2SQL approach and a robust, graph-structure-aware benchmark for evaluating analytical reasoning depth on enterprise schemas.

title: CLON: Cue-Calibrated Linguistic Object Onboarding for Zero-Shot 6D Pose Front-Ends
summary: Zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipelines increasingly rely on strong downstream pose solvers, but their performance is often limited by the front-end: object proposals must preserve partially visible true positives while rejecting semantically plausible distractors. We introduce Cue-Calibrated Linguistic Object Onboarding (CLON), a front-end requiring no task-specific training for new objects. Given rendered templates of the onboarded object set, CLON constructs a linguistic semantic memory for top-down proposal generation and object-set cue weights for calibrated proposal scoring. The linguistic memory guides SAM 3 toward high-recall proposals for onboarded objects, while cue weights are computed once from the onboarded object set before scene inference and kept fixed during online scoring. On seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets, CLON improves detection AP by 8.1 percentage points (pp), segmentation AP by 6.2 pp, and downstream 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 pp over CNOS and SAM-6D front-ends.

AI.tldr: A task-agnostic front-end (CLON) for zero-shot 6D pose estimation that uses rendered templates to build a linguistic memory and fixed cue weights to improve proposal generation and scoring, boosting detection, segmentation, and pose accuracy without extra training.
AI.motivation: Front-end proposals must preserve true positives while rejecting distractors in zero-shot settings; existing methods (CNOS, SAM-6D) can be limited; a training-free front-end for new objects can improve downstream pose accuracy.
AI.method: CLON constructs a linguistic semantic memory from rendered object templates to guide a SAM-3 proposal generator toward high-recall detections. It also computes fixed cue weights from the onboarded object set prior to inference, used during scoring to calibrate proposals. No task-specific training required for new objects.
AI.result: On seven BOP-Classic-Core datasets, CLON improves detection AP by 8.1 percentage points, segmentation AP by 6.2 points, and downstream 6D pose AR by up to 4.1 percentage points compared to CNOS and SAM-6D front-ends.
AI.conclusion: A training-free front-end that leverages linguistic memory and cue calibration can substantially boost zero-shot 6D pose pipelines, effectively enhancing recall-distractor discrimination and downstream pose accuracy without object-specific training.

title: Too Rare to Learn: Prescribed Cyclone Tracks Degrade a Bay of Bengal Ocean Emulator
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures. In review at the NeurIPS 2026 Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop
summary: Neural ocean emulators are being proposed for regional forecasting in cyclone-exposed coastal seas, and a natural design choice is to hand the network the cyclone as a prescribed input. We test that choice in the Bay of Bengal and find it harmful. We withhold 15 whole cyclones spanning 65 to 150 kt from GLORYS12 reanalysis and compare two U-Nets that are identical except for four prescribed cyclone-track channels. Across three seeds the ocean-only model beats persistence in every run and the storm-conditioned model loses to it in every run, with the two skill ranges disjoint (p = 3.1e-5, paired across storms). The cause is exposure frequency rather than signal content: the channels are non-zero on only 7.9% of training days, so they are out of distribution the moment they activate. The extra error falls inside the prescribed storm footprint, and replacing the real cyclone map with a no-storm map at inference improves held-out storm forecasts by 7.5 to 16.4% in every seed. The conditioned network has learned a response to a rare signal that is confidently wrong.

AI.tldr: Conditioning neural ocean emulators on rare cyclone-input channels harms generalization; an ocean-only model beats a storm-conditioned model; distribution shift due to 7.9% non-zero channel activity; replacing cyclone maps with no-storm maps at inference improves forecasts; the model learns a wrong response to a rare signal.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether prescribing cyclone state improves regional forecasts in cyclone-exposed seas and identify failure modes in the presence of rare conditioning signals.
AI.method: Two U-Nets identical except for four cyclone-track input channels; withheld 15 cyclones (65–150 kt) from GLORYS12 reanalysis; train and test across three seeds; compare ocean-only vs storm-conditioned models; assess against persistence; conduct ablation by using a no-storm map at inference; analyze training-channel activity frequency (7.9%); note out-of-distribution issues.
AI.result: Ocean-only model beats persistence on all runs; storm-conditioned model loses to ocean-only on all runs; skill ranges are disjoint; p = 3.1e-5 (paired across storms); cyclone channels are non-zero on only 7.9% of training days; when activated, they fall out-of-distribution; replacing cyclone maps with no-storm maps at inference improves held-out storm forecasts by 7.5–16.4% across seeds.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning on a rare, out-of-distribution signal can degrade performance; the network learns a confidently wrong response to a rare cue; avoid relying on explicit cyclone-input channels; ensure training distribution matches inference or use robust conditioning and evaluation that tests for distribution shift.

title: Development of a Humanoid Robot Prototype for Multimodal Human-Robot Interaction
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Published in the 2025 RIVF International Conference on Computing and Communication Technologies (RIVF 2025)
summary: Human-robot interaction (HRI) enables intuitive and intelligent collaboration between humans and robots in real-world environments. This paper introduces a humanoid robot prototype designed as a flexible testbed for developing and integrating artificial intelligence (AI) modules in HRI tasks. The system features a 12 degree-of-freedom (DOFs) dual-arm mechanism and a 2 DOFs head with an expressive LCD screen to express facial emotions. All hardware components are controlled by a custom-designed controller board with real-time AI processing supported by an onboard Jetson module. The system incorporates three AI modules: (1) gesture recognition using MediaPipe Pose and an LSTM classifier, (2) object detection with YOLO and 3D localization, and (3) voice-command processing through speech recognition and large language model(LLM)-based semantic parsing. The platform is validated through experiments on positioning accuracy, with results showing average manipulation errors of approximately 1.83 cm. To demonstrate its versatility, experimental results show over 90% task accuracy, with gesture recognition reaching 96%, speech recognition reaching 92%. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed system as a reproducible and accessible humanoid platform for research and prototyping in HRI.

AI.tldr: A reproducible humanoid robot testbed with 12-DOF dual arms, 2-DOF head, and on-board Jetson for real-time AI. Integrates gesture recognition (MediaPipe Pose + LSTM), object detection (YOLO + 3D localization), and speech-command processing (ASR + LLM parsing). Validated with ~1.83 cm positioning error and >90% task accuracy (gesture 96%, speech 92%).
AI.motivation: To provide a flexible, accessible, and reproducible platform for developing and integrating AI modules in real-world HRI tasks, enabling rapid prototyping and benchmarking.
AI.method: Hardware: humanoid with 12-DOF dual arms, 2-DOF head with expressive LCD; custom controller board; onboard Jetson for real-time AI processing. AI modules: (1) gesture recognition via MediaPipe Pose and LSTM, (2) object detection with YOLO and 3D localization, (3) voice-command processing through speech recognition and LLM-based semantic parsing. Validation through positioning accuracy experiments and task metrics.
AI.result: Average manipulation error ~1.83 cm. Task accuracy >90%, with gesture recognition 96% and speech recognition 92%.
AI.conclusion: The work presents an effective, reproducible, and accessible humanoid platform for HRI research and prototyping, demonstrating integrated AI modules and solid performance.

title: Continual Graph Memory for Adaptive Recommendation under Intent Drift
summary: This paper studies adaptive recommendation under intent drift, where feedback from each recommendation outcome can reveal whether the relational evidence used for ranking is useful, missing, or misleading. While Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide essential semantic structure to handle these shifts, traditional KG-enhanced systems treat the graph as a static retrieval substrate, making it brittle to evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns. This paper proposes CGM-Rec, a continual graph memory framework for adaptive recommendation. CGM-Rec treats the graph state as a writable memory and maintains two complementary components. Therein, a Semantic Graph Memory is updated conservatively through quality-gated typed operations for storing stable and high-confidence relational knowledge. Meanwhile, an Episodic Lesson Memory acts as a fast reactive memory that learns recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. During testing, model parameters remain frozen and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. We evaluate CGM-Rec under a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol, where encoders and prompts remain fixed during testing and adaptation occurs only through memory writes. Experiments across multiple recommendation settings show that CGM-Rec improves over evaluated neural and LLM-based baselines on most metrics. Particularly, under sampled-candidate reranking, CGM-Rec improves HR@1 by up to 29.58% over the strongest LLM baseline on Bundle, and outperforms K-RagRec on metadata-rich ML-100K with HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746.

AI.tldr: CGM-Rec introduces a continual graph memory framework with a semantic memory and an episodic memory to adapt recommendation under intent drift, achieving notable gains in one-pass frozen-parameter reranking experiments.
AI.motivation: To address brittleness of static knowledge-graph–driven retrieval under evolving intents, noisy metadata, and recurring failure patterns, by enabling writable, continual memory updates without retraining.
AI.method: Two-memory design: a Semantic Graph Memory updated conservatively with quality-gated typed operations to store stable, high-confidence relational knowledge; an Episodic Lesson Memory as a fast reactive memory capturing recent outcomes, failure cases, and corrective hints. Testing uses frozen parameters with adaptation only via memory writes; evaluation in a frozen-parameter, one-pass reranking protocol.
AI.result: CGM-Rec outperforms evaluated neural and LLM baselines across multiple settings; up to 29.58% HR@1 improvement over the strongest LLM baseline on the Bundle dataset in sampled-candidate reranking; on ML-100K (metadata-rich) it achieves HR@5 of 0.5941 versus 0.4746 for K-RagRec.
AI.conclusion: A memory-driven continual graph memory framework enables effective adaptation to intent drift without updating model parameters, yielding significant gains in reranking tasks, particularly in sampled-candidate and metadata-rich settings.

title: An Attention-Guided Global and Local Fusion Framework for Lesion-Focused Image Classification
summary: Lesion-focused image classification presents a core analytical challenge, as discriminative signals are often sparse, spatially dispersed, and easily obscured by background noise, while conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process entire images uniformly and may dilute signal relevance. This study hypothesizes that adaptive fusion of global contextual information and lesion-focused local information can improve classification performance compared with using either representation independently. We propose a three-branch, attention-guided deep learning framework built on Densely Connected Convolutional Network-121 (DenseNet-121) to improve feature attribution, interpretability, and classification reliability. The architecture consists of a global branch that learns representations from full images, followed by Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to generate attention maps that highlight prediction-relevant regions and produce masked inputs, and a local branch enhanced with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to extract refined spatial and channel-wise features from these focused regions. An adaptive fusion branch integrates global and local representations by learning instance-specific weights, allowing dynamic prioritization between contextual and localized information. The framework is evaluated on a synthetic Spot Pattern Dataset (SSPD) and three benchmark datasets, including skin lesion, guava leaf, and grape leaf image datasets, where the fusion branch outperformed the individual global and local branches, reaching 97.75% accuracy on the skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on the guava leaf dataset. The results highlight the value of attention-guided architectures in healthcare analytics by improving model transparency, strengthening feature relevance, and supporting more reliable data-driven decision-making in medical image analysis.

AI.tldr: An attention-guided three-branch fusion framework built on DenseNet-121 combines global image context with lesion-focused local features to improve lesion classification. It uses Grad-CAM to generate attention masks and masked inputs for a local CBAM-enhanced branch, with an adaptive fusion module that learns instance-specific weights to merge global and local representations. The method outperforms individual branches on multiple datasets, achieving 97.75% accuracy on skin lesions and 99.64% on guava leaves (and high performance on synthetic SSPD).
AI.motivation: Discriminative lesion signals are sparse and easily obscured by background noise; standard CNNs process full images uniformly, risking diluted signal relevance. An adaptive fusion of global context and lesion-focused local information is hypothesized to improve attribution, interpretability, and classification reliability.
AI.method: Three-branch architecture based on DenseNet-121: a global branch processes full images; Grad-CAM generates attention maps to produce masked inputs highlighting relevant regions; a local branch with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) refines features from these regions; an adaptive fusion branch learns instance-specific weights to fuse global and local representations, enabling dynamic prioritization of contextual versus localized information.
AI.result: The fusion branch outperformed individual branches, with high accuracies on the evaluated datasets: 97.75% on the skin lesion dataset and 99.64% on the guava leaf dataset; the approach improved feature attribution, interpretability, and decision reliability.
AI.conclusion: Attention-guided, multi-branch fusion frameworks can enhance transparency and reliability in medical image analysis by effectively combining global context and localized lesion signals, supporting more trustworthy data-driven clinical decisions.

title: SMILE: Bridging Continuous Optimization and Discrete Symbolic Recovery
summary: Symbolic regression (SR) discovers closed-form mathematical expressions from data, offering interpretability beyond black-box models. Existing methods suffer from slow convergence in combinatorial search spaces and lack mechanisms to exploit compositional structure in the data. We introduce SMILE (Sine, Multiplication, Identity, Logarithm, Exponential), a hybrid framework that unifies continuous gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery through three stages: structural analysis of the data to identify the compositional hierarchy of the target expression, continuous optimization to learn parameters of a network that encodes the target expression using interpretable activations, and symbolic recovery through structured pruning, coefficient optimization, and rounding. This final stage distills the learned network into a compact expression with exact symbolic constants. We evaluate SMILE on SRBench across ground-truth and black-box datasets, with ablation studies validating each component. SMILE achieves the highest symbolic solution rate at the largest noise levels, demonstrating strong robustness where competing methods degrade substantially. It consistently lies on the Pareto front of accuracy versus complexity, recovering significantly simpler expressions in a fraction of the time required by the competing methods.

AI.tldr: Hybrid symbolic regression framework SMILE unifies gradient-based optimization with discrete symbolic recovery to yield robust, compact expressions with exact constants; achieves state-of-the-art symbolic solution rate, especially under high noise, and favorable accuracy/complexity trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Symbolic regression methods face slow convergence in combinatorial search spaces and often miss exploitation of compositional structure in data; a hybrid approach that leverages both continuous optimization and discrete symbolic recovery can improve efficiency, interpretability, and robustness.
AI.method: Three-stage SMILE: (1) structural analysis to uncover the compositional hierarchy of the target expression; (2) continuous optimization using a network with interpretable activations to model the target expression; (3) symbolic recovery via structured pruning, coefficient optimization, and rounding to distill the network into a compact symbolic expression with exact constants.
AI.result: Evaluated on SRBench with ground-truth and black-box datasets; ablation studies validate each component; SMILE achieves the highest symbolic solution rate at large noise levels, showing robustness where competing methods degrade; lies on the Pareto front of accuracy versus complexity, recovering simpler expressions much faster than competitors.
AI.conclusion: SMILE demonstrates robust, efficient symbolic regression by exploiting compositional structure and hybrid optimization, delivering accurate, interpretable, compact expressions and advancing SR performance on challenging benchmarks.

title: Towards Neuro-Symbolic Procedural Reasoning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
comment: Accepted as an oral presentation at the X-Reason Workshop, ECCV 2026. Non-archival extended abstract. 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute short manipulation skills, but remain brittle in long-horizon procedures requiring persistent task state, dependency-aware reasoning, conditional decisions, and reliable grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic framework that combines learned VLA control with explicit task graphs and multimodal procedural memory. Task graphs encode action dependencies, valid transitions, and branch conditions, while memory maintains the active step, completed actions, textual context, and task-relevant visual evidence. Together, these structures guide object selection, destination grounding, subgoal dispatch, and verification of expected state transitions. Human demonstrations provide additional spatial and temporal guidance through gaze or saliency cues. To isolate their effect on policy learning, our initial study bypasses cross-view gaze transfer and directly annotates pseudo-gaze in robot-view teleoperation videos. The resulting guidance is used during VLA fine-tuning and inference. We study two long-horizon manipulation domains, workspace clearing and surgical-instrument handling, which require ordered execution, visually grounded decisions, and conditional branching. We evaluate correct-object and destination selection, subtask completion, task progress, step-order consistency, complete-task success, and procedural or execution mistakes. This work positions structured symbolic reasoning and demonstration-derived visual guidance as complementary mechanisms for reliable long-horizon VLA manipulation.

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic VLA framework integrating explicit task graphs and multimodal procedural memory with pseudo-gaze guidance to improve long-horizon manipulation reliability; evaluated on workspace clearing and surgical-instrument handling; demonstrates improvements in grounding, branching decisions, and task progress.
AI.motivation: Address brittleness of vision-language-action models in long-horizon tasks requiring persistent task-state tracking, dependency-aware reasoning, conditional branching, and reliable grounding; propose a hybrid approach combining learned VLA control with symbolic structures and memory, plus demonstration-derived guidance.
AI.method: Combine a learned VLA controller with explicit task graphs that encode action dependencies, valid transitions, and branch conditions, plus a multimodal procedural memory that stores the active step, completed actions, textual context, and task-relevant visual evidence. Use these structures to guide object selection, destination grounding, subgoal dispatch, and verification of state transitions. Incorporate human demonstrations as spatial/temporal guidance via gaze cues; in the initial study, bypass cross-view gaze transfer and annotate pseudo-gaze in robot-view teleoperation videos for use in VLA fine-tuning and inference.
AI.result: The approach yields improved long-horizon manipulation reliability by leveraging the symbolic task graphs and procedural memory, enhancing correct-object and destination selection, subtask completion, progress tracking, and step-order consistency, while reducing procedural or execution mistakes.
AI.conclusion: Structured symbolic reasoning and demonstration-derived visual guidance act as complementary mechanisms to neuro-VLA control, boosting reliability and robustness in long-horizon manipulation tasks and offering a pathway for better generalization through explicit task-state modeling and guided grounding.

title: Harness-agnostic detection and immunization of reward hacking in self-evolving language models
summary: Self-evolving language models improve by proposing candidate updates and keeping whatever raises a visible score. When that score is an imperfect proxy for the capability one actually wants, sustained selection widens the gap between the two. This is reward hacking. We introduce HackProbe, a monitor that attaches to an arbitrary self-evolving loop through two black-box hooks, with no access to weights or activations. It keeps a secret, distribution-fixed comparison core, whose frozen distribution makes its capability proxy comparable across generations, alongside a rotated fresh layer that hardens the bank against co-adaptation. Four tests built on that proxy cover the level gap, a scale-aligned divergence with online change-point detection, capability stagnation, and a conditional confidently-wrong rate; a Sidak correction turns them into a calibrated family-wise p-value. Diagnosis alone recovers nothing, so a risk-aware immunization layer reselects an honest candidate from the proposal pool using the core together with a purely structural gaming footprint, disclosing at most log2 Pi bits per generation to the host. We prove a detectability bound that converts a target error rate into an explicit probe-size budget, and we delimit what probe rotation does and does not buy. On a controlled prompt-level host with four injected hacking channels and ground-truth labels, HackProbe reaches 0.763 AUROC against 0.663 for the strongest baseline and cuts the false-positive rate from 0.706 to 0.434. Its bandwidth-limited reselection is the only immunization level that returns more true capability under hacking, 5.2 points on average, than it forfeits on clean runs, 4.7; per-channel effects are mostly not individually significant.

AI.tldr: HackProbe introduces a black-box monitor for self-evolving LMs to detect and immunize against reward hacking by using a secret, fixed comparison core and a rotated fresh layer; it performs four calibrated tests and a risk-aware reselection, achieving improved AUROC and reduced false positives under hacking with only limited information leakage.
AI.motivation: Reward hacking in self-evolving language models arises when the objective proxy diverges from actual capabilities; there is a need for a modality-agnostic monitor that can be attached to evolving loops without access to weights/activations, and that can calibrate across generations while resisting co-adaptation.
AI.method: Attach HackProbe via two black-box hooks to a self-evolving loop. Use a secret, distribution-fixed comparison core with a frozen distribution and a rotated fresh layer to impede co-adaptation. Implement four tests (level gap, scale-aligned change-point detection, capability stagnation, conditional confidently-wrong rate) with Sidak correction to yield calibrated p-values. Diagnosis is followed by a risk-aware immunization layer that reselects an honest candidate using the core and a structural gaming footprint, disclosing at most log2 Pi bits per generation. Prove a detectability bound translating target error rate to probe-size budget and characterize the effects of probe rotation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on a controlled prompt-level host with four injected hacking channels and ground-truth labels shows HackProbe achieving 0.763 AUROC compared to 0.663 for the strongest baseline, and reducing false positives from 0.706 to 0.434. Bandwidth-limited reselection yields net gain in true capability under hacking (≈5.2 points) versus loss on clean runs (≈4.7 points); per-channel effects are largely non-significant.
AI.conclusion: HackProbe provides a statistically calibrated, bandwidth-limited immunization mechanism for self-evolving LMs against reward hacking by pairing a hidden comparison core with rotation-based defenses and a risk-aware reselection strategy, achieving superior detection and net capability retention under hacking; the approach is supported by a formal detectability bound and controlled experiments.

title: Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation of CLIP for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval
summary: Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR) aims to retrieve untrimmed videos that contain moments relevant to a text query. Since the target moment occupies only a portion of the video, PRVR requires retrieval based on fine-grained understanding beyond coarse video-level matching. However, existing methods often rely on frozen CLIP frame features, which lack temporal understanding. Even with recent progress in parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation, video-level predictions can still be supported by imprecise frame-level evidence. In this paper, we propose an Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation (ITA) framework for PRVR. First, our Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation allows the last few visual transformer layers to attend over groups of neighboring frames. This provides temporally aware frame embeddings while keeping CLIP frozen and training only adaptation parameters. Second, we introduce Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation to address the weakly supervised nature of PRVR, softly aggregating top-$k$ frames based on text-frame affinities and propagating learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and retrieves substantially more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth query-relevant moments. Our code is available at github.com/hynnsk/ITA.

AI.tldr: ITA for partially relevant video retrieval combines (1) backbone-internal temporal adaptation by letting the last ViT layers attend over neighboring frames while keeping CLIP frozen, and (2) affinity-weighted gradient propagation for weak supervision, yielding state-of-the-art PRVR results and better frame-level evidence.
AI.motivation: PRVR requires fine-grained temporal understanding to locate moments within untrimmed videos; existing CLIP-based methods lack temporal context due to frozen features, limiting evidence quality and transferability.
AI.method: (i) Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation: enable the final visual transformer layers to attend over groups of nearby frames, producing temporally aware frame embeddings without updating CLIP parameters; (ii) Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation: softly select top-k frames by text-frame affinities and propagate learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames, improving supervision signal in weakly labeled data.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and yields more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth moments.
AI.conclusion: ITA effectively injects temporal awareness into frozen CLIP representations for PRVR while addressing weak supervision through affinity-guided gradient propagation, enabling better moment localization and evidence retrieval without full-end fine-tuning.

title: Interpretability for Turing Machines
comment: 75 pages, 31 figures, 3 tables. Interactive companion: https://tminterp.timaeus.co. Code and data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22205895
summary: We show that susceptibilities, an interpretability technique developed for neural networks, can identify the presence of algorithmic structure in Turing machines by probing the local loss landscape of a learning problem for noisy Turing machines introduced by Murfet and Troiani (arXiv:2504.08075). We prove that symmetries and path separation in the algorithm implemented by a Turing machine induce permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks in its susceptibility matrix. We study this empirically on a set of deterministic finite automata (DFAs) and demonstrate that algorithmic features can be recovered by principal component analysis and clustering methods in susceptibility space.

AI.tldr: Susceptibilities reveal algorithmic structure in Turing machines by showing symmetry- and path-induced patterns in the susceptibility matrix; dimensionality reductions (PCA) and clustering in susceptibility space can recover underlying algorithmic features from DFAs.
AI.motivation: Extend interpretability techniques to computational systems to detect underlying algorithmic structure in noisy Turing machines and automata, using local loss landscape analysis.
AI.method: Theoretically prove that algorithmic symmetries and path separation induce permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks in the susceptibility matrix; empirically validate on a set of DFAs by applying PCA and clustering to susceptibility representations to recover algorithmic features.
AI.result: Establishes that susceptibility matrices exhibit structured patterns (permutation symmetries and low-rank blocks) due to algorithmic symmetries; empirically, PCA and clustering in susceptibility space can recover underlying algorithmic features in DFAs.
AI.conclusion: Susceptibility-based analysis is a viable tool for probing algorithmic structure in Turing machines/automata; symmetries and path separations manifest in the susceptibility matrix and can be leveraged to recover the underlying algorithm.

title: What Matters, When? Diagnosing and Improving Conditional Visual Grounding in Visuomotor Imitation Policies
comment: Accepted as an extended abstract at the DexHAND Workshop, ECCV 2026. Non-archival, non-proceedings. 4 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: Visuomotor imitation policies can achieve high performance under in-distribution visual conditions yet fail when visually similar objects or receptacles are introduced. We study this behavior as a problem of conditional visual grounding: the visual target required for successful control changes with the manipulation phase and, in more complex tasks, with the observed task state. Using Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), we systematically introduce distractor objects and receptacles with controlled color and shape similarity and localize failures to picking and placement. We find that distractor sensitivity is specific to both the type of visual similarity and the manipulation stage. Guided by this diagnosis, we evaluate distractor augmentation, phase-dependent attention regularization, and appearance-based visual prompting as complementary interventions for improving target selection while preserving spatial information required for control. These interventions substantially improve robustness in simulation and on a physical UR3e. We further examine the same failure pattern in a pretrained vision-language-action policy on a state-conditioned instrument-handling task, where the observed state of a medical instrument determines the correct destination. Together, the results show that visual distractors can cause incorrect object or destination selection even when the underlying manipulation skill remains intact, and that explicitly improving target selection can substantially recover performance across distinct visuomotor policy-learning regimes.

AI.tldr: Distractor-induced failures in visuomotor imitation arise from phase/state-dependent visual grounding; targeted interventions on target selection improve robustness across simulators and hardware, and transfer to another policy.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies often succeed in clean, in-distribution visuals but fail when distractors resemble targets; understanding the grounding failures and how to mitigate them is crucial for robust manipulation.
AI.method: Use Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to systematically inject distractor objects/receptacles with controlled color/shape similarity and varying manipulation stages; diagnose failures at picking/placement; evaluate interventions—distractor augmentation, phase-dependent attention regularization, appearance-based visual prompting; validate in simulation and on a UR3e; extend analysis to a pretrained vision-language-action policy on instrument-handling tasks.
AI.result: Distractor sensitivity depends on the type of visual similarity and manipulation stage; the proposed interventions substantially improve target selection and overall robustness in both simulation and hardware; the same failure pattern appears in a state-conditioned policy, indicating broader applicability of targeting improvements.
AI.conclusion: Visual distractors can derail target selection without breaking the underlying manipulation skill; explicitly improving target grounding yields robustness gains across distinct visuomotor policy-learning regimes.

title: ERPBench: Evaluating LLM Agents for Enterprise Decision-Making Across Competitive Market Ecologies
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed for enterprise workflows, yet existing evaluations rarely test whether business-decision conclusions transfer across competitive market ecologies. We introduce ERPBench, an execution-instrumented benchmark for enterprise decision agents in a six-round Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) simulation with coupled pricing, production, procurement, inventory, finance, and shared-market competition. ERPBench evaluates the same 100 fixed problems in two matched competitive market ecologies: Solo, where each evaluated LLM agent competes against fixed rule-based opponents, and Arena, where six evaluated LLM agents compete in a shared market. Across six model families, this yields 1,200 model-level trajectories spanning 7,200 decision rounds. Under the observed service configuration, the leading model differs between ecologies: DeepSeek leads in Solo (252.29M mean valuation; mean rank 1.67), whereas Gemini leads in Arena (263.95M; 1.76). The two ecologies identify the same task-level winner on only 21 of 100 problems, and Gemini's bottom-rank rate falls from 22 % to 0 % in Arena. ERPBench supports paired evaluation of whether enterprise-agent rankings transfer across competitive market ecologies, supplemented by aggregate execution-intervention analysis. Code and benchmark resources are available in our https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/erp-bench.

AI.tldr: ERPBench: an execution-instrumented benchmark for enterprise decision agents in a six-round ERP simulation across Solo and Arena ecologies; reveals limited transfer of task-level winners between ecologies; ecology-specific performance dominates.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether enterprise decision agents' conclusions transfer across competitive market ecologies and quantify how rankings shift between paired market environments.
AI.method: Six-round ERP simulation with coupled pricing, production, procurement, inventory, finance; 100 fixed problems; six model families; two ecologies (Solo: against fixed rule-based opponents; Arena: six agents in a shared market); 1,200 model trajectories across 7,200 decision rounds; metrics include mean valuation and mean rank; cross-ecology comparison of winners and bottom-rank rates; execution-intervention analysis; code available in GitHub.
