AI.result: Leading model differs by ecology: DeepSeek leads in Solo (252.29M mean valuation; mean rank 1.67); Gemini leads in Arena (263.95M; 1.76). Only 21 of 100 problems share the same top winner across ecologies. Gemini's bottom-rank rate decreases from 22% in Solo to 0% in Arena.
AI.conclusion: ERPBench enables paired evaluation of cross-ecology transfer of enterprise-agent rankings and supports execution-intervention analysis; results indicate ecology-specific performance substantially alters top winners, underscoring the importance of cross-ecology benchmarking; resources are available at the linked GitHub repository.

title: Linguistic Trajectory Encoding for Efficient Long-Horizon Spatial Memory in Embodied Agents
summary: Embodied agents performing long-horizon tasks require a memory representation in which the state transitions of dynamic objects remain queryable in natural language across hours-to-days observation horizons. Existing systems either drop fine-grained motion (clip-level video-language embeddings), keep it only as raw coordinates (geometric SLAM), or organise it around immediate task context (agent working memories). None of them gives the agent a per-object timeline whose state transitions are themselves queryable in language. Our key contribution is \textbf{Linguistic Trajectory Encoding} (LTE), which compresses dynamic object motion histories via a hybrid representation combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. LTE adapts compression to motion complexity by anchoring periods without reliable observations to the last seen location, while representing motion with geometric waypoints and linguistic descriptions to preserve accuracy. To evaluate these capabilities across extended time horizons, we construct the \textbf{Spatial Memory Benchmark} (SMB) from EgoLife multi-day recordings, targeting capabilities absent in existing benchmarks: semantic trajectory retrieval and long-horizon object retrieval. On SMB, the LTE-based system achieves $45.3\%$ success in semantic trajectory retrieval and $48.7\%$ in long-horizon object retrieval, outperforming structured-memory and VLM baselines (best prior: $31.9\%$ and $34.4\%$). LTE achieves trajectory compression by factors of $8.7\times$ to $26.1\times$ with sub-second query latency on $24$\,h video. On Ego4D natural-language queries, the system reaches $28.75\%$ / $55.10\%$ R@1/R@5, $+15.80$ / $+31.30$ pts over EgoVLPv2.

AI.tldr: LTE provides per-object, queryable linguistic trajectories for long-horizon reasoning, enabling strong semantic trajectory and long-horizon object retrieval with substantial compression and fast query latency.
AI.motivation: Existing memory architectures underutilize per-object, language-queryable trajectories for long-horizon tasks, often sacrificing granularity, raw geometry, or immediate-task focus. There is a need for a compact, per-object timeline that supports natural-language queries over hours-to-days of observations.
AI.method: Introduce Linguistic Trajectory Encoding (LTE): a hybrid representation combining natural language descriptions, sparse spatial anchors, and visual anchors. LTE compresses object motion by anchoring unobserved periods to the last seen location, while representing motion with geometric waypoints and linguistic descriptions to preserve accuracy; evaluate on Spatial Memory Benchmark (SMB) derived from EgoLife multi-day recordings; compare against structured-memory and VLM baselines.
AI.result: LTE achieves 45.3% semantic trajectory retrieval and 48.7% long-horizon object retrieval on SMB (vs best prior 31.9% and 34.4%). Trajectory compression factors range 8.7x–26.1x with sub-second query latency on 24-hour video. On Ego4D natural-language queries, LTE attains 28.75% R@1 and 55.10% R@5, exceeding EgoVLPv2 by +15.80 and +31.30 points.
AI.conclusion: LTE enables effective, language-queryable per-object histories for long-horizon tasks, outperforming baselines in semantic trajectory and long-horizon object retrieval, with strong compression and low-latency queries.

title: WEECFP-SuRGE: Wide Embedded Extended Connectivity Fingerprint with Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding
summary: We introduce WEECFP, a parameter-free 1024-dimensional continuous molecular fingerprint that scatters each Morgan substructure across roughly thirty-two signed positions of a single vector, and WEECFP-SuRGE, a transformer architecture whose self-attention applies SuRGE (Substructure Rotary Graph-distance Encoding) -- a RoPE-like rotation parameterized by molecular shortest-path graph distance -- to WEECFP substructure tokens. A 7-model blend of this architecture (the WEECFP-SuRGE Blend) achieves the lowest average regression rank on the TDC ADMET leaderboard; is #2 overall on the TDC ADMET leaderboard (behind only pretrained MapLight+GNN), and is #1 overall among methods that use no external pretraining; takes leaderboard #1 finishes on Pgp, Lipophilicity, CYP2D6 Substrate, Clearance Microsome, and LD50 (with the WEECFP-NoSuRGE Blend separately reaching #1 on HIA) across the full 22-benchmark suite -- without any external pretraining. On MoleculeNet, WEECFP-SuRGE beats every classical-fingerprint baseline on 3 of 4 regression tasks (ESOL, Lipophilicity, QM9). We further show that WEECFP tokenization is near-lossless: a greedy overlap reconstruction recovers the exact canonical SMILES of 99.9% of in-distribution molecules across 9 MoleculeNet datasets and 98.93% of molecules in a cross-dataset holdout (HIV->Lipophilicity), and that a three-reference farthest-first encoding of graph distance correlates at Pearson r = 0.901 with the true pairwise distance, enabling O(S) positional memory at matching accuracy.

AI.tldr: WEECFP is a parameter-free 1024-D molecular fingerprint with SuRGE-enhanced transformer encoding, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive results on ADMET benchmarks without external pretraining; demonstrates near-lossless tokenization and distance-encoded substructure memory.
AI.motivation: To create accurate, parameter-efficient molecular representations that preserve substructure information and enable scalable, pretraining-free transformer models for ADMET and MoleculeNet tasks.
AI.method: Construct WEECFP: a 1024-dimensional fingerprint where each Morgan substructure is scattered across roughly 32 signed vector positions. WEECFP-SuRGE applies a RoPE-like rotation parameterized by shortest-path graph distance to WEECFP tokens. A 7-model blend (WEECFP-SuRGE Blend) achieves top ADMET performance; includes WEECFP-NoSuRGE variant. Uses three-reference farthest-first encoding for graph distance to enable O(S) positional memory. Tokenization accuracy assessed via greedy overlap reconstruction.
AI.result: WEECFP-SuRGE Blend attains the lowest average regression rank on the TDC ADMET leaderboard and is #2 overall (behind a pretrained MapLight+GNN), and #1 among methods without external pretraining. It secures #1 on several tasks (Pgp, Lipophilicity, CYP2D6 Substrate, Clearance Microsome, LD50) and WEECFP-NoSuRGE reaches #1 on HIA. On MoleculeNet, WEECFP-SuRGE outperforms classical fingerprints on 3/4 regression tasks (ESOL, Lipophilicity, QM9). Tokenization is near-lossless: 99.9% exact SMILES recovery in-distribution across 9 MoleculeNet datasets and 98.93% in a cross-dataset holdout (HIV→Lipophilicity). Three-reference farthest-first distance encoding yields Pearson r = 0.901 with true distances, enabling O(S) positional memory at matching accuracy.
AI.conclusion: WEECFP-SuRGE provides a competitive, pretraining-free molecular representation that combines efficient substructure tokenization with distance-aware RoPE-like encoding, yielding strong ADMET and MoleculeNet performance and robust token reconstruction, with scalable, memory-efficient positional encoding.

title: Same Trajectory, Contradictory Rewards (ROBORMBENCH): Paraphrase Fragility in Vision Language Reward Models
summary: Vision-language models are increasingly used as reward functions for robotic learning, but this role requires paraphrase invariance: the same trajectory should receive the same reward under semantically equivalent goal descriptions. We show that current VLM reward models often violate this property. Paraphrasing the instruction alone can substantially change predicted progress scores, and can even flip identical robot behavior between failure and success. To measure this failure mode, we introduce ROBORMBENCH, a benchmark with 2,390 real-robot trajectories, ground-truth progress labels, and 21,673 verified paraphrases spanning lexical, syntactic, and action-goal rewrites. Across proprietary and open-source VLMs, paraphrase-induced instability is widespread and severe, grows under more divergent rewrites, and is not reliably reduced by scale or explicit reasoning. Dedicated reward models trained with trajectory-grounded supervision are substantially more stable. These results show that paraphrase robustness is a core requirement for reliable VLM-based reward modeling in robotics.

AI.tldr: Paraphrase robustness is essential for VLM-based robot rewards; current VLM reward models are sensitive to textual paraphrase, causing unstable progress scores and even flips in outcome. A benchmark (ROBORMBENCH) with real trajectories and large paraphrase coverage shows widespread instability across models; trajectory-grounded supervised rewards are more stable.
AI.motivation: To enable reliable use of vision-language models as reward signals in robotic learning, it is crucial that rewards be invariant to semantically equivalent goal descriptions. The paper demonstrates that existing VLM rewards fail this invariance, risking misleading progress signals.
AI.method: Introduce ROBORMBENCH with 2,390 real-robot trajectories, ground-truth progress labels, and 21,673 verified paraphrases spanning lexical, syntactic, and action-goal rewrites. Evaluate both proprietary and open-source VLM reward models, analyze stability under paraphrases, and compare against trajectory-grounded supervised reward models.
AI.result: Paraphrase-induced instability is widespread and severe across VLMs; progress scores change substantially with paraphrase, can flip successful/failed behavior; instability grows with more divergent rewrites and is not reliably mitigated by scaling or explicit reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Paraphrase robustness is a core requirement for reliable VLM-based reward modeling in robotics; dedicated trajectory-grounded reward models substantially improve stability, suggesting future work should prioritize paraphrase-invariant reward learning.

title: Train What You Deploy:Token-Faithful Post-Training of a Production Coding
summary: Existing post-training pipelines for coding and terminal agents suffer severe token and control fidelity errors: simplified training environments mismatch production deployments, and offline token reconstruction from agent logs distorts original prompts and conflates policy calls with background model operations. We present a fidelity-aware training coupling framework that retains trainer-side sampling over original prompts, eliminates spurious model calls via a negotiated training protocol, and restricts loss computation to verifiable token spans with closed-failure guarantees. We further propose Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO), which establishes tight two-sided TV certification bounds, adaptive-K rules, budget-aware sequence guarantees, and error-robust policy masking atop standard DPPO. Evaluated on matched Baize5B and Baize10B models with identical training and test protocols on TMax-100, C-DPPO yields a consistent +3.0-point performance gain over standard DPPO across model scales. Certificate audits validate the reliability and full operational coverage of our certified training pipeline.

AI.tldr: Introduces fidelity-aware training coupling and Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO) to reduce token/control fidelity errors in post-training pipelines for coding/terminal agents; reports +3.0-point gains on Baize models with TV bounds and certificate audits.
AI.motivation: Address severe token and control fidelity errors arising from offline-to-online deployment, mismatched training environments, and reconstruction of prompts; improve reliability, verifiability, and safety of post-training pipelines for decision-making agents.
AI.method: Fidelity-aware training coupling that preserves trainer-side sampling on original prompts, uses a negotiated training protocol to eliminate spurious model calls, and confines loss to verifiable token spans with closed-failure guarantees. Introduces Certified Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (C-DPPO) with tight two-sided total variation bounds, adaptive-K rules, budget-aware sequence guarantees, and error-robust policy masking on top of standard DPPO.
AI.result: Evaluated on matched Baize5B and Baize10B models with identical training and test protocols on TMax-100. C-DPPO achieves a consistent +3.0-point performance gain over standard DPPO across scales. Certificate audits validate the reliability and full operational coverage of the certified training pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The fidelity-aware training coupling combined with C-DPPO enhances training reliability and performance in production-like settings, with verifiable guarantees and auditable pipelines; results suggest potential benefits for scalable, robust post-training workflows.

title: Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything
summary: Monocular depth estimation foundation models, such as the Depth Anything series, have achieved remarkable performance across diverse domains. However, they still suffer from critical failures under adverse weather conditions, such as fog, rain, snow, or at night. To address this, we present Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything (DA-W), a framework that explicitly disentangles style from content for weather-robust depth estimation. Specifically, we introduce a Style Filter trained on a curated mix of real and synthetic degradation datasets to extract content-independent, degradation-aware weather embeddings. This style embedding is then injected into the Depth Anything backbone using a parameter-efficient, zero-initialized adapter. Such a lightweight modulation allows a single unified model to robustly adapt to diverse conditions, including fog, rain, snow, and low-light, while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of its core generalization abilities in normal conditions. We train the adapter using a pseudo-label distillation and alignment strategy. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DA-W achieves state-of-the-art robust depth estimation, improving AbsRel by an average of 3.7% on our curated weather benchmarks, while matching or slightly outperforming performance on standard clean benchmarks. Our project page is available at https://zhaoming-tamu.github.io/WCDA/.

AI.tldr: DA-W introduces Weather-Conditioned Depth Anything: a style-filter based degradation-aware embedding injected via a lightweight adapter into Depth Anything, enabling robust monocular depth estimation across fog, rain, snow, and low light; achieves state-of-the-art robustness with ~3.7% AbsRel improvement on weather benchmarks while maintaining or slightly improving performance on clean data.
AI.motivation: Monocular depth estimation foundation models exhibit vulnerabilities under adverse weather; need robust, cross-condition performance without catastrophic forgetting of standard capabilities.
AI.method: A Style Filter is trained on a mix of real and synthetic degraded data to produce content-independent, degradation-aware weather embeddings. This embedding is injected into the Depth Anything backbone through a zero-initialized, parameter-efficient adapter. Training uses pseudo-label distillation and alignment to fuse the style with content.
AI.result: DA-W achieves state-of-the-art robust depth estimation, with an average AbsRel improvement of 3.7% on curated weather benchmarks, while matching or slightly outperforming on standard clean benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling style and content via a lightweight, adapter-based modulation enables robust, weather-conditioned monocular depth estimation without sacrificing normal performance, offering a compact, adaptable solution.

title: Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport with General Growth Penalty
summary: Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth or death. Unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) addresses this by penalizing growth along transport paths, making the choice of growth penalty a key way to encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis. However, existing UDOT solvers either rely on computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or depend on analytical solutions of conditional paths, restricting their efficiency solely to quadratic penalties, i.e. Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geodesics. To enable an efficient UDOT solver for general growth penalties, we first show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. We then introduce \textbf{S}imulation-free \textbf{U}nbalanced \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{O}ptimal transport (SUDO), a simulation-free framework for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties. SUDO learns the conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and subsequently leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient, analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors and produce more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.

AI.tldr: SUDO is a simulation-free unbalanced dynamic OT framework enabling general convex growth penalties beyond Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao, achieving fast and accurate UDOT by learning conditional paths and transport costs and solving a semi-coupling with unbalanced flow matching; it supports asymmetric growth priors and yields plausible trajectories on single-cell data.
AI.motivation: Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth/death. Existing UDOT methods are either computationally expensive (NeuralODE simulations) or restricted to quadratic penalties (WFR geodesics), limiting efficiency and applicability.
AI.method: Demonstrate that concave growth penalties cause separation of growth and transport. Introduce SUDO (Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport): a framework that learns conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and then applies unbalanced flow matching to obtain a simulation-free solution. Supports general non-quadratic convex growth penalties and avoids simulations (e.g., NeuralODE).
AI.result: On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient analytic-solution–driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, it supports asymmetric penalties encoding proliferation-dominant priors, producing more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.
AI.conclusion: SUDO extends unbalanced dynamic OT to general convex growth penalties with simulation-free computation, delivering competitive accuracy and speed, greater modeling flexibility, and plausible growth dynamics for single-cell trajectory inference.

title: Predicting Spatiotemporal Mobile Sensing-Based PM2.5 Concentrations Using Low-Rank Adapted Spatially Attentive Graph Neural Network
comment: 24 Pages, 14 Figures, World Conference of Transport Research2026 Transport Research
summary: Urban air quality can vary significantly along transit corridors, necessitating high-resolution monitoring. This work introduces a novel mobile-sensing dataset from Surat, Gujarat, India, comprising PM$*{2.5}$ concentrations, meteorological variables (temperature, humidity, wind speed, wind direction), and land-use features. To represent the spatiotemporal data as a graph, two node-definition strategies were used: (i) uniform segmentation (200--400~m intervals) and (ii) DBSCAN clustering to adaptively group dense observations. For each node, rolling mean and standard deviation of meteorological variables were computed. To model this high-dimensional data, we propose a SA-GNN for fine-grained, short-term PM$*{2.5}$ forecasting and hotspot identification. We compared SA-GNN with LSTM, RNN, GRU, and ANN models. These models performed well on low-resolution data but had difficulty capturing rapidly changing patterns in urban air quality. SA-GNN employs cluster-specific GRUs to capture localized temporal dependencies and a Graph Attention Network to learn spatial heterogeneity. This hybrid architecture effectively models rapid fluctuations and complex spatial interactions. On our dataset, SA-GNN achieved $R^2 = 0.95$, RMSE $= 6.8$, and MAE $= 4.2~\si{\micro\gram\per\meter\cubed}$, outperforming all baseline models. Combining spatial clustering with adaptive attention significantly improves forecasting, enabling real-time, fine-grained monitoring and supporting personalized exposure tracking and timely alerts for healthier cities.

AI.tldr: A novel mobile-sensing PM2.5 dataset in Surat for fine-grained, short-term forecasting using SA-GNN with cluster-specific GRUs and graph attention; outperforms LSTM/RNN/GRU/ANN (R2=0.95, RMSE=6.8, MAE=4.2 µg/m3).
AI.motivation: Urban air quality varies along transit corridors and at high spatiotemporal resolution; traditional models struggle with rapid urban fluctuations; new approaches are needed for real-time monitoring and personalized exposure.
AI.method: Collect mobile PM2.5 data along with meteorological variables and land-use. Define nodes via uniform segmentation (200–400 m) or DBSCAN clustering. Compute rolling mean/std for weather variables per node. Propose SA-GNN with cluster-specific GRUs and a Graph Attention Network; compare against LSTM, RNN, GRU, and ANN.
AI.result: SA-GNN achieved R^2=0.95, RMSE=6.8 µg/m3, MAE=4.2 µg/m3, outperforming all baselines; adaptive spatial clustering and attention enhance modeling of rapid fluctuations and spatial heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Combining spatial clustering with adaptive graph attention yields accurate, fine-grained short-term forecasts and supports real-time exposure tracking and alerts in healthier城市.

title: PAPT++: Risk-Aware Adversarial Tuning and Generation for Single Domain Generalization
summary: Single domain generalization (SDG) aims to learn a model from one labeled source domain that generalizes to unseen target domains. A common strategy is to enrich the source distribution with augmented or generated samples, and recent text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models provide a strong generative prior for this purpose. However, diversity alone is insufficient for robust generalization, because useful generated samples should also capture variations that the current classifier finds difficult. Motivated by distributionally robust optimization (DRO), we define a semantic ambiguity set in the class-conditional generative space of a pretrained T2I model and search it for samples with high classification loss under the current classifier. To this end, we introduce PAPT++, a risk-aware adversarial generation-training framework for SDG. PAPT++ first learns diverse semantic reference images for each class through image-text alignment and intra-class diversity regularization. These references then serve as denoising targets during classifier-guided diffusion synthesis, reducing semantic drift while guiding generation toward challenging variations. The generated samples are combined with the source data to update the classifier, and the updated classifier guides the next synthesis round in return. In this way, PAPT++ progressively exposes the classifier to challenging yet semantically consistent variations. Extensive experiments on standard SDG benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of the proposed PAPT++ method and the effectiveness of its main components.

AI.tldr: PAPT++ is a risk-aware adversarial generation-training framework for single domain generalization that uses semantic-ambiguity search in a pretrained T2I model to synthesize challenging yet semantically consistent samples, leveraging diverse semantic references and denoising targets to iteratively train the classifier.
AI.motivation: Diversity alone is insufficient for robust SDG; standard augmentation fails to cover hard variations. Inspired by distributionally robust optimization, define a class-conditional semantic ambiguity set in a T2I space and seek high-loss samples to harden the classifier.
AI.method: 1) Learn diverse semantic reference images per class via image-text alignment and intra-class diversity regularization. 2) Use these references as denoising targets during classifier-guided diffusion synthesis to reduce semantic drift and steer generation toward challenging variations. 3) Combine generated samples with source data to update the classifier; use the updated classifier to guide the next synthesis round, forming an iterative training loop.
AI.result: Experiments on standard SDG benchmarks show that PAPT++ outperforms baselines; ablations confirm the effectiveness of semantic reference learning, denoising targets, and risk-aware generation.
AI.conclusion: PAPT++ progressively exposes the classifier to challenging yet semantically consistent variations, improving SDG generalization by integrating semantic-aware diffusion synthesis with DRO-inspired adversarial sampling.

title: Locating and Steering Refusal Beyond Attention
comment: 33 pages, 6 figures, 26 tables; 10-page main text plus technical appendix
summary: Where inside a language model does refusal live, and does that place change when the architecture does? In a transformer, refusal is governed by a single direction in the residual stream, a finding that safety and interpretability tooling now depend on. State-space models (SSMs) route information through a recurrent update instead of attention, sharing no token-mixing mechanism with a transformer. Does the same safety representation survive this shift, or must it be rediscovered per architecture? It survives. A single rigid rotation, which can only reorient a space and not reshape it, aligns one model's representation space with another's, so the two genuinely share the representation. A harm probe trained on a transformer then flags an SSM's harmful inputs, and removing the aligned direction makes a model answer attacks it would otherwise refuse, while a random direction of the same size does far less. What is architecture-specific is not where the direction is steered but where it must be read. Each layer computes a fresh output that is then added into the residual stream, and harm is cleanly readable at this output, the write site, before the addition. A control that holds the intervention's strength fixed shows that what matters is where the direction is estimated, not where it is applied. Applied through a detector-triggered gate, this direction lowers jailbreak success in all four architecture families we test (SSM, transformer, recurrent, hybrid), and on the SSM it holds against an attacker that tunes its prompt against the defense. The gate only matches a trivial rule that returns a fixed refusal whenever the same detector fires, so what transfers across architectures is the direction itself, not defense strength. Safety tooling built on refusal therefore ports to a new architecture by re-estimating the direction at that architecture's write site, not by rebuilding it.

AI.tldr: Safety representations for refusal are architecture-agnostic in LMs; a single rotation aligns representations across transformers, SSMs, and other architectures; safety tooling can transfer by re-estimating the direction at each architecture’s write site.
AI.motivation: Determine whether refusal representations survive architecture shifts and where they reside in the model's computation.
AI.method: Train a harm probe on a transformer, align representations across architectures with a rigid rotation, test a detector-triggered gate for refusal, and analyze transfer across four architectures (transformer, SSM, recurrent, hybrid).
AI.result: A single rigid rotation aligns spaces across architectures; the same direction transfers; removing the aligned direction enables refusals to fail; the read-out point is at the write site (before residual addition); defense effectiveness depends on where the direction is estimated, not where applied; the gate reduces jailbreak across architectures; safety tooling ported by re-estimation at the new architecture's write site.
AI.conclusion: Refusal safety representations are architecture-invariant in terms of the direction; porting safety tooling requires re-estimation of the direction at the new architecture's write site rather than rebuilding the defense strength.

title: SQL-Zero: Self-Evolving Text-to-SQL
summary: Training a competitive Text-to-SQL agent usually depends on human-annotated natural-language/SQL pairs, which are expensive, domain-specific, and a bottleneck for scaling to new databases. We show it is possible to train a competitive solver with zero annotated pairs. We introduce SQL-Zero, a proposer-solver self-play in which a challenger and a solver start from the same base LLM and the only ground truth is execution against the database itself. The challenger generates SQL pairs calibrated to the solver's current difficulty (targeting "hard but solvable"), and both roles are updated with GRPO in alternating turns, with a template-level repetition penalty on the challenger to prevent diversity collapse. Training on BIRD databases with no labels, self-play improves over the zero-shot base on BIRD dev by 6.6 points at 3B and 7.3 points at 7B. It also scores higher than a matched control trained under the same recipe on human BIRD gold over the same databases, although an exact paired test does not resolve that margin. Transfer depends on scale: at 3B every iteration outperforms the base on unseen Spider databases and under lexical perturbation (Spider-Syn), where it also degrades less than the matched BIRD-gold control, whereas at 7B only the first iteration preserves transfer.

AI.tldr: Zero-annotated Text-to-SQL training via proposer-solver self-play (SQL-Zero); uses execution as ground truth; yields competitive performance and transfer gains on BIRD and Spider, with results scaling with model size.
AI.motivation: Eliminate the need for expensive NL/SQL labels to scale Text-to-SQL to new databases; exploit self-play and execution feedback to train competitive solvers from a base LLM.
AI.method: Proposer-solver self-play starting from a base LLM. A challenger generates SQL pairs calibrated to the solver's current difficulty; the solver attempts to solve; both roles are updated with GRPO in alternating turns. A template-level repetition penalty on the challenger mitigates diversity collapse. Training on BIRD without labels; evaluation on BIRD dev and comparison to gold and control baselines; transfer tests on Spider datasets and Spider-Syn.
AI.result: Self-play improves BIRD dev scores by 6.6 points at 3B and 7.3 points at 7B. It surpasses a matched gold-trained control on human BIRD gold over the same databases, though a precise paired test is inconclusive. Transfer is scale-dependent: at 3B, iterations outperform the base on unseen Spider and Spider-Syn with less degradation than the gold-control; at 7B, only the first iteration retains transfer.
AI.conclusion: Zero-annotated self-play can yield competitive Text-to-SQL performance and transfer, particularly at smaller scales; results highlight scale sensitivity and the need for careful design to maintain diversity and generalization. Further work could explore ablations (GRPO, penalty effects), robustness to diverse databases, and stronger evaluation on transfer datasets.

title: LetOccVote: Learning Weakly Supervised 3D Occupancy through Consensus
summary: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy prediction reduces the reliance on costly 3D annotations by learning from 2D pseudo-labels generated by vision foundation models. However, existing methods typically use these imperfect pseudo-labels directly as supervision, making occupancy learning vulnerable to erroneous geometric and semantic targets. We observe that agreement across repeated observations provides an inexpensive and reliable cue for assessing pseudo-label reliability. Based on this observation, we propose \textbf{LetOccVote}, a weakly supervised Gaussian-based occupancy framework that leverages cross-frame voting to improve both geometric and semantic supervision. For geometry, Depth Vote exploits cross-frame geometric agreement to refine supported pseudo depth and reject contradictory estimates before volumetric lifting and depth supervision. For semantics, Semantic Vote aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to identify reliable and contested evidence, strengthening reliable semantic supervision while filtering unreliable pseudo-label segments. The entire framework is trained solely with 2D pseudo-label supervision without requiring 3D occupancy annotations. On Occ3D-nuScenes, LetOccVote achieves 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU, establishing state-of-the-art performance among methods with 2D pseudo-label supervision.

AI.tldr: Weakly supervised 3D occupancy using LetOccVote with cross-frame Gaussian-based voting to refine 2D pseudo-labels for geometry (Depth Vote) and semantics (Semantic Vote); achieves SOTA among 2D-pseudo-label methods on Occ3D-nuScenes (53.27 IoU, 20.39 mIoU).
AI.motivation: Reduce reliance on costly 3D occupancy annotations by exploiting inexpensive cross-frame agreement as a reliability cue for 2D pseudo-labels.
AI.method: LetOccVote introduces cross-frame voting with Gaussian-based modeling. Depth Vote refines pseudo depths by leveraging geometric agreement across frames before volumetric lifting and depth supervision. Semantic Vote aggregates pseudo-semantic observations in a shared 3D space to distinguish reliable evidence from contested signals, enhancing semantic supervision.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance among methods using 2D pseudo-label supervision on Occ3D-nuScenes, achieving 53.27 IoU and 20.39 mIoU.
AI.conclusion: A fully weakly supervised framework trained with 2D pseudo-labels that improves both geometry and semantics through cross-frame agreement, demonstrating effective suppression of erroneous targets and robust 3D occupancy estimation.

title: Training Large Language Models for Small-Molecule Design with Synthetic Task Scaling
summary: Designing viable drug candidates requires searching a combinatorially large and rugged chemical space for molecules that satisfy multiple, often competing, objectives. Large language models (LLMs) provide a useful generative prior for this problem because of their representational capacity, reasoning ability, and flexibility when incorporating information from the external environment. While reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can be used to improve the capabilities of LLMs, many chemically relevant scoring functions require hours or even days per evaluation, making them prohibitively expensive to use directly during online training. Here, we investigate whether LLMs can learn molecular design strategies from cheaper synthetic tasks that generalize to expensive molecular lead optimization settings. We find that curriculum-based training recipes that gradually incorporate more challenging synthetic design tasks enable strong performance that surpasses that of much larger frontier models on structure-based lead optimization. Our results suggest that scaling post-training using synthetic tasks is an effective strategy for adapting LLMs to high-cost experimental scenarios that are too expensive to directly train on.

AI.tldr: Curriculum-guided synthetic-task pretraining lets LLMs learn molecular design strategies that generalize to expensive lead-optimization tasks, outperforming larger models when high-cost evaluations are involved.
AI.motivation: Designing viable drug candidates requires navigating an enormous, rugged chemical space with multiple objectives, while many scoring functions are expensive to evaluate; cheaper but representative training signals are needed to adapt LLMs for high-cost experimental scenarios.
AI.method: Create a sequence of increasingly challenging synthetic design tasks that mimic real molecular design objectives. Train LLMs with a curriculum on these tasks, then assess their performance on structure-based lead optimization with expensive scoring. Compare against much larger frontier models to evaluate generalization from cheap tasks to costly evaluations.
AI.result: LLMs trained via the curriculum on synthetic tasks achieve strong performance in structure-based lead optimization, surpassing much larger frontier models. The approach scales post-training with synthetic tasks to adapt LLMs to high-cost experiments that are impractical to train on directly.
AI.conclusion: Curriculum-based synthetic-task training is an effective, cost-efficient strategy to adapt LLMs for high-cost molecular design settings, enabling better transfer to expensive lead-optimization tasks and suggesting directions for refining curricula and synthetic task design.

title: Sound-based Multi-Person 3D Pose Estimation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026, Project Page: https://oumi03.github.io/sound-mhpe/
summary: Can we recover the 3D poses of multiple people using only sound? This paper presents the first attempt to estimate multi-person 3D poses solely from acoustic signals. Estimating the poses of multiple individuals using acoustic signals is inherently challenging due to the superposition of motion-dependent signal variations. Unlike single-person scenarios, the presence of multiple subjects leads to overlapping acoustic signatures, making it difficult to attribute specific signal changes to an individual's pose. Furthermore, the complexity is compounded by inter-person reflections, which introduce intricate propagation delays that obscure the temporal motion-acoustic relationship. To address these issues, we propose SoundMHPE (Sound-based Multi-person Human Pose Estimator), a novel encoder-decoder framework consisting of two key components. First, the Acoustic Multi-scale Encoder captures diverse temporal and fine-grained frequency features to isolate subtle acoustic signatures from complex, overlapping signals. Second, the Temporal Pose Decoder employs an attention mechanism to disentangle multi-person information across successive frames. By jointly accounting for temporal dynamics and inter-person dependencies, this component precisely reconstructs frame-wise individual poses. To validate our approach, we constructed the 6-hour Acoustic Multi-person Pose (AMP) dataset consisting of 432K synchronized frames of multi-person pose and acoustic data, and demonstrated that our SoundMHPE outperforms baseline models. Project page: https://oumi03.github.io/sound-mhpe/

AI.tldr: Pioneering work on multi-person 3D pose estimation from audio using SoundMHPE; an encoder-decoder with a multi-scale acoustic encoder and a temporal pose decoder; validated on a new AMP dataset (6 hours, 432k frames); outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Estimate 3D human poses solely from acoustic signals in multi-person settings, addressing challenges of overlapping signatures and inter-person reflections that hinder attribution of motion cues.
AI.method: Acoustic Multi-scale Encoder captures diverse temporal and frequency features; Temporal Pose Decoder uses attention to disentangle multi-person information across frames; jointly models temporal dynamics and inter-person dependencies to reconstruct per-frame poses.
AI.result: Creation of the Acoustic Multi-person Pose (AMP) dataset (6 hours, 432K synchronized frames) and empirical demonstration that SoundMHPE surpasses baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of acoustic-only multi-person pose estimation; introduces a dataset and architecture that show promise; future work could explore ablations, robustness, and broader generalization.

title: Model Retirement Creates Reproducibility Risk in Biomedical AI Publications
summary:
Background. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted in biomedical research at a rapid and accelerating pace, yet commercial services that host many widely used models operate under deprecation schedules that can complicate scientific reproducibility.
  Methods. We searched PubMed for original research articles from 2022 through March 2026 that applied a specific LLM to a biomedical task. An extraction agent identified model names from 61,077 article abstracts with human reviewers validating a subset for extraction accuracy. Extracted model names were normalized to canonical model identifiers. Lifecycle data (release date, retirement date, status) were compiled for the 50 most frequently used models.
  Results. We identified 8,931 paper-model mentions spanning 5,242 unique publications after restricting the analysis to the 50 most frequently used models. Among these mentions, 77.7% cited a commercial closed-weight model. Overall, 42% involved a model that was already retired by the time of official publication or is scheduled to retire within two years of publication. The median interval from publication to model retirement was 538 days.
  Conclusion. Many biomedical publications using LLMs are on a trajectory toward computational non-reproducibility after publication. Model deprecation should be treated as a core reporting and preservation issue for biomedical research.

AI.tldr: Many biomedical papers using LLMs rely on models that retire or will retire soon, threatening reproducibility; a lifecycle-aware reporting approach is needed.
AI.motivation: Address reproducibility challenges in biomedical LLM research due to model deprecation and commercial hosting schedules.
AI.method: Systematic bibliometric study identifying LLM usage in PubMed abstracts (2022–Mar 2026); automated extraction of model names from 61,077 abstracts; normalization to canonical IDs; construction of lifecycle data for top 50 models; validation on a subset.
AI.result: 8,931 paper–model mentions across 5,242 publications; 77.7% use commercial closed-weight models; 42% use models retired or retiring within 2 years of publication; median time to retirement ≈ 538 days.
AI.conclusion: Model deprecation poses reproducibility risks; lifecycle reporting/preservation should be integrated into biomedical research practices.

title: Mitigating Performance Discrepancy in Cross-Domain 3D Class-Incremental Learning
summary: 3D perception plays a crucial role in real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and AR/VR. In practical scenarios, 3D perception models need to continually adapt to newly emerging 3D object categories, making class-incremental learning (CIL) particularly important. However, unlike 2D images, 3D point clouds are inherently heterogeneous: objects from the same class may not only come from the clean CAD domain, but also from RGB-D camera scans of varying quality, video reconstructions, or even corrupted observations. We discover that such heterogeneity introduces a new challenge beyond catastrophic forgetting: the degree of performance degradation can vary substantially across domains, a phenomenon we term performance discrepancy. To investigate this problem, we establish the Domain3D-CIL training and evaluation protocol, which contains point cloud categories from heterogeneous domains. We further adapt a wide range of mainstream CIL methods to the 3D modality. The results demonstrate that this performance discrepancy consistently appears across these baselines. To mitigate this issue, we introduce PolyMem, an exemplar-free approach that implicitly models rich high-order statistics of the feature distribution to enhance cross-domain robustness. Experiments demonstrate that our method effectively alleviates the performance discrepancy while improving the model's performance across domains. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: 3D class-incremental learning across heterogeneous domains; PolyMem reduces cross-domain performance discrepancy without using exemplars.
AI.motivation: 3D perception must continually adapt to new object categories. Point clouds are inherently heterogeneous (CAD, RGB-D scans, reconstructions, corrupted observations). This heterogeneity causes a performance discrepancy across domains that goes beyond catastrophic forgetting. A protocol to evaluate domain-robust CIL for 3D is needed.
AI.method: Introduce Domain3D-CIL training/evaluation protocol with heterogeneous domain point clouds. Adapt mainstream CIL methods to 3D. Propose PolyMem, an exemplar-free approach that implicitly models high-order feature distribution statistics to improve cross-domain robustness.
AI.result: The performance discrepancy persists across baseline CIL methods in Domain3D-CIL. PolyMem effectively alleviates the cross-domain performance gap and improves overall performance across domains.
AI.conclusion: PolyMem provides a robust, exemplar-free solution for cross-domain 3D CIL, addressing a new domain-heterogeneity challenge and enhancing cross-domain generalization; code will be released after acceptance.

title: A Fairness Audit of the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern Method: Format-Specific and Gender-Differential Bias, with an Interpretable Calibration Layer for Cricket Target Revision
comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (JQAS); forthcoming
summary: The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method has been the international standard for revising target scores in rain-interrupted limited-overs cricket since 1999. Despite over two decades of operational use, no large-scale empirical audit of its prediction bias has been published. We conduct such an audit on 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet, generating 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. We document two structured biases. First, DLS prediction error spans a 137-run range across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) match-state buckets. Second, DLS exhibits a gender-differential bias on ODIs that has not previously been quantified: on the training split, mean over-prediction is +1.51 runs for men but +7.63 runs for women, a gap of +6.13 runs (F = 195.16, p < 10^-43). We benchmark DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble, and propose DLS-Cal, a lightweight interpretable calibration layer (27K parameters) outputting a state-conditioned correction added to DLS. DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I, and a gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs while leaving men's calibration unchanged. We release code, models, and data.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical audit of the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method finds structured biases in target-revision predictions, including a 137-run spread across match-state buckets and a notable gender-differential bias in ODIs. The work introduces DLS-Cal, a lightweight calibration layer, and a gender-aware variant that substantially reduce bias, outperforming several modern ML baselines; authors release code, models, and data.
AI.motivation: Despite decades of operational use, there has been no comprehensive, large-scale audit of DLS prediction bias. The study aims to quantify magnitude and structure of biases, assess gender disparities, and explore calibrated and ML-based alternatives to improve accuracy and fairness.
AI.method: They assemble 8,150 international matches (3,095 ODIs, 5,055 T20Is) from Cricsheet and generate 233,550 synthetic interruption scenarios with temporal splits. They benchmark DLS against five modern alternatives: Bi-LSTM, XGBoost, an enriched XGBoost variant, a deep context-aware model, and a stacking ensemble. They propose DLS-Cal, a 27k-parameter, state-conditioned calibration layer that outputs a correction added to DLS; they also evaluate a gender-aware variant. They report joint biases and statistical significance (e.g., F = 195.16, p < 1e-43) on training data.
AI.result: Two structured biases are documented: (1) DLS prediction error spans 137 runs across (overs-remaining, wickets-lost) state buckets. (2) A gender-differential bias on ODIs; mean over-prediction is +1.51 runs for men vs +7.63 runs for women on the training split (+6.13 run gap; F = 195.16, p < 1e-43). DLS-Cal reduces absolute bias by 31% on ODI and 19% on T20I; a gender-aware variant reduces women's ODI residual bias from +6.19 to +0.65 runs, leaving men's calibration unchanged. Baselines are provided; data, models, and code are released.
AI.conclusion: DLS exhibits structured, addressable biases in rain-interrupted matches. Calibration-based approaches (DLS-Cal) and gender-aware calibration substantially reduce bias with modest parameter counts, supporting their deployment to improve fairness and accuracy. The authors provide resource release for reproducibility.

title: One Diffusion Model, Two Roles: Guided Trajectory Planning and Safety-Critical Scenario Generation in Closed-Loop Simulation
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026 workshop. Arka and Rajesh have equal contribution
summary: Diffusion probabilistic models can capture the multi-modal, interaction-rich distribution of joint future trajectories in driving scenes. We show that a single pretrained diffusion traffic model can serve two complementary roles in the autonomous driving development loop: as an ego motion planner, and as a controllable generator of safety-critical scenarios for stress-testing the planners. On the planning side, we introduce a Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) diffusion-transformer decoder that fuses scene context via joint attention rather than late cross-attention, improving closed-loop performance on nuPlan. We further propose Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy (DAPSE), a training-free guidance scheme that injects arbitrary energy functions at the clean-sample level, avoiding the first-order approximation errors while requiring no auxiliary networks. Beyond planning, we leverage the same diffusion model as a controllable scenario generator to create realistic long-tail driving interactions for closed-loop evaluation. Through inference-time guidance, selected agents are steered toward safety-critical behaviors, including aggressive cut-ins, lead-vehicle braking, and combined longitudinal-lateral interactions, while preserving realistic traffic behaviors. Evaluated in closed-loop nuPlan simulations with independent black-box planners, the generated scenarios expose failure modes that remain hidden under standard benchmarks. Although the SSDS-based planner achieves stronger nominal performance, it experiences larger degradation under these challenging scenarios, demonstrating that benchmark superiority does not necessarily translate to robustness. These results demonstrate that a single learned traffic prior can simultaneously improve motion planning and provide a realistic framework for systematic planner robustness evaluation.

AI.tldr: A single pretrained diffusion-based traffic model can both plan ego motion and controllably generate safety-critical driving scenarios for stress-testing planners, using a novel SSDS decoder and a training-free DAPSE guidance, with robust evaluation showing nominal gains but reduced robustness under challenging conditions.
AI.motivation: Address the need for unified, probabilistic modeling of multi-modal joint future trajectories in driving scenes and provide an actionable stress-testing framework for planners, using a single learned prior to improve planning while enabling controllable scenario generation for robustness evaluation.
AI.method: Introduce Single-Stream Dual-Stream (SSDS) diffusion-transformer decoder that fuses scene context via joint attention (not late cross-attention). Propose Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling with Energy (DAPSE), a training-free guidance scheme injecting energy functions at clean-sample level to steer samples without first-order approximation errors or extra networks. Use inference-time guidance to steer selected agents toward safety-critical behaviors during long-horizon scene generation. Evaluate on nuPlan in closed-loop simulations with independent black-box planners to assess planning performance and robustness.
AI.result: SSDS improves closed-loop planning performance on nuPlan. DAPSE enables flexible guidance without training, preserving realism. The diffusion model also acts as a controllable scenario generator, revealing failure modes under stress tests not visible in standard benchmarks. However, though SSDS has stronger nominal performance, it shows larger degradation under safety-critical scenarios, indicating benchmark superiority does not guarantee robustness.
AI.conclusion: A single learned traffic prior can enhance motion planning and serve as a realistic framework for systematic planner robustness evaluation. The study highlights the separation between nominal planning gains and robustness under adversarial or long-tail scenarios, emphasizing the need for stress-testing with controllable scenario generation.

title: FinalityBench: An Effect-Level Benchmark for Agent Decisions Under Delayed and Conflicting Financial Finality
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code, corpus generator and all result files: https://github.com/abhisheksharma2411/finalitybench Archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22262591
summary: A merchant's payment processor, ledger, ERP and bank feed are updated by messages that get delayed, duplicated, dropped and reordered, so for minutes at a time the four hold contradictory beliefs about the same order. An agent resolving the exception must decide whether to ship goods, re-submit a capture, refund or wait, knowing some of those cannot be undone. We present FinalityBench, an executable benchmark for that decision. It keeps a hidden canonical event log and derives each system's view from a separately faulted delivery stream, so disagreement follows from specified fault semantics rather than being authored. Grading is on executed monetary effects: an episode is scored by the merchant's terminal economic position, relative to a privileged reference told when the pending capture resolves. The corpus of 321 tasks includes 45 twin pairs (90 tasks): tasks whose four system views are identical at the decision instant, whose authoritative probes both return unknown, and whose eventual correct dispositions differ. That snapshot indistinguishability is checked under every evaluation seed rather than assumed; equivalence over all interaction traces is not claimed. Over 14,445 graded episodes from nine programmatic policies, ranking by single-task accuracy and by paired loss disagree in 7 places: a ship-on-first-sign policy is second-best by accuracy at 65.7% and worst in the suite by paired loss, because it cannot tell the two members apart. A runtime gating irreversible actions on an authoritative finality probe reaches 85.4% and, unlike every polling policy, loses nothing to pass^5; its residual loss is almost entirely one archetype, which prices finality information directly. Language models reach the same exact rate as the hand-written gate on a stratified subset, lose about twice as much money, and discover the finality-gating strategy without being told it.

AI.tldr: FinalityBench is an executable benchmark that evaluates decision policies for order finality under asynchronous, fault-prone multi-system views, scoring monetary outcomes and incorporating an authoritative finality gate.
AI.motivation: To study how agents resolve exceptions when four interconnected systems (merchant processor, ledger, ERP, bank feed) may disagree due to delays, drops, and reordering, and to quantify policy performance by economic impact rather than nominal correctness.
AI.method: Construct a benchmark with a hidden canonical event log and separate fault-injected delivery streams; create 321 tasks (including 90 twin pairs) that induce divergent system views; evaluate policies via 14,445 graded episodes across nine policies; measure outcomes by merchant terminal position at resolution; include an authoritative finality probe (gate) and assess whether different policies can distinguish indistinguishable snapshots; compare hand-written policies to language-model-based policies.
AI.result: Gating irreversible actions using a finality probe reaches 85.4% effectiveness with minimal residual loss; twin-pair tasks reveal policies differing in paired loss vs accuracy (e.g., ship-on-first-sign) due to indistinguishability; language models reach comparable accuracy to a hand-written gate on stratified subsets but incur higher monetary loss, yet can discover the finality-gating strategy autonomously.
AI.conclusion: Finality-aware decision policies that leverage an authoritative finality signal substantially improve monetary outcomes; the benchmark exposes trade-offs between prompt action and correctness under fault semantics, and demonstrates that language models can learn effective finality strategies without explicit instruction.

title: SimFuse3D: Source-Guided Target Simulation and Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting for Cross-Platform 3D Object Detection
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
summary: Changes in sensor height and viewpoint alter object-level point distributions, making cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) difficult. Self-training uses labeled source scans and unlabeled target scans, yet a retained prediction may provide a useful target location while enclosing sparse foreground returns, background clutter, or points inconsistent with the predicted box. We refer to this mismatch as box-point inconsistency. We introduce SimFuse3D, which preserves the target placement and repairs the associated pseudo-object using measured geometry from labeled source scans. Object Memory retrieves a compatible labeled source instance. Target Simulation places its ground-truth box at the target location, aligns its points with the target viewing geometry, and filters the aligned crop to approximate the target observation. Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) maps each target pseudo-object confidence score to a bounded weight shared by RPN localization and R-CNN box regression. All components operate only during adaptation, leaving the detector architecture and inference graph unchanged. Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D exceeds Pi3DET-Net on every reported AP metric and ranks first among the compared adaptation methods on nearly all metrics. On nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first among the compared adaptation methods with both evaluated detectors.

AI.tldr: SimFuse3D is a domain-adaptive framework for cross-platform LiDAR that repairs pseudo-objects during self-training using source geometry, memory retrieval, target simulation, and confidence-guided reweighting, achieving state-of-the-art results across six transfers.
AI.motivation: Cross-platform LiDAR unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) is hindered by changes in sensor height and viewpoint, which alter object-level point distributions and create box-point inconsistency between predicted boxes and target observations.
AI.method: Introduce three adaptation-only components: Object Memory to retrieve compatible labeled source instances, Target Simulation to align ground-truth boxes and crops to the target view, and Confidence-Guided Multi-Stage Localization Reweighting (CMLR) to map pseudo-object confidence to a bounded weight shared by RPN localization and R-CNN regression. All components operate during adaptation without changing detector architecture or inference graph.
AI.result: Across six cross-platform transfers, SimFuse3D outperforms Pi3DET-Net on all reported AP metrics and ranks first among compared methods on most metrics. In nuScenes-to-KITTI, it ranks first among comparators for both evaluated detectors.
AI.conclusion: SimFuse3D effectively mitigates box-point inconsistency and improves cross-platform LiDAR UDA without modifying the detector, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple transfers.

title: Resilience Beyond Stationary Client Unavailability: Unlocking Efficient and Unbiased Federated Learning
summary: Due to resource constraints or external and internal uncertainties, clients in real-world federated learning systems are often intermittently available edge devices. In highly dynamic environments, the parameter server lacks prior real-time knowledge of clients' availability, making it challenging to adapt traditional federated learning algorithms to be resilient to uncertainties in client availability. If not carefully addressed, complex client availability can introduce significant bias, potentially harming the performance of the trained model. Most prior work either fails to account for non-stationary client availability dynamics or demands significant memory and computational overhead. This paper aims to develop efficient federated learning algorithms that are provably resilient to heterogeneous and non-stationary stochastic client availability. We propose FedSWE, which admits novel algorithmic structures to (i) compensate for missed computations, (ii) stabilize and diffuse the global updates over rounds, and (iii) evenly mix the local updates through implicit gossiping, despite being agnostic to non-stationary dynamics. Compared with the standard FedAvg, FedSWE introduces light additional memory and computation overhead. We show that FedSWE converges to a stationary point of non-convex objectives while achieving the desired linear speedup property in certain special cases. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments over diversified client unavailability dynamics on real-world data sets.

AI.tldr: FedSWE is a lightweight robust federated learning algorithm designed for heterogeneous, non-stationary client availability. It achieves convergence to a stationary point in non-convex settings and exhibits linear speedup in certain regimes, using three mechanisms: compensation for missed computations, diffusion of global updates, and implicit gossiping to mix local updates.
AI.motivation: In real-world federated learning, client devices are intermittently available and lack real-time knowledge of their availability. This non-stationary, heterogeneous client participation can bias learning and degrade performance. There is a need for algorithms with provable resilience that operate with low additional memory and computation.
AI.method: FedSWE introduces three algorithmic structures: (i) compensation for missed computations to handle unavailable clients, (ii) stabilization and diffusion of global updates across rounds to reduce variance and drift, and (iii) implicit gossiping to mix local updates evenly. The approach is agnostic to non-stationary dynamics and aims for low overhead compared to FedAvg. Theoretical analysis shows convergence to a stationary point for non-convex objectives and linear speedup in certain special cases; empirical evaluations validate performance under diverse availability dynamics on real datasets.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantee: convergence to a stationary point of non-convex objectives; potential linear speedup in certain regimes. Empirical results: numerical experiments on real-world datasets with various non-stationary client unavailability patterns demonstrating robustness and competitive performance relative to standard FedAvg.
AI.conclusion: FedSWE provides provable resilience to heterogeneous, non-stationary client availability with modest memory and computation overhead, improving robustness of FL in dynamic environments. It complements FedAvg and offers a concrete mechanism to mitigate bias from intermittent participation; conclusions assume stochastic availability patterns and may depend on liquidity of communications and system parameters.

title: MINT: A Unified Model for World-Space Camera and Hand Motion Estimation from Scalable Egocentric Pipeline Supervision
summary: Recovering camera and hand motion in world coordinates from egocentric video is a key capability for activity understanding, robot learning, and augmented reality. Existing systems typically decompose this problem into separate stages for camera motion, depth, hand reconstruction, and trajectory refinement, resulting in substantial computational overhead and preventing the joint modeling of camera and hand motion. We introduce MINT (Minting IN-the-Wild Trajectories), the first foundation model that directly produces complete world-space two-hand trajectories from ego-centric RGB video. From a single shared spatiotemporal video representation, MINT jointly predicts the camera trajectory, camera-frame hand states, and per-frame hand presence, and then produces world-space hand motion via explicit coordinate transformations. Training such a model at scale is challenging, since paired world-space camera and hand annotations are scarce. We therefore develop an open-source labeling EGOPIPELINE that converts large collections of public egocentric videos into structured camera-and-hand trajectory supervision. MINT is first pretrained on these large-scale pseudo-labels and then fine-tuned on a small set of high-quality joint annotations. Across public benchmarks, MINT achieves [xxx] improvement in world-space hand trajectory accuracy, [xxx] improvement in camera trajectory estimation, and [xxx] faster end-to-end trajectory generation than the labeling pipeline, while generalizing zero-shot to unseen egocentric datasets. We release the model, training and inference code, labeling pipeline, and a curated 1,021-hour egocentric trajectory dataset.

AI.tldr: MINT is a foundation model that directly outputs world-space two-hand trajectories from egocentric video by jointly predicting camera motion, hand states, and per-frame hand presence from a single spatiotemporal representation, using pseudo-label pretraining via EGOPIPELINE and fine-tuning on limited annotations.
AI.motivation: Enable joint, efficient estimation of camera and hand motion in world coordinates from ego-centric video to support activity understanding, robot learning, and AR, while avoiding costly multi-stage pipelines and enabling zero-shot generalization.
AI.method: Unified spatiotemporal video representation that jointly predicts: (i) camera trajectory, (ii) camera-frame hand states, and (iii) per-frame hand presence; world-space hand motion obtained through explicit coordinate transformations. Training uses an open-source labeling pipeline (EGOPIPELINE) to convert large public egocentric videos into structured camera-and-hand trajectories (pseudo-labels) for large-scale pretraining, followed by fine-tuning on a smaller set of high-quality joint annotations. End-to-end trajectory generation is faster than the labeling pipeline and zero-shot generalizes to unseen egocentric datasets.
AI.result: The paper reports improved world-space hand trajectory accuracy and camera trajectory estimation, with faster end-to-end trajectory generation compared to the labeling pipeline, and zero-shot generalization across unseen datasets; it also releases the model, code, labeling pipeline, and a 1,021-hour dataset.
AI.conclusion: MINT introduces a scalable, joint modeling framework for world-space hand and camera motion from egocentric video, backed by a practical data-labeling pipeline and open resources, enabling broader research and applications in activity understanding and robotics.

title: PLUME: Parameter-Efficient Personalization of Large Language Models via Low-Rank User Modulation in Shared Subspaces
summary: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) is essential for delivering AI assistance that aligns with individual users' styles, intents, and preferences. While per-user fine-tuning can substantially enhance personalization quality, it introduces significant parameter and storage overhead, limiting scalability to large user populations. We propose PLUME (Personalized Low-Rank Adaptation through User Modulation and Shared Subspace), a lightweight framework that achieves efficient and expressive per-user adaptation by leveraging a shared task-specific subspace. Specifically, PLUME first learns a global task subspace from aggregated user data. Personalization is then achieved by training only a lightweight small square matrix within this subspace, enabling each user to obtain a tailored model while keeping shared components fixed. Cross-layer shared parameters and rank-1 residual terms are further introduced to significantly reduce redundancy while maintaining expressiveness. Experiments on multiple personalized text generation benchmarks demonstrate that PLUME achieves comparable or superior performance to strong baselines, while reducing per-user parameters by over 95%. These results establish shared-subspace modulation with minimal residuals as a scalable and semantically grounded approach to LLM personalization.

AI.tldr: PLUME introduces a shared-subspace, low-rank per-user adaptation for LLMs, enabling efficient personalization by training a per-user small square matrix within a global task subspace, with cross-layer sharing and rank-1 residuals to reduce redundancy. It achieves comparable or superior personalization while reducing per-user parameters by >95%.
AI.motivation: Personalizing LLMs is essential to align with individual users, but per-user fine-tuning is parameter- and storage-intensive and scales poorly to large user populations.
AI.method: Learn a global task subspace from aggregated user data. For each user, train only a lightweight small square matrix inside this subspace, with shared components kept fixed. Apply cross-layer shared parameters and rank-1 residuals to minimize redundancy while preserving expressiveness.
AI.result: In experiments across multiple personalized text generation benchmarks, PLUME achieves comparable or superior performance to strong baselines while reducing per-user parameters by over 95%.
AI.conclusion: Shared-subspace modulation with minimal residuals offers a scalable and semantically grounded approach to LLM personalization.

title: A Robust Watermark-based Fingerprint Framework for GNNs Ownership Verification
summary: The high training cost of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has raised growing concerns regarding model ownership infringement, such as model stealing and unauthorized misuse. To verify model ownership and prevent significant economic losses, two groups of GNN Ownership Verification (OV) methods have been proposed: watermark-based methods and fingerprint-based methods. However, these methods typically face three limitations: (1) the performance degradation of protected models caused by out-of-distribution (OOD) watermark graphs with respect to the training set; (2) the unrealistic assumption that surrogate models have been trained on a watermark-containing training set; and (3) over-reliance on specific output levels for fingerprint extraction. In this paper, we propose a Robust watErMArk-based fingeRprint frameworK for GNNs, named REMARK. REMARK first generates carefully crafted in-distribution watermark graphs that maximize output differences between GNN models, thus mitigating OOD-induced performance degradation. REMARK then extracts robust fingerprints from these output differences to verify GNN ownership, thereby removing the assumptions that surrogate models must be trained on a watermark-containing dataset or expose specific output levels. Extensive experiments across widely used real-world datasets and GNN architectures demonstrate that REMARK achieves state-of-the-art OV accuracy and robustness while preserving the utility of protected models.

AI.tldr: Introduces REMARK, a robust watermark/fingerprint framework for GNN ownership verification that uses in-distribution watermark graphs and output-difference fingerprints to achieve high OV accuracy/robustness without requiring watermark training data or fixed output levels.
AI.motivation: Overcomes three core limitations of prior GNN OV methods: (i) performance drop under out-of-distribution watermark graphs, (ii) assumption that surrogate models are trained on watermark-containing data, and (iii) dependence on predefined output levels for fingerprint extraction.
AI.method: 1) Generate in-distribution watermark graphs designed to maximize output differences between GNN models; 2) Extract robust fingerprints from the resulting output differences; 3) Verify ownership by matching fingerprints, without relying on watermark-training data or specific outputs.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets and architectures show state-of-the-art OV accuracy and robustness, while preserving protected model utility.
AI.conclusion: REMARK provides a practical, robust solution for GNN ownership verification, mitigating OOD-related performance issues and reducing reliance on restrictive assumptions; suitable for broad deployment in model protection.

title: CrossDepth: Geometry-Constrained Attention for Generalizable Multi-View Surround Depth Estimation
summary: Reliable 3D understanding of the surrounding environment is a core requirement for autonomous driving. Multi-view surround camera rigs provide broad scene coverage, but the spatially adjacent images typically overlap only minimally. Consequently, the depth of most pixels must be inferred from monocular appearance cues. These cues can appear differently across images and may therefore be interpreted differently by the depth estimation model. We target two main sources of cross-image inconsistency: differences in camera intrinsics and the limited receptive field of each image. We address the former by conditioning the features on per-pixel camera-aware ray embeddings, enabling the network to account for camera-dependent variations in monocular cues. We address the latter by extending each pixel's context beyond its own image through cross-image attention constrained to geometrically plausible regions, derived from the calibrated rig setup. The model is trained in a fully self-supervised manner based on photometric consistency. Evaluations on DDAD and nuScenes show improved overall depth accuracy and cross-image depth consistency over state-of-the-art self-supervised methods under in-domain and cross-domain evaluation. Code is available at https://abualhanud.github.io/CrossDepthPage/.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised cross-view depth estimation method for multi-view surround cameras using camera-aware ray embeddings and geometry-constrained cross-image attention, improving depth accuracy and cross-image consistency on DDAD and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving requires robust 3D understanding. Multi-view surround rigs have limited overlapping views, causing monocular cues to be interpreted inconsistently across images. Differences in camera intrinsics and small receptive fields exacerbate cross-image inconsistency. The goal is to align monocular cues across views and leverage cross-view context within geometric constraints.
AI.method: Introduce per-pixel camera-aware ray embeddings to condition features on camera intrinsics. Extend each pixel's context using cross-image attention constrained to geometrically plausible regions derived from the calibrated rig. Train the model in a fully self-supervised fashion using photometric consistency.
AI.result: On DDAD and nuScenes, the approach achieves improved depth accuracy and cross-image depth consistency compared to state-of-the-art self-supervised methods, in-domain and cross-domain. The authors also release code at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: Camera-aware ray conditioning plus geometry-constrained cross-image attention effectively mitigate cross-image inconsistency in multi-view surround setups, enhancing self-supervised depth estimation and generalization across domains.

title: Aplaud: Adaptive Personalized Low-Rank Decomposition for User-Specific LLM
summary: In this paper, we study the problem of personalized survey response prediction using fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). This task poses unique challenges: limited per-user training data, scalability of model storage, and the need to exploit shared structure across survey questions. To address these issues, we propose Aplaud (Adaptive Personalized Low-rank and User-specific Nested Decomposition), a lightweight and scalable framework for LLM personalization. Aplaud extends the LoRA paradigm by separating adaptation into a frozen, shared low-rank basis and a compact user-specific correction, augmented with a rank-one residual for finer personalization. To further reduce per-user parameter cost and mitigate overfitting, the correction matrix can be factorized into an even lower-rank form. Empirical results demonstrate that Aplaud achieves efficient, scalable personalization across users while outperforming state-of-the-art LoRA-based personalized LLM approaches in both generalization and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Aplaud is a scalable, personalized LLM adaptation framework that extends LoRA with a shared low-rank basis plus user-specific correction and an optional rank-one residual, with possible further factorization to reduce per-user parameters, achieving better generalization and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Personalization of LLMs with very limited per-user data, scalability of model storage, and leveraging shared structure across survey questions.
AI.method: Aplaud decomposes adaptation into a frozen, shared low-rank basis and a compact user-specific correction; augments with a rank-one residual for fine personalization; the correction can be factorized into an even lower-rank form; extends LoRA's paradigm for scalable personalization.
AI.result: Empirical results show that Aplaud enables efficient, scalable personalization across users and outperforms state-of-the-art LoRA-based personalized LLM approaches in generalization and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Aplaud offers a lightweight, scalable personalization framework that reduces per-user parameters, mitigates overfitting, and improves generalization and efficiency for personalized LLM deployment.

title: InterSing: Explicit Interaction Dynamics for 3D Duet Singing Animation and Beyond
summary: We present InterSing, a framework for generating realistic 3D head animations for duet singing performances. Unlike solo singing, duet performance requires each singer to balance individual expressiveness with intermittent interaction at musically salient moments, such as phrase boundaries, synchronized rhythms, and call-and-response passages. Because these interactions are sparse and rhythm-dependent, existing audio-driven animation methods and conversational interaction models do not adequately capture their structure. Our key insight is that duet coordination can be represented as a time-varying signal that reflects how strongly performers engage with one another throughout a song.
