Based on this observation, we introduce interaction logits, an interpretable latent representation that models the degree of cross-performer engagement at each time step. We learn these logits using weak supervision and use them to condition an interaction-aware diffusion model jointly driven by audio features and interaction dynamics. This formulation enables unified multi-mode generation, spanning independent motion, coordinated behavior, and smooth transitions between them. Experiments show that InterSing generates realistic and expressive singing head animations with stronger coordination and musical alignment than existing methods, while preserving each performer's characteristic motion style. We further demonstrate that the same formulation generalizes to multi-singer performances and provides intuitive control over when and how performers engage.

AI.tldr: Diffusion-based duet singing head animation using interaction logits; interpretable latent for cross-performer engagement enabling independent, coordinated, and transitioning motion with weak supervision; generalizes to multi-singer and offers intuitive control.
AI.motivation: Duet coordination is sparsely interactive and rhythm-dependent, not well captured by solo-focused audio-driven or conversational models; a time-varying engagement signal is needed.
AI.method: Introduce interaction logits learned with weak supervision; condition an interaction-aware diffusion model on audio features and logits; supports multi-mode generation across independent/coordinated/transition; extends to multi-singer.
AI.result: Empirically shows improved realism, coordination, and musical alignment over baselines; preserves each performer's motion style; generalizes to multi-singers; provides intuitive control of engagement timing.
AI.conclusion: InterSing provides an interpretable latent representation for duet interaction, enabling unified generation and potential applicability to broader multi-performer scenarios.

title: Persistent Teacher Anchoring for Tool-Using Agents
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference)
summary: Distillation is common in LLM post-training, where on-policy knowledge distillation (OPKD) uses student-generated trajectories to prepare the student for downstream RL. At each state, the student matches a next-token distribution supplied by the teacher. As the rollout enters states the teacher would not visit, the teacher-student distribution gap can accumulate. In tool use, this gap becomes consequential because student-written calls execute before supervision and their observations shape later prefixes. Proposer-verifier generation addresses this drift by letting the teacher decide which student-proposed text is retained during generation. Existing formulations govern text but leave tool execution outside their scope. We propose Persistent Teacher Anchoring (PTA), a student-induced but teacher-committed rollout construction. PTA retains chunk-level verification and adds turn-level commitment, allowing a call to reach the environment only after the teacher has verified the entire turn. Treating verified chunks as atomic generation units, we introduce persistent lookahead, which fills idle rollout capacity by advancing future samples and carrying unfinished ones across student updates under the fixed verifier. Across Search-R1-style retrieval and DeepEyes-style perception RL, applying PTA before downstream RL improves macro best@4 by 2.5 and 2.8 points over OPKD under the same downstream RL budget, while lookahead improves throughput by 24%.

AI.tldr: Persistent Teacher Anchoring (PTA) mitigates teacher-student drift in on-policy knowledge distillation with tool use, by chunk-level verification, turn-level commitment, and persistent lookahead; it improves downstream RL performance and throughput compared with OPKD.
AI.motivation: Teacher-student distribution mismatch accumulates when rollout visits states the teacher wouldn't, and tool execution adds complexity since actions precede supervision; existing text-only formulations neglect tool execution.
AI.method: Proposes PTA: a rollout construction with chunk-level verification and turn-level commitment; calls reach environment only after full turn verification; treats verified chunks as atomic units; introduces persistent lookahead to advance futures and carry unfinished samples across updates under fixed verifier.
AI.result: Empirical gains in macro best@4 for two settings (Search-R1-style retrieval and DeepEyes-style perception RL): +2.5 and +2.8 points over OPKD; lookahead increases throughput by 24%.
AI.conclusion: PTA effectively reduces drift and enhances downstream RL performance and throughput in tool-augmented LLM RL; persistent lookahead complements PTA by utilizing idle capacity and stabilizing generation across updates.

title: DCFA: Dual-view Causal-inspired Attribution for Failure Reasoning in LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have experienced rapid growth in recent years. Despite their promise, such systems remain fragile, frequently exhibiting reasoning and coordination errors that can lead to system-level failures. Failure attribution in such systems relies on tracing natural language interactions among agents to identify the decisive error, which refers to the earliest action whose correction can reverse system failure. There are two key challenges: 1) Shallow attribution: Existing methods often capture only minor deviations, such as incomplete retrievals or formatting errors, which verification mechanisms can correct, while missing the decisive cause of system failure. 2) Contextual degradation: As the length of the system traces increases, the model's reasoning ability rapidly deteriorates. To address these challenges, we propose DCFA, a training-free framework for failure attribution. DCFA integrates a global module that constructs structured causal-inspired dependency graphs from system traces to identify the initial decisive error, and a local module that applies local counterfactual-inspired reasoning to refine causal-inspired attribution. Experiments on the Who&When benchmark across six LLMs show that DCFA improves step-level accuracy by up to 8.27% over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: DCFA: training-free failure attribution for LLM-based multi-agent systems, using a global causal graph plus local counterfactual reasoning to locate the initial decisive error, improving step-level attribution accuracy by up to 8.27% on Who&When across six LLMs.
AI.motivation: Two challenges: shallow attribution that misses decisive causes, and context degradation as traces grow, undermining model reasoning and attribution reliability.
AI.method: Global module constructs structured causal-inspired dependency graphs from system traces to identify the initial decisive error; local module applies local counterfactual-inspired reasoning to refine attribution; training-free.
AI.result: On Who&When benchmark across six LLMs, DCFA increases step-level accuracy by up to 8.27% over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: DCFA offers a training-free, two-module approach to robust failure attribution, addressing shallow errors and long-context degradation, enhancing reliability of LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: Methane Detection On Board Satellites from Unorthorectified Imagery
summary: As a potent greenhouse gas, methane is a major driver of climate change. Its effective mitigation relies on timely detection. Conventional detection methods rely on orthorectification to correct geometric distortions and matched filters to enhance plume signals, which are steps designed for ground processing and poorly suited to onboard execution. We introduce UnorthoDOS, a dataset and approach for training machine learning models directly on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery, bypassing both orthorectification and matched-filter products. Our U-Net models trained on unorthorectified data approach the performance of models trained on orthorectified data (IoU 16.91% vs. 18.47% on all plumes), while both substantially outperform the mag1c matched-filter baseline (IoU 4.76%). We further demonstrate the feasibility of onboard deployment: FP16 compression halves model size with under 0.3% output deviation. The trained ML models and two ML-ready datasets -- orthorectified and unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery from the EMIT sensor -- are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SpaceML/UnorthoDOS, with code at https://github.com/spaceml-org/plume-hunter.

AI.tldr: UnorthoDOS enables training on unorthorectified hyperspectral imagery for methane plume detection, yielding comparable performance to orthorectified models and superior to mag1c, with onboard deployment feasibility; datasets and code released.
AI.motivation: Overcome reliance on orthorectification and matched-filter products that hinder onboard, real-time methane detection; enable efficient onboard ML inference.
AI.method: Train U-Net models on unorthorectified EMIT hyperspectral data; compare to orthorectified training; evaluate IoU; demonstrate FP16 compression for onboard deployment; public datasets on HuggingFace and code on GitHub.
AI.result: IoU for unortho models: 16.91% vs 18.47% (ortho) on all plumes; both > mag1c baseline 4.76%; FP16 reduces model size by 2x with <0.3% output deviation.
AI.conclusion: Unortho approach approaches orthorectified performance and enables feasible onboard deployment; provides open datasets and code to accelerate adoption.

title: Dynamic Heterogeneous Graph Representation Learning: A Survey
summary: Graph representation learning (GRL) serves as a canonical paradigm for modeling complex networks. However, real-world AI systems inherently manifest as evolving heterogeneous entities with complex interactions, posing significant challenges to static or homogeneous modeling. To address these complexities, representation learning for Dynamic Heterogeneous Graphs (DHGs) has emerged as a vital approach for learning low-dimensional representations that simultaneously preserve structural semantics and temporal dynamics. This survey presents the first systematic review of DHG representation learning methods. We first introduce a unified formal definition that encompasses both discrete-time and continuous-time DHGs from the perspective of temporal granularity. Building upon this formulation, we propose a novel algorithm-centric taxonomy that categorizes existing literature, including early embedding-based approaches, graph neural network (GNN)-based models, and relatively recent Transformer-based DHG methods, while explicitly highlighting their intrinsic modeling biases with respect to dynamic granularity. Furthermore, we summarize representative applications of DHG representation learning, along with commonly used datasets and benchmarks. Finally, we discuss promising research directions that guide future advances in this rapidly evolving field.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of dynamic heterogeneous graphs (DHGs) representation learning, defining a unified temporal framework for discrete/continuous time, proposing an algorithm-centric taxonomy (embedding-based, GNN-based, Transformer-based), analyzing biases with respect to granularity, and outlining datasets, benchmarks, and future directions.
AI.motivation: Real-world AI systems manifest as evolving heterogeneous networks requiring dynamic, granular modeling; there is a lack of a systematic review for DHG representation learning.
AI.method: Introduce a unified formal definition of DHGs across discrete and continuous time via temporal granularity, develop an algorithm-centric taxonomy categorizing existing methods (embedding-based, GNN-based, Transformer-based), highlight intrinsic biases with respect to dynamic granularity, and summarize applications, datasets, and benchmarks; discuss future directions.
AI.result: First systematic review of DHG representation learning; provides formal DHG definitions, a taxonomy of methods, analysis of modeling biases linked to granularity, and a compilation of datasets, benchmarks, and potential research directions.
AI.conclusion: The work advances DHG representation learning by offering a formal framework, a structured taxonomy, and practical guidance on datasets and directions, thereby facilitating standardization and progress in modeling dynamic heterogeneous networks.

title: Shadow Queries for Private Retrieval in Vector Databases
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on information retrieval (IR) systems, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), to incorporate domain-specific knowledge without costly re-training. These systems often store pre-computed document embeddings in cloud-based vector databases. However, such embeddings are vulnerable to embedding inversion attacks (EIAs), which can reconstruct their underlying text. Existing defenses, such as adding noise or scaling embeddings, often provide limited privacy or significantly reduce retrieval utility.
  We propose SHAQ (shadow query generation), a semantic-decomposition and embedding-decoupling defense against EIAs. SHAQ is based on the insight that EIAs rely on the strong coupling between an embedding and its original text. Instead of storing document embeddings directly, SHAQ uses a generative language model to create diverse shadow queries that capture different semantic aspects of each document. These queries are then encoded and stored in place of the original document embeddings, thereby decomposing document semantics and decoupling stored embeddings from the source text.
  Experiments across diverse IR datasets show that SHAQ substantially improves privacy while preserving retrieval utility, achieving a recovery rate as low as 0.2104, defending up to 19.50% more tokens than baseline defenses, and reaching up to 0.7967 MAP@10 with up to 5.53% utility improvement. These results demonstrate that semantic decomposition and embedding decoupling provide an effective alternative to directly modifying embeddings for defending against EIAs.

AI.tldr: SHAQ uses shadow query generation to decouple document semantics from embeddings, reducing vulnerability to embedding inversion attacks (EIAs) while preserving or improving retrieval performance.
AI.motivation: EIAs threaten privacy of vector embeddings in recall-augmented IR; existing defenses (noise, scaling) often degrade retrieval utility or offer limited privacy. A need exists for a defense that decouples semantics from embeddings.
AI.method: Generate diverse shadow queries per document with a generative LM to capture different semantic aspects. Encode these queries and store them instead of the original document embeddings, effectively semantic-decomposing and decoupling stored embeddings from source text.
AI.result: On diverse IR datasets, SHAQ reduces EIA recovery rate (as low as 0.2104), defends up to 19.50% more tokens than baseline defenses, and achieves MAP@10 up to 0.7967 with up to 5.53% utility improvement.
AI.conclusion: Semantic decomposition and embedding decoupling via SHAQ offer an effective alternative to modifying embeddings for defending against EIAs, achieving privacy gains with preserved or improved retrieval utility.

title: TourPhysics: Bringing Physics to World Models for Exploration and Manipulation from a Single Image
summary: Interactive visual world models must distinguish observation from physical intervention. Camera motion reveals new surfaces, whereas intervention changes object motion, contact, and deformation. Current video world models are largely driven by appearance priors and often lose physical or spatial consistency over long horizons. We present TourPhysics, an online framework initialized from a single image and a declarative physical configuration. TourPhysics extends PhysOmni, our ACM Multimedia 2026 work, from finite physics-grounded video synthesis to persistent exploration and manipulation. TourPhysics combines deterministic simulation with video generation while assigning separate roles to simulator state, geometric evidence, generator controls, and appearance memory. For each action, the simulator computes a finite physical and camera trajectory before the corresponding observation is generated. Accepted observations publish the terminal state and update the appearance memory and subsequent generator controls, while the committed state and simulator geometry remain fixed throughout synthesis and retry. We further separate the simulator geometry used for projection and visibility from the relative depth used to condition the generator. A reference-anchored memory retrieves accepted static appearance through geometric cross-view correspondence and incorporates it through a bounded residual that reverts to the native path when no valid correspondence exists. On simulator-defined camera tours and object manipulations, TourPhysics follows prescribed camera and object trajectories more closely than the evaluated baselines, preserves the input scene, and reduces appearance drift during long-horizon revisits.

AI.tldr: TourPhysics is an online, physically grounded video synthesis framework that separates observation from intervention to achieve persistent, long-horizon consistency in scene appearance and geometry during camera tours and object manipulations. It extends PhysOmni from finite physics-grounded video synthesis to persistent exploration and manipulation.
AI.motivation: Current video world models lean on appearance priors and struggle with physical/spatial consistency over long horizons; distinguishing observation from intervention and maintaining consistent geometry is essential for robust planning and manipulation in interactive settings.
AI.method: Initialize from a single image and a declarative physical configuration; extend PhysOmni to combine deterministic simulation with video generation. Assign distinct roles to simulator state, geometric evidence, generator controls, and appearance memory. For each action, compute a finite physical and camera trajectory before observation is generated. Accepted observations publish terminal state and update appearance memory and subsequent generator controls; committed state/geometry fixed during synthesis. Separate simulator geometry used for projection/visibility from relative depth used to condition the generator. Use a reference-anchored memory via geometric cross-view correspondence to retrieve static appearance and apply a bounded residual when correspondence exists; otherwise revert to native path. Follow simulator-defined camera tours and manipulations, adhering to prescribed trajectories more closely than baselines, preserving the input scene, and reducing appearance drift over long horizons.
AI.result: Qualitatively, TourPhysics follows simulator-defined tours more closely than evaluated baselines, preserves the input scene, and reduces appearance drift during long-horizon revisits.
AI.conclusion: TourPhysics provides persistent exploration and manipulation with improved long-horizon physical-consistency by decoupling projection geometry from depth conditioning, and by integrating a reference-anchored appearance memory into an online, sampler-based generation loop, extending PhysOmni to continuous video synthesis.

title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications
summary: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of learning-augmented algorithms across domains, proposing interfaces, error measures, and trade-offs; introduces a theorem-level axis separating achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence; separates formal guarantees from empirical evidence; outlines open problems and benchmarking needs.
AI.motivation: Unify prediction interfaces, error metrics, and performance guarantees for learning-augmented algorithms, and articulate conditions under which end-to-end reasoning can be reliable across diverse problem settings.
AI.method: Systematic literature synthesis across five domains—online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design; introduces an orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishing upper bounds from asymptotic dependence; explicitly treats prediction cost, feedback, and composition; separates formal guarantees from empirical systems evidence.
AI.result: States sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning; clarifies cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking; provides a framework for evaluating when predictions can be integrated without compromising guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Offers a structured synthesis that guides design and evaluation of learning-augmented systems, emphasizing explicit consideration of prediction cost, feedback, and composition, and outlining key open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

title: Diffusion Language Models for Mobile Edge Agentic AI: Foundations, Applications, and Challenges
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a non-autoregressive alternative for mobile edge agentic artificial intelligence (AI) by refining tokens through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right decoding. Compared with autoregressive Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), DLMs can update multiple uncertain tokens in parallel and exploit bidirectional context throughout the generation process, enabling more flexible quality-latency trade-offs beyond fixed sequential decoding. These properties are particularly attractive for edge agents, where partial refinement, early exit, and constraint-guided correction can reduce response delay and communication overhead while improving robustness under noisy, incomplete, or dynamic contexts. This survey reviews DLM foundations and analyzes their suitability for edge settings under latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability constraints. We cover resource-efficient architectures, training and inference acceleration, compression, edge/cloud deployment, communication-aware serving, Internet of Things (IoT)/wireless applications, and evaluation of DLM-based agents. We further discuss open issues in long-context state management, split inference, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and reproducible benchmarking. The goal is to connect DLM modeling properties, including bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, and quality-latency elasticity, with system-level requirements of future mobile edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: DLMs offer non-autoregressive, bidirectional, parallel token refinement for edge AI, enabling flexible quality-latency trade-offs; the paper surveys foundations, architectures, deployment, and open issues for mobile edge intelligence.
AI.motivation: Address latency, memory, energy, bandwidth, privacy, and reliability constraints in edge AI by leveraging diffusion-based language models as an alternative to autoregressive LLMs.
AI.method: Survey and analysis of DLM foundations, architectures, training and inference acceleration, compression, edge/cloud deployment, communication-aware serving, IoT/wireless applications, and evaluation of DLM-based agents, plus discussion of open issues.
AI.result: Synthesis of design space, guidelines for edge deployment, and open research questions.
AI.conclusion: DLMs show promise for edge constraints due to bidirectionality, parallel refinement, controllability, and quality-latency elasticity; realizing this potential requires addressing long-context state management, split inference, trustworthy execution, multimodal grounding, and reproducible benchmarking.

title: How Faithful Is Attribution for Sales Forecasting? A Counterfactual Study
summary: Deep models for sales forecasting, such as WaveNet-style dilated convolutional networks, are accurate but opaque: when a single model predicts sales for one of many series, it offers no account of why. We add a post-hoc, architecture-agnostic counterfactual interpretability layer to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster trained on the full Corporacion Favorita grocery dataset (174,685 series over 1,688 days). The method decomposes each forecast into contributions that sum exactly to the predicted value, avoiding the allocation artifacts we observed with additive SHAP-style attribution. We evaluate faithfulness with a deletion/insertion protocol and find a statistically significant effect on both tests (deletion gap 0.22, p<0.001; insertion gap 0.27, p<0.01; robust across five background-sampling seeds), establishing that the attributions reflect genuine model behavior rather than plausible-looking artifacts. We then characterize, honestly, where attribution is and is not informative: reliance on the promotion signal is heterogeneous across series (median ratio approximately 1.0, with roughly 20% of series showing a strong effect), and the model captures the shape of the weekly sales cycle (day-of-week r=0.78) while systematically under-predicting its amplitude. Our contribution is not improved accuracy but an interpretability layer with a rigorous faithfulness evaluation and a candid account of its limits.

AI.tldr: Post-hoc, architecture-agnostic counterfactual interpretability layer added to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster on a large grocery dataset. It decomposes forecasts into exact, faithful contributions, avoiding additive attribution artifacts. Faithfulness evaluated via deletion/insertion tests showing significant effects. Finds heterogeneous reliance on promotions and a good capture of weekly cycles but underestimates amplitude. Contribution: an interpretable layer with rigorous faithfulness evaluation and transparent limitations, not improved accuracy.
AI.motivation: Address opacity of deep forecasting models and provide faithful, interpretable attributions across many time series, avoiding artifacts from additive attribution methods like SHAP.
AI.method: Introduce a post-hoc counterfactual interpretability layer that is architecture-agnostic and ensures that per-series forecasts are decomposed into contributions summing to the prediction. Apply to a multi-series WaveNet forecaster trained on the Corporacion Favorita grocery dataset (174,685 series across 1,688 days). Evaluate faithfulness with deletion/insertion tests across multiple background seeds. Analyze when attribution is informative (e.g., promotion signal) and how well the model captures seasonality (weekly cycles).
AI.result: Attribution decompositions sum to predictions (no additive artifacts). Deletion gap = 0.22 (p<0.001); insertion gap = 0.27 (p<0.01); robust across five seeds. Promotion signal shows heterogeneous influence (median ~1.0, ~20% of series strong). Day-of-week correlation with actuals r=0.78; amplitude of weekly cycle under-predicted. The layer provides faithful interpretability with transparent limitations; no accuracy gains claimed.
AI.conclusion: The interpretability layer is faithful and informative for diagnosing model behavior across many series, but it has limits (promotion effects vary by series; weekly shape captured but amplitude underestimates). It advances interpretability in time-series forecasting without claiming improved accuracy.

title: DODR: Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space
summary: Autoregressive (AR) large language models formulate reasoning as token-level probabilistic sampling, which induces three fundamental defects in complex logical reasoning: error accumulation, probability substituting necessity, and the linear-chain information bottleneck. This paper proposes the Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space architecture (DODR), which reconstructs reasoning as reasoning-graph computation in a high-dimensional linear-algebraic space. Reasoning states are represented as snapshot vectors whose primitives are semantic units (phrases or sentences) rather than tokens, and each inference step is a deterministic matrix operation with no token sampling. Peirce's three inference types are formalized as three trainable matrix operators: a rank-deficient deduction operator (information collapse), a full-rank induction operator (information expansion), and an abduction operator defined as the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of deduction (information hypothesizing). We prove that the operator set is minimal and complete given Peirce's trichotomy, that no single "super-operator" can realize all three types (a rank obstruction), and that reasoning graphs are Turing-complete with contractive backflow converging by Banach's fixed-point theorem. Experiments on 503 sample records (420 deduplicated samples) across dedicated and end-to-end settings show: deduction loss converges to 1.40e-05; induction achieves 0.9996 generalization coverage with 20/20 hard vetoes on counterexamples; abduction solutions exceed the random baseline by 28x with judgment accuracies of 72.5% (58/80, Wilson 95% CI [61.9%, 81.1%]) and 81.7% (49/60, CI [70.1%, 89.4%]); frozen operators attain 100% (60/60) on unseen cross-domain deduction. The architecture provides a structural zero-hallucination guarantee and a three-layer continual-learning mechanism. All data and code are released.

AI.tldr: Deterministic Operator-Driven Reasoning in Latent Space (DODR) replaces token-level sampling with deterministic, matrix-based reasoning in a latent, graph-structured space, achieving zero hallucinations and strong generalization across deduction, induction, and abduction.
AI.motivation: AR LMs suffer from error accumulation, reliance on probabilistic token sampling, and a linear-chain information bottleneck in reasoning; a structured, deterministic framework is proposed to overcome these defects.
AI.method: Reasoning states are snapshot vectors built from semantic units (phrases/sentences). Inference steps are deterministic matrix operations governed by three trainable operators: (1) rank-deficient deduction (information collapse), (2) full-rank induction (information expansion), and (3) abduction via Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse of deduction. The operator set is proven minimal and complete under Peirce's trichotomy; reasoning graphs are Turing-complete with contractive backflow ensuring convergence by Banach's fixed-point theorem.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 503 samples (420 deduplicated) shows: deduction loss ~1.4e-05; induction generalizes with 0.9996 coverage and 20/20 hard vetoes on counterexamples; abduction improves over random baseline by 28x with judgments of 72.5% (58/80) and 81.7% (49/60) under Wilson CIs [61.9%, 81.1%] and [70.1%, 89.4%] respectively; frozen operators achieve 100% on unseen cross-domain deduction. The architecture guarantees zero hallucination and features a three-layer continual-learning mechanism; all data and code are released.
AI.conclusion: DODR provides a principled, complete operator-based alternative to probabilistic token sampling, delivering structural guarantees (zero hallucination, convergence) and strong cross-domain generalization, supported by reproducible data and code.

title: LensStyle: Learning the Optical Aesthetics for Controllable Stylized Lens Effect Rendering
summary: The visual aesthetics of photographs are deeply influenced by lens characteristics such as aperture shape, optical vignetting and optical diffraction, which together define a camera's unique optical style. Existing lens effect rendering methods primarily focus on accurately simulating the blur transition from small to large apertures but overlook the stylistic aspects of lens effects. As a result, they fail to produce diverse bokeh effects under large apertures or capture distinctive photographic phenomena such as starbursts that emerge under small apertures. In this work, we introduce LensStyle, a unified framework for controllable stylized lens effect rendering that explicitly models lens aesthetics through joint continuous-discrete control. Our model incorporates a Dual-Path Controller that disentangles continuous optical parameter modulation (e.g., focus distance and blur strength) from discrete lens-style conditioning (e.g., circular, polygonal, donut, cat-eye, and starburst effects), enabling fine-grained, interpretable, and physically grounded lens manipulation within a single unified framework. To support model training, we curate a comprehensive MultiLens dataset containing multi-lens image pairs synthesized under real optical constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LensStyle achieves superior realism, controllability, and aesthetic quality compared with existing lens effect rendering approaches and diffusion-based image editing models, advancing computational photography toward multiple-lens-style simulation.

AI.tldr: Unified framework LensStyle for controllable stylized lens effects using continuous-discrete control and a Dual-Path Controller, trained on a MultiLens dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing lens-effect methods focus on blur transitions with large apertures and neglect stylistic, aesthetic lens phenomena (e.g., diverse bokeh shapes, starbursts). A controllable, interpretable model is needed to capture lens aesthetics.
AI.method: Joint continuous optical-parameter modulation (e.g., focus distance, blur strength) with discrete lens-style conditioning (circular, polygonal, donut, cat-eye, starburst) via a Dual-Path Controller. Trains on a curated MultiLens dataset of multi-lens image pairs synthesized under real optical constraints.
AI.result: LensStyle achieves superior realism, controllability, and aesthetic quality compared with existing lens-effect rendering methods and diffusion-based editing models.
AI.conclusion: Provides a physically grounded, interpretable, unified framework for stylized lens-effect rendering with diverse artistic styles and fine-grained control, advancing multi-lens-style simulation in computational photography.

title: Federated Attack Campaign Detection via Contrastive Encoding of Threat Indicators in Gradient Updates
comment: Accepted to ECML-PKDD 2026, 4th Workshop on Advancements in Federated Learning - Towards Trustworthy Federated Learning
summary: Detecting orchestrated cyberattack campaigns that span multiple organizations traditionally requires sharing sensitive telemetry and threat intelligence across institutional boundaries and country borders, a barrier that Federated Learning removes by training shared threat detectors directly on local data. We propose FedIoC, a modular framework in which clients fold locally available structured threat indicators into their gradient updates; we instantiate the client-side encoder with a supervised contrastive loss over IoC-matched flows. Within each training batch, flows that match any known indicator pattern form the positive set; the contrastive objective pulls their learned embeddings together and pushes non-IoC embeddings away, so that campaign-relevant structure is, by design, expressed in the gradient direction. Clients sharing indicators for the same attack campaign then produce aligned gradient components, which the server clusters by the cosine similarity of their updates to recover global campaign patterns without any direct IoC transmission. We evaluate FedIoC on two public threat-detection benchmarks distributed across FL clients that each observe only a fragment of every active campaign and hold disjoint indicator sets derived from their local telemetry. In this regime the FL server recovers cross-organizational campaign cohorts directly from gradient geometry. We contribute FedIoC as a modular framework for this setting, and use it to pinpoint the non-IID gradient structure as the main driver of recovery and to define the open problem of designing encoders that improve on it.

AI.tldr: FedIoC enables cross-organization threat detection in a privacy-preserving federated setting by using a client-side supervised contrastive encoder over IoCs; global campaign patterns emerge from gradient similarity without sharing IoCs, though non-IID gradient structure drives recovery and encoder design remains open.
AI.motivation: Coordinated cyberattack campaigns span multiple organizations, requiring sensitive data sharing. Federated Learning can train detectors locally, but extracting campaign-level structure without IoC exposure is challenging; FedIoC aims to reveal cross-organizational patterns from gradients alone.
AI.method: A modular FL framework where clients incorporate locally available threat indicators into gradient updates via a supervised contrastive loss on IoC-matched flows. Positive samples are flows matching any IoC within a batch; the encoder learns embeddings that pull IoC-matched flows together and push non-IoC flows apart. The server clusters clients' gradient updates by cosine similarity to recover global campaign cohorts, without transmitting IoCs.
AI.result: Evaluations on two public threat-detection benchmarks distributed across FL clients with fragmented and disjoint local IoCs. The server recovers cross-organizational campaign cohorts from gradient geometry, demonstrating that non-IID gradient structure enables this recovery.
AI.conclusion: FedIoC provides a modular framework for gradient-based cross-organizational campaign discovery in FL and identifies non-IID gradient structure as the main driver of recovery, while highlighting the open problem of designing encoders that further improve performance.

title: ProtLingo: Efficient Protein Language Modeling via Conditional Memory and Expert Routing
summary: Proteins perform diverse cellular functions, and even single amino-acid substitutions can alter stability, activity, or molecular interactions. Protein language models (PLMs) provide a scalable approach for modeling such sequence--function relationships from unlabeled sequences, but increasing the size of dense Transformer backbones often brings substantial computational cost without consistently improving mutation-sensitive prediction. We introduce ProtLingo, an efficient PLM framework that augments a pretrained single-sequence backbone with conditional local memory and sparse expert routing. ProtLingo maps contextual residue representations into route-specific discrete codes, composes centered local windows into latent $N$-gram addresses, and retrieves reusable residual signals associated with recurring local sequence contexts. In parallel, selected feed-forward blocks are upcycled into sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers with shared and routed experts, enabling residue-dependent computation while activating only a subset of parameters. Experiments on protein fitness prediction, FLIP benchmarks, and supervised contact prediction show that ProtLingo achieves competitive performance with a 150M-scale backbone, including strong parameter efficiency on mutation-effect prediction and preserved long-range structural representations.

AI.tldr: ProtLingo is an efficient protein language model that augments a pretrained backbone with conditional local memory and sparse routing to improve mutation-effect predictions, achieving competitive performance with a 150M-scale backbone while reducing parameters and preserving long-range representations.
AI.motivation: Protein sequence–function mapping with large dense transformers is computationally expensive and often does not yield proportional gains for mutation-sensitive predictions; a parameter-efficient architecture is desirable.
AI.method: ProtLingo augments a pretrained single-sequence backbone with conditional local memory and sparse expert routing. It maps contextual residue representations into route-specific discrete codes, forms latent N-gram addresses from centered local windows, and retrieves reusable residual signals tied to recurring local contexts. Simultaneously, select feed-forward blocks are converted into sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers with shared and routed experts, enabling residue-dependent computation by activating only a subset of parameters.
AI.result: Experiments on protein fitness prediction, FLIP benchmarks, and supervised contact prediction show ProtLingo achieves competitive performance with a 150M-scale backbone, offering strong parameter efficiency on mutation-effect prediction and preserving long-range structural representations.
AI.conclusion: ProtLingo provides a parameter-efficient PLM framework that maintains competitive performance while reducing computational cost, particularly for mutation-sensitive predictions and structural representations.

title: Learning 3D Editing without Paired Supervision via Generative Prior Distillation
summary: Instruction-guided 3D editing is essential for interactive content creation, yet it faces a significant bottleneck: the severe scarcity of high-quality paired training data. Existing approaches attempt to bypass this by either relying on slow test-time optimization or training on pseudo-pairs constructed via complex pipelines, which often introduce structural drift and geometric artifacts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that learns feed-forward 3D editing without paired 3D supervision via Generative Prior Distillation. Instead of relying on ground-truth 3D pairs, our core idea is to distill visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from powerful foundation models directly into a 3D editing model. Specifically, through a differentiable rendering pipeline, we supervise the 3D representation using two complementary signals: a 2D visual prior from an image editing model at the main editing view, and a semantic prior from a Vision-Language Model at novel views to ensure strict instruction following and source identity preservation. Crucially, to address the geometric collapse and multi-view inconsistencies inherent in 2D projection supervision, we introduce a 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization. Acting as a geometric prior, this term operates in the 3D latent space, constraining the edited output to remain within the manifold of realistic 3D assets defined by a pretrained image to 3D teacher model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior instruction fidelity and cross-view consistency, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Our project is available at: https://github.com/thiamine128/PriorEdit3D.

AI.tldr: A feed-forward 3D editing framework that distills visual, semantic, and geometric priors from foundation models into a 3D editor trained without paired 3D data, leveraging differentiable rendering, 2D and 3D priors, and a 3D-aware distribution matching regularization for view-consistent, instruction-faithful edits.
AI.motivation: Severe shortage of high-quality paired 3D data for instruction-guided editing. Existing methods rely on slow optimization or pseudo-pairs that introduce geometric artifacts, hindering real-time, faithful edits across views.
AI.method: Generative Prior Distillation: distill knowledge from image editing models and vision-language models into a 3D editing model via a differentiable rendering pipeline. Supervises 3D representation with a 2D visual prior at the main view and a 3D semantic prior from a Vision-Language Model for novel views, plus a 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization in the 3D latent space to constrain outputs to a manifold of realistic 3D assets defined by a pretrained image-to-3D teacher model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show superior instruction fidelity and cross-view consistency, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines; the method is non-pair-supervised and feed-forward, enabling fast, robust 3D edits. Project available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a non-paired, feed-forward 3D editing framework that leverages distillation of powerful foundation-model priors (visual, semantic, geometric) into a 3D editor, with a 3D-aware regularization to maintain geometric realism and multi-view consistency; it advances instruction-guided 3D editing and offers practical applicability.

title: Communication-Efficient Personalized Federated Learning via Layer-Wise Multi-Threshold Random Sketching
summary: Personalized federated learning (PFL) is a promising paradigm for collaborative learning over distributed devices, where edge nodes collaboratively train personalized models without sharing raw data. Although PFL addresses data heterogeneity by learning client-specific models, it still suffers from substantial uplink and downlink communication costs when exchanging high-dimensional parameters in bandwidth-constrained systems. Recent one-bit methods achieve extreme compression, but they usually rely on a single thresholding rule applied to the whole model. This design has two limitations. First, it overlooks layer-wise differences in parameter distributions and quantization sensitivities. Second, a single threshold provides only coarse binary information and cannot capture fine-grained variations in parameter distributions. To address these issues, we propose a communication-efficient PFL framework via layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching. In the proposed method, each layer is assigned its own set of quantization thresholds, so that the compressed representation can adapt to layer-specific statistics while using multiple intervals to provide a finer low-bit description of sketched parameters. The proposed method supports bidirectional communication using compact low-bit sketches and improves the communication-accuracy tradeoff compared with existing one-bit compression approaches.

AI.tldr: Layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching for personalized federated learning (PFL) that assigns per-layer thresholds and multiple quantization intervals to compress updates with finer low-bit detail, enabling bidirectional communication and improved communication-accuracy tradeoffs compared with single-threshold one-bit methods.
AI.motivation: In PFL, client-specific models mitigate data heterogeneity but high-dimensional updates cause substantial uplink/downlink costs. One-bit compression with a single threshold is limited by neglecting layer-wise variations in parameter distributions and by coarse information.
AI.method: For each layer, allocate its own set of quantization thresholds forming multiple intervals; apply random sketching to the compressed representation of layer parameters; support bidirectional communication using low-bit sketches; aim to improve the communication-accuracy tradeoff over existing one-bit approaches by capturing layer-specific statistics.
AI.result: The proposed framework reportedly achieves a better trade-off between communication efficiency and model accuracy than existing one-bit compression methods, by using layer-aware thresholds and multi-interval quantization to provide a finer low-bit description.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise multi-threshold random sketching offers an effective, adaptable compression strategy for PFL, addressing layer heterogeneity and enabling bidirectional low-bit communication with improved performance over single-threshold schemes.

title: Whose record is this? Diagnosing and authorizing record use in personalized multimodal models
summary: Contextualized visual personalization can retrieve a true record yet apply it to the wrong visual subject. We formalize when a record may condition an answer as \emph{record authorization}: subject presence ($P$), record-edge validity ($E$), and answer support ($S$) must all hold. We call violations visual memory misbinding (VMM). We construct RecordAuth-Diag, a 3,690-case matched diagnostic suite that changes one image--record edge while holding the query, question, record text, and image multiset fixed. Card removal and nonce relabeling attribute these failures to supplied records. Raw-bank failures span Qwen-, Phi-, and Gemma-family interfaces: Gemma-3-4B-IT reaches 63.69\% local unauthorized use at 25.75\% clean recall. CoViP remains at 26.02\%, versus 22.49\% for its Qwen backbone at similar clean recall. Typed pre-generation authorization reduces Qwen card exposure on RecordAuth-Diag from 43.63\% to 3.06\%, while positive recall changes from 86.26\% to 60.90\%. Full $P\wedge E\wedge S$ validation uses 560 localized DAVIS cases: top-1 relevance and typed authorization have comparable release (28.93\% and 28.39\%) but 6.79\% and 0.89\% unsafe release, respectively. Of the 33 additional unsafe cases removed, 27 are support, 4 edge, 2 clean, and 0 boundary cases. Thus the observed increment is an $E\wedge S$ decision dominated by support, not an edge check alone. Appearance supplies $E$ evidence only conditional on $P$; authenticated subject tokens instantiate the missing presence witness as a sufficiency control. The claims concern the evaluated contracts, not natural prevalence, consent, or visual identity

AI.tldr: Formalizes record authorization (P, E, S) for visual-memory misbinding (VMM); introduces RecordAuth-Diag (3,690 cases) to probe how a single image–record edge perturbation affects answers; shows substantial unauthorized responses across backbones and datasets; demonstrates that pre-generation authorization reduces exposure but lowers recall; concludes that E evidence is only meaningful under P and requires a presence witness for sufficiency control.
AI.motivation: To prevent contextualized visual personalization from asserting a record-based answer when the subject or edge evidence is missing or misbound; to quantify the conditions under which a supplied record can legitimately authorize an answer.
AI.method: Construct RecordAuth-Diag by perturbing one image–record edge while keeping query, question, record text, and image multiset fixed; use card removal and nonce relabeling to attribute failures to provided records; evaluate raw-bank interfaces (Gemma-3/4B-IT, CoViP, Qwen-family) and measure local unauthorized use and clean recall; apply typed pre-generation authorization to reduce card exposure; validate with 560 localized DAVIS cases for P∧E∧S decision, analyzing top-1 relevance and unsafe release; categorize unsafe removals by reason (edge, edge+S, support, etc.).
AI.result: Gemma-3/4B-IT: 63.69% local unauthorized use at 25.75% clean recall. CoViP: 26.02% (unsafe) vs 22.49% backbones at similar clean recall. Typed pre-generation reduces Qwen card exposure from 43.63% to 3.06%, while recall drops from 86.26% to 60.90%. Full P∧E∧S validation on 560 DAVIS: top-1 relevance 28.93%, typed authorization 28.39% release; unsafe releases 6.79% and 0.89% respectively. Of 33 additional unsafe cases removed, 27 were support, 4 edge, 2 clean, 0 boundary. The increment is driven by E∧S decision dominated by support, not edge alone.
AI.conclusion: Evidence (E) is meaningful only given the presence condition (P); authenticated subject tokens can provide a missing presence witness as a sufficiency control. The study emphasizes that attempted releases hinge on support and S, rather than edge checks alone; thus claims pertain to the evaluated contracts rather than natural prevalence, consent, or visual identity.

title: MCPO: Modality-Contrastive Preference Optimization for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Compression
summary: Recently, multimodal large-scale reasoning models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks through long Chains-of-Thought (M-CoT). However, excessively long reasoning trajectories incur substantial computational costs and significant KV-cache pressure. Existing CoT compression and alignment paradigms mainly rely on static rules or single-dimensional preferences, lacking fine-grained cross-modal constraints; as a result, they are prone to inducing visual laziness and hallucinatory reasoning. To address these issues, we propose Modality-Contrastive Preference Optimization (MCPO), a highly sample-efficient two-stage length-compression method that requires fewer than 900 training samples. In the compression stage, we introduce a step-level Normalized Cross-Modal Mutual Information (NCMI) pruning algorithm, which automatically identifies and removes visual-independent reasoning steps by comparing the reasoning discrepancies between with-image and no-image contexts. This significantly reduces redundancy and hallucinatory content in the reasoning chains. In the alignment stage, the model first undergoes supervised fine-tuning to achieve domain-adaptive initialization, followed by optimization using an asymmetric multimodal length-controlled preference loss. This objective adopts a highly nonlinear odds-ratio formulation that provides steep gradients in the with-image context to reinforce length constraints for preferred trajectories, while applying a scaled, flat-gradient linear difference in the no-image context to maintain modality consistency, thereby achieving stable cross-modal preference alignment. Extensive experiments on mainstream base models such as Qwen3-VL-Thinking show that our method can reduce CoT length by up to 69.5% and achieve up to 3.34x end-to-end inference speedup while preserving original accuracy.

AI.tldr: A two-stage, sample-efficient multimodal CoT length-compression method (MCPO) using NCMI pruning and asymmetric length-controlled preference loss to reduce CoT length and accelerate inference while preserving accuracy; claims up to 69.5% length reduction and 3.34x speedup with <900 labeled samples on base models such as Qwen3-VL-Thinking.
AI.motivation: Long multimodal reasoning causes heavy compute and KV-cache pressure; existing compression methods rely on static rules and lack cross-modal constraints, leading to visual laziness and hallucinations.
AI.method: Stage 1: NCMI pruning compares reasoning with and without images to prune visual-independent steps. Stage 2: supervised fine-tuning for domain-adaptive initialization, then optimize with asymmetric multimodal length-controlled preference loss: steep gradients in with-image context to enforce length constraints; scaled flat-gradient in no-image context to maintain modality consistency.
AI.result: Significant CoT length reduction (up to 69.5%), up to 3.34x end-to-end speedup, preserving original accuracy; validated on base models like Qwen3-VL-Thinking; sample-efficient (<900 samples).
AI.conclusion: MCPO provides effective cross-modal constrained CoT compression, mitigating visual laziness and hallucinations while achieving faster inference with minimal loss in accuracy.

title: PACE: Propagation-Aware Collaborative Correction for One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning
summary: Client heterogeneity creates both an opportunity and a risk in personalized federated graph learning. Knowledge held by other subgraphs may complement a receiver's Local model, but an incompatible transfer can override reliable predictions. One-shot communication sharpens this tension because an unsuitable server return cannot be corrected later. We introduce PACE, which treats collaborative knowledge as a compact correction to a complete Local predictor rather than as its replacement. Each client uploads a rank-r update carrier and a diagonal sketch of propagated message moments. The server uses them to construct a propagation-aware, receiver-anchored correction, while the receiver retains its full Local model. Convex negative-log-likelihood calibration (CNLL) then selects one coefficient between Local and External logits using validation nodes; model parameters remain fixed and no feedback is sent. At Rank-6, personalized returns occupy 9.6-17.6% of dense tensor bytes across the six evaluated datasets. The correction receives nonzero weight and improves both Accuracy and weighted-F1 over Local on five datasets; on ogbn-arxiv, CNLL assigns zero predictive weight to the correction and preserves Local predictions exactly. Applying the same CNLL rule to matched baselines on three citation datasets does not account for these gains. The central result is therefore that a small transported correction can augment a complete Local model when receiver evidence supports it while leaving the Local prediction unchanged otherwise.

AI.tldr: PACE introduces a minimal, propagation-aware correction for personalized federated graph learning that complements a full Local predictor without overriding it. It uses rank-r update carriers and diagonal moment sketches, gated by CNLL, achieving gains on most datasets with limited communication; on ogbn-arxiv the correction is ignored by design.
AI.motivation: Address client heterogeneity in personalized federated graph learning with one-shot communication, avoiding detrimental transfers while leveraging complementary knowledge from other subgraphs.
AI.method: Clients upload a rank-r update carrier and a diagonal sketch of propagated moments. The server constructs a propagation-aware, receiver-anchored correction and the receiver maintains its Local model. CNLL selects a single coefficient between Local and External logits using validation nodes; parameters are fixed and no feedback is sent. Evaluation includes Rank-6 where external corrections occupy 9.6-17.6% of dense tensor bytes across six datasets.
AI.result: The correction carries nonzero weight and improves Accuracy and weighted-F1 over Local on five datasets; on ogbn-arxiv CNLL assigns zero weight to the correction, preserving Local predictions. Matching CNLL rules on baselines do not yield similar gains. Overall, a small transported correction can augment a complete Local model when receiver evidence supports it while leaving Local predictions unchanged otherwise.
AI.conclusion: A compact, propagation-aware correction can meaningfully augment a strong local model in personalized federated graph learning when justified by receiver evidence, without compromising Local performance in its absence.

title: Hierarchical Possession-Aware Graph Pointer Network for Pass Receiver Selection
comment: This paper has been accepted by the 27th International Conference on Web Information Systems Engineering (WISE 2026)
summary: Pass receiver selection is a fundamental task in football analytics, aiming to predict the intended receiver under a given game state. This task is challenging with event-centered freeze-frame observations, a broadcast-like setting that provides only partial and variable player visibility without complete trajectories or stable player identities. The model must therefore reason over anonymous visible candidates, opponent pressure, and recent context under partial observation. To address this setting, we propose a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN), which formulates pass receiver selection as variable-size candidate prediction over visible teammates. HPGPN jointly models current player interactions, local event context, and possession-level temporal dynamics. It represents the current pass situation with a graph, incorporates fixed event context, and uses dynamic possession history to capture how the attacking sequence evolves. Candidate representations are refined hierarchically by integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence, and a glimpse pointer head scores the receiver candidates. Experiments on public football event and freeze-frame data show that HPGPN improves pass receiver selection performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and dual-branch dynamic possession-history modeling.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical graph-based pointer network for pass receiver selection under partial observation, combining current interactions, fixed context, and possession history to predict the intended receiver among visible teammates.
AI.motivation: To address pass receiver prediction under event-centered freeze-frame observations where actor identities are incomplete and only a subset of players are visible, requiring reasoning over anonymous candidates and temporal dynamics.
AI.method: Proposes HP GPN: a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network. It models the pass situation as a graph of interactions, integrates fixed event context, and uses dynamic possession history to capture temporal evolution. Candidate representations are refined via spatial, contextual, and historical cues; a glimpse pointer head scores candidates, producing variable-size predictions over visible teammates.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on public football event and freeze-frame datasets shows improved pass receiver prediction performance. Ablation studies indicate the importance of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and a dual-branch dynamic possession-history component.
AI.conclusion: HP GPN effectively handles pass receiver selection under partial observation by jointly modeling spatial interactions, event context, and possession dynamics; graph structure and hierarchical candidate refinement are key to performance gains.

title: VICAL: Vicinal Consistency Alignment for Long-Tailed Visual Recognition
summary: Multi-expert models have become the dominant paradigm for long-tailed learning, largely attributed to their presumed ability to benefit from expert diversity. However, we revisit this central assumption and reveal that diversity induced by logit adjustment or explicit regularizers does not guarantee better ensemble accuracy. Our work suggests that multi-expert models benefit more from variance reduction than diversity maximization. We introduce \textbf{VICAL}, a \textbf{VI}cinal \textbf{C}onsistency \textbf{AL}ignment framework that improves long-tailed recognition not by enforcing expert diversity, but by reducing prediction variance. Specifically, our approach comprises two key components: Self-Consistency Learning and Deep Ensemble Distillation. Self-Consistency Learning discourages reliance on unstable high-frequency information, smoothing the local loss landscape and mitigating overfitting, especially for tail classes. Deep Ensemble Distillation promotes cross-expert low-frequency semantic agreement using a low-resolution view, thereby sidestepping optimization conflicts with established knowledge. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 show that VICAL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of our consistency-driven design. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/FlamieZhu/Vicinal-Consistency-Alignment}{VICAL}.

AI.tldr: A variance-reduction, consistency-driven multi-expert framework (VICAL) improves long-tailed recognition by reducing prediction variance rather than maximizing diversity, via Self-Consistency Learning and Deep Ensemble Distillation; achieves state-of-the-art on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018.
AI.motivation: Challenges the core assumption that diversity among experts yields better ensemble performance in long-tailed settings. Diversity induced by logit adjustments or explicit regularizers does not guarantee improvement; proposes focusing on variance reduction instead.
AI.method: Introduce Vicinal Consistency Alignment (VICAL) with two components: (1) Self-Consistency Learning to dampen reliance on unstable high-frequency information, smoothing the local loss landscape; (2) Deep Ensemble Distillation to promote cross-expert low-frequency semantic agreement using a low-resolution view, avoiding conflicts with established knowledge.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018 show VICAL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: A consistency-driven framework with variance reduction outperforms diversity-centric approaches for long-tailed recognition in multi-expert models; code available.

title: KVMem: Virtualizing Million-Token Agent Workspaces on a Consumer GPU
summary:
Modern LLM agents operate in persistent workspaces whose accumulated history can exceed both GPU KV capacity and the model's native context window. Existing systems typically compact older context into summaries or retrieve it later as text, either losing fine-grained execution evidence or repeatedly prefilling content that the model has already processed. We present KVMem, a KV-context virtualization system that preserves overflowed workspace history as paged KV state across GPU memory, host memory, and NVMe. KVMem uses lightweight, model-native attention-space indexes to select relevant historical blocks and materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model's native context window. Extensive evaluations on long-context agent benchmarks spanning histories up to one million tokens, including LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, and AgentLongBench, show that KVMem generally achieves higher task utility and greater inference efficiency than compaction-based approaches, the de facto standard for handling context overflow. In the DeepSWE long-context test with Qwen3.8-27B, KVMem improves task success from 43.8% with compaction-only context management to 48.4%.
  In our local-deployment evaluation, KVMem runs Qwen3.6/3.8-27B NVFP4 with MTP on an off-the-shelf laptop equipped with a 24\,GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU, virtualizing agent workspaces of up to 1M tokens-four times the model's native 256K-token context window. In a single-session setting, KVMem generates $\sim$50 tokens/s, providing interactive responsiveness for local agent execution. More broadly, by decoupling addressable workspace size from the LLM's native context window, KVMem provides a practical path toward long-running agents whose workspaces can grow beyond that window.

AI.tldr: KVMem introduces a KV-context virtualization approach to overflowed LLM workspaces, storing history as paged KV state across GPU, host memory, and NVMe. It uses model-native attention-space indexes to assemble a query-dependent execution view within the model’s native context window, outperforming compaction-based methods on long-context benchmarks and enabling interactive local deployment.
AI.motivation: Persistent workspaces can exceed GPU KV capacity and the model’s native context window, causing loss of fine-grained evidence or repeated processing with compaction. A scalable, efficient method is needed to preserve long-term history for long-running agents.
AI.method: KVMem stores overflow history as paged key-value blocks across GPU/host/NVMe. It employs lightweight, model-native attention-space indexes to select relevant blocks and materializes a query-dependent execution view bounded by the model’s context window, effectively virtualizing the workspace size independent of the model’s native context length.
AI.result: Evaluations on long-context benchmarks (LongMemEval, MemoryAgentBench, AgentLongBench) with histories up to 1M tokens show higher task utility and inference efficiency than compaction-based approaches. In DeepSWE tests with Qwen3.8-27B, task success rose from 43.8% (compaction) to 48.4%. Local deployment on a laptop (Qwen3.6/3.8-27B NVFP4 with MTP) on a 24 GB RTX 5090 Laptop GPU achieved ~50 tokens/s, enabling interactive responses and supporting workspaces up to 1M tokens (four times the 256K native window).
AI.conclusion: Decoupling addressable workspace size from the LLM’s native context window enables practical long-running agents with larger histories, delivering better task performance and interactive efficiency than compaction-based context management.

title: MedFlow: Class-Aware Multi-Scale Generation for Medical Time-Series Synthesis
summary: Synthetic medical time-series generation can alleviate data scarcity and support the development of reliable clinical prediction models. However, existing methods mainly focus on matching the overall distribution and temporal dynamics of real data, which does not necessarily ensure strong downstream utility on imbalanced medical datasets. Clinically informative patterns often occur at heterogeneous temporal scales, while rare minority-class characteristics can be obscured by dominant population patterns. To address these challenges, we propose MedFlow, a class-aware multi-scale flow matching framework for medical time-series synthesis. MedFlow employs a vector-quantized multi-scale tokenizer to represent medical sequences at complementary temporal resolutions, capturing both coarse clinical trends and fine-grained dynamics. We further introduce Token Marginal Guidance, which incorporates class-conditional token statistics directly into the flow matching process to steer generation toward class-specific regions of the learned tokens. This mechanism strengthens minority-class patterns, while preserving the global and tail distributions of real data. Experiments on four public datasets covering electronic health records, EEG, and ECG signals demonstrate that MedFlow consistently outperforms recent state-of-the-art diffusion-based baselines across downstream prediction tasks. On average, it improves AUPRC by 5.8%, reduces Context-FID by 88.6%, and achieves 3.8$\times$ higher sampling throughput.

AI.tldr: MedFlow is a class-aware, multi-scale flow-based model for synthetic medical time-series that addresses imbalance by using a vector-quantized multi-scale tokenizer and token marginal guidance, achieving better downstream utility and higher throughput than diffusion baselines.
AI.motivation: Medical time-series data are often scarce and highly imbalanced. Existing methods focus on matching overall distributions and temporal dynamics but fail to preserve or enhance minority-class patterns, especially at heterogeneous temporal scales.
AI.method: Introduce MedFlow, a class-aware multi-scale flow matching framework. It uses a vector-quantized multi-scale tokenizer to represent sequences at multiple temporal resolutions and a Token Marginal Guidance mechanism that injects class-conditional token statistics into the flow matching process to bias generation toward class-specific regions of the token space.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four public datasets (EHR, EEG, ECG) shows MedFlow consistently outperforms recent diffusion-based baselines on downstream prediction tasks: +5.8% in AUPRC, -88.6% in Context-FID, and ~3.8x faster sampling throughput.
AI.conclusion: MedFlow effectively enhances minority-class patterns in synthetic medical time-series while preserving global data distributions, delivering improved downstream utility across diverse modalities and demonstrating strong scalability and efficiency.

title: When Genomic Masking Priors Fail to Transfer: Strong Variant Prediction, Weak Functional Generation
summary: Bidirectional discrete diffusion model appears naturally suited to genomic modeling because it can reconstruct missing sequence from both flanks. We developed GenDA (Genomic Density-optimized Absorbing Diffusion) under the additional hypothesis that entropy-guided span placement would concentrate reconstruction pressure on compositionally complex regions, improving both downstream variant-effect prediction and functional sequence generation. Our results only partially support this premise. After supervised fine-tuning, the 202M-parameter GenDA model reaches a pooled ClinVar SNV AUROC of 0.774, exceeding a similarly scaled autoregressive model by 0.103. However, a matched random-span variant reaches 0.777, providing no evidence that entropy guidance causes the ClinVar improvement. More unexpectedly, GenDA fails a zero-shot functional inpainting stress test: across promoters, enhancers, exon boundaries, and intron boundaries, it does not consistently outperform a control that shuffles the native gap while exactly preserving 3-mer composition. Failure is already present for 50--500-bp gaps, although enhancer degradation worsens at longer gaps. Diagnostics identify several boundary conditions: entropy measures local sequence complexity rather than functional importance; 1-mer tokenization limits physical context; training spans are capped at 300 bp; and high absolute AlphaGenome fidelity can coexist with negative control-normalized restoration. These results show that strong fine-tuned variant prediction, a plausible corruption prior, and functional generation are distinct claims that require separate validation.

AI.tldr: GenDA shows partial gains in ClinVar SNV prediction but fails functional inpainting; entropy guidance lacks clear benefit; results separate prediction from functional generation.
AI.motivation: Investigate bidirectional discrete diffusion for genomic sequence reconstruction to enhance variant-effect prediction and functional sequence generation by targeting compositionally complex regions.
AI.method: Develop GenDA (201M parameters) with entropy-guided span placement; supervised fine-tuning; compare to autoregressive baselines; conduct zero-shot functional inpainting stress tests across promoters, enhancers, exons/introns; analyze boundary conditions via sequence tokenization and span length diagnostics.
AI.result: ClinVar SNV AUROC 0.774, exceeding a similarly scaled autoregressive model by 0.103; random-span variant reaches 0.777, offering no evidence that entropy guidance improves ClinVar. Zero-shot functional inpainting fails across multiple genomic contexts; degradation with longer enhancer gaps; boundary-condition findings: entropy reflects local sequence complexity, 1-mer tokenization limits context, training spans capped at 300 bp, high alphabet fidelity can coexist with poor restoration when controlled against negative baselines.
AI.conclusion: Results underscore that strong fine-tuned variant prediction, a plausible corruption prior, and functional sequence generation are distinct goals requiring separate validation; predictive performance does not guarantee functional generation improvements.

title: When Financial Fine-tuning Fails: A Three-Level Detectability Analysis of Numerical Hallucination in Domain-Adapted Language Models
summary: Financial large language models are increasingly deployed for summarization of reports and disclosures, where numerical hallucination poses significant practical risks. While prior work often attributes such hallucination to insufficient numerical reasoning, this assumption has not been systematically tested under controlled fine-tuning settings. In this paper, we conduct a cost-effective, controlled study of numerical hallucination in financial summarization across three model variants: a base instruction-tuned model, a domain language-adapted model (FT-A), and a numeracy-enhanced domain model (FT-A+B+C). We introduce a three-level detectability taxonomy distinguishing between overt hallucination (currency-denominated fabrication), covert-explicit hallucination (professional-convention numbers), and covert-implicit hallucination (ungrounded quantitative claims). Our results reveal that domain fine-tuning substantially degrades numerical restraint at all detectability levels. While the Base model maintains near-zero hallucination rates (5.4\%), FT-A exhibits 82.5\% overt hallucination and FT-A+B+C reaches 98\%. Contrary to intuition, numeracy supervision amplifies rather than mitigates hallucination across all levels. We identify template injection---the insertion of memorized canonical values regardless of input content---as a primary hallucination mechanism in fine-tuned models. These findings demonstrate that numerical hallucination in financial summarization is driven by the degradation of numerical restraint through domain adaptation, not by insufficient numerical reasoning. We recommend that evaluation protocols assess hallucination across all detectability levels and that deployment practices include explicit mechanisms for grounding-aware generation or abstention.

AI.tldr: Domain-tuned financial LLMs show dramatic numerical hallucination, worsened by numeracy supervision; domain adaptation degrades numerical restraint and enables template injection as a key mechanism; grounding or abstention is needed.
AI.motivation: Systematically test whether numerical hallucination in financial summarization stems from insufficient numerical reasoning or from domain adaptation under controlled fine-tuning.
AI.method: Compare three model variants (base instruction-tuned, FT-A domain-adapted, FT-A+B+C numeracy-enhanced) across three detectability levels (overt, covert-explicit, covert-implicit) in financial summarization; quantify hallucination rates; analyze mechanism.
AI.result: Base model ~5.4% hallucination; FT-A ~82.5% overt hallucination; FT-A+B+C ~98% hallucination; numeracy supervision increases hallucination across levels; template injection identified as primary mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination arises from degraded numerical restraint due to domain-adaptation, not missing numerical reasoning; recommend evaluating across all detectability levels and implementing grounding-aware generation or abstention in deployment.

title: ARC-Loc: Leveraging Azimuthal Ray Convergence as a Geometric Cue for Direct Cross-View Localization
summary: Cross-view localization (CVL) estimates the pose of a ground image by matching it to a geo-referenced satellite image. To bridge the extreme viewpoint gap, mainstream pipelines rely on Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) transformations or 2D-to-3D lifting. However, deriving 3D structures from a single ground image is fundamentally ill-posed, causing these methods to endure geometric distortions and computational costs during 3D lifting or BEV projection. Furthermore, relying on external depth foundation models to resolve this introduces latency and remains susceptible to noisy predictions. In this work, we present a different approach inspired by a human navigation technique called resection, that can perform direct ground to satellite image matching and localization without relying on external depth foundation models. The key insights of our method are that (i) ground keypoints can be translated into azimuthal rays on the satellite map, and (ii) these rays ideally converge at the user location. Exploiting this geometric constraint through direct line-to-point correspondences, we introduce a minimal Azimuthal Ray Convergence (ARC) solver to identify the intersection, alongside an ARC loss to optimize the matching network. By eliminating dependencies on computationally heavy BEV transformations and external depth foundation models, our approach achieves faster, memory-efficient inference, while its explicit feature matching ensures straightforward compatibility with existing frameworks. Experiments on VIGOR and KITTI demonstrate that ARC-Loc maintains competitive localization accuracy compared to recent approaches, highlighting its practicality.

AI.tldr: Introduces Azimuthal Ray Convergence (ARC) for direct ground-to-satellite localization without BEV/3D lifting or depth models; uses ground keypoint→azimuthal ray transformations and a minimal ARC solver to find the user location via line-to-point convergence; efficient and compatible with existing frameworks, with competitive accuracy on VIGOR and KITTI.
