The Domain-Aware Win-rate Network (DAWN) employs a Domain-Aware Knowledge Extractor (DAKE) to compile target-mode attributes into learnable representations, feeding Domain-Aware Temporal/Spatial/Permutation OmniNet Encoders (DATOE/DASOE/DAPOE). A single online model serves all modes with per-mode thresholds; offline evaluation shows 67.73% win-rate prediction accuracy, outperforming attention and sequence baselines.
AI.result: Offline: 67.73% win-rate prediction accuracy, outperforming evaluated baselines. Online A/B tests across the League ladder show consistent reductions in imbalanced matches. For lower-tier players, CHAMP reduces the 5-minute kill-crushing rate by up to 20.73%.
AI.conclusion: CHAMP effectively mitigates cold-start, distribution shift, and data-sparsity bottlenecks in cross-domain MOBA matchmaking; DAWN enables domain-aware, jointly learned representations that generalize across modes, yielding measurable improvements in match balance in real-world deployments.

title: VoxelFix: Post-Hoc Semantic Correction of Completed 3D Voxel Maps
summary: Semantic 3D maps are increasingly constructed automatically for aerial robotics by integrating learned semantic predictions into 3D representations. While this avoids costly manual 3D annotation, errors in the perception and mapping pipeline can persist in the resulting map, reducing its reliability for downstream autonomous tasks. Existing 3D semantic map refinement methods either rely on the original observations, treat occupancy as part of the prediction problem, or apply non-learned local regularization to completed maps. Instead, we study post-hoc semantic correction, asking whether semantic accuracy can be recovered directly from the completed map while keeping its geometry and occupancy fixed. We introduce \method, a graph-based model that corrects voxel labels based on local geometry and neighboring semantic information. To obtain training pairs, we corrupt contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. We evaluate \method on completed OccuFly maps generated from predictions of four independently trained 2D segmentation models. \method consistently improves mIoU by 4.23--5.00 percentage points, with gains broadly distributed across the evaluated semantic classes and particularly strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall. Results on an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene further suggest that the learned correction can transfer beyond the environments seen during training.

AI.tldr: Post-hoc semantic correction for completed 3D semantic maps (OccuFly), using a graph-based model to refine voxel labels while keeping geometry and occupancy fixed; achieves ~4.2–5.0 pp IoU gains across classes with strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall; shows transfer to out-of-distribution scenes.
AI.motivation: Semantic 3D maps for aerial robotics suffer residual labeling errors after automatic construction. Existing refinements rely on original observations, treat occupancy as prediction, or apply non-learned local regularization. A post-hoc correction that preserves geometry/occupancy aims to recover semantic accuracy directly from the completed map.
AI.method: A graph-based model, named (presumably) [31m? (the placeholder in the abstract is \method). It corrects voxel labels using local geometry and neighboring semantic information. Training pairs are generated by corrupting contiguous regions of annotated OccuFly maps according to class confusions observed in upstream maps. Evaluation on completed OccuFly maps from four independently trained 2D segmentation models.
AI.result: Consistent improvement of mean IoU by 4.23–5.00 percentage points across evaluated maps. Gains are broadly distributed across semantic classes with particularly strong improvements for tree, roof, and wall. Transfer to an independently reconstructed out-of-distribution aerial scene suggests the learned correction generalizes beyond training environments.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc semantic correction is viable for improving semantic map accuracy without altering geometry or occupancy. The approach generalizes across different upstream segmentation models and environments, indicating robustness and potential for deployment in aerial robotic perception pipelines.

title: Confounding-Valid Conformal Inference for Counterfactual KPIs in Wireless Networks
summary: Conformal counterfactual inference enables network operators to use logged telemetry to reliably answer 'what-if' questions about network operation. These answers typically take the form of prediction sets that contain, with a user-defined probability, the key performance indicators (KPIs) that would have been observed under alternative control actions. A key challenge is that logged telemetry may omit variables used by the controller, resulting in hidden confounding and invalidating the statistical guarantees of counterfactual analysis. In principle, this issue can be addressed using randomized telemetry, collected by assigning control actions independently of the network state. However, because such randomization may disrupt normal operation, randomized telemetry is typically scarce, causing counterfactual analysis based solely on it to produce uninformative prediction sets. To address these challenges, we propose Confounding-Valid Counterfactual Conformal Inference (CV-CCI), which combines abundant, potentially confounded observational telemetry with limited randomized data through the General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI) principle. CV-CCI leverages observational data to improve efficiency while using randomized data to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees under arbitrary hidden confounding. Experiments on two representative radio access network (RAN) control tasks show that CV-CCI remains valid under hidden confounding while producing more efficient prediction sets than state-of-the-art confounding-valid baselines.

AI.tldr: CV-CCI fuses observational (potentially confounded) telemetry with limited randomized data to enable conformal counterfactual inference under hidden confounding, improving efficiency while maintaining finite-sample coverage.
AI.motivation: Hidden confounding from unobserved variables undermines causal counterfactual guarantees in network telemetry; randomized telemetry can fix it but is scarce and disruptive; need method that uses both data sources to guarantee coverage.
AI.method: General Synthetic-Powered Inference (GESPI) blends abundant observational data with limited randomized data to produce valid counterfactual conformal prediction sets; CV-CCI yields efficiency gains vs baselines while preserving coverage guarantees.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on two RAN control tasks demonstrates validity under hidden confounding and increased efficiency (smaller prediction sets) relative to state-of-the-art confounding-valid baselines.
AI.conclusion: CV-CCI offers a practically viable framework for conformal counterfactual inference in network settings with hidden confounding and scarce randomized data; likely extensible to other domains with similar data characteristics.

title: AutoLR: Automating the Path from Research to Launch Review in Industrial Recommender Systems
summary: Improving an industrial recommender is an iterative research-and-engineering process rather than a direct path from idea to deployment. In \textbf{DASHEN, NetEase's gaming-community app}, algorithm engineers typically identify promising directions from research papers, technical reports, and prior production experiments; reproduce or adapt the underlying methods; implement them in the production codebase; and evaluate the resulting models through training and offline experiments. Promising candidates are then advanced to online A/B tests, and those demonstrating robust gains are submitted to Launch Review---the internal gate for full-traffic rollout. Large language models (LLMs) can assist with individual stages of this workflow, but the overall process remains human-dependent without a harness that can reliably coordinate them across long-running, often multi-day experimental cycles. We present \textbf{AutoLR}, initially built as \textbf{Auto Launch Review} and later extended upstream into an autonomous research-to-launch harness. AutoLR combines three system mechanisms: a \textbf{multi-expert council} that debates and adversarially reviews proposals; a \textbf{deterministic evidence-weighted exploration--exploitation selector} that allocates a limited trial budget across candidate directions and uses Council reranking; and a layered knowledge system that combines external research, production-system knowledge, and DASHEN-specific domain knowledge---such as game communities, player characteristics, and content-interaction patterns---with posterior evidence from configurations, patches, logs, failures, and offline outcomes. LLM agents perform semantic reasoning and code generation, while deterministic controllers retain authority over execution, metric extraction, guardrails, and persistent state transitions.

AI.tldr: An autonomous research-to-launch harness (AutoLR) for industrial recommender systems using a multi-expert council, deterministic exploration-exploitation, and layered knowledge with LLMs for reasoning and code, governed by deterministic controllers.
AI.motivation: To coordinate long-running, multi-stage experiments from ideas to deployment in production-grade recommender systems, reducing human bottlenecks while ensuring safety, reproducibility, and scalable governance.
AI.method: Three mechanisms: (1) a multi-expert council for debate and adversarial reviews; (2) a deterministic evidence-weighted exploration–exploitation selector that allocates limited trial budgets across candidate directions and uses council reranking; (3) a layered knowledge system combining external research, production-system knowledge, and DASHEN-specific domain knowledge with posterior evidence from configurations, patches, logs, failures, and offline outcomes. LLM agents perform semantic reasoning and code generation, while deterministic controllers retain authority over execution, metric extraction, guardrails, and persistent state transitions.
AI.result: Not specified in abstract.
AI.conclusion: AutoLR provides an autonomous research-to-launch harness that coordinates end-to-end experimentation for industrial recommender systems, balancing autonomous reasoning with deterministic governance and human oversight.

title: WeAgent-MMGenEdit: A Full-Stack Recipe for Multimodal Agentic Image Generation and Editing
summary: Image generation and editing models have advanced rapidly, yet remain unreliable when prompts require external world knowledge. Bounded and long-tail parametric knowledge prevents direct or reason-then-generate approaches from recovering the required facts and visual appearances. Existing agentic generation and editing methods mitigate this limitation with retrieval tools, yet remain constrained by insufficient visual verification, overloaded policy models, and weak integration of retrieved textual and visual evidence. To address these limitations, we present WeAgent-MMGenEdit, a full-stack recipe including a multimodal harness, a scalable data construction pipeline, a comprehensive benchmark, and post-training methods for the agent policy and image backend. We first introduce WeAgent-Harness, a multimodal runtime with persistent evidence management and dedicated verification and integration tools that organize retrieved multimodal evidence into a dense carrier. Upon this, we develop a scalable pipeline for prompt synthesis and agentic trajectory collection, yielding 23K supervised trajectories and 14.7K RL tasks with three-layer verifiable checklists. We further introduce WeBench-MMGenEdit, a bilingual benchmark covering both knowledge-intensive image generation and multi-image editing. Finally, a two-sided post-training recipe based on SFT and RL improves the agent policy and image backend. Together, WeAgent-MMGenEdit enables a 30B-total/3B-active policy to outperform similarly sized policy models and approach the performance of a 1T-parameter agent.

AI.tldr: A multimodal agent framework (WeAgent-MMGenEdit) for knowledge-intensive image generation/editing, comprising a multimodal harness (WeAgent-Harness), scalable data pipeline, bilingual benchmark (WeBench-MMGenEdit), and a post-training recipe (SFT + RL) that yields strong efficiency gains: a 30B total / 3B active policy outperforms similarly sized models and nears a 1T-parameter agent.
AI.motivation: Current agentic generation struggles with external/world knowledge, verification, and integrating retrieved textual/visual evidence; existing systems are limited by weak retrieval integration, insufficient visual verification, and policy bottlenecks.
AI.method: Develop WeAgent-Harness for persistent evidence management and multimodal evidence integration into a dense carrier; build a large-scale data pipeline producing 23k supervised trajectories and 14.7k RL tasks with three-layer verification; introduce WeBench-MMGenEdit, a bilingual benchmark for knowledge-intensive generation and multi-image editing; apply a two-sided post-training regimen (SFT and RL) to improve both the agent policy and the image backend.
AI.result: Empirical claim: 30B-total / 3B-active policy outperforms similarly sized policy models and approaches a 1T-parameter agent; extensive data and benchmark resources support evaluation and improvement of knowledge-aware multimodal generation/editing.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive, scalable, full-stack framework that enhances reliability and performance of knowledge-driven multimodal generation/editing at smaller model sizes through integrated evidence handling, large-scale supervised/RL data, bilingual benchmarking, and post-training.

title: Deep Microcompression: Structured Pruning and Bit-packed Quantization for Microcontrollers
comment: Presented at the Global South ML Workshop at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Seoul, South Korea
summary: This paper introduces Deep Microcompression (DMC), a hardware-aware pipeline for deep learning inference on bare-metal microcontrollers. DMC integrates structured pruning, quantization-aware training, and fixed-length bit-packing to achieve a 55.8$\times$ weight compression ratio on LeNet-5 (98.77\% accuracy), generating a dependency-free C library with deterministic latency. On the RP2040 (Cortex-M0+), DMC reduces binary size by 3$\times$ versus TensorFlow Lite while matching its accuracy. Critically, DMC enables the first documented deployment of a standard CNN on the ATmega328P, a device constrained to 2KB SRAM, previously considered infeasible for CNN inference.

AI.tldr: DMC delivers 55.8x weight compression on LeNet-5 with 98.77% accuracy, plus a dependency-free C library enabling deterministic, low-latency inference on microcontrollers; also achieves 3x smaller binaries than TensorFlow Lite on RP2040 and documents the first CNN deployment on ATmega328P (2KB SRAM).
AI.motivation: Enable practical CNN inference on ultra-constrained bare-metal microcontrollers by drastically reducing memory, code size, and latency while preserving accuracy and determinism.
AI.method: Integrate structured pruning, quantization-aware training, and fixed-length bit-packing into a hardware-aware inference pipeline; generate a dependency-free C library; evaluate on LeNet-5 (for compression/accuracy) and RP2040; compare binary size and latency to TensorFlow Lite; demonstrate deployment on ATmega328P.
AI.result: 55.8× weight compression on LeNet-5 achieving 98.77% accuracy; deterministic latency; RP2040 binary size ≈3× smaller than TensorFlow Lite while preserving accuracy; documented CNN deployment on ATmega328P with 2KB SRAM.
AI.conclusion: DMC enables feasible CNN inference on ultra-constrained microcontrollers, delivering substantial compression and size reductions without accuracy loss, enabling new deployments on resource-limited hardware.

title: MARLA: A Conceptual Scaffold for Regulatory Learning under the EU AI Act
summary: The EU AI Act positions regulation as part of the infrastructure for safe, trustworthy and market-ready innovation. Realising this ambition requires regulatory learning: the evidence generated during implementation must be translated into governance and legal knowledge that supports consistent interpretation, effective oversight, and adaptation as technologies evolve. Yet the actors who produce this evidence and those who rely on it operate in different professional worlds. This paper proposes MARLA (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt), a conceptual scaffold organising regulatory learning as a five-stage cycle centred on the implementation of legal requirements into socio-technical practices, situated at the Local, National and European levels of the AI Act's governance architecture. Deliberately non-prescriptive, MARLA gives technical and legal stakeholders a shared vocabulary in which each of the first three stages generates its own documentable form of regulatory learning. We illustrate the scaffold with two piloted case studies and a prospective National-to-European illustration.

AI.tldr: MARLA is a non-prescriptive five-stage regulatory-learning scaffold (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt) for implementing the EU AI Act across Local, National, and European levels, illustrated by two pilots and a prospective National-to-European case.
AI.motivation: Regulatory learning translates implementation evidence into governance and legal knowledge. Actors operate in different professional worlds, so a shared vocabulary is needed to support consistent interpretation, oversight, and adaptation as technologies evolve.
AI.method: Proposes a five-stage cycle (Map, Assess, Report, Learn, Adapt) centered on implementing legal requirements into socio-technical practices. It is deliberately non-prescriptive and yields a documentable form of regulatory learning at each of the first three stages. Applied at Local, National, and European levels of the AI Act governance architecture; illustrated with two piloted case studies and a prospective National-to-European illustration.
AI.result: A conceptual scaffold that provides a shared vocabulary and structure to organize regulatory learning, bridging technical and legal stakeholders and supporting consistent interpretation, oversight, and adaptation.
AI.conclusion: MARLA offers a practical framework to organize regulatory learning within AI Act governance, enabling cross-level coordination and adaptation as technologies evolve.

title: SMILE: Self-Explainable Multimodal Information Bottleneck for Medical Diagnosis
summary: Explainability is increasingly seen as a crucial requirement in AI-based medical diagnosis, particularly in safety-critical clinical decision-making. Most existing explainability methods in healthcare operate in a post-hoc manner and are predominantly designed for unimodal data, which limits their applicability in increasingly prevalent multimodal diagnostic settings. This paper addresses the problem of self-explainable multimodal diagnosis by formulating it within the information bottleneck (IB) framework. We propose a unified learning paradigm that jointly optimizes predictive performance and modality-specific explainability by identifying the most informative elements inside each modality that contribute to diagnostic decisions. To enable tractable and stable optimization, we employ a matrix-based Renyi's $α$-order entropy functional under the assumption of sufficiently expressive encoders. Extensive experiments on representative medical datasets spanning heterogeneous modalities demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves strong diagnostic performance, including an absolute accuracy improvement of 9.1 percentage points on the iCTCF dataset. Moreover, the learned explanations provide transparent and modality-aware insights into feature relevance, thereby improving both the explainability and generalization.

AI.tldr: Self-explainable multimodal diagnosis via information bottleneck with matrix Renyi entropy; improves accuracy and provides modality-aware explanations.
AI.motivation: Explainability in AI-based medical diagnosis; current post-hoc and unimodal limitations hinder multimodal clinical settings.
AI.method: Unified IB-based learning paradigm jointly optimizes predictive performance and modality-specific explainability; selects informative elements in each modality; uses matrix-based Renyi α-order entropy for tractable optimization; assumes expressive encoders.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on heterogeneous multimodal medical datasets; strong diagnostic performance; +9.1 percentage points accuracy on iCTCF; explanations offer modality-aware insights and improve generalization.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a coherent framework for self-explainable multimodal diagnosis, achieving high accuracy while providing transparent, modality-specific explanations; potential for better clinical trust and deployment.

title: NEAT-POCKET: Pocket-Conditioned Autoregressive 3D Molecular Generation with a Neighborhood-Guided Set Transformer
summary: AI-driven de novo molecular design offers a promising route to accelerate early-stage drug discovery by generating novel ligands directly within target protein binding pockets. We present NEAT-POCKET, a pocket-conditioned extension of the autoregressive NEAT model for 3D molecular generation. NEAT-POCKET generates molecules atom by atom in protein pocket environments while preserving atom permutation invariance and explicitly modeling hydrogen atoms. Benchmarks on the CrossDocked and SPINDR datasets show that NEAT-POCKET achieves competitive structure-based generation performance while sampling substantially faster than existing baselines. Beyond full-molecule generation, NEAT-POCKET naturally enables pocket-conditioned fragment completion, a task directly relevant to lead optimization and scaffold elaboration. These results position NEAT-POCKET as a fast, flexible, and practical framework for structure-based drug design.

AI.tldr: NEAT-POCKET extends NEAT to pocket-conditioned 3D molecular generation, enabling atom-by-atom design inside protein pockets with hydrogen modeling and permutation invariance; it achieves competitive structure-based generation and faster sampling, with pocket-conditioned fragment completion for lead optimization.
AI.motivation: To accelerate structure-based drug design by enabling rapid, accurate de novo design inside protein binding pockets, preserving key geometric symmetries and explicitly modeling hydrogens.
AI.method: Pocket-conditioned autoregressive generation: NEAT-POCKET extends NEAT to generate molecules atom-by-atom within protein pockets, preserving atom permutation invariance and explicitly modeling hydrogen atoms. It operates in 3D space and is benchmarked on CrossDocked and SPINDR datasets.
AI.result: NEAT-POCKET achieves competitive structure-based generation performance on CrossDocked and SPINDR benchmarks and samples substantially faster than existing baselines; it also enables pocket-conditioned fragment completion relevant to lead optimization and scaffold elaboration.
AI.conclusion: NEAT-POCKET is a fast, flexible, and practical framework for structure-based drug design, capable of rapid de novo molecule generation and fragment completion directly conditioned on protein pockets.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Sequential Solar PV Policy Design under Uncertainty: An Agent-Based Approach
summary: Designing effective and fiscally sustainable policies for solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption requires balancing adoption gains against public expenditure under uncertainty and heterogeneous decision-making. This study formulates PV policy design as a sequential decision problem and integrates reinforcement learning (RL) with a stochastic agent-based model (ABM) that simulates yearly solar PV adoption under uncertainty. A policymaker agent selects annual incentives, including capital grants, subsidised loan rates, and feed-in tariffs, over a 16-year horizon. Adoption--cost trade-offs are explored by varying policy preferences within a scalarised reward framework. Policies are learned using PPO, SAC, and TD3 and evaluated under stochastic simulation. The results show that this approach produces a clear trade-off structure: the highest-adoption policy (TD3, $w_{\text{cost}}=0.5$) achieves approximately 4,145 adopters at a cost of EUR 41.73 million, while the lowest-cost policy (PPO, $w_{\text{cost}}=2.0$) reduces expenditure to EUR 7.27 million with 2,682 adopters. The balanced policy (PPO, $w_{\text{cost}}=1.6$) achieves 3,495 adopters at a cost of EUR 22.47 million. Across algorithms, consistent trade-off patterns are observed, indicating robustness of the adoption--cost relationship. Compared with static baseline policies, the RL framework explores a broader range of policy configurations. These findings demonstrate the potential of RL as a flexible tool for adaptive policy design under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: RL-based design of solar PV adoption policies using ABM under uncertainty; PPO, SAC, TD3 learn incentive policies over 16 years, revealing a robust adoption–cost trade-off and outperforming static baselines.
AI.motivation: Address uncertain adoption dynamics and fiscal constraints in solar PV deployment; enable adaptive, data-driven policy design that accounts for heterogeneity and stochasticity.
AI.method: Formulates PV policy design as a sequential decision problem with a policymaker agent selecting annual incentives (capital grants, subsidised loan rates, feed-in tariffs) over 16 years. Uses a stochastic agent-based model to simulate adoption; scalarised reward combines adoption gains and costs; policies learned with PPO, SAC, and TD3 and evaluated under stochastic simulation.
AI.result: Identified a clear trade-off between adoption and cost. Highest-adoption policy (TD3, w_cost=0.5) yields ~4,145 adopters at EUR 41.73m; lowest-cost policy (PPO, w_cost=2.0) yields 2,682 adopters at EUR 7.27m; balanced policy (PPO, w_cost=1.6) yields 3,495 adopters at EUR 22.47m. Trade-off patterns consistent across algorithms, RL explores broader policy configurations than static baselines.
AI.conclusion: RL provides a flexible, robust framework for adaptive policy design under uncertainty in PV adoption, capable of balancing adoption gains with fiscal costs and exploring policy configurations beyond static approaches.

title: Conserved Immune Topology Improves Pathology Foundation Model Generalization for Cross-Cancer MSI-H Prediction
comment: Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Medical Foundation Models and Benchmarks (MedFM-Bench). 15 pages, 2 figures
summary: Pathology foundation models integrated with multiple instance learning achieve competitive accuracy within single-cancer cohorts, yet cross-cancer generalization remains unresolved due to organ-specific histological and architectural differences. In this paper, we propose Conserved Immune Topology (CIT), a lightweight spatial representation for cross-cancer MSI-H prediction that augments foundation-model embeddings with biologically motivated immune descriptors. CIT uses unsupervised clustering to identify immune-associated tiles, then encodes tertiary lymphoid structures, peritumoral immune reactions, multi-scale tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, and immune-tumor mixing from frozen foundation-model embeddings and tile coordinates without requiring annotations or target-domain data. The proposed method was evaluated under cross-site and cross-cancer settings using CPTAC-COAD and TCGA-STAD cohorts, which introduce scanner variability, distribution shifts, and organ-specific architectural variations. Zero-shot cross-cancer transfer with CIT increased TransMIL AUC from 0.6627 to 0.7161, an absolute gain of 0.0534 (p=0.003), with consistent improvements across all three MIL aggregators. These results suggest that spatial immune topology provides potentially an organ-invariant representation for MSI-H prediction, supporting cross-cancer generalization of pathology foundation models.

AI.tldr: CIT augments foundation-model embeddings with unsupervised immune topology descriptors to enable cross-cancer MSI-H prediction; shows significant zero-shot cross-cancer AUC gains.
AI.motivation: Cross-cancer generalization gaps in pathology foundation models arise from organ-specific histology; propose an organ-invariant representation via immune topology to improve MSI-H prediction.
AI.method: Unsupervised clustering identifies immune-associated tiles and encodes features such as tertiary lymphoid structures, peritumoral immune reactions, multi-scale tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, and immune-tumor mixing from frozen foundation-model embeddings and tile coordinates; requires no annotations or target-domain data; evaluates cross-site/cancer CPTAC-COAD and TCGA-STAD with three MIL aggregators.
AI.result: Zero-shot cross-cancer transfer improved MIL AUC from 0.6627 to 0.7161 (Δ=0.0534, p=0.003); consistent improvements across all three MIL aggregators.
AI.conclusion: Spatial immune topology may provide an organ-invariant representation for MSI-H prediction, supporting cross-cancer generalization of pathology foundation models.

title: A Comparative Study of Counterfactual Explainers for Graph Neural Networks Enabling Multiple Types of Graph Edit
summary: Counterfactual explanations for graph-structured data seek to determine minimal and realistic modifications required in an input graph to alter a model's prediction to a predefined output. Although counterfactual explainers that support modifying the graph by both adding and removing edges have recently emerged, there is still a lack of general and efficient methods, especially when considering the quality of the generated explanations. Moreover, the problem remains far from solved, as existing methods exhibit different strengths and weaknesses, often trading off between explanation size, coverage and quality. For this reason, it is important to identify where each method performs well and where it falls short, so as to guide future research in the field. Thus, our study compares six state-of-the-art (SOTA) models on a diverse set of real-world and synthetic datasets, covering both binary and multi-class graph and node classification tasks, and evaluates their performance using diverse quantitative and qualitative metrics.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive empirical comparison of six state-of-the-art counterfactual explainers for graph-structured data across diverse datasets and tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of general, efficient, and high-quality counterfactual explanations for graphs; understand trade-offs among explanation size, coverage, and quality; identify strengths and weaknesses of existing methods to guide future work.
AI.method: Conduct a broad empirical evaluation of six SOTA counterfactual graph explainers on real-world and synthetic datasets, covering binary and multi-class graph and node classification tasks; use diverse quantitative and qualitative metrics.
AI.result: The study performs a comprehensive comparative analysis across methods and datasets, revealing varying strengths/weaknesses and illustrating trade-offs among explanation size, coverage, and quality.
AI.conclusion: Insights from the comparison help indicate where each method excels or falls short, guiding future research toward improving generality, efficiency, and explanation quality.

title: From Language Models to World-Acting Systems: Progress and Limits of Agentic AI across Digital, Social, Virtual, and Physical Environments
comment: Review article. 29 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Literature cutoff: 31 August 2026
summary: Large language models become consequential agents when surrounding systems let outputs change external state. Models now call tools, operate interfaces, delegate work, retain state, inhabit generated worlds, and control robots or laboratory equipment. Such advances are often narrated as one march toward autonomy, conflating model competence, system integration, persistence, and safe authority. This critical review synthesizes primary research and official technical specifications available by 31 August 2026. We organize the evidence along delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling, while separating model, harness, and environment. Within the evidence examined, action-interface expansion is documented more convincingly than robust completion, recovery, authorization, or independent verification. Model Context Protocol and Agent2Agent improve interoperability but do not establish trustworthy delegation; multi-agent organization adds specialization alongside cost and correlated failure. Persistent simulations and world models support training and planning but do not themselves demonstrate agency; robotics and self-driving laboratories establish bounded feasibility rather than unattended open-world reliability. We propose justified delegation as an analytical and normative heuristic, not an observed law or certified score: expand action scope only where evidence supports provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control. This framing yields a research agenda for coupled model-harness evaluation, capability-based permissions, durable state, cross-agent accountability, and staged physical validation.

AI.tldr: Current evidence shows action-interface expansion outpaces robust autonomous agency; justify delegation with provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control; outline a research agenda for coupled model-harness evaluation and accountability.
AI.motivation: Critically assess claims that LLMs with tools, persistence, and embodiment yield true autonomy, and provide normative criteria and a forward-looking research agenda.
AI.method: Critical synthesis of primary research and official technical specifications available up to 31 August 2026; organizing evidence along delegated authority, temporal persistence, and environmental coupling, while separating model, harness, and environment; evaluating protocols (Model Context Protocol, Agent2Agent) and multi-agent organization.
AI.result: Action-interface expansion is more convincingly evidenced than robust completion, recovery, authorization, or independent verification; current interoperability improvements do not establish trustworthy delegation; persistent simulations and world models aid training/planning but do not demonstrate agency; robotics/self-driving labs show bounded feasibility rather than unattended open-world reliability.
AI.conclusion: Propose justified delegation as a normative heuristic: expand action scope only where provenance, bounded authority, failure detection, safe recovery, and calibrated human control are supported; articulates a research agenda on coupled model-harness evaluation, capability-based permissions, durable state, cross-agent accountability, and staged physical validation.

title: BLASt3R: Bundle Adjustment of Any Image Set with Multi-View Matching and Monocular Priors
summary: Recent hybrid Structure-from-Motion (SfM) systems combine the robustness of feed-forward 3D reconstruction with the accuracy of traditional bundle adjustment (BA) with pixel matching. They are usually the best performing methods however their scalability and usability remains limited since estimating dense correspondences between views is prohibitively costly, especially considering time constraints inherent to online applications like Visual SLAM (VSLAM). In this paper, we introduce a regularized BA framework that leverages a fast multi-view matcher and monocular priors for initialization and regularization. In contrast to existing systems, our unified approach seamlessly supports both online VSLAM and offline reconstruction from unordered image collections within the same optimization framework and sharing common hyperparameters for all tasks. Extensive experiments across both domains demonstrate improved performance and speed tradeoffs over traditional, feed-forward, and hybrid baselines. Notably for VSLAM, our uncalibrated method outperforms all previous calibrated approaches.

AI.tldr: A unified, regularized BA framework that uses a fast multi-view matcher and monocular priors to combine online VSLAM and offline SfM in one optimization, improving speed and accuracy over baselines and enabling uncalibrated VSLAM to outperform calibrated methods.
AI.motivation: Current hybrid SfM methods rely on dense pixel correspondences, which are too costly for online use; a single framework with shared hyperparameters for online and offline workflows is highly desirable.
AI.method: Introduce a regularized bundle adjustment that leverages a fast multi-view matcher and monocular priors for initialization and regularization, enabling seamless online VSLAM and offline reconstruction within one optimization framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show improved performance and favorable speed-accuracy tradeoffs compared with traditional, feed-forward, and hybrid baselines; the uncalibrated VSLAM approach surpasses prior calibrated methods.
AI.conclusion: A unified optimization framework can robustly handle both online and offline SfM tasks, delivering better accuracy-speed balance and simplifying deployment across VSLAM and offline reconstruction.

title: Single-Query Black-Box Calibration Auditing via Logit Bias
summary: Evaluating the calibration of Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for their safe deployment as zero-shot classifiers. Yet, commercial API providers increasingly hide the continuous output probabilities required by standard calibration metrics. To bypass this opacity, we demonstrate that any LLM API exposing a logit\_bias parameter can be mathematically manipulated to evaluate exact probability thresholds using strictly one query per sample. Leveraging this mechanism, we introduce a novel and provably consistent estimator of the True Calibration Error for binary tasks. Our approach therefore provides an efficient framework for auditing black-box foundation models.

AI.tldr: Efficient, provably consistent estimator of True Calibration Error for binary tasks by exploiting logit_bias in LLM APIs to retrieve exact probabilities with a single query, enabling auditing of black-box models.
AI.motivation: Calibration of LLMs as zero-shot classifiers is essential for safe deployment, yet API opacity hides continuous probabilities needed for standard calibration metrics, hindering evaluation of black-box systems.
AI.method: Demonstrate that any LLM API exposing a logit_bias parameter can be manipulated to read exact probability thresholds with one query per sample; derive a provably consistent estimator of True Calibration Error for binary tasks.
AI.result: Introduces a provably consistent estimator for True Calibration Error in binary settings and an efficient framework for auditing black-box foundation models.
AI.conclusion: The work enables reliable calibration assessment of opaque LLM APIs by extracting exact probabilities via logit_bias, supporting safer deployment and auditing of black-box models.

title: Compact-Memory LLM Agents via Online Max-Member Clustering and Atom-Aware Packing
summary:
Many long-horizon LLM deployments face tight prompt budgets: latency, cost, and context limits make full-context prompting impractical as interaction length grows. The key question is then not raw recall alone, but which memory design gives the best quality--token trade-off in the compact-memory regime. We present \textbf{RSM-full}, an online clustered-memory pipeline designed for a strong quality--token Pareto point.
  RSM-full combines two design choices: a cosine-gated \emph{max-member merge} write rule and an atom-aware grouped context packer. On AMA-Bench, our primary compact-memory benchmark, it reaches $83%$ of Full-Context quality at $32%$ of the token cost at a $4$k budget; under four-seed averaging it beats the closest streaming-clustered baseline (Online K-Means) by $+3.5$--$6.0$,pp ($p{<}.001$) across the whole ${\sim}2.6$k--${\sim}5$k regime. Three-seed ablations show most of this gain comes from the merge rule ($+5.7$,pp over Online K-Means and matched-$τ$ DP-means) and the grouped packer ($+5.0$,pp over flat concatenation).
  The pattern reproduces on RealMem, an independent long-horizon persona-memory benchmark: RSM-full improves on Budget-RAG ($+0.69$,pp, $p{=}.006$), is on par with BM25-RAG (paired $Δ{=}{+}0.27$,pp, $p{=}.47$; we do \emph{not} claim BM25 equivalence in the equivalence-test sense), and significantly outperforms Streaming-Proto ($+2.97$,pp) and the closest reproduced 2025 agentic-memory baseline A-MEM ($+1.65$,pp, $p{<}.001$). Across benchmarks the message is consistent: under tight budgets, compact-memory performance is driven mainly by how streaming memories are merged and how retrieved content is assembled.
  Overall, RSM-full is most useful when answeroughly $2k$--$5k$ prompt tokens, where itdefines a strong compact-memory Pareto point; higher-token baselines remain stronger outside this regime.

AI.tldr: RSM-full is an online clustered-memory pipeline that achieves a favorable quality–token Pareto frontier for long-horizon prompts by using a cosine-gated max-member merge and an atom-aware grouped context packer, showing strong gains in compact-memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM deployments face strict prompt budgets (latency, cost, and context limits). The key challenge is selecting a memory design that maximizes quality per token under tight memory constraints.
AI.method: Propose RSM-full: online clustered-memory pipeline with a cosine-gated max-member merge write rule and an atom-aware grouped context packer. Evaluate on AMA-Bench (compact-memory benchmark) and RealMem (long-horizon persona-memory benchmark), comparing against Online K-Means, Budget-RAG, BM25-RAG, Streaming-Proto, and A-MEM. Include four-seed averaging and three-seed ablations.
AI.result: AMA-Bench: 83% of Full-Context quality at 32% of token cost at a 4k budget. Four-seed averaging beats Online K-Means by +3.5 to +6.0 pp (p<0.001) across ~2.6k–~5k tokens. Three-seed ablations show merge rule and grouped packer provide most gains (+5.7 pp and +5.0 pp vs baselines). RealMem: Budget-RAG improves by +0.69 pp (p=0.006); BM25-RAG is at parity (+0.27 pp, p=0.47); Streaming-Proto (+2.97 pp) and A-MEM (+1.65 pp, p<0.001) are outperformed. Across benchmarks, gains come primarily from how memories are merged and content is retrieved. In the 2k–5k token regime, RSM-full defines a strong compact-memory Pareto point; beyond that, higher-token baselines may be stronger.
AI.conclusion: RSM-full delivers a practical Pareto-efficient memory design for compact-context prompting, with notable gains in the 2k–5k token regime. It should be favored when prompt budgets are tight, though not necessarily superior when token budgets exceed this range.

title: First Things First: Teaching LLM-Based Agents to Prioritize Must-Haves before Nice-to-Haves
summary: Recent progress in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has fueled significant enthusiasm in their potential to act as autonomous agents for real-world tasks. However, scenarios requiring agents to fulfill users' complex, structured requirements remain largely underexplored. In this work, we examine reasoning tasks under three distinct requirement scenarios: (i) Must-have requirements uniquely determine a unique feasible solution; (ii) Multiple answers satisfy the must-have requirements and are prioritized via the nice-to-have requirements; and (iii) No candidate solution satisfies the must-have requirements, in which case the agent should abstain from generating a response. We evaluate state-of-the-art MLLMs on 3,649 carefully constructed problems that reflect realistic service scenarios, including e-commerce, booking, and map-based or ride-hailing. Our evaluation reveals that existing MLLMs exhibit catastrophic failures in all scenarios. They frequently misinterpret task requirements, violate must-have requirements, and produce invalid solutions. To address this critical gap, we propose First Things First Reinforcement Learning FTF-rl that explicitly optimizes reasoning over multi-priority user requirements. Experimental results show that our method substantially improves the task success rate compared to strong baselines. Moreover, FTF-rl yields general effectiveness on popular logical and mathematical reasoning tasks, including LogicVista, MathVision, and InfoQA. Our findings suggest that enhancing requirement-aware reasoning capability provides a simple yet effective pathway to improve generalization of MLLM agents. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/claire62/FTF-RL.

AI.tldr: FTF-rl is a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes reasoning under multi-priority user requirements for multimodal LLM agents, improving task success and generalizing to logical/mathematical reasoning tasks; code and dataset are released.
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs struggle with autonomous task execution when user requirements are structured and multi-faceted (must-have vs nice-to-have). They often misinterpret requirements, violate constraints, or abstain. There is a need for requirement-aware reasoning to improve reliability and generalization.
AI.method: Propose First Things First Reinforcement Learning (FTF-rl), which explicitly optimizes reasoning over multi-priority user requirements (must-have and nice-to-have). The agent learns to satisfy must-have constraints, leverage nice-to-have preferences, and abstain when no solution exists. Evaluated on 3,649 carefully constructed problems across e-commerce, booking, and map-based/ride-hailing tasks, and tested for broader logical/mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.result: FTF-rl substantially improves task success rate over strong baselines. It demonstrates generalization to LogicVista, MathVision, and InfoQA. Ablations suggest the approach effectively aligns multi-priority constraints.
AI.conclusion: Emphasizes that requirement-aware reasoning is a simple yet effective path to enhance generalization of MLLM agents; provides code and dataset for reproducibility.

title: Coarse-Graining Hidden Representations: Unsupervised Neuron Selection via Mapping Entropy
summary: Overparameterized neural networks carry far more hidden units than a task nominally requires, raising the question of which neurons are essential and whether that distinction is legible in the representation itself, without labels or gradients. We cast neuron selection as the problem of coarse-graining the hidden layer by retaining a subset of its neurons, and score each putative selection by the mapping entropy (ME). This quantity measures the loss of discriminatory power inherent in discarding part of the network neurons, and the selection that minimises the ME is taken as particularly informative. This criterion is fully unsupervised, in that it depends only on hidden-activation statistics. In teacher-student networks, ME optimisation recovers the minimal teacher-consistent representation and retains extra units in proportion to the hidden layer's residual variability; in a non-linear Gaussian process task, it selects coherent functional-class mappings whose preferred class shifts across training. On this task and on translation-augmented MNIST, ME-selected subnetworks outperform random subsets of equal size, most clearly under strong compression - linking configurational distinguishability to predictive performance.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised neuron selection via mapping entropy (ME) identifies essential hidden units in overparameterized nets; ME-optimized subnetworks outperform random ones and recover minimal teacher-consistent representations under compression.
AI.motivation: To determine which neurons are functionally essential without labels or gradient-based cues, by linking representation distinguishability to predictive power under compression.
AI.method: Define a subset selection over the hidden layer and score it with the mapping entropy (ME), measuring the loss of discriminatory power when discarding neurons; optimize ME to select informative subnetworks. Apply to teacher-student networks and a non-linear Gaussian process task, plus translation-augmented MNIST.
AI.result: ME optimization recovers minimal teacher-consistent representations and preserves units according to residual variability; in a non-linear GP task the preferred class shifts with training; on translation-augmented MNIST, ME-selected subnetworks outperform random equal-size subsets, especially under strong compression.
AI.conclusion: ME provides a fully unsupervised criterion for identifying informative hidden units; strengthens the link between configurational distinguishability of hidden units and predictive performance, and reveals how representations adapt during training under compression.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Equity and Crypto Markets: Progress, Profitability Evidence, and the Limits of Automated Investing
comment: Review article. 32 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Literature cutoff: 31 August 2026
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) now supports investment workflows from data and prediction through research, portfolios, execution, and tool use. Technical capability, however, is not evidence of investment profitability. This critical state-of-the-art review examines public research available through 31 August 2026 on listed equities, exchange-traded funds, centralized crypto spot, perpetual futures, and on-chain markets. We organize evidence with an alpha-translation chain: point-in-time information must yield a stable signal, feasible positions, executable orders, and risk-adjusted returns after costs. Across machine learning, time-series foundation models, financial language models, reinforcement learning, and agents, the examined record shows real but mainly upstream progress in prediction, text processing, portfolio design, and workflow integration. Evidence is thinner for durable net performance. Temporal contamination, repeated selection, survivorship, weak benchmarks, implementation costs, venue mechanics, and capacity can break translation to net alpha. Strong historical results coexist with predictor decay, corrected look-ahead failures, mixed prospective evidence, and few audited live-capital records. Crypto adds informative state but requires separate treatment of spot, perpetual, and decentralized cash flows and execution. Within the public evidence examined here, no general AI architecture is shown to deliver persistent, cross-regime, capacity-aware net alpha. More credible claims require point-in-time data and models, decision-aligned objectives, joint portfolio--execution evaluation, controlled adaptation, prospective tests, and authority-matched governance. These conditions can improve evidence and implementation; they do not guarantee profit.

AI.tldr: Public AI-in-finance research shows early upstream gains in prediction and workflow integration but no robust, persistent alpha across regimes; rigorous, prospective, decision-aligned evaluation is needed.
AI.motivation: Assess whether AI advances translate into durable investment performance across asset classes; identify translation bottlenecks and governance requirements.
AI.method: Critical synthesis of public research through Aug 31, 2026; organize evidence along an alpha-translation chain; assess classes: listed equities, ETFs, centralized crypto spot, perpetual futures, on-chain markets; cover ML, time-series foundation models, financial LMs, RL, agents; discuss biases and implementation constraints.
AI.result: Real but mainly upstream progress; weaker evidence for durable net returns; risk of biases (temporal contamination, look-ahead, survivorship, benchmarks, costs, venue mechanics, capacity) undermines translation to net alpha; crypto adds informative state but requires separate treatment; no AI architecture shown to deliver persistent, cross-regime, capacity-aware net alpha; credible claims require point-in-time data, decision-aligned objectives, joint portfolio-execution evaluation, controlled adaptation, prospective tests, and governance.
AI.conclusion: Future work should demand point-in-time data, decision-aligned objectives, joint portfolio-execution evaluation, prospective tests, governance; these improve evidence but do not guarantee profitability.

title: Measured Sliders: Learning Continuous Controls from Differentiable Image Measurements
summary: Continuous sliders are useful only when coefficient changes produce predictable image changes. Yet most diffusion sliders derive their axes from text or learned representations, leaving their scales disconnected from observable image properties. Consequently, we cannot tell in advance which attributes are learnable, compare control strengths directly, or anticipate interference when multiple controls are combined. We propose Measured Sliders, a framework that defines continuous controls through closed-form differentiable image measurements. A common measurement space unifies the pipeline. Before training, an observability test identifies usable supervision. During training, a measurement-guided objective learns target movement while suppressing non-target changes. After training, decoded calibration expresses controls in comparable units of realized image change. Multiple LoRA branches are stored in one checkpoint and composed without training on joint activations. Across SDXL and FLUX.1-dev, the resulting controls are ordered, selective, and composable. On 553 prompts, lighting direction reaches rho = 0.995 and 98.9% monotone sweeps. A five-attribute checkpoint achieves average selectivity 2.59, compared with 1.50 for the strongest baseline, and preserves every requested direction in 96.7% of pair and 86.1% of triple compositions. The observability test also separates every subsequently successful measurement from the failed candidate. Overall, image-space measurement provides a common basis for learning, diagnosing, calibrating, and composing continuous generative controls.

AI.tldr: Measured Sliders define continuous diffusion controls via closed-form image measurements, creating a common measurement space for learning, diagnosing, calibrating, and composing attributes. An observability test selects usable supervision; training optimizes movements toward targets while suppressing side changes; post-training calibration yields comparable units. LoRA branches can be stored in one checkpoint and composed without joint retraining. Demonstrated across SDXL and FLUX.1-dev with strong monotonicity and selectivity metrics.
AI.motivation: Diffusion sliders often derive axes from text or learned representations, misaligning with observable image properties. This makes it hard to predict learnable attributes, compare control strengths, or anticipate interference when combining controls. A unified, image-space measurement framework with an observability check can make controls interpretable, comparable, and composable.
AI.method: Define continuous controls via closed-form differentiable image measurements in a common measurement space. Before training, perform an observability test to identify usable supervision signals. During training, use a measurement-guided objective to move target attributes while suppressing non-target changes. After training, recover calibration that maps controls to comparable units of realized image change. Store multiple LoRA branches in a single checkpoint and enable composition without retraining on joint activations. Validate across SDXL and FLUX.1-dev; evaluate on 553 prompts for lighting direction (rho=0.995; 98.9% monotone sweeps); a five-attribute checkpoint achieves average selectivity 2.59 vs 1.50 for strongest baseline; preserves each requested direction in 96.7% of pair and 86.1% of triple compositions. The observability test also discriminates successful measurements from failed candidates.
AI.result: The framework yields ordered, selective, and composable controls with strong empirical performance. It provides a unified, image-space basis for learning and diagnosing controls, enabling reliable composability and predictable attribute changes across prompts and models.
AI.conclusion: Measured Sliders deliver interpretable, cross-model, and composable diffusion controls by tying them to observable image measurements, supported by an observability test and a measurement-guided optimization. This approach improves predictability, comparability, and efficiency of diffusion controls.

title: MomentQuant: an even more minimalist interval method with linear time complexity for time series classification
summary: Time series data is very common in many real-world applications and in numerous domains, with increasing interest for automated information extraction using machine learning. One of these subfields is time series classification, which consists in assigning a label to each new, unseen time series. Many algorithms have been developed over the past decades, with the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost being consistently discussed. Quant, an interval-based algorithm extracting quantiles from recursive, fixed, dyadic intervals, was shown to achieve high accuracy, while being very fast. We propose two changes to make this algorithm even faster. The first one is a better optimized implementation of the exact same algorithm. The second one is to derive approximate quantiles, using the Cornish-Fisher expansion, instead of exact quantiles. This change removes the necessity to sort the time series, leading to a smaller computational complexity. We call this novel algorithm MomentQuant. We provide evidence that our implementation of Quant is faster than the original one, and that MomentQuant is even faster than our implementation of Quant, at the cost of a tiny decrease in predictive performance. These improvements are especially relevant for real-life applications, where inference is performed much more often than training.

AI.tldr: Introduces MomentQuant, a faster variant of Quant for time series classification by optimizing exact quantile computation and using Cornish-Fisher approximations to avoid sorting, achieving faster inference with a small accuracy trade-off.
AI.motivation: Address the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost in time series classification, with emphasis on inference efficiency in real-world deployments.
AI.method: Two enhancements to Quant: (1) a highly optimized implementation of the exact algorithm; (2) derivation of approximate quantiles via Cornish-Fisher expansion to avoid sorting and reduce complexity, yielding MomentQuant.
AI.result: Quant is faster than the original; MomentQuant is faster than the optimized Quant; minor decrease in predictive performance; results favor inference speed in real-world usage.
AI.conclusion: MomentQuant offers a practical speed–accuracy trade-off for deployment where inference speed is critical, supporting real-world applications with frequent predictions.

title: Solving Hard XAI Queries Based on a Compiled Dual-Rail Encoding
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, full version of a submitted conference paper with detailed proofs
summary: The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) within real-world applications has raised a lot of concerns regarding their trustworthiness, especially in critical applications. The field of eXplainable AI (XAI) has emerged with the objective of providing explanations to the users about the decisions made by AI systems. Several explanations for boolean classifiers have been introduced in the literature, including abductive and contrastive explanations, each giving a different insight on the decision of the classifier. However, computing an explanation for a decision of a boolean classifier is a hard problem in general. One way to deal with this complexity is to rely on a compiled representation of the classifier for which each explanation can be computed efficiently. Unfortunately, we prove in this paper that several classes of abductive explanations, remain hard to compute even for Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams, one of the most tractable subsets of the knowledge compilation map. Included in such classes are shorter abductive explanations or abductive explanations that include the explainee's preferences. To recover the benefits of working with compiled representations, we show that a proper representation of the dual-rail encoding of the classifier can be used to compute efficiently these classes of explanations.

AI.tldr: Hardness persists for several abductive explanations of boolean classifiers even with Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams; dual-rail encoding enables efficient computation.
AI.motivation: Improve trust in AI by explaining decisions. Abductive and contrastive explanations are important for XAI, but computing explanations is hard; compiled representations reduce complexity only for some problems; need methods to recover efficiency.
AI.method: Provide hardness proofs for multiple abductive explanation classes on OBDDs. Introduce a dual-rail encoding of the classifier and demonstrate how it enables efficient computation of these explanations within compiled representations.
AI.result: Proves intractability for shorter abductive explanations and explanations incorporating explainee preferences on OBDDs; shows that a proper dual-rail encoding of the classifier can be used to compute these explanations efficiently.
AI.conclusion: A dual-rail encoding of the classifier can recover computational efficiency for certain abductive explanations in compiled representations, offering a practical avenue for scalable XAI for boolean classifiers.

title: Cross-Domain Tracker Adaptation Without Target-Domain Labels via Vision-Language Agents
summary: We present a system that uses a Vision-Language Model (VLM) as a diagnostic agent for adapting a detect-to-track pipeline to a new target domain without access to target-domain labels. Rather than optimizing against annotated metrics, the VLM directly inspects rendered tracking outputs, identifies visual failure modes, and recommends parameter updates through an iterative tuning loop. We first demonstrate that ground-truth-supervised hyperparameter transfer can be brittle. On MOT17->MOT20, applying a source-derived oracle configuration reduces mean HOTA by 0.090, from a target-domain ceiling of 0.357, to 0.267. Without using any target-domain labels, our VLM-based tuner recovers 67.8% of this lost headroom, finishing within 0.029 HOTA of the target ceiling; on the highest-density target sequence, it recovers up to 86.7%. We further show that label-free Bayesian optimization with handcrafted proxy objectives struggles under large domain shifts and can degrade configurations that are already strong. In contrast, the VLM tuner acts selectively: when its visual diagnosis reveals no clear failure mode, it declines to modify the configuration, preserving performance on easy transfers while improving hard ones. Finally, we characterize the conditions under which this approach succeeds, namely, when domain shift manifests through exposed detection-level parameters, versus where it is less effective, such as MOT17->DanceTrack, where the source oracle is already near-optimal.

AI.tldr: A Vision-Language Model serves as a label-free diagnostic tuner for a detect-to-track system, recovering substantial target-domain performance headroom without target labels, and outperforming label-free Bayesian optimization in large shifts while being selective about when to modify configurations.
AI.motivation: Ground-truth supervised hyperparameter transfer can be brittle under domain shift. Label-free BO can degrade performance and lacks interpretability. A diagnostic VLM can inspect rendered outputs to guide tuning.
AI.method: Iterative tuning loop where a Vision-Language Model inspects rendered tracking outputs, diagnoses visual failure modes, and recommends parameter updates. It compares against a source-derived oracle, and is evaluated on domain shifts such as MOT17→MOT20, examining when to modify configurations and when not to.
AI.result: VLM tuner recovers 67.8% of lost headroom, finishing within 0.029 HOTA of the target ceiling; on the highest-density target sequence, recovery reaches 86.7%. Ground-truth-supervised oracle transfer can reduce mean HOTA from 0.357 to 0.267 (−0.090). Without target labels, the VLM tuner approaches the target ceiling. Label-free Bayesian optimization struggles under large domain shifts and may degrade strong configurations. The tuner acts selectively and preserves easy transfers while improving hard ones; success is contingent on domain shift manifesting through detection-level parameters (less effective when the source oracle is near-optimal, e.g., MOT17→DanceTrack).
AI.conclusion: A VLM-based diagnostic tuner offers a robust, label-free approach to adapt detect-to-track pipelines across domains, outperforming traditional label-free optimization in many shifts and providing interpretable failure-mode guidance; its effectiveness depends on whether domain shift affects detectable detection-level parameters.

title: From 80x to 385x: A Best-Matching-Unit Search at the L2 Roof, Measured Against a Symmetrically Tuned Baseline
comment: 15 pages, 8 tables, 3 figures. Companion to arXiv:2608.24067. Both implementations were tuned symmetrically; cuSPARSE became 2-3x faster in the process. Code, data and frozen results: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22245712 (tag v2.0)
summary: Comparisons between GPU implementations are usually asymmetric: one side is tuned by its author, the other is run as found. I report a programme that tuned both a novel SOM algorithm (SparseBin) and the baseline algorithm it was being compared to (cuSPARSE). The best-matching-unit search that dominates self-organizing map training was tuned through four levers - tile size, tile-membership clustering, neuron-axis chunking and vectorised loads - reaching 5.6-10.1x per epoch over the previously published configuration at map sizes from 32x32 to 512x512, and lifting the margin over the CUDA implementation behind our earlier MEDLINE atlases from ~80x to ~385x. cuSPARSE, the implementation SparseBin is compared against, received every lever with an analogue on its side, and became 2-3x faster in the process. The tuned kernel pressed the L2 bandwidth roof at 77% of peak with every other unit at 40-65%, bounding any further lever at ~1.3x - a terminal result rather than a waypoint, and every untested lever was either capped by that bound by construction or measured null.

AI.tldr: Auto-tuning both a novel SOM kernel (SparseBin) and its baseline cuSPARSE yields large per-epoch speedups and exposes a hardware-bound limit driven by memory bandwidth; untuned levers saturate, suggesting near-peak performance is approached.
AI.motivation: Address the common asymmetry in GPU benchmarking by tuning both compared implementations to reveal true performance potential and practical limits of the kernel on contemporary GPUs.
AI.method: Four tuning levers for the best-matching-unit search kernel: tile size, tile-membership clustering, neuron-axis chunking, and vectorised loads. Evaluations conducted across map sizes from 32x32 to 512x512. Both SparseBin and cuSPARSE were tuned with analogous levers. Per-epoch time and L2 bandwidth utilization (aiming toward peak) were measured.
AI.result: SparseBin achieved 5.6-10.1x per-epoch speedups over the previously published configuration; the margin over a CUDA implementation behind earlier MEDLINE atlases increased from ~80x to ~385x. cuSPARSE benefited from tuning with analogous levers, improving by 2-3x. The tuned kernel saturated about 77% of peak L2 bandwidth, with other units at 40-65%, implying that further gains are bounded by memory bandwidth; untested levers were bounded by that limit or yielded null gains.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that fair, bidirectional tuning can dramatically alter perceived performance, but hardware-imposed bandwidth limits cap further gains. Auto-tuning reveals both substantial speedups and the practical terminus of optimization on current GPUs.

title: Why We Care About Understanding: Competence through Predictive Compression
summary: What is the relation between understanding and compression, and why does human understanding take such a heavily compressed form? Across information theory, machine learning, and AI research, a substantial tradition identifies understanding with compression-a thought captured in Gregory Chaitin's dictum that "comprehension is compression." Philosophers, by contrast, have characterized understanding in terms of grasping connections, giving explanations, and handling novelty. This paper bridges the two pictures through three interlocking theses. The first concerns the concept of understanding: it serves as an efficient proxy for a distinctive form of robust competence, enabling us to identify whom to trust and whom to learn from. The second concerns the state of understanding: to understand a domain is to possess a mental model of its relational structure that enables prediction, and what enables prediction enables compression, because what becomes predictable need not be stored separately. Compression is therefore not identical with comprehension, but its representational shadow. The third concerns the characteristically human form of understanding: the fiduciary and transmission functions highlighted by the first thesis impose pressures of demonstrability and transmissibility that drive human understanding toward principled simplicity. The resulting framework explains both the appeal and the limits of compressionist accounts of understanding while shedding light on the inscrutability of AI systems.

AI.tldr: Understanding and compression are closely linked yet distinct: understanding is an efficient, robust proxy for trust and learning; compression is the shadow of predictive structure; human understanding evolves under demands of demonstrability and transmissibility, explaining AI inscrutability.
AI.motivation: Bridge information-theoretic and philosophical notions of understanding; explain why compression is appealing and its limits; illuminate human cognition and AI system behavior.
AI.method: Conceptual synthesis across information theory, ML, and AI; articulate three interlocking theses about concept of understanding, state of understanding, and human form of understanding; derive consequences for predictability, compression, and transmission.
AI.result: A unified framework in which understanding is tied to predictive, relizable structure; compression serves as a practical byproduct; human cognitive design pushes toward simplicity and demonstrability; clarifies why compressionist views work and where they fail, and why AI systems are inscrutable.
AI.conclusion: Compression is not identical to understanding but a shadow of it, rooted in predictive structure and robust competence; human cognition is shaped by fiduciary and transmissibility pressures, favoring principled simplicity and demonstrability; the framework explains the appeal and limits of compressionist accounts and sheds light on AI inscrutability.

title: Few-Shot Video Recognition via Hierarchical Metric Learning
summary: Few-shot action recognition (FSAR) aims to recognize unseen action categories with only a small number of annotated video samples. Recent works typically apply single-prototype supervision at the network output and fail to sufficiently exploit rich cross-frame global spatial information in videos. Even existing multi-level metric schemes only impose parallel prototype constraints on intermediate layers, without progressive supervision along the full feature pipeline, which results in limited generalization ability of the learned class prototypes. Inspired by this, we present a novel method, hierarchical metric learning for few-shot action recognition (HML-FSAR). First, a spatial-enhanced module is developed to capture cross-frame global spatial representations. Combined with temporal MHA, heterogeneous alignment, spatial-temporal feature fusion and dictionary learning modules, it constructs the complete feature processing pipeline. Second, a hierarchical metric learning (HML) strategy is embedded into HML-FSAR. Composed of center metric, alignment metric, contrastive metric, dictionary metric and prototype metric, HML imposes progressive multi-stage complementary constraints from frame-level representations to final class prototypes, so as to jointly optimize feature compactness, heterogeneous spatial-temporal alignment, inter-class discriminability and anti-noise robustness. The proposed HML-FSAR method is validated on five widely-used FSAR datasets, and experimental results fully demonstrate its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Proposes HML-FSAR, a hierarchical metric learning framework with spatial-enhanced representation and progressive multi-metric supervision across frame-level to prototypes to improve few-shot action recognition.
AI.motivation: Current FSAR methods rely on single-prototype supervision and limited cross-frame spatial modeling; multi-level metric schemes often provide only intermediate-layer supervision and lack progressive guidance through the feature pipeline, limiting prototype generalization.
AI.method: Introduce a spatial-enhanced module to capture cross-frame global spatial representations, paired with temporal multi-head attention, heterogeneous alignment, spatial-temporal feature fusion, and dictionary learning. Embed a hierarchical metric learning (HML) strategy comprising center, alignment, contrastive, dictionary, and prototype metrics to impose progressive constraints from frame-level representations to final class prototypes.
AI.result: Validated on five widely-used FSAR datasets, with experimental results indicating clear effectiveness and improved generalization compared with baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed HML-FSAR framework combines spatial enhancement, temporal modeling, and a multi-stage hierarchical metric learning scheme to improve feature compactness, cross-domain alignment, discriminability, and robustness for few-shot action recognition.

title: Beyond Stationarity in Time Series: Discovering Causal Structures and Latent Regimes via Markov Blankets
comment: Accepted at the 11th AALTD Workshop at ECML PKDD 2026, Naples, Italy
summary: This paper introduces Regime-aware Constraint-Based and Noise-Based causal discovery with Markov Blankets (RCBNB-MB), a novel causal discovery algorithm for time series that relaxes the common assumption of a single, time-consistent causal structure. Time series are typically observed at discrete time points and often exhibit regime changes that challenge the assumption of a static causal structure, a limitation in many real-world dynamic systems. To address this challenge, RCBNB-MB identifies latent causal regimes, defined as subsets of time points within which a stable causal structure holds. The algorithm follows an iterative strategy that segments the time series into regimes and discovers the causal graph within each regime. By leveraging the Markov blanket rather than direct parents, RCBNB-MB gains robustness to errors in causal discovery and preserves predictive information. We provide theoretical guarantees for RCBNB-MB's ability to recover both regime transitions and causal graphs under reasonable assumptions. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on simulated datasets with known ground truth and real-world IT monitoring data, where taking into account regime shifts is critical. Empirical results show that RCBNB-MB systematically outperforms baseline approaches in accurately detecting regime changes and their associated causal graphs, positioning it as a robust and versatile framework for non-stationary time series analysis.

AI.tldr: A regime-aware, time-series causal discovery framework (RCBNB-MB) that segments non-stationary data into latent causal regimes and learns per-regime graphs using Markov blankets, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation showing improved detection of regime changes and causal structure.
AI.motivation: Non-stationarity and regime shifts break static causal assumptions in time-series; there is a need for robust methods to detect regime changes and infer regime-specific causal graphs.
AI.method: Iterative regime segmentation to identify latent causal regimes; within each regime, perform causal discovery using constraint-based and noise-based approaches that leverage Markov blankets for robustness and information preservation; theoretical guarantees for recovering regime transitions and graphs.
AI.result: The method provides theoretical guarantees for recovering regime transitions and causal graphs under reasonable assumptions; empirical validation on simulated data and real IT monitoring data shows systematic improvement over baselines in detecting regime changes and the associated causal graphs.
AI.conclusion: RCBNB-MB offers a robust, versatile framework for non-stationary time-series causal discovery, suitable for dynamic systems with regime shifts; demonstrated effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world IT data, with potential applicability to other domains.

title: Global to Local: Topology-Preserving Adaptive Graph Pooling via Granular-Ball
summary: Graph pooling aims to compress the graph, including both node embeddings and their underlying topological patterns, into a more compact representation. Previous works focus primarily on the overly fine-grained representation of nodes, progressively coarsening the graph by removing nodes or merging them into clusters, thus neglecting the global-to-local patterns and adaptive granularity of the graph's topological structure. In the real scenario, graphs as a whole can be considered the coarsest level of granularity, encapsulating the global topological structure, with progressively finer-grained local topological structures represented from top to bottom. This process continues until the adaptive granularity for each subdomain is reached. To this end, we propose a novel Topology-Preserving Adaptive Graph Pooling (TPAGP) method that dynamically partitions graphs into granular balls by integrating node features and topological information, enabling the generation of multi-granularity representations that effectively capture both local and global structural patterns. Additionally, we design a multi-granularity graph network model that facilitates feature interaction and optimization across different granularities, significantly enhancing performance in graph classification tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that TPAGP outperforms existing pooling methods across various benchmark datasets, effectively mitigating information loss caused by fixed-granularity strategies.

AI.tldr: A topology-preserving adaptive pooled graph representation via granular balls with multi-granularity networks, achieving superior graph classification by preserving global-local patterns and reducing granularity-induced information loss.
AI.motivation: Current graph pooling emphasizes fine-grained node reduction and cluster merging, which overlooks global-to-local topology and adaptive granularity.
