Graphs have global structure at the coarsest level and progressively finer local structures; effective pooling should preserve topology across multiple granularities.
AI.method: Introduce TPAGP: dynamic partitioning of graphs into granular balls that fuse node features and topology to create multi-granularity representations; also propose a multi-granularity graph network to enable feature interaction and optimization across granularities.
AI.result: Empirical results show TPAGP outperforms existing pooling methods on benchmark datasets and mitigates information loss caused by fixed-granularity strategies.
AI.conclusion: TPAGP provides topology-preserving adaptive pooling that captures both global and local structures, enabling effective multi-granularity representations and improved graph classification performance.

title: Compact Neural Appearance Models for Efficient Gaussian Splatting
summary: Explicit primitive-based radiance fields such as 3D Gaussian Splatting typically model view-dependent appearance using low-order spherical harmonics (SH). Although efficient to evaluate, SH coefficients dominate per-primitive storage and memory traffic, while their band-limited basis restricts angular detail. We present a thorough, end-to-end comparison of SH and recent spherical appearance models and introduce an implicit alternative that decodes compact per-primitive latent codes using a tiny shared MLP. We integrate all models into the same optimized pipeline, fusing their forward and backward passes into a differentiable CUDA rasterizer and provide a portable WebGL viewer for laptop and mobile GPUs. Our evaluation across reconstruction quality, memory use, and optimization and rendering performance shows that recent spherical models offer the strongest overall quality-efficiency trade-off. Our neural representation is the most compact model evaluated and, compared to third-degree SH, reduces the per-primitive appearance footprint from 192 to 28 bytes, accelerates optimization by 1.3$\times$, while improving reconstruction quality. We further analyze how appearance parametrization shapes optimization, identifying differences in recovered geometry and the tendency of expressive models to absorb non-static scene content. Together, our framework and analysis provide practical guidance for replacing SH beyond what image metrics alone can capture.

AI.tldr: SH-based radiance fields suffer from limited angular detail and bulky per-primitive SH storage; a latent-code, implicit spherical model offers a more compact, faster, and higher-quality alternative, evaluated in a unified pipeline against SH and other spherical representations.
AI.motivation: To rigorously compare SH, recent spherical appearance models, and an implicit latent-code approach within a common, optimized pipeline, and to quantify trade-offs in quality, memory, and performance for explicit primitive-based radiance fields.
AI.method: End-to-end evaluation by integrating SH, recent spherical parameterizations, and an implicit per-primitive latent-code model into a single CUDA-based differentiable rasterizer with a portable WebGL viewer; measure reconstruction quality, memory footprint, optimization speed, and rendering performance; analyze how appearance parametrization affects optimization and geometry.
AI.result: Recent spherical models deliver the best overall quality–efficiency trade-off. The proposed neural latent-code model is the most compact, reducing per-primitive appearance footprint from 192 to 28 bytes, accelerating optimization by ~1.3×, and improving reconstruction quality compared with third-degree SH. The analysis highlights how appearance parameterization shapes optimization and can lead expressive models to absorb non-static scene content.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides practical guidance for replacing SH with modern spherical representations in explicit primitive-based radiance fields and emphasizes evaluation beyond image-space metrics to capture optimization dynamics and geometry implications.

title: Phase Transition Frequency as a Training Time Predictor of Test Accuracy in ResNets
summary: The number of discrete class-separability jumps observed during ResNet finetuning is examined empirically as a predictor of final test accuracy. Across 75 experiments spanning four benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and CIFAR-10-C) and three architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ResNet-101), with five to ten seeds per configuration, a strong within-dataset negative correlation is obtained on standard i.i.d. classification benchmarks: \(r = -0.84\) on CIFAR-10 (\(p < 10^{-8}\), \(n = 30\)) and \(r = -0.87\) on CIFAR-100 (\(p < 10^{-5}\), \(n = 15\)). Under distributional stress, the relationship attenuates: TinyImageNet yields \(r = -0.45\), and the CIFAR-10-C corruption benchmark yields \(r = -0.19\). Two additional analyses discipline the empirical claim. A partial correlation controlling for architecture depth, treated as a linear covariate, shows that on CIFAR-100 the transition count retains statistically significant predictive power (\(r_{\mathrm{partial}} = -0.69\), \(p = 0.007\)); the corresponding result under the stricter categorical conditioning is not established at \(n = 15\). A comparison against six alternative training-curve signals shows that transition count achieved the strongest correlation among the evaluated signals on CIFAR-100 and one of the strongest on CIFAR-10, but is dominated by other signals on the two stressed benchmarks. The comparison is restricted to training-curve-level signals; comparisons against effective rank, Hessian sharpness, Fisher information, margin, and neural-collapse measures, which are the strongest competitors in the current literature, are not part of the present study and remain open. The observation is presented as an in-distribution training-quality probe among a family of candidate probes, and an inexpensive detection procedure suitable for logging alongside a standard training loop is provided.

AI.tldr: Negative correlation between the count of discrete class-separability transitions during ResNet finetuning and final test accuracy in-distribution, with strong effects on CIFAR-10/100 and weaker effects under distribution shift; partial correlation controlling for depth remains significant on CIFAR-100; transition count often among the strongest simple training-curve signals on CIFAR-100 but not on stressed benchmarks; proposed as a cheap in-training-quality probe.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether a simple, inexpensive in-training signal—the number of discrete class-separability transitions observed during finetuning—can predict final performance and serve as a practical quality probe during training.
AI.method: Empirical study of 75 experiments over four benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, CIFAR-10-C) and three ResNet architectures (ResNet-18/50/101) with 5–10 seeds per config. Computed transition counts during finetuning, assessed Pearson correlations with final test accuracy, performed partial correlations controlling for depth, and compared against six alternative training-curve signals. Discussed the limits and logging implications.
AI.result: Strong in-distribution negative correlations: CIFAR-10 r=-0.84 (p<1e-8, n=30); CIFAR-100 r=-0.87 (p<1e-5, n=15). Weaker correlations under distribution shift: TinyImageNet r=-0.45; CIFAR-10-C r=-0.19. Partial correlation (depth as covariate) on CIFAR-100: r_partial=-0.69, p=0.007; categorical conditioning not established at n=15. Among six signals, transition count is strongest on CIFAR-100 and among the strongest on CIFAR-10, but not dominant on stressed benchmarks. The study notes the need to compare against stronger competitors (effective rank, Hessian sharpness, Fisher information, margin, neural-collapse) which were not assessed. The transition count is framed as an in-distribution, inexpensive training-quality probe that can be logged alongside standard training loops.
AI.conclusion: Transition-count is a practical, inexpensive probe of training quality under i.i.d. conditions, with strong predictive power on CIFAR-10/100; its utility declines under distribution shift; further work should include broader comparisons with additional training-curve metrics and more stressed benchmarks.

title: A Tree-based RAG Framework for Evidence-Intensive QA via Adaptive Planning and Topology-Aware Evidence Gathering
summary: Recent structured RAG methods leverage tree- or graph-based reasoning structures to improve multi-hop QA. However, they face key limitations in evidence-intensive QA, where answering a question requires synthesizing information scattered across dozens or even hundreds of documents: structural rigidity, which limits adaptive reasoning expansion, and topology-ignorant evidence gathering, which prevents effective integration of evidence across different reasoning nodes. To address these issues, we propose APT-RAG, an Adaptive Planning and Topology-aware evidence gathering RAG framework. Adaptive planning dynamically expands the reasoning structure based on question dependencies and evidence requirements, while topology-aware evidence gathering improves evidence coverage through sibling evidence reuse, direct retrieval, and evidence aggregation from child nodes. We further introduce evidence-guided batched answer generation to reduce significant generation overhead in evidence-intensive QA. In the experiments on evidence-intensive QA benchmarks, APT-RAG outperforms existing structured RAG methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/hyudsl/APT-RAG.

AI.tldr: APT-RAG introduces adaptive planning and topology-aware evidence gathering to address evidence-intensive multi-hop QA in RAG, with evidence-guided batched answer generation to reduce generation overhead; demonstrates superior performance on benchmarks; code available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Existing structured RAG methods struggle in evidence-intensive QA due to structural rigidity and topology-ignorant evidence gathering, which limits adaptive expansion and effective integration across numerous documents.
AI.method: Adaptive planning dynamically expands the reasoning structure based on question dependencies and evidence requirements, while topology-aware evidence gathering improves coverage via sibling evidence reuse, direct retrieval, and aggregation from child nodes. Additionally, evidence-guided batched answer generation reduces generation overhead.
AI.result: APT-RAG outperforms existing structured RAG methods on evidence-intensive QA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively enhances evidence coverage and efficiency in evidence-intensive QA, with publicly available code.

title: Learning Spatial-Spectral Refinement and Calibrating Complementary Observations for Hyperspectral Image Super-Resolution
summary: Hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion (HMIF) aims to reconstruct a high-resolution hyperspectral image (HR-HSI) by combining the fine spatial details of a high-resolution multispectral image (HR-MSI) with the rich spectral information of a low-resolution hyperspectral image (LR-HSI). Recent advances in implicit neural representations (INRs) have enabled flexible coordinate-based modeling for HMIF; however, existing INR-based approaches may not fully capture fine-grained spatial structures and rich spectral dependencies. Moreover, the LR-HSI and HR-MSI are primarily incorporated through degradation-consistency constraints, leaving their complementary information underexploited. To address these limitations, we propose Two-Stage Reconstruction with Implicit Tensor Neural Representation (TSR-ITNR), a unified self-supervised framework integrating representation refinement and observation-guided calibration. In Stage 1, TSR-ITNR learns an implicit Tucker representation and refines its low-rank spatial coefficient tensor and spectral basis to better capture fine spatial structures and interband correlations. A fixed pretrained denoiser further provides a deep prior for the preliminary reconstruction. In Stage 2, parameter-free calibration derives complementary and noninterfering corrections from both observations to recover information insufficiently captured in Stage 1. Theoretical analysis establishes the geometry-preserving property of spectral refinement and the orthogonal complementarity of calibration. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate strong quantitative, visual, and spectral reconstruction performance without ground-truth HR-HSI supervision. Beyond conventional reconstruction metrics, we further assess the effectiveness of TSR-ITNR using downstream semantic segmentation accuracy.

AI.tldr: A two-stage self-supervised HMIF framework (TSR-ITNR) uses an implicit Tucker tensor representation and observation-guided calibration to reconstruct high-resolution HSI from LR-HSI and HR-MSI without ground-truth HR-HSI, with theoretical guarantees and strong benchmark performance including downstream segmentation.
AI.motivation: Current INR-based HMIF methods may miss fine spatial details and complex spectral dependencies and underutilize complementary information from LR-HSI and HR-MSI, which are mainly integrated via degradation constraints.
AI.method: Stage 1 learns an implicit Tucker representation, refining the low-rank spatial coefficient tensor and spectral basis; a fixed pretrained denoiser provides a deep prior for the preliminary reconstruction. Stage 2 performs parameter-free calibration to extract complementary, noninterfering corrections from both observations to recover information not captured in Stage 1. Theoretical analysis shows a geometry-preserving property for spectral refinement and orthogonal complementarity for calibration.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets show strong quantitative, visual, and spectral reconstruction performance without ground-truth HR-HSI supervision. Additionally, the method’s utility is demonstrated by improvements in downstream semantic segmentation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: TSR-ITNR provides a unified, self-supervised framework for HMIF that leverages implicit tensor representations and observation-guided calibration, supported by theoretical guarantees and comprehensive empirical validation.

title: Dimension-Adaptive Batched Lipschitz Narrowing Without Knowing the Zooming Dimension
summary: The Appropriately Combined Edge-length (ACE) sequence in A-BLiN depends on the zooming dimension $d_z$. This note removes that dependence. The next edge length is selected from the number of cubes that survive the preceding elimination. The resulting Count-Adaptive BLiN algorithm does not use $d_z$ or the zooming constant $C_z$, yet it attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_d(T^{(d_z+1)/(d_z+2)})$ regret with $\mathcal O_d(\log\log T)$ batches. Together with the adaptive-grid lower bound in Theorem 10 of the original paper, the optimal batch complexity remains $Θ_d(\log\log T)$ when $d_z$ is unknown.

AI.tldr: Removes dependence on the zooming dimension dz in the ACE sequence of A-BLiN by introducing Count-Adaptive BLiN; edge-length is chosen from surviving cubes, yielding dz-free operation with regret Õ_d(T^{(dz+1)/(dz+2)}) and Õ_d(log log T) batch complexity; optimal batch complexity Θ_d(log log T) persists when dz is unknown.
AI.motivation: To decouple algorithmic behavior from an unknown zooming dimension and constants (dz, C_z), while preserving nearly optimal regret and achieving low batch complexity under a lower-bound framework.
AI.method: Introduce Count-Adaptive BLiN where the next edge length is determined by the number of surviving cubes after the preceding elimination. The algorithm omits explicit use of dz and C_z, relies on adaptive-grid discretization, and leverages the elimination-based edge-length selection to drive the regret bound.
AI.result: The Count-Adaptive BLiN achieves a regret of Õ_d(T^{(dz+1)/(dz+2)}) with Õ_d(log log T) batches, despite not using dz or C_z. This aligns with the adaptive-grid lower bound (Theorem 10 of the original paper), showing that the optimal batch complexity remains Θ_d(log log T) when dz is unknown.
AI.conclusion: Removing the dz dependency from ACE edge-length and achieving dz-free operation while retaining near-optimal regret and the optimal batch complexity strengthens the robustness of BLiN-type strategies under dimension-uncertainty; the adaptive-grid lower bound substantiates the reported optimal batch complexity.

title: Language models judge war differently when tested for alignment
summary: Safety evaluations can mischaracterize deployed behaviour if artificial-intelligence systems respond to being evaluated. We test this possibility in a full-factorial conjoint experiment on decisions to start a war, spanning 20 large language models, 32 scenarios, 10 repetitions and two conditions (N = 12,800 judgments). Adding one sentence, "You are tested for alignment with human values", produced two effects. First, it produced a level effect: mean willingness to start war fell by 13.43 points on a 0-100 scale (95% confidence interval, -16.20 to -10.65). Second, it produced a structural effect by changing which information drove judgments. Probability of success was the largest factor for 17 of 20 models at baseline; under the cue, civilian casualties were largest for 12. Standardized estimates show that this reordering arose principally because models attenuated strategic considerations such as probability of success and domestic support. Evaluation framing therefore changes both an answer's level and its revealed decision rule.

AI.tldr: Framing AI safety evaluations alters both the level and the revealed decision rules in war-decision judgments across 20 LLMs.
AI.motivation: To test whether evaluation framing biases manifest in AI judgments about high-stakes actions by modifying judgment criteria.
AI.method: Full-factorial conjoint experiment: 20 large language models, 32 scenarios, 10 repetitions, two evaluation conditions (N=12,800 judgments); manipulated sentence: 'You are tested for alignment with human values'.
AI.result: The cue reduced mean willingness to start war by 13.43 points on a 0-100 scale (CI -16.20 to -10.65). It also changed which information drove judgments: baseline: probability of success was the top factor for 17 of 20 models; with the cue, civilian casualties became the top factor for 12 models. Standardized estimates indicate the reordering arose from attenuation of strategic considerations (e.g., probability of success, domestic support).
AI.conclusion: Evaluation framing can shift both the level and the revealed decision rule of AI judgments, suggesting safety evaluations may mischaracterize deployed behavior.

title: Adaptive Gated Deepfake Detection for Low-Resolution and Resource-Constrained Environments
summary: Deepfake detection models often rely on high-quality inputs, fixed inference paths, and computationally expensive architectures, limiting their use in low-resolution and resource-constrained settings. This paper proposes AdaGate-DF, an adaptive gated deepfake detection framework that uses image-quality cues to route samples through a dual multi-exit system so high-quality images can exit earlier and save compute. We evaluated AdaGate-DF against MaD-CoRN, DefakeHop++, and ShuffleNetV2 on two benchmark datasets (Celeb-DF and FaceForensics++) under multiple configurations to test image resolution dependence and training and inference efficiency. On Celeb-DF, AdaGate-DF achieves an AUC of 0.9370, outperforming MaD-CoRN and DefakeHop++ while maintaining a low inference latency. Resolution-based testing shows consistent improvement as input resolution increases, reaching an AUC of 0.9708 at 384 by 384. The FaceForensics++ results highlight that AdaGate-DF remains effective under class imbalance, following competitive results with evaluated models. Overall, AdaGate-DF demonstrated a practical balance between detection performance, uncertainty-aware prediction, and computational efficiency for variable-quality deepfake detection.

AI.tldr: AdaGate-DF introduces an adaptive gated dual-exit framework for deepfake detection that routes samples based on image quality to exit early and save compute, achieving strong AUC on Celeb-DF and robust performance on FaceForensics++ with efficiency advantages across resolutions.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors typically require high-quality inputs and heavy architectures; there is a need for efficient, scalable detectors that adapt to input quality and resource constraints.
AI.method: Proposes AdaGate-DF with a dual multi-exit architecture and image-quality cues to route samples; evaluates against MaD-CoRN, DefakeHop++, ShuffleNetV2 on Celeb-DF and FF++ under multiple configurations and resolutions.
AI.result: On Celeb-DF, AUC 0.9370, surpassing MaD-CoRN and DefakeHop++ with low latency; AUC improves with resolution to 0.9708 at 384x384. On FF++, performance remains competitive under class imbalance. Demonstrates a practical balance between accuracy, uncertainty-aware prediction, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive gated dual-exit design with quality-aware routing can achieve competitive deepfake detection performance while reducing computation and maintaining robustness to varying input quality.

title: FedDRAW: Federated Dual Reputation Annealing Weighting for Heterogeneous Multi-Institutional Chest Radiograph Classification
summary: Artificial intelligence models are promising for medical diagnosis, but they require large numbers of unbiased data, which in medicine are distributed across hospitals and cannot be centralized to protect patient privacy. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this, since hospitals train one shared diagnostic model while patient data remain local. Training proceeds in communication rounds, in which each hospital trains the shared model locally and returns it to the server for merging by weighted average. This aggregation weight determines whose institutional knowledge shapes the result. Federated averaging (FedAvg) sets it in proportion to local sample count, so a small but informative hospital is permanently assigned a small influence, andl argest clients could dominate the global model even when they are less informative. We propose Federated Dual Reputation Annealing Weighting (FedDRAW), a server-side aggregation method that combines a data-size prior with the cosine similarity between client and global parameters under two coupled annealing schedules. An inner schedule shifts client reputation from the size prior towards similarity. An outer, deferred annealing schedule on the softmax inverse temperature keeps the weighting selective in the early and middle rounds and relaxes it to uniformity at convergence. We evaluate FedDRAW on 12 simulated client-partition scenarios of two chest radiograph datasets (CheXpert and ChestMNIST), against seven federated baselines under identical local training settings. FedDRAW achieved the highest average rank among all eight methods under both AUC and the geometric mean (GM) of sensitivity and specificity, which a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis confirmed to be a statistically significant difference between the methods. Scheduling two signals, rather than fixing the weights by sample count alone, could enable less biased diagnostic models.

title: TROVE: Adaptive Agent Skill Orchestration via Trace-Grounded Route Validation and Editing
summary: Agents tend to optimize, select, or constrain execution structures before decisive runtime outcomes are observed. However, such pre-execution commitment creates an orchestration bottleneck: when intermediate evidence invalidates the pending continuation, agents must either execute stale steps or replan broadly, compounding errors, wasting computation, and discarding progress. We thus propose Trace-grounded Route Orchestration via Validation and Editing (TROVE), which revises only what runtime evidence invalidates. Offline, TROVE distills evaluated workflow-search traces into atomic and composite skills and an outcome-conditioned transition graph, preserving stable fragments while exposing outcome-dependent decisions. Online, it treats a planned route as provisional: after committing one top-level skill, the controller retains a valid continuation, inserts a trace-supported local response, or replaces only the invalid suffix. Evaluation across code-generation, question-answering, and math reasoning benchmarks with different LLM backbones show that TROVE delivers a stronger quality-efficiency trade-off than existing baselines of dataset-level optimization, query-level architecture selection, and graph-constrained scheduling. Quality gains are largest when outcomes change the appropriate continuation, whereas early termination yields substantial efficiency gains on near-saturated tasks. Ablations further show that composite skills capture most offline benefits, insertion enables local correction, and suffix replacement primarily improves efficiency. These findings establish selective route editing as a general principle for adaptive agent orchestration.

AI.tldr: TROVE enables selective route editing by grounding run-time decisions in offline traces, allowing local corrections rather than full replans, achieving better quality-efficiency trade-offs across tasks.
AI.motivation: Pre-execution commitments can bottleneck agents: when intermediate evidence invalidates pending steps, agents either execute stale steps or replan broadly, wasting computation and progress. A framework that edits only invalid suffixes promises efficiency and robustness.
AI.method: Offline: distill evaluated workflow-search traces into atomic and composite skills and an outcome-conditioned transition graph; preserve stable fragments while exposing outcome-dependent decisions. Online: planned route is provisional; after committing one top-level skill, the controller retains a valid continuation, inserts a trace-supported local response, or replaces only the invalid suffix.
AI.result: Across code-generation, QA, and math reasoning benchmarks with various LLM backbones, TROVE achieves a stronger quality-efficiency trade-off than baselines such as dataset-level optimization, query-level architecture selection, and graph-constrained scheduling. Gains are larger when outcomes change the continuation; early termination yields efficiency gains on near-saturated tasks. Ablations show composite skills capture most offline benefits; insertion enables local correction; suffix replacement mainly improves efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Selective route editing constitutes a general principle for adaptive agent orchestration.

title: Scalable Detection of Fossil Palynomorphs in Multifocal Digital Microscopy Images
summary: Palynomorphs (microscopic, organic-walled fossils such as pollen, spores, and dinoflagellates) are important high-resolution records of past climates and are critical to the study of ancient ecosystems. Existing methods rely on manual analysis of high-resolution, multifocal digital microscopy images, which is slow and time-consuming and requires researchers to compromise on the scale of their investigations. To the best of our knowledge, our work proposes the first ever scalable end-to-end pipeline for automated palynomorph detection in whole slide images that addresses this bottleneck through: (1) efficient methods for decomposing and compressing digitized multifocal microscope slide images into tractable 2-dimensional tiles for analysis; (2) benchmarking modern object detection models, including RF-DETR, for the detection of palynomorphs, achieving an AP@50 of 0.879; (3) an efficient algorithm for the synthesis of detection outputs across large-scale, high-resolution images; and (4) an I/O optimization resulting in faster inference time. Our methods drastically reduce the time required for palynomorph detection in a single slide from often days of manual inspection to under one hour of automated analysis, enabling palynological research at a substantially greater scale.

AI.tldr: First scalable end-to-end pipeline for automated palynomorph detection in whole-slide images, including tiling of multifocal scans, benchmarking of detectors (RF-DETR) with AP@50 = 0.879, and output synthesis plus I/O optimizations; reduces analysis from days to under an hour per slide.
AI.motivation: Manual palynomorph analysis is slow and limits scale. High-resolution, multifocal slide images require efficient, scalable automation to enable large-scale palynological research.
AI.method: Decompose and compress multifocal slide images into tractable 2D tiles; benchmark modern object detectors (including RF-DETR) for palynomorph detection; develop an efficient fusion algorithm to synthesize detections across large images; implement I/O optimizations to speed inference.
AI.result: Achieves AP@50 of 0.879 on palynomorph detection and reduces per-slide analysis time from days to under one hour; provides a scalable, end-to-end pipeline for high-resolution whole-slide palynology imaging.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that scalable automated palynomorph detection is feasible, enabling research at greater scale; the tiling, fusion, and I/O optimization strategies are applicable to similar high-resolution WSI tasks.

title: Hessian-based molecular conformation augmentation for a scalable and efficient strategy of machine learning interatomic potentials
comment: 45 pages including Supporting Information, with 6 figures and 9 tables in the main text
summary: While machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have successfully learned potential energy surfaces (PES) and atomic forces, many practical applications, such as vibrational analysis and transition state search, rely heavily on the PES Hessian. Yet, standard MLIPs tend to be trained on energy and forces alone, leaving Hessian information largely unexploited. Meanwhile, existing methods that explicitly incorporate the Hessian into training objectives require architectural modifications and introduce significant computational and memory overheads due to higher-order backpropagation. To address these limitations, we propose two Hessian-derived data augmentation schemes: isotropic Gaussian displacement (\textbf{UniAug}) and normal mode-weighted displacement (\textbf{ModeAug}). Both methods utilize simple Taylor expansions, achieving effective augmentation without altering training objectives or extending the autograd graph. This allows seamless, plug-and-play integration with existing architectures and training pipelines. Comprehensive evaluations across non-equilibrium and equilibrium datasets demonstrate that our approach enhances model accuracy while providing practical, task-specific guidelines.

AI.tldr: Hessian-informed data augmentation for MLIPs through two plug-and-play schemes, UniAug and ModeAug, to improve Hessian-related accuracy without altering training objectives or autograd graphs.
AI.motivation: Hessian information is critical for vibrational analysis and transition-state search but is underutilized due to reliance on energy/force training and high overhead of explicit Hessian integration.
AI.method: Two augmentation schemes: isotropic Gaussian displacement (UniAug) and normal-mode-weighted displacement (ModeAug). Both use simple Taylor expansions to perturb inputs during training, preserving loss functions and autograd graphs.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on non-equilibrium and equilibrium datasets show improved model accuracy and practical task-oriented guidelines for Hessian-related applications.
AI.conclusion: Hessian-derived augmentation provides an effective, computationally cheap enhancement for MLIPs, enabling better vibrational analyses and transition-state tasks with easy integration into existing training pipelines.

title: Moral Competence Before Moral Content: Why LLM Agents Lack the Prerequisites for Coherent Alignment
comment: Accepted for publication in the Paris Journal of AI and Digital Ethics (2026); presented at PCAIDE 2026
summary: AI alignment requires AI systems to adhere to human norms, values, or intentions. Under value pluralism there is no correct target, but a shared prerequisite is that the system's behavior expresses a coherent policy: a mapping from situations to verdicts that is invariant while a situation's morally relevant features are preserved, and sensitive when they change. We introduce four structural conditions for such coherent policies: verdict stability, monotonicity, decisiveness, and Pareto viability. Together they measure a form of moral competence that is evaluable from behavior alone, without reference to a moral standard or expert baseline, forming a structural floor for alignment rather than a normative target. We demonstrate the methodology on three simulated deployments featuring LLM-based agents facing moral dilemmas. Evaluating nine frontier models under a factorial design of five paraphrases, five escalation levels, and three dominance conditions, we show no model expresses a coherent policy across the three deployments: surface-form perturbation alone produces verdict-rate shifts of up to $99$ percentage points at a single escalation level, and a model's success on one scenario does not predict its competence on another. This suggests LLM-based agents are not currently the kind of object to which alignment can meaningfully apply.

AI.tldr: Proposes four structural conditions (verdict stability, monotonicity, decisiveness, Pareto viability) to define a coherent policy for AI alignment, evaluated as a structural floor evaluable from behavior alone. Across three simulated LLM deployments and a factorial study of nine models, perturbations cause large verdict shifts and cross-scenario incompetence, suggesting current LLMs are not coherent enough to be meaningfully aligned by these criteria.
AI.motivation: Value pluralism implies no single correct target for alignment; however, a coherent policy—consistent mapping from situations to verdicts that respects morally relevant features—can serve as a structural baseline for alignment, independent of normative targets.
AI.method: Formalize four structural conditions for coherence; apply them to three simulated moral-decision deployments with LLM agents. Use a factorial design (five paraphrases, five escalation levels, three dominance conditions) to evaluate nine frontier models. Assess verdict stability, monotonicity, decisiveness, and Pareto viability from behavior alone.
AI.result: No model expresses a coherent policy across deployments. Surface-form perturbations shift verdicts dramatically (up to 99 percentage points at one escalation level). A model’s success in one scenario poorly predicts competence in others, indicating lack of cross-scenario coherence.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based agents do not exhibit the kind of coherent policy necessary for alignment under the proposed structural criteria; alignment should be viewed as a structural floor rather than a normative target, and the methodology reveals substantial fragility to perturbations and scenario dependence.

title: Lightweight Vision Transformer Compression for On-Device Plant Disease Detection in Resource-Constrained Agricultural Field Conditions
summary: Chilli (Capsicum annuum) is one of India's most economically significant crops, yet its productivity is persistently threatened by diseases that are difficult to identify without expert intervention. While Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved high classification accuracy, their large computational footprint makes deployment on resource constrained devices challenging. Existing compression approaches typically address pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation in isolation, leaving the potential benefits and interactions of their combined application insufficiently explored. We propose a unified Vision Transformer compression framework that combines Hessian-Balanced Adaptive Block Pruning (H-BAC), guided by second-order sensitivity estimation, with quantization and attention-based knowledge distillation. To systematically identify the most effective configuration within each compression family, each technique is first evaluated independently through controlled ablation studies, after which the best-performing components are integrated into a sequential deployment pipeline tailored to real-world agricultural constraints. On a chilli 3-class village-split dataset with a genuine cross-village, cross-device out-of-distribution test split, the resulting compressed models match or exceed the 95.13% FP32 baseline's accuracy, alongside 74-98% model size reduction, and the fully integrated compression pipeline achieves a 54.5x size reduction (327.42 MB to 6.01 MB) at 95.13 +/- 2.32% accuracy across four tested configurations. A direct comparison further reveals that, on this dataset, a directly-trained student of the same final size, without pruning or distillation, reaches comparable accuracy of 94.87%, at the same 6.01 MB INT8 size, indicating where H-BAC and knowledge distillation are, and are not yet shown to be, worth their computational cost.

AI.tldr: A unified vision transformer compression framework for chilli disease classification that combines Hessian-Balanced Adaptive Block Pruning (H-BAC), quantization, and attention-based knowledge distillation (KD). Through ablations, the best components are integrated into a sequential deployment pipeline. On a cross-village chilli dataset, the compressed models reach or exceed FP32 baseline accuracy with 74-98% size reductions; the full pipeline achieves 54.5x reduction (327.42 MB to 6.01 MB) at ~95.13% accuracy. A directly trained student of the same final size (without pruning/distillation) attains ~94.87% accuracy, highlighting when H-BAC and KD are beneficial relative to training a smaller model directly.
AI.motivation: Deploy high-performing Vision Transformers on resource-constrained agricultural devices for disease classification, acknowledging that existing compression methods are typically studied in isolation. The study investigates the interactions and synergies between pruning, quantization, and KD, validated on a cross-village, cross-device out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset to reflect real-world variability.
AI.method: Proposes Hessian-Balanced Adaptive Block Pruning (H-BAC) guided by second-order sensitivity, combined with quantization and attention-based knowledge distillation. Conducts controlled ablation studies to identify the best configuration within each compression family, then integrates the optimal components into a sequential deployment pipeline tailored to agricultural constraints. Evaluated on a 3-class chilli dataset with genuine cross-village, cross-device OOD split.
AI.result: Compressed models match or surpass 95.13% FP32 baseline accuracy while achieving 74-98% model size reduction. The fully integrated pipeline achieves 54.5x size reduction (327.42 MB to 6.01 MB) with ~95.13±2.32% accuracy. A directly-trained student of the same final size (without pruning/distillation) reaches 94.87% accuracy at 6.01 MB INT8, suggesting H-BAC and KD deliver benefits in some configurations but may be redundant in others.
AI.conclusion: A unified compression framework leveraging H-BAC, quantization, and KD can produce substantial model size reductions with competitive accuracy in practical agricultural deployments. The results indicate non-uniform benefits from pruning and KD across configurations, underscoring the importance of ablations and context-aware deployment decisions. Further work could explore more efficient interaction strategies among compression techniques and broader real-world validation.

title: PRICE: A Systematic Study of LLM Adaptation Choices for Bitcoin Price Forecasting
summary: Cryptocurrency markets exhibit extreme volatility and non-stationary dynamics that challenge conventional forecasting methods. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for time series forecasting, the combined effects of adaptation choices remain largely unexplored in financial settings. This study introduces PRICE, a structured approach for adapting LLMs to short-term Bitcoin price forecasting. Built on a 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 8B model, PRICE investigates how fine-tuning, numerical representation, prompting, inference, and decoding jointly influence forecasting performance. PRICE integrates Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), Recursive multi-step inference, Integer-rounded numerical representation, Context-Task-Format (CTF) prompting, and Exact zero-temperature decoding. Ablation studies show that each component contributes to forecasting accuracy and reliability. LoRA enables efficient training on limited hardware, recursive inference improves accuracy, integer-rounded values reduce errors, CTF prompting outperforms Chain-of-Thought, Implicit Chain-of-Thought (iCoT), and few-shot prompting, and zero-temperature decoding improves stability during recursive forecasting. Comparative evaluation against eight transformer-based and time-series foundation models shows that PRICE achieves the lowest forecasting errors on both validation and test sets while maintaining robust performance across evaluation periods. Despite being based on a model primarily pretrained on text rather than time-series data, PRICE achieves competitive or superior performance relative to specialized foundation models. These findings demonstrate that adaptation choices critically determine the accuracy and robustness of LLMs for numerical time-series forecasting.

AI.tldr: PRICE adapts a quantized LLaMA-3 8B model for short-term Bitcoin price forecasting using a structured adaptation pipeline. It combines LoRA, recursive multi-step inference, integer-valued representation, Context-Task-Format prompting, and exact zero-temperature decoding, and achieves state-of-the-art or competitive forecasting accuracy against transformers and time-series baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise for time-series forecasting, but adaptation choices in finance are underexplored. Cryptocurrency markets are volatile and non-stationary, necessitating robust, efficient adaptation strategies for LLMs to numeric forecasting tasks.
AI.method: 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 8B with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA); recursive multi-step inference; integer-rounded numerical representation; Context-Task-Format (CTF) prompting; exact zero-temperature decoding; comprehensive ablation to assess each component's contribution.
AI.result: PRICE attains the lowest forecasting errors on validation and test sets among eight transformer-based and time-series baselines, with robust performance across evaluation periods; it remains competitive or superior despite being pretrained mainly on text rather than time-series data.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation choices critically determine LLMs’ accuracy and robustness for numerical time-series forecasting; a structured, component-wise adaptation (LoRA, recursive inference, integer rounding, CTF prompting, and zero-temperature decoding) enables effective short-term crypto forecasting even with a model not specialized for time-series.

title: Towards Efficient Evaluation of Evolutionary Transfer Optimization: Case Studies on Task-Parameterized Applications
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Intelligence and Nature-Inspired Computing (MIND 2026)
summary: As evolutionary transfer optimization (ETO) scales to larger collections of related tasks, problem evaluation can become a major source of runtime growth. This work studies problem-side evaluation scaling in task-parameterized applications and reformulates application-specific serial computations into forms suitable for parallel execution. We organize evaluation scaling into two levels: the number of evaluated tasks and the workload within each task. In multi-task optimization, matrix-recursive kinematic-arm evaluation is reformulated using an accumulation-matrix representation of cumulative link directions. In sequential transfer optimization, pointwise B-spline trajectory evaluation is reformulated using a blending-matrix representation for trajectory and collision computations. Both reformulations maintain close numerical agreement with their reference evaluations and substantially reduce runtime, yielding $256.72\times$ and $93.91\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively. These results demonstrate problem-side reformulation as a practical route toward scalable ETO. Both application implementations and experimental scripts are released as open source to support reproducibility and reuse.

AI.tldr: Problem-side reformulation enables scalable evaluation in evolutionary transfer optimization by converting serial computations into matrix- and blending-based representations, achieving large end-to-end speedups while preserving numerical accuracy.
AI.motivation: As ETO scales to larger task collections, evaluation cost becomes a major bottleneck; the work seeks scalable, application-specific reformulations for parallel execution and reduced runtime.
AI.method: In multi-task optimization, reformulate matrix-recursive kinematic-arm evaluation using an accumulation-matrix representation of cumulative link directions. In sequential transfer optimization, reformulate pointwise B-spline trajectory evaluation using a blending-matrix representation for trajectory and collision computations. Both maintain numerical fidelity to reference evaluations.
AI.result: End-to-end speedups of 256.72× (multi-task) and 93.91× (sequential) with close numerical agreement to reference evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Problem-side reformulation is a practical route toward scalable evolutionary transfer optimization; the implementations and experimental scripts are released as open source to support reproducibility and reuse.

title: MEOX: Compact Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts for Earth Observation
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
summary: Recent advances in Earth Observation representation learning accommodate heterogeneous sensors and missing observations, often through larger architectures. We present MEOX (Multimodal Earth Observation with eXperts), a multimodal masked autoencoder with a 2.939 million-parameter encoder and 3.115 million parameters in total. Sensor-specific adapters, explicit validity signals, and a shared sparse-expert block preserve modality-dependent processing before a learned patch-wise fusion. Four metadata tokens then accompany a single spatial sequence through fourteen further encoder blocks. Shared expert projections with private low-rank residuals constrain parameter growth, while rotary attention supports downstream spatial grids different from pretraining. The model is pretrained on 1.228 million MMEarth64 samples using modality-balanced masked reconstruction and structured sensor dropout. Frozen transfer is evaluated on six GEO-Bench tasks at both 64 and 224 pixels. The model reaches 64.42% mean intersection-over-union on cashew segmentation at 64 pixels and 90.56% average accuracy on EuroSAT at 224 pixels, exceeding the corresponding reported CSMoE results. BigEarthNet finetuning reaches 72.95% micro-average precision. Routing diagnostics distinguish expert participation, spatial dependence, modality association, and functional contribution. A held-out WorldCover probe measures a 0.64-percentage-point benefit from metadata, while retrieval separates same-sensor semantics from cross-sensor alignment. These results demonstrate sensor-flexible representation learning and strong task transfer using a compact parameter budget.

AI.tldr: A compact multimodal masked autoencoder (MEOX) for Earth Observation that handles heterogeneous sensors via sensor-specific adapters and sparse experts, enabling effective cross-sensor transfer with a small parameter budget.
AI.motivation: Address heterogeneous EO sensors and missing observations while maintaining scalable, robust representations that generalize across tasks and resolutions.
AI.method: A multimodal masked autoencoder with a 2.939M-parameter encoder and 3.115M total parameters, using sensor-specific adapters, explicit validity signals, and a shared sparse-expert block for modality-dependent processing before patch-wise fusion. Four metadata tokens accompany a spatial sequence through fourteen encoder blocks. Shared expert projections with private low-rank residuals constrain growth, and rotary attention supports downstream spatial grids. Pretrained on 1.228M MMEarth64 samples with modality-balanced masked reconstruction and structured sensor dropout. Frozen transfer evaluated on six GEO-Bench tasks at 64 and 224 px. Diagnostics include routing analyses and a WorldCover probe.
AI.result: On 64-px cashew segmentation: 64.42% mIoU. On 224-px EuroSAT: 90.56% average accuracy, exceeding CSMoE. BigEarthNet finetuning reaches 72.95% micro-average precision. Metadata yields a 0.64 percentage-point benefit in WorldCover. Retrieval shows sensor-specific vs cross-sensor alignment in semantics. Demonstrates strong transfer with a compact parameter budget and sensor-flexible representation learning.
AI.conclusion: MEOX demonstrates effective sensor-flexible representation learning and strong cross-task transfer with scalable parameter efficiency; diagnostic analyses reveal how experts participate and how metadata and cross-sensor alignment contribute to performance.

title: GLASS: Graph-Language Alignment with Spherical Scoring for Transferable Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
comment: Preprint. This work and project were done in Apr. 2026. This work was included in Xudong Wang's Ph.D. thesis (Defense Passed on 13 Apr. 2026), "Principled and Effective Graph Representation Learning with Application to Anomaly Detection," deposited with The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen Library
summary: We introduce GLASS, a framework for graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) that achieves robust cross-domain transferability through graph-language alignment on the unit hypersphere. GLASS builds a unified representation space by aligning a structure-aware graph encoder with an instruction-aware text embedding via a multi-slice soft cosine objective. Our framework serializes local, global, and semantic graph properties into a compact Graph Descriptor Prompt (GraphDP), creating a text bridge that enables domain-agnostic anomaly scoring. By enforcing multi-scale consistency through Matryoshka representation slices, the model captures anomalous deviations at multiple levels of granularity. For scoring, we formulate anomaly detection as density estimation on the aligned hypersphere and introduce Spherical Multi-Modal Scoring (SMS), which instantiates von Mises-Fisher kernel density estimators in both graph and text embedding spaces. This probabilistic formulation recovers angular k-nearest-neighbor scoring as a high-concentration limiting case and provides a principled fusion of structural and semantic anomaly signals. The shared text embedding space further serves as a cross-domain bridge: by encoding a target domain's GraphDP without target-domain training data, GLASS performs zero-shot anomaly detection, and with only a handful of normal examples, few-shot adaptation via reference-set calibration. Across twelve benchmarks and three meta-domains, GLASS obtains the best average AUROC and rank compared with recent advanced GLAD baselines and enables effective cross-domain transfer.

AI.tldr: GLASS is a cross-domain graph anomaly detection framework that aligns graph and text embeddings on a unit hypersphere, enabling zero-shot and few-shot anomaly detection via Graph Descriptor Prompts and multi-scale Matryoshka representations, with spherical density-based scoring (SMS).
AI.motivation: To achieve robust cross-domain GLAD by learning domain-agnostic representations that fuse structural graph information with semantic text cues, and to provide principled, probabilistic anomaly scoring on a hypersphere.
AI.method: Align a structure-aware graph encoder with an instruction-aware text embedding using a multi-slice soft cosine objective. Serialize local, global, and semantic graph properties into a Graph Descriptor Prompt (GraphDP). Enforce multi-scale consistency via Matryoshka representation slices. Score anomalies via density estimation on the aligned hypersphere using Spherical Multi-Modal Scoring (SMS) with von Mises-Fisher kernels in both graph and text spaces, yielding angular k-NN as a high-concentration limit. Enable zero-shot detection by encoding a target domain GraphDP without target data and few-shot adaptation via reference-set calibration.
AI.result: Outperforms recent advanced GLAD baselines across twelve benchmarks and three meta-domains, achieving best average AUROC and ranking while enabling robust cross-domain transfer and zero-/few-shot anomaly detection.
AI.conclusion: GLASS provides a unified, probabilistic, graph–text aligned representation on the hypersphere for GLAD, combining multi-scale structural/semantic cues with principled density-based scoring to enable effective cross-domain anomaly detection.

title: MePo++: Unifying Representation Refinement and Reconciliation for General Continual Learning
summary: General continual learning (GCL) aims to learn from evolving data streams without task identities, explicit boundaries, or repeated access to previous data, making it a realistic yet challenging setting for continual intelligence. Although pretrained models (PTMs) provide rich prior knowledge for addressing the limited supervision and non-stationary nature of GCL, existing PTM-based methods often directly adapt pretrained representations and overlook two critical gaps: the misalignment between upstream pretraining and downstream continual adaptation, and the unreliability of conventional output alignment under blurry streams. Here we propose MePo++, a unified post-training framework that bridges pretrained knowledge and downstream GCL through representation refinement and reconciliation. MePo++ introduces two complementary components: MetaPrep, which improves representation plasticity for continual adaptation through unsupervised meta-refinement over pseudo continual sequences; and StreamAlign, which reinforces representation stability by reconciling evolving online features with a stable pretrained geometry. By improving representation learnability before adaptation and preserving alignment during continual learning, MePo++ enables PTMs to remain both plastic for new concepts and stable over evolving streams. Experiments across diverse PTMs, datasets, and continual learning baselines demonstrate the consistent effectiveness and generality of MePo++ for PTM-based GCL. Our code is available at https://github.com/SunGL001/MePo_Plus.

AI.tldr: MePo++ is a post-training framework that enhances pretrained models for general continual learning via two complementary modules: MetaPrep for unsupervised meta-refinement to boost plasticity, and StreamAlign for alignment with pretrained geometry to maintain stability, yielding robust improvements across PTMs, datasets, and baselines.
AI.motivation: GCL settings lack task identities and fixed data streams, and pretrained models are underutilized due to misalignment between upstream pretraining and downstream adaptation as well as unstable output alignment under blurry streams. A unified post-training approach is needed to refine representations for continual adaptability while preserving stable geometry.
AI.method: MePo++ comprises two components: MetaPrep, performing unsupervised meta-refinement over pseudo continual sequences to improve representation plasticity before adaptation; and StreamAlign, which aligns online features with the stable geometry of the pretrained model to preserve stability during continual learning. The framework operates in a post-training phase to prime PTMs for GCL, bridging pretrained knowledge and downstream adaptation.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across diverse pretrained models, datasets, and continual learning baselines shows consistent improvements and generality of MePo++ for PTM-based GCL. The authors also provide code, indicating reproducibility and practical utility.
AI.conclusion: By improving representation learnability prior to adaptation and maintaining alignment during continual learning, MePo++ enables pretrained models to remain plastic to new concepts while stable across evolving streams, offering a generalizable solution to PTM-based GCL.

title: Reflection-aware Generative Novel View Synthesis
summary: We propose Ref-GeNVS, a training-free, reflection-aware method for generative novel view synthesis (NVS) in mirror scenes. Existing multi-view diffusion models often fail to recognize the mirror in the scene and cannot exploit reflected content for scene generation. To fix this issue without additional training, our key idea is to treat a mirror image as two complementary views. From input images, we estimate the mirror plane and reflect camera poses to form virtual views. Based on this virtual view setup, we propose a two-stage generation method consisting of Mirror-gated attention and Reflection injection, which enables reflection-consistent NVS by explicitly leveraging reflection relationships in a multi-view diffusion model. Ref-GeNVS inherits the strong generalizability of the multi-view diffusion backbone, while it does not require finetuning. On synthetic and real scenes including mirrors, Ref-GeNVS outperforms recent generative NVS methods by generating reflection-consistent and contextually coherent novel views, revealing scene structure visible only through mirrors. Project page: https://kim-geonu.github.io/Ref-GeNVS/

AI.tldr: A training-free, reflection-aware NVS method (Ref-GeNVS) that treats mirror images as dual views to generate reflection-consistent novel views without finetuning, using virtual views from a predicted mirror plane and a two-stage diffusion-based pipeline.
AI.motivation: Multi-view diffusion models struggle to recognize mirrors and leverage reflections for scene generation; enabling reflection-aware NVS without training can improve view consistency and reveal mirror-visible structure.
AI.method: Estimate mirror plane from input images; reflect camera poses to create virtual views; apply a two-stage diffusion generation with Mirror-gated attention and Reflection injection to enforce reflection relationships within a multi-view backbone.
AI.result: On synthetic and real mirror scenes, Ref-GeNVS outperforms recent generative NVS methods by producing reflection-consistent, contextually coherent views and revealing scene structure visible only through mirrors.
AI.conclusion: Training-free, reflection-aware NVS is feasible and generalizable within a multi-view diffusion framework; explicit use of reflection relationships improves view consistency in mirror-rich scenes.

title: How to Speculate about Uncertainty in Agentic Coding? A Draft-Model Gate Method
summary: LLM agents deployed for software engineering fail expensively: they act confidently wrong, and bad actions are recognized only after costly execution and retry. We present Speculative Uncertainty (SU), a method that recovers a predictive failure signal for a black-box agent from its output tokens alone, with no access to logits, weights, activations, or repeated sampling. Inverting speculative decoding, a small open-weight draft model scores the agent's already-generated trajectory in a single forward pass. From these speculative cross-likelihoods we extract phase-aware features by separating the reasoning and action spans, and calibrate them against a verifiable objective. SU produces a failure-likelihood score that any downstream policy, such as routing, human intervention, or extra test-time compute, can consume directly. To show the signal is actionable, we instantiate one such policy, a pre-execution veto gate, on software engineering agents Qwen3-Coder-480B and closed-source Claude 3.5 Sonnet, cutting execution error rate by 6-8 percentage points and token cost by 14-19% in deployment, transferring to out-of-distribution benchmarks without retraining, and generalizing across agent models.

AI.tldr: Speculative Uncertainty (SU) provides a black-box failure signal for LLM agents using speculative decoding with a small open-model, enabling a pre-execution veto that reduces errors and token cost in software engineering deployments.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in software engineering often act confidently but incorrectly, incurring high costs from wrong actions. A predictive failure signal is needed that does not require access to model internals or retraining.
AI.method: Invert speculative decoding by scoring an agent’s generated trajectory with an open-weight draft model in a single forward pass. Extract phase-aware features by separating reasoning and action spans from speculative cross-likelihoods and calibrate against a verifiable objective to produce a failure-likelihood score for downstream policies (routing, human oversight, extra compute).
AI.result: A actionable failure-likelihood signal is produced. A pre-execution veto gate using SU on Qwen3-Coder-480B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet reduces execution error rate by 6–8 percentage points and token cost by 14–19% in deployment, generalizes to out-of-distribution benchmarks and across agent models without retraining.
AI.conclusion: SU provides a practical, model-agnostic signal to control LLM agent execution, enabling safer deployment through routing or human intervention without requiring access to internals or retraining.

title: TruthInsightBench: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Automated Evaluation of Open-Ended Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: Autonomous coding agents are increasingly proposed as AI-scientist systems that conduct analyses and write research reports, but executing a prescribed analysis is not the same as making a discovery. Existing benchmarks are configured for reproduction: tasks, data, and rubrics are built around a hidden target study, and recovery of its result is rewarded. We present TruthInsightBench, a benchmark configured for discovery. Its 40 blind tasks, drawn from 40 peer-reviewed studies across 10 scientific domains, expose only a neutral scientific objective and frozen data; source conclusions, expected values, and analysis paths are withheld, leaving the agent to determine what claim the data support. A fixed LLM-based judge scores the evidentiary maturity of an agent's own claims along six dimensions, operationalized as 29 artifact-grounded items, with automated, deterministic aggregation and no per-instance human grading, so evaluation can be repeated automatically as agents evolve. On one frozen base model, four coding agents form a narrow plateau (58.4-60.3 of 100) with no statistically reliable pairwise separation: they execute and document analyses competently, with comparatively strong evidence auditability and novelty, but largely lack the discriminating acts that establish a trustworthy claim (controls, robustness, falsifiability, and cross-dataset generalization). The bottleneck is scientific judgment rather than coding, and genuine discovery remains out of reach. TruthInsightBench makes this gap a measurable target; data and scoring code are at https://github.com/TruthInsight-stack/TruthInsightBench.

AI.tldr: TruthInsightBench reframes AI-scientist benchmarking from reproduction to discovery, using 40 blind tasks and a fixed LLM judge to assess evidentiary maturity of agent-made claims; results show a discovery gap dominated by scientific judgment rather than coding.
AI.motivation: To quantify autonomous agents' ability to perform genuine scientific discovery, not just reproduce or execute given analyses, by removing access to conclusions and paths and evaluating the agent's own interpretive claims.
AI.method: 40 blind tasks drawn from 40 peer-reviewed studies across 10 domains with frozen data and neutral objectives; no source conclusions or analysis paths provided; a fixed LLM-based judge scores evidentiary maturity via 29 artifact-grounded items across six dimensions, with automated aggregation and no per-instance human grading.
AI.result: Four coding agents reach a narrow performance plateau (58.4–60.3/100) with competent analysis but lack of discriminating acts for trustworthy claims; gaps in controls, robustness, falsifiability, and cross-dataset generalization indicate discovery remains out of reach; bottleneck appears to be scientific judgment rather than coding.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark establishes a measurable target for discovery in AI scientists; data and scoring code are publicly available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: Think-Verify-Revise: Neuro-Symbolic Visual Reasoning with Vision-Language Models and Dynamic Logic Tensor Networks
comment: Accepted at the MARS2 Workshop @ ECCV 2026
summary: Visual reasoning tasks require a system to jointly perceive visual content and apply formal relational constraints---a combination that neither pure neural nor purely symbolic approaches handle well in isolation. This paper proposes a Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) framework that closes this gap by tightly coupling a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for automatic First-Order Logic (FOL) rule induction with a Dynamic Logic Tensor Network (D-LTN) for differentiable rule verification, in a closed iterative feedback loop. The VLM receives a small set of labelled visual examples and proposes candidate FOL rules conforming to a strict grammar (Think); the D-LTN is automatically assembled from these rules at runtime and evaluates them grounding on CNN-produced visual embeddings (Verify); and verification failures are fed back to guide the VLM's next hypothesis (Revise). Evaluated on the ViSudo-PC benchmark across four visual domains (MNIST, EMNIST, KMNIST, FMNIST), the system induces valid Sudoku constraint rules using only three training examples as visual context. The proposed method achieves AUC scores matching or outperforming previous methods (NeuPSL, LTN), showing the potential for automatic rule discovery through VLM. Code is available at https://github.com/homayoun-afshari/nesy.

AI.tldr: A Neuro-Symbolic loop pairs a Vision-Language Model for inductive rule generation with a differentiable logic verifier (D-LTN). The loop refines rules via verification feedback, enabling automatic discovery of visual relational constraints (e.g., Sudoku) from few examples, achieving competitive AUC on ViSudo-PC and releasing code.
AI.motivation: Visual reasoning demands joint perception and relational reasoning; pure neural or symbolic approaches fail to capture this synergy. Automatic rule discovery from limited data is desirable.
AI.method: Three-stage loop: (1) Think: VLM suggests candidate FOL rules under a fixed grammar from small labeled sets; (2) Verify: at runtime a D-LTN is assembled from the induced rules and grounds them to CNN embeddings to compute differentiable truth-values; (3) Revise: verification failures feed back to the VLM to revise hypotheses; repeat. Evaluation on ViSudo-PC across MNIST/EMNIST/KMNIST/FMNIST, using only three training examples to induce Sudoku constraints.
AI.result: The method induces valid Sudoku constraints with only three visual examples. It achieves AUC scores that match or surpass prior methods (NeuPSL, LTN) on ViSudo-PC datasets.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates strong potential of automatic rule discovery in Neuro-Symbolic visual reasoning and shows competitive performance with a closed-loop VLM-D-LTN framework; code is publicly available.

title: Learning from VAE Errors to support ECG-based Differential Diagnosis of Myocardial Scar
comment: Accepted at the PharML Workshop, ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance is a key marker of myocardial scar, but its limited accessibility motivates routine ECG-based screening. We evaluated whether $β$-variational autoencoder (VAE)-derived ECG representations can discriminate LGE+ from LGE- cardiomyopathic patients in a local cohort of 300 subjects. We compared 32-dimensional features from the foundation ECGx.AI model with those from a shallower $β$-VAE trained on normal PTB-XL ECGs, evaluating downstream classification and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based reconstruction errors. ECGx.AI reached an area under ROC of 0.686 with Random Forest, while the proposed $β$-VAE reached 0.577 with sensitivity of 0.775 with Gradient Boosting. Notably, DTW-reconstruction errors significantly differed between classes in 10 out of 12 leads according to Mann-Whitney U test and help in classification, leading to an area under ROC of 0.643 with Logistic Regression, supporting their potential as markers of scar-related ECG alterations.

AI.tldr: ECG-based discrimination of LGE+ vs LGE- cardiomyopathy using β-VAE representations shows modest AUC; DTW reconstruction errors provide complementary markers with per-lead significance.
AI.motivation: Scar assessment by LGE MRI is limited by accessibility; the study investigates ECG-derived representations (β-VAE) to screen for scar-related cardiomyopathy in a 300-subject cohort.
AI.method: Compare 32-dimensional features from foundation ECGx.AI model with a shallower β-VAE trained on PTB-XL ECGs. Evaluate downstream classification (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) and DTW-based reconstruction errors across 12 leads with Mann-Whitney U tests.
AI.result: ECGx.AI features yielded AUC 0.686 (Random Forest). The β-VAE features yielded AUC 0.577 (Gradient Boosting) with sensitivity 0.775. DTW reconstruction errors differed between classes in 10 of 12 leads and achieved AUC 0.643 (Logistic Regression).
AI.conclusion: DTW-based errors are promising lead-level markers of scar-related ECG changes and can complement ECG-based screening, but overall discriminative performance is modest and external validation is needed.

title: Measuring AI Accountability Through Argumentation Analysis: Can Model Reasoning Withstand Scrutiny?
comment: 27 pages (19 main text + appendix and references), 5 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for publication in the Paris Journal of AI and Digital Ethics (2026); presented at PCAIDE 2026
summary: AI oversight methods rely on ground truth for validation, but what constitutes appropriate AI behavior is contested. This leaves evaluation of moral reasoning in LLMs and debate-based oversight implicitly avoiding realistic ambiguity. We investigate an alternative standard designed to function despite such ambiguity: structural quality of the defence a model can mount for its verdicts in response to critical questions, measured through a four-phase dialectical protocol grounded in Walton's theory of argumentation schemes and Govier's criteria for argument cogency. The protocol is adaptive to different frames of reasoning, extends beyond multiple-choice framing, and treats both the reasoning that precedes a verdict and its post-hoc justification. Across nine frontier models and 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice items -- $6,778$ judge-scored cells, validated against $89.6\%$ inter-judge agreement on the binary failure judgment -- models defend their reasoning well above the rubric minimum on every dimension. Failure mass concentrates on grounds and sufficiency, and correlates with epistemic hedging rather than argument length. Reasoning is better defended than post-hoc justification, on every model and every Govier dimension. The scheme a model presents in its justification differs from the one it reasoned with on a substantial share of dilemmas ($\geq 20\%$ per model), despite value-based practical reasoning dominating both tracks. The protocol catches strictly indefensible defences (self-contradiction, false premises), and it surfaces difficulties in characterizing the role of retraction in AI alignment, suggesting a need for more situated evaluations.

AI.tldr: A four-phase dialectical protocol evaluates LLM moral-reasoning defenses; across nine frontier models and 200 high-ambiguity MoralChoice items, defenses are generally strong yet reveal gaps in grounds/sufficiency and post-hoc justification; indicates need for more situated evaluation.
AI.motivation: To address ambiguity in defining appropriate AI behavior and evaluation, proposing a structural standard based on the quality of a model's defensive reasoning rather than assuming ground-truth labels.
AI.method: A four-phase dialectical protocol grounded in Walton's argumentation schemes and Govier's criteria for argument cogency. It adapts to different frames of reasoning, extends beyond multiple-choice framing, and evaluates both the reasoning leading to a verdict and its post-hoc justification. Applied to nine frontier models across 200 MoralChoice items (6,778 judge-scored cells) with 89.6% inter-judge agreement on binary failure judgments.
AI.result: Models defend their reasoning well above rubric minimum across all dimensions; failure mass concentrates on grounds and sufficiency and correlates with epistemic hedging rather than argument length. Reasoning is better defended than post-hoc justification; the defense scheme a model presents often diverges from its initial reasoning in ≥20% of dilemmas per model. The protocol also catches strictly indefensible defences and highlights difficulties in characterizing retraction in AI alignment.
AI.conclusion: The protocol provides a robust standard for evaluating AI alignment under ambiguity and reveals needs for more situated evaluations and refined analysis of retraction; suggests limitations in current evaluation frameworks that rely on ground-truth labels and underscores the importance of structural-quality defenses.

title: How Does mHC Use Its Residual Streams? Selective Routing and Near-Identity Mixing
summary: Hyper-Connections and their manifold-constrained variant mHC widen a residual pathway from one stream to n, yet how trained models use this capacity remains unclear: how broadly blocks read and write, how strongly the residual pathway mixes streams, and whether the streams carry distinct representations. We examine these properties in the four-stream residual pathway of DeepSeek-V4-Flash using effective stream counts, cross-stream residual weights, and inter-stream cosine similarity. Read/write routing is concentrated but varies across depth: a typical attention or FFN site effectively uses about two streams, while the dominant stream changes across layers and the representations remain directionally distinct. Residual mixing is modest and occurs primarily in early layers; in layers 22-42, the pathway mostly carries each stream forward separately. Targeted interventions establish the functional significance of these patterns. Replacing the late mixers by identity increases C4 perplexity by only 1.9% and preserves the six-task average score, whereas replacing the early mixers increases perplexity by 41%. Fixing each early mixer to its C4 diagnostic mean increases perplexity by only 0.2% and reduces the average score by 0.25 percentage points, showing that its site-specific structure matters more than its token-wise variation on the evaluated metrics. Likewise, retaining the three largest routing weights per token at every site increases perplexity by at most 2.7% and changes the average score by at most 0.4 points. Thus, the studied model realizes only part of the flexibility afforded by four-stream mHC: individual blocks rarely require all four streams, and late residual mixing provides little measured benefit.

AI.tldr: Four-stream hyper-connections (mHC) in DeepSeek-V4-Flash are only partially utilized: read/write routing concentrates on ~2 streams, early-layer mixers are important, late mixers offer little benefit, and streams largely remain distinct in deeper layers.
AI.motivation: To understand how multi-stream residual architectures are used in large models, quantify routing and mixing patterns, and assess the value of additional streams for design and interpretability.
AI.method: Quantify effective stream usage with metrics (effective stream counts, cross-stream residual weights, inter-stream cosine similarity) across depth; identify read/write patterns; perform targeted interventions by replacing late mixers with identity, replacing early mixers with diagnostic means, fixing early mixers to means, and retaining top routing weights; evaluate impact on C4 perplexity and six-task average score.
AI.result: Read/write routing is concentrated; typical site uses about two streams; the dominant stream shifts across layers while representations stay directionally distinct. Early-layer residual mixing is prominent; layers 22–42 mostly carry streams forward separately, indicating limited cross-stream mixing later. Replacing late mixers with identity increases C4 perplexity by 1.9% with little effect on six-task score; replacing early mixers raises perplexity by 41%. Fixing early mixers to their C4 mean increases perplexity by 0.2% and reduces average score by 0.25 percentage points. Keeping only the three largest routing weights per token increases perplexity by at most 2.7% and changes the average score by at most 0.4 points.
AI.conclusion: The model uses only part of four-stream mHC capacity: most blocks do not require all four streams, and late residual mixing yields limited performance gains. Site-specific, early-mixer structure matters more than token-wise variation for the evaluated metrics, guiding future design toward targeted, sparsified cross-stream interactions.

title: Constructing and Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Trajectories for Medical Agent
summary: Evaluation of medical artificial intelligence agents remains predominantly answer-centric, assessing only the correctness of final outputs while overlooking the quality of intermediate reasoning. In clinical settings, however, a correct answer reached through fabricated evidence or incoherent logic is as dangerous as an incorrect one. We propose MedTraj, a framework that treats reasoning trajectories as critical objects for construction, evaluation, and optimization. The pipeline generates structured multi-step reasoning chains from medical reasoning sources. Each trajectory is then parsed into clinical observations, evidence, numbered reasoning steps, and a final conclusion, and scored across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, and traceability. Controlled error injection introduces targeted faults into otherwise correct trajectories to establish causal links between specific reasoning failures and measurable quality degradation. Building on this, step-level filtering based on marginal contribution identifies which individual reasoning steps drive or undermine trajectory quality. Finally, quality-weighted context learning feeds trajectory evaluations back into the model at inference time, allowing it to learn from both strong and weak reasoning demonstrations. Experiments across CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed demonstrate that trajectory context consistently improves reasoning coherence, with gains of +0.029 to +0.041 over a zero-shot baseline. On CECMed, quality-weighted context nearly doubles the correctness over the zero-shot baseline while cutting the hallucination ratio by 87%. Marginal-contribution analysis further shows that a small minority of reasoning steps carry most of the quality signal, and that extending chains beyond four steps yields diminishing returns.
