AI.tldr: MedTraj: a framework to evaluate and optimize medical AI reasoning trajectories, not just final answers; introduces five quality dimensions, error injection, marginal-contribution analysis, and context-aware learning to improve correctness and reduce hallucinations across medical QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Current medical AI evaluation focuses on final answers, ignoring reasoning quality and traceability. Flawed or incoherent reasoning can be dangerous in clinical settings. There is a need to systematically construct, evaluate, and optimize multi-step reasoning trajectories.
AI.method: Propose MedTraj pipeline that (1) generates structured multi-step reasoning chains from medical sources; (2) parses trajectories into observations, evidence, numbered steps, and final conclusion; (3) scores trajectories across five quality dimensions: coherence, evidence support, hallucination, completeness, traceability; (4) uses controlled error injection to study causal effects of reasoning failures; (5) performs step-level marginal-contribution analysis to identify influential steps; (6) applies quality-weighted context learning to feed trajectory evaluations back into the model at inference time.
AI.result: Across CareQA, PubMedQA, and CECMed, trajectory context improves reasoning coherence with gains of +0.029 to +0.041 over a zero-shot baseline. On CECMed, quality-weighted context nearly doubles correctness over zero-shot and cuts hallucination by 87%. Marginal-contribution analysis indicates a small minority of steps carry most of the quality signal, with diminishing returns beyond four steps.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating and optimizing reasoning trajectories yields substantial gains in correctness and reduced hallucinations in medical QA. A small subset of steps dominates quality, and longer chains offer limited additional benefit. MedTraj establishes a framework for trajectory-based evaluation and learning to enhance clinical safety and reliability.

title: From Interpretability Methods to Interpretable Models
summary: More than a decade in, explainable AI (XAI) for computer vision has assembled a mature toolbox: attribution, feature visualization, concept-based, and circuit-based methods. Yet almost all of the field's effort has gone into building and comparing these methods, and little into the question they were meant to answer---how interpretable are our models, and are we making progress as they evolve? We argue for shifting the field's focus from methods to models, along two complementary lines. One is already within reach: existing tools let us characterize and compare what different models represent and compute. The other is harder, and largely neglected: whether a model can actually be understood by the humans who rely on it---the independent evaluators on whom trust and certification depend, not the experts confirming what they already expect. It can only be measured, not inferred. We review why the toolbox is mature enough to support both, survey the thin body of work comparing models, draw a parallel to systems neuroscience, and close with a model-centric XAI agenda.

AI.tldr: Shift XAI from method-focused comparisons to model-centric evaluation, combining existing tools for model characterization with independent, human-centered assessment to measure actual interpretability and trust.
AI.motivation: Although the XAI toolbox for vision is mature, it largely assesses methods rather than how interpretable models truly are to humans. Progress requires evaluating models' understandability by independent evaluators, which is essential for trust and certification.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis and literature review: argue for a two-pronged agenda. (1) Use existing interpretability tools to characterize and compare models. (2) Develop human-centered, independent evaluations to measure actual understandability. Draw a systems neuroscience analogy and survey existing model-comparison work to motivate a model-centric XAI framework.
AI.result: Articulates a two-line strategy for progress: (i) leverage tools to characterize model representations and computations; (ii) establish independent human evaluations of interpretability. Reviews sparse prior model-comparison work and outlines a model-centric XAI agenda.
AI.conclusion: A model-centric XAI agenda is needed. Progress requires measuring interpretability by independent evaluators, not just confirming what experts expect, and aligning toolbox capabilities with human-centered evaluation for trust and certification.

title: Optimal Rates for Agentic Networked Information Aggregation
comment: Initial version submitted to SODA 2027 on July 9, 2026
summary:
Building on the pioneering paper of Kearns, Roth, and Ryu (SODA'26), we study information aggregation in a networked learning model. The model captures a central pattern in agentic AI: each agent sees only part of the data and passes on only its own conclusion. Their model considers a linear regression problem with the mean squared error (MSE) loss. Agents sit in a DAG and each sees only a subset of the features and its parents' predictions, fits a linear predictor, and passes only its prediction forward. The benchmark is the full-feature learner that sees all raw features. A path of depth $D$ is $M$-covered if every block of $M$ consecutive agents collectively sees all raw features. Kearns, Roth, and Ryu proved that the excess mean squared error of the last agent on such a path is $O(M/\sqrt D)$, and gave a cyclic instance with excess error $Ω(M/D)$ for $D<M^2$.
  We close this gap: the correct rate is constant up to depth $M^2$, and $Θ(M^2/D)$ beyond it. We first give a sharper analysis of the cyclic instance and improve its lower bound to $Ω(\sqrt{M/D})$ for $D<M^2$. We then construct, for every depth $D\ge M^2$, an $M$-covered path of depth $D$ with excess error $Ω(M^2/D)$. The same instance gives the constant lower bound for all $D < M^2$. We also show that for any fixed distribution the excess error contracts geometrically along the path, ruling out any single instance that witnesses any polynomial lower bound at every depth.
  Finally, we prove the same optimal rate for logistic classification in the logit-passing model of Bateni et al., which considers the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss. The same improved upper bound of $O(M^2/D)$ holds, and we transfer all the regression lower bounds by showing that on those examples the logistic path follows the least-squares path up to rescaling.

AI.tldr: Optimal information-aggregation rate on DAG paths: constant excess MSE up to depth M^2, then Θ(M^2/D) for deeper paths; results extend to logistic/BCE as well.
AI.motivation: Resolve how excess error scales with path depth D under M-covered feature visibility in networked learning; close a gap between previously known bounds in regression and extend to logit classification.
AI.method: Sharper cyclic-instance analysis, construction of M-covered paths achieving lower bounds, contraction arguments for fixed distributions, and reduction/transfer to logistic (BCE) via least-squares path alignment.
AI.result: For regression (MSE): excess error is constant for D ≤ M^2 and Θ(M^2/D) for D ≥ M^2. Improved lower bound Ω(√(M/D)) for D < M^2 on cyclic instance; constant lower bound for all D < M^2 via another construction; geometric contraction for any fixed distribution; logistic/BCE extends with the same O(M^2/D) upper bound and path equivalence up to rescaling.
AI.conclusion: The M^2 threshold is fundamental: rates are constant up to it and decay as M^2/D beyond. The results unify regression and logistic settings and illuminate limits of distributed, decoupled feature processing in DAG-based networked learners.

title: LLM-Guided Program Evolution for Circle Packing: Breaking 10 Packomania Records for $28
summary: We present Discovery Loop, a lightweight system that uses a large language model (LLM) to iteratively evolve optimization algorithms. Starting from a simple seed solver, the LLM proposes algorithmic improvements guided by a scoreboard of results and a history of prior ideas. Each candidate is evaluated against an independent verifier; improvements are kept and failures discarded. Applied to the Packomania circle-packing benchmark (csqv: maximize the sum of radii of N variable-radius circles in the unit square), the system improved the best known solutions for 10 values of N in the range 101-114, with gains of 2.4%-5.4% over prior records, all within 15 iterations and at a total LLM cost of $27.72. These results have been independently accepted by Packomania. We describe the method, analyze cost-efficiency dynamics including an adaptive plateau-detection mechanism, and discuss implications for democratizing automated scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: An LLM-guided, iterative optimization-loop evolves algorithms from a seed solver; evaluated by an independent verifier; achieves new best-known circle-packing results for N in 101–114 with 2.4–5.4% gains in 15 iterations at a total LLM cost of $27.72.
AI.motivation: Automate discovery of effective optimization heuristics to accelerate scientific progress, reduce human effort, and democratize access by lowering computational and expertise barriers in combinatorial optimization.
AI.method: Seed solver serves as the starting point. The LLM proposes algorithmic improvements, guided by a scoreboard of results and a history of prior ideas. Each candidate is evaluated by an independent verifier; successful improvements are retained, failures are discarded. The system adapts cost through a plateau-detection mechanism. Applied to the Packomania circle-packing benchmark (maximize the sum of radii of N variable-radius circles in the unit square), it explores N in 101–114 and completes within 15 iterations with a total LLM expenditure of $27.72.
AI.result: The approach yields improved best-known solutions for 10 values of N in 101–114, with gains of 2.4%–5.4% over prior records, all achieved within 15 iterations and verified independently. Packomania has accepted these results.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that short, low-cost, LLM-guided iterative exploration can surpass prior heuristics on a concrete optimization benchmark and points toward broader potential for automated discovery in science, subject to reliable verification and reproducibility.

title: A Generalizable Feature Extractor for Alzheimer's-Related Brain MRI Tasks
comment: 26 pages (excluding the references section), 7 figures (excluding sub-figures)
summary: When there is not enough labeled data to properly train deep learning models, transfer learning can help. We still do not fully understand how effective it is in neuroimaging, especially for Alzheimer's disease research. It is also not clear if these transferred models can work on new datasets without being retrained for each specific task. We evaluate whether a compact, supervised pretrained model can serve as a reusable foundation model for downstream neuroimaging tasks. We freeze the 7.18 million weights of a 3D CNN previously trained for brain-age prediction, and adapt it to each task using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), requiring only ~1% additional trainable parameters. We evaluate generalizability in six experiments. Adapting the model to classify cognitively normal versus Dementia on ADNI gave an AUC of 0.964 on held-out folds (Experiment #1). Applying that adapted model unchanged to OASIS-3, with no retraining, gave an AUC of 0.871 (Experiment #2). Reusing its output logit together with age and a cognitive score distinguished stable from progressing MCI with an AUC of 0.828 (Experiment #3). Adapting the same backbone to predict amyloid positivity from structural MRI gave an AUC of 0.804 (Experiment #4). Finally, the same approach estimated ICV-normalized hippocampal and white matter hypointensity volumes directly from the T1w image, with R^2 of 0.80 and 0.91 respectively, tasks normally addressed with much larger U-Net networks (Experiments #5 and #6). A compact model supervised on brain age can therefore serve as a reusable backbone, adapting to each task with ~1% additional parameters and transferring to an unseen cohort without any training. Our findings suggest that a carefully trained brain age model can serve as an effective foundation model for Alzheimer's related tasks, even under strict data constraints.

AI.tldr: A compact brain-age backbone, adapted with LoRA (~1% extra parameters), can serve as a reusable foundation model for diverse Alzheimer's-related neuroimaging tasks, enabling cross-cohort transfer without retraining across six experiments.
AI.motivation: Neuroimaging faces limited labeled data and dataset heterogeneity. A reusable foundation model could improve transfer learning across tasks and cohorts in Alzheimer's disease research.
AI.method: Start from a 3D CNN pretrained on brain age (7.18M weights). Freeze weights and apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) per task. Evaluate six experiments spanning ADNI and OASIS-3, with downstream tasks including CN vs Dementia, progression prediction, amyloid positivity, and MRI-derived biomarker estimation (hippocampal volume, white matter hypointensity). Use task-specific inputs like age and cognitive scores where applicable.
AI.result: Experiment 1: AUC 0.964 (CN vs Dementia on ADNI). Experiment 2: AUC 0.871 on OASIS-3 without retraining. Experiment 3: AUC 0.828 using combined logit, age, and cognitive score to distinguish stable vs progressing MCI. Experiment 4: AUC 0.804 for predicting amyloid positivity. Experiments 5 & 6: R^2 0.80 (hippocampal volume) and R^2 0.91 (white matter hypointensity) from T1-weighted MRI. Overall, ~1% additional trainable parameters; the backbone transfers to unseen cohorts without training.
AI.conclusion: A carefully trained brain-age model can serve as an effective foundation for Alzheimer’s-related tasks under data constraints, enabling cross-dataset transfer without retraining and requiring minimal task-specific parameters.

title: Embedded Graph Flows for Categorical Graph Generation
summary: Generating categorical graphs requires choosing node and edge types that form a coherent structure without depending on node order. Many graph generators encode categories as fixed one-hot vectors, which can impose an artificial geometry in which categories are equidistant. We propose Embedded Graph Flows (EGF), a generative model that learns continuous embeddings for node and unordered-edge categories and transports Gaussian noise towards these learnt endpoints using a permutation-equivariant graph transformer. A terminal readout maps the embeddings back to discrete graph categories. Across molecular benchmarks, EGF achieved competitive performance. On QM9, EGF gives the best result on all four reported metrics among the three methods, including a Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD) of 0.150, compared with 0.717 for the categorical-diffusion baseline DiGress and 0.812 for the bridge-based baseline GruM. When applied to larger molecules in ZINC250k, EGF retains the lowest maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) using the neighbourhood subgraph pairwise distance kernel (NSPDK), indicating close agreement with the local substructures of the reference molecules. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trusted-System-Lab/EGF.

AI.tldr: EGF learns continuous embeddings for node and unordered-edge categories and uses a permutation-equivariant graph transformer to transport Gaussian noise to learned endpoints; achieves strong results on QM9 and ZINC250k; code released.
AI.motivation: Discrete, one-hot encodings impose artificial geometry and restrict the modeling of category relationships. EGF proposes continuous embeddings for categories and permutation-equivariant generation to better capture graph structure.
AI.method: A permutation-equivariant graph transformer learns continuous embeddings for node and unordered-edge categories; Gaussian noise is transported toward learned endpoints; a terminal readout maps embeddings back to discrete graph categories.
AI.result: On QM9, EGF achieves the best performance across all four reported metrics among three methods, including FCD = 0.150 (DiGress 0.717; GruM 0.812). On ZINC250k, EGF has the lowest maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) using NSPDK, indicating closer alignment with reference substructures. Code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: EGF provides a scalable, permutation-invariant framework that generates categorical graphs via continuous embeddings, achieving competitive or state-of-the-art results on molecular benchmarks.

title: ProCA: Progressive Contrastive Alignment for Robust EEG Visual Decoding
summary: Electroencephalogram (EEG) visual decoding aims to recover visual semantics from non-invasive neural time-series signals, for which robust alignment between noisy neural responses and stable semantic representations is key to achieving high-performance decoding. Despite recent advances in contrastive learning, robust EEG decoding remains challenging because existing methods rely on fixed visual or textual anchors whose semantic relations may become misaligned with EEG representations that vary across trials, subjects, and learning stages. Our empirical evidence shows that this instability appears across both standard EEG decoding protocols and more challenging robustness settings, including strict cross-subject transfer and realistic personalized continual adaptation. We provide a formal analysis showing that fixed semantic supervision can bias optimization when EEG-specific relations evolve, and that structure-agnostic perturbations may distort semantically important EEG components. To address these issues, we propose Progressive Contrastive Alignment (ProCA), a unified and model-agnostic framework for adaptive neural-semantic alignment. ProCA progressively refines class-level contrastive supervision from frozen vision-language priors to EEG-aware semantic relations, and introduces structure-consistent interpolation to constrain feature mixing according to channel-wise and temporal importance. Across subject-dependent, subject-independent, strict cross-subject transfer, and continual adaptation settings, ProCA achieves average relative Top-1/Top-5 gains of 7.4%/3.9%, 10.0%/4.6%, 28.1%/17.8%, and 16.8%/11.6%, respectively.

AI.tldr: ProCA: a model-agnostic Progressive Contrastive Alignment framework for EEG decoding that progressively tunes from vision-language priors to EEG-specific semantics, with structure-consistent interpolation to align neural signals with semantic classes. It significantly improves performance across subject-dependent/independent, cross-subject transfer, and continual adaptation settings.
AI.motivation: Fixed semantic supervision and structure-agnostic perturbations cause instability when EEG-to-semantics relations drift across trials, subjects, or learning stages; robust EEG decoding requires adaptive, EEG-aware alignment.
AI.method: ProCA gradually refines class-level contrastive supervision from frozen vision-language priors to EEG-aware semantic relations and introduces structure-consistent interpolation that constrains feature mixing according to channel-wise and temporal importance; model-agnostic framework.
AI.result: Average relative gains in Top-1/Top-5 accuracy across settings: 7.4%/3.9% (subject-dependent), 10.0%/4.6% (subject-independent), 28.1%/17.8% (strict cross-subject transfer), 16.8%/11.6% (continual adaptation).
AI.conclusion: ProCA provides robust, adaptive neural-semantic alignment for EEG decoding, addressing instability from fixed anchors and perturbations, with substantial performance gains and broad applicability across EEG decoding paradigms.

title: UniMate: One Unified Model to Animate Diverse Skeletons
summary: Recent advances in automatic rigging now deliver animation-ready 3D assets at scale, yet generating the motion to drive them remains a bottleneck. Existing learned animators are topology-constrained: they rely on category-specific templates or require per-skeleton fine-tuning and reference motions at inference. We present UniMate, a unified foundation model that synthesizes articulated motion for arbitrary skeletons from a rigged 3D asset and a text prompt, with no test-time optimization or per-skeleton retraining. UniMate introduces a topology-aware diffusion transformer, which integrates skeletal topology into attention via three mechanisms: (1) a graph-aware attention bias from pairwise joint relations and geodesic distances; (2) a spectral rotary position embedding generalizing RoPE to arbitrary kinematic trees via the graph Laplacian; and (3) a global topological conditioner attention-pooled from the rest-pose skeleton. We also curate UniML3D, 13,006 motion sequences spanning bipedal, quadrupedal, avian, marine, insectoid, serpentine, and articulated rigid objects with unified canonicalization and text pairing. Trained on this dataset, UniMate outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in quality, generalization, and efficiency, and supports zero-shot cross-topology transfer, in-betweening, expansion, and text-guided editing. Our project page is available at https://linzhanmou.com/unimate/.

AI.tldr: UniMate is a topology-aware diffusion transformer-based foundation model that synthesizes motion for arbitrary skeletal topologies from rigged 3D assets and text prompts without test-time optimization, using graph-aware attention, graph-Laplacian-based spectral RoPE, and a global topological conditioner, trained on UniML3D across diverse articulated subjects.
AI.motivation: Current learned animators are topology-constrained, relying on category-specific templates or per-skeleton tuning and reference motions, which hampers generalization to arbitrary skeletons. A unified, test-time-optimized motion synthesis model is needed.
AI.method: A topology-aware diffusion transformer with three mechanisms: (1) graph-aware attention bias from pairwise joint relations and geodesic distances; (2) a spectral rotary position embedding generalizing RoPE to arbitrary kinematic trees via the graph Laplacian; (3) a global topological conditioner attentive-pooling from the rest pose. Training data UniML3D (13,006 motion sequences) across bipedal, quadrupedal, avian, marine, insectoid, serpentine, and articulated rigid objects with unified canonicalization and text pairing.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in motion quality, generalization across topologies, and efficiency; enables zero-shot cross-topology transfer, in-betweening, expansion, and text-guided editing.
AI.conclusion: Introduces UniMate and UniML3D to enable unified, topology-general motion synthesis for arbitrary skeletons without per-skeleton retraining, advancing scalable, text-driven animation pipelines.

title: Variational Continuation for Double Pendulum Periodic Orbits
summary: We present a Hessian-based approach to numerically continue periodic orbits in dynamical systems. A loop (periodic orbit candidate) is parametrized as a Fourier series; a loss function is defined based on the deviation of the loop from the physical differential equations. Unlike previous work relying on hand-derived Jacobians, our method automates the process by leveraging automatic differentiation, a common machine learning technique. The continuation direction can be determined by the flat directions of the loss landscapes (directions with zero eigenvalues), making the search of periodic orbits efficient and guided. Our method is integrator-free, precisely initializes oscillations around unstable fixed points, and efficiently detects orbit family intersections and subharmonic bifurcations. As a demonstration, we present full continuations of periodic double pendulum oscillations from fixed points, showing bifurcations along orbit families and categorizing branches of periodic orbits. In particular, we find periodic orbits where both pendulum masses are never simultaneously at rest, which to our knowledge has been missing in the literature.

AI.tldr: Hessian-based, AD-powered continuation of periodic orbits via Fourier-parameterized loops, enabling integrator-free, efficient discovery and bifurcation analysis of orbit families in a double pendulum; uncovers new non-resting periodic orbits.
AI.motivation: Need robust, Jacobian-free methods to continue periodic orbits, detect bifurcations and intersections, including unstable points, without manual Jacobian derivations.
AI.method: Represent periodic loop with Fourier series; define a loss measuring deviation from the governing ODE; use automatic differentiation to obtain Hessians/flat directions; continue along loss-landscape null directions; integrator-free; initialize near unstable fixed points; detect bifurcations and orbit intersections.
AI.result: Successful full continuations of periodic double pendulum oscillations along orbit families; classification of branches; discovery of periodic orbits where both masses are never simultaneously at rest, previously unreported.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effectiveness and generality of Hessian-AD-based continuation for periodic orbits, providing a Jacobian-free, efficient framework for exploring dynamical systems and identifying novel orbit families.

title: Compact Bellman-Grounded Cognitive Maps for Cost-Aware Navigation
summary: Biological agents navigate familiar environments not by re-solving routes for each new goal, but by reusing a learned map built once and read off as goals change. Existing artificial cognitive-map models mimic this reuse, yet their guidance is not explicitly grounded in additive heterogeneous route costs. Furthermore, they often struggle with memory efficiency: representative state-indexed and high-rank spectral constructions incur substantial storage growth as the environment scales. We present BCM, which grounds a reusable cognitive map in local edge costs through a self-supervised Bellman-grounded objective and a compact coordinate encoding, supporting changing goal queries without per-goal retraining. On weighted grids of up to $N=1600$ nodes, BCM maintains full success and only a 5\% mean Gap relative to exact Dijkstra search, compared with about $45\%$ for a connectivity-based spectral baseline. Notably, as the graph size increases from $N=400$ to $N=3600$, its memory footprint grows sublinearly while maintaining competitive performance, making our method scalable to complex environments. Together, these results show that additive route costs can be written into a compact, reusable cognitive-map representation, bridging the gap between biological flexibility and optimal path planning.

AI.tldr: BCM provides a compact, reusable cognitive map grounded in additive edge costs, enabling goal-changing queries without retraining and achieving near-optimal planning with sublinear memory growth on large graphs.
AI.motivation: To overcome two limitations of existing cognitive-map models: (1) lack of explicit grounding in additive route costs, and (2) high memory cost for representative or spectral constructions, which hinder scalability and efficient goal-directed planning.
AI.method: Introduce BCM with a self-supervised Bellman-grounded objective and a compact coordinate encoding to bind local edge costs into a reusable map. The model supports changing goals without per-goal retraining and is evaluated on weighted grids up to N=1600 nodes, comparing against exact Dijkstra and a spectral baseline.
AI.result: BCM maintains full success and ~5% mean gap to exact Dijkstra (vs ~45% for the spectral baseline) on tested grids. Memory footprint grows sublinearly with graph size (from N=400 to N=3600), indicating favorable scalability while retaining competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: Additive route costs can be encoded into a compact, reusable cognitive-map representation, reconciling biological flexibility with optimal path planning and enabling scalable, goal-adaptive navigation.

title: WorldSculpt: Generating Compositional Worlds from Grounded Videos
summary: We study the problem of generating a compositional 3D representation of a cluttered scene containing hundreds of objects. The goal is to represent the scene as a collection of individual object meshes placed in a shared world frame, as required by downstream applications such as gaming, AR/VR, simulation, and robotics. This task is challenging in densely cluttered scenes, where objects heavily occlude one another and each view reveals only a fraction of their geometry. Geometry-based approaches typically reconstruct the scene as a single representation and leave incomplete geometry in occluded regions, while existing compositional methods with generative priors are largely limited to relatively simple scenes. We show that complex scenes with hundreds of objects can instead be generated compositionally by adapting a strong single-object 3D generative prior to multi-view observations. We instantiate this paradigm with Pixal3D, extending it with a multi-view conditioning pathway that grounds object generation in multiple posed observations. Although the model is finetuned entirely on single objects in canonical space, it generalizes to large scenes with severe occlusion without any scene-level training, demonstrating the feasibility and scalability of this paradigm. We further introduce UE-MeshyScene, a photorealistic benchmark of densely cluttered scenes with hundreds of objects, per-object annotations, and ground-truth meshes. Across single-object, controlled multi-object, and UE-MeshyScene evaluations, our method consistently outperforms prior approaches, with larger gains as scene complexity and occlusion increase. Finally, we demonstrate broader applicability by converting generated 3DGS worlds, such as Marble and HY-World 2.0, into compositional mesh scenes.

AI.tldr: Proposes compositional generation of hundreds-object 3D scenes by adapting a strong single-object prior (Pixal3D) with multi-view conditioning; introduces UE-MeshyScene benchmark; demonstrates scalability, generalization without scene-level training, and applicability to converting existing 3D worlds into compositional meshes.
AI.motivation: Cluttered scenes with heavy occlusion yield incomplete geometry when using single representations. Prior geometry-based methods struggle to fill occluded regions, while compositional priors are often limited to simple scenes. A scalable approach that can generate per-object meshes in a shared world frame is needed for downstream tasks (gaming, AR/VR, robotics).
AI.method: Extend Pixal3D with a multi-view conditioning pathway to ground single-object priors in multiple posed views, finetune only on single objects in canonical space, and apply to multi-object scenes without scene-level training. Represent scenes as a collection of individual object meshes in a common world frame. Introduce UE-MeshyScene, a photorealistic benchmark with hundreds of objects, per-object annotations, and ground-truth meshes. Demonstrate cross-evaluation (single-object, controlled multi-object, UE-MeshyScene) and show the ability to convert generated 3D worlds (e.g., Marble, HY-World 2.0) into compositional mesh scenes.
AI.result: The approach outperforms prior methods across single-object, controlled multi-object, and UE-MeshyScene benchmarks, with larger performance gains as scene complexity and occlusion increase. It can scale to scenes with hundreds of objects, generalizes to heavily occluded environments without scene-level training, and enables transforming existing generative worlds into compositional mesh scenes.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility and scalability of compositional 3D scene generation for densely cluttered environments by leveraging a single-object prior with multi-view grounding. The introduced UE-MeshyScene benchmark supports robust evaluation and the framework offers broad applicability to AR/VR, gaming, simulation, and robotics, including converting other 3D generative worlds into compositional mesh representations.

title: Distill Globally, Adapt Locally: Reasoning Distillation and Product-Type Test-Time Training for Scalable Trade-Up Recommendation
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on Agentic and Generative AI for E-Commerce (GenAIECommerce 2026), co-located with ACM RecSys 2026
summary: Trade-up recommendation identifies higher-quality alternatives that preserve a customer's purchase intent while offering upgraded benefits. Large language models (LLMs) can reason about such distinctions, but applying them directly to hundreds of millions of product pairs is operationally impractical. We introduce a two-level framework that distills LLM reasoning into an efficient non-generative student and adapts its decision boundary to product-type-specific trade-up criteria. At Level 1, a retrieval-augmented few-shot LLM teacher generates structured relation labels and natural-language rationales. These rationales supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier through alignment and contrastive objectives; at inference, the student uses only two precomputed 768-dimensional product embeddings, with no LLM calls or text generation. On a fixed human-annotated benchmark of 8,352 pairs, a 15.5M-parameter four-class reasoning-distilled student achieves AUC 0.924 (95% CI [0.918, 0.929]), compared with 0.912 for the four-class label-only student. At Level 2, product-type test-time training (PT-TTT) uses few-shot demonstrations to optimize lightweight category-specific adapters over the frozen student. PT-TTT improves AUC from 0.924 to 0.941 and average precision from 0.920 to 0.940. On a 100K-pair proxy catalog, the distilled student on a single eight-GPU machine is approximately 5,000x faster and 10,000x lower in estimated cost than direct LLM inference.

AI.tldr: A two-level distillation framework converts LLM reasoning for trade-up recommendations into a fast, embedding-based student with per-product-type adapters, achieving high accuracy and massive speed/cost gains.
AI.motivation: To scale trade-up reasoning to hundreds of millions of product pairs by avoiding direct LLM inference while preserving decision quality and adapting to product-type criteria.
AI.method: Level 1 uses a retrieval-augmented LLM teacher to generate relation labels and rationales; these supervise a compact embedding-pair classifier via alignment and contrastive losses. The inference-time student relies on two fixed 768-d embeddings per product, with no LLM calls. Level 2 (PT-TTT) optimizes lightweight, category-specific adapters over the frozen student using few-shot demonstrations.
AI.result: On an 8,352-pair benchmark, a 15.5M-parameter four-class student achieves AUC 0.924 (CI 0.918–0.929), surpassing a label-only student (AUC 0.912). On a 100K-pair proxy catalog, the distilled student on eight GPUs is ~5,000x faster and ~10,000x cheaper than direct LLM inference. PT-TTT raises AUC to 0.941 and AP to 0.940.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-level distillation with Level-2 product-type adapters delivers scalable, high-performance trade-up recommendations, combining efficiency with strong predictive accuracy and adaptable criteria across product types.

title: Unifying ICL, SFT, KL-Regularized RL Through a Bayesian Lens
summary: Large language models are now trained and evaluated under a diverse set of paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), few-shot in-context learning (ICL), KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, on-policy distillation (OPD), and test-time reasoning with search and chain-of-thought. These methods are often discussed as fundamentally different, and recent empirical results--such as the mixed impact of few-shot prompting on RL-tuned reasoning models--can appear puzzling. This note develops a Bayesian perspective that puts these procedures on the same footing. At the core is a two-step template: (i) construct a (generalized) Bayes or Gibbs posterior q* over outputs or actions given a context, using a prior/reference model and a utility signal (log-likelihood, reward, or advantage); and (ii) approximate q* by a forward-KL projection onto a parametric family, either in-weights (SFT/RL) or in-context (ICL). Part I formalizes few-shot ICL and SFT as amortized and-weights projections onto the Bayes posterior predictive. Parts II-IV show that KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward-weighted SFT, reward-weighted ICL (RW-ICL), and advantage-weighted SFT (AWSFT) are all instances of forward-KL projection onto posteriors induced by rewards or advantages. We disentangle where these equivalences hold (objectives and first-order updates) and where they do not (source and granularity of the learning signal). Part V sketches implications for modern reasoning pipelines: RLHF/RLVR recipes as "posterior design + projection", why cold-start or supervised warm-up is practically unavoidable for importance-weighted KL projections, and DeepSeek-R1 and o1-style reasoning models as combining test-time Bayesian search with training-time KL amortization.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian framework shows that supervised fine-tuning (SFT), few-shot in-context learning (ICL), KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, on-policy distillation (OPD), and test-time reasoning with search and chain-of-thought are unified as forward-KL projections of generalized Bayes posteriors; it clarifies when equivalences hold and provides design implications for modern reasoning pipelines.
AI.motivation: Resolve apparent fragmentation among diverse LLM training/evaluation paradigms, offering a principled, unified account that connects supervision, in-context strategies, RL-based alignment, and test-time reasoning.
AI.method: Two-step template: (i) construct a generalized Bayes/Gibbs posterior q* over outputs/actions given a context, using a prior/reference model and a utility signal (log-likelihood, reward, or advantage); (ii) approximate q* by a forward-KL projection onto a parametric family, either in-weights (SFT/RL) or in-context (ICL). Part I formalizes ICL and SFT as amortized/weight projections onto posterior predictive; Parts II–IV show KL-regularized RLHF/RLVR, reward-weighted SFT, reward-weighted ICL (RW-ICL), and AWSFT are instances of forward-KL projections; Part V discusses implications for reasoning pipelines and practical considerations like cold-start warm-ups and the interpretation of certain reasoning models as combinations of test-time Bayesian search with training-time KL amortization.
AI.result: Frames KL-regularized and reward-weighted methods as forward-KL projections from Bayes posteriors; disentangles when equivalences hold (objective/first-order updates) versus when they do not (granularity of learning signal); provides design principles for posterior design and projection in modern LLM pipelines; links to reasoning architectures like DeepSeek-R1/o1-style models.
AI.conclusion: A unifying Bayesian perspective situates SFT, ICL, RLHF/RLVR, and test-time reasoning within a single posterior-design + projection paradigm, clarifying when different methods coincide and offering practical guidance for building and diagnosing modern reasoning systems.

title: RegionFed: Federated Learning for Personalized Query Understanding in Heterogeneous Retail Environments
summary: Retail search systems serve diverse geographic regions with distinct query patterns, vocabularies, and product preferences, creating significant data heterogeneity that challenges both privacy-preserving training and model personalization. Federated learning offers a natural solution for privacy, but standard FL methods produce global models that sacrifice regional performance, while existing personalized FL approaches operate at the parameter level and catastrophically collapse on modern transformers (below 10\% accuracy on T5) due to tied embeddings and LayerNorm interactions. We introduce RegionFed, an \textit{architecture-robust} federated learning framework that sidesteps this failure by operating entirely at the gradient level. RegionFed uses the $\ell_2$ conflict between regional and global gradients as a unified signal that (i) diagnoses heterogeneity, (ii) routes each region to the cheapest sufficient personalization strategy, and (iii) adaptively controls personalization strength. Because it treats models as differentiable black boxes, RegionFed deploys on T5-Small, T5-3B, RoBERTa, and CNN with zero code changes, providing large gains on transformers (where parameter-level methods collapse) and consistent improvements on CNNs. Across three public datasets (Amazon ESCI, Amazon Reviews, LEAF-FEMNIST) and four architectures, RegionFed-Meta achieves 92.27\%, closing the gap to the privacy-violating centralized upper bound (Centralized + Regional Weighting: 92.04\%, $Δ$=0.23pp, within 1$σ$) while providing $(ε{\approx}0.60)$-differential privacy and $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence.

AI.tldr: RegionFed is a gradient-level, architecture-robust FL framework that addresses regional heterogeneity and transformer instability by using gradient conflicts for adaptive personalization, achieving near-centralized accuracy with differential privacy.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous regional data in retail search creates privacy-preserving training challenges and poor regional personalization. Standard FL's global models underperform locally, and parameter-level personalization fails on modern transformers due to embedding and LayerNorm interactions.
AI.method: Operate entirely at the gradient level. Use the L2 conflict between regional and global gradients as a unified signal to diagnose heterogeneity, select a minimal sufficient personalization strategy for each region, and adapt personalization strength. Treat models as differentiable black boxes, enabling zero-code-change deployment across architectures (T5-Small, T5-3B, RoBERTa, CNN).
AI.result: RegionFed-Meta achieves 92.27% across three public datasets (Amazon ESCI, Amazon Reviews, LEAF-FEMNIST) and four architectures, closing the gap to the centralized bound (Centralized + Regional Weighting: 92.04%; Δ = 0.23pp). It provides ~0.60-differential privacy and O(1/√T) convergence.
AI.conclusion: RegionFed offers an architecture-robust, gradient-based personalization that outperforms parameter-level methods (which collapse on transformers) and yields strong, privacy-preserving performance across diverse models and datasets.

title: SciDocBench: A Workflow-Centered Benchmark and Data Pipeline for Scientific Document Understanding
comment: 52 pages, 21 figures, and 20 tables. Project page: https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench
summary: Scientific papers require models to reason jointly over text, equations, figures, tables, code, and datasets while preserving the provenance of supporting evidence. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate these capabilities in isolation, leaving unclear whether multimodal models can support realistic scientific-reading workflows. We introduce SciDocBench, a workflow-centered benchmark for scientific document understanding. It contains 124 expert-authored and difficulty-screened questions organized into seven research-assistant capability groups and 19 subtasks across five scientific domains. Each question is instantiated under four matched conditions combining English or Chinese questions with all-images-first or interleaved document representations, yielding 496 evaluation instances for controlled analysis. The strongest evaluated system achieves only 62.6/100, with pronounced weaknesses in document perception, evidence grounding, verification, and cross-document reasoning. To translate these diagnostics into scalable training signals, we introduce SciDocIR, a typed evidence-graph representation that preserves scientific document objects, layout and cross-reference relations, and provenance. Building on SciDocIR, we construct SciDocDataset, comprising approximately 15K supervised fine-tuning samples and 8K reinforcement-learning samples across 14 verifiable subtasks. Together, SciDocBench, SciDocIR, and SciDocDataset form an evaluation-to-training framework for diagnosing and improving scientific-document assistants. The project page is available at https://github.com/InternLM/SciDocBench.

AI.tldr: A multimodal, workflow-centered benchmark suite for scientific document understanding (SciDocBench) complemented by an evidence-graph representation (SciDocIR) and a large fine-tuning/RL dataset (SciDocDataset) to diagnose and improve scientific-document assistants across multilingual and cross-document tasks.
AI.motivation: To move beyond isolated multimodal capabilities and evaluate end-to-end scientific-reading workflows with provenance, while enabling scalable training signals.
AI.method: SciDocBench: 124 expert-authored questions, 7 capability groups, 19 subtasks, 5 domains; 496 instances across four matched conditions (English/Chinese questions) × (all-images-first vs interleaved representations). SciDocIR: a typed evidence-graph encoding document objects, layout, cross-reference relations, and provenance. SciDocDataset: ~15k supervised fine-tuning samples and ~8k RL samples across 14 subtasks. Framework combines evaluation with training data.
AI.result: Best-performing system reaches 62.6/100; notable weaknesses in document perception, evidence grounding, verification, and cross-document reasoning."
AI.conclusion: SciDocBench, SciDocIR, and SciDocDataset constitute an end-to-end evaluation-to-training framework to diagnose and improve scientific-document assistants; project page available at the provided repository.

title: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
comment: 39 pages, 14 pages main text. Code, data, and pre-registrations: https://github.com/nebula-1999/Interface-Induced-Trajectory-Censoring
summary:
Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.

AI.tldr: Tool-call rates in agent evaluations are dominated by the model-interface stack, not the model alone; interface censorship and silent failures can mask calls. A targeted 98-line preflight check helps detect these failures. Across multiple models and datasets, changing adapters, templates, or parsers shifts observed calls and outcomes in scale- and interaction-dependent ways; repairs improve parsing but do not guarantee performance gains.
AI.motivation: To determine whether observed tool usage is an intrinsic property of the model or an artifact of the surrounding interface, and to quantify silent failures introduced by serving adapters and parsers across scales and models.
AI.method: Experimentally vary serving adapters, templates, and parsers across multiple models and datasets (BFCL v4, tau-bench, Qwen2.5-Coder, Llama-3.1-8B, Verl AgentLoop) while keeping model/seed/weights fixed. Measure server-parsed calls, emitted tool calls, acceptance, execution, and observations. Use a 2x2 evaluation design for templates/parsers, calibrate against adjudicated gold standards, and deploy a 98-line preflight check to detect silent failures.
AI.result: Observed tool-call rates hinge on interface components: (i) BFCL v4 shows 0.00 vs 0.96/0.19 depending on serving adapter; (ii) tau-bench swaps yield 0→636 server-parsed calls and 0→103 tool-executions; (iii) Qwen2.5-Coder exhibits 0/100 server parses at all sizes while well-formed emitted calls reach 80/100 at 32B (≈72 after calibration) and silent fraction stays 0–2 with matched envelopes; (iv) Llama-3.1-8B shows 23% tool function calls drop to 0 under strict true; (v) Verl AgentLoop sees many generations with a complete call but zero acceptance/execution/observation; repairs restore parsing but with limited outcome gains (parsing 0→84, rescues 0→9, pass rate 53→62, not statistically significant). The 98-line preflight catch detects silent failures; overall, the observed tool-call rate is a property of the model-interface stack, not the model alone.
AI.conclusion: Tool usage is an emergent property of the software stack around the model; silent failures can hide tool calls and distort evaluation. To obtain meaningful tool-use measurements, end-to-end preflight checks and careful matching of interfaces are essential; improving parsing alone may not improve outcomes without addressing downstream acceptance and execution.

title: A Hybrid Predictive Ensemble of Machine Learning and Deep Neural Networks for Early Cardiovascular Disease Risk Assessment
summary: This study introduces an intelligent framework that integrates machine learning and deep neural network ensemble techniques for early detection and prognosis of cardiovascular diseases. The system utilizes real-time physiological data collected from Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices, including ECG sensors, heart rate monitors, and blood pressure trackers. To ensure the accuracy and reliability of input data, preprocessing steps such as noise reduction, normalization, and missing value imputation are employed. The most significant health indicators are identified through effective feature selection methods and then processed using optimized classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), which are combined in an ensemble architecture to improve diagnostic precision. The framework demonstrates remarkable performance in predicting cardiovascular disease risk, achieving higher accuracy, reduced false positives, and enhanced consistency compared to conventional methods. It is designed on a cloud-based infrastructure that ensures scalability and real-time processing for continuous patient monitoring. Experimental evaluation on real-world cardiovascular datasets confirms the framework's efficiency in early-stage risk assessment and clinical decision support. The results highlight the potential of combining traditional machine learning and deep learning paradigms to achieve proactive healthcare management and improve patient outcomes.

AI.tldr: An IoMT-enabled, cloud-based ML/DL ensemble framework for early cardiovascular disease detection and prognosis, achieving higher accuracy and fewer false positives than traditional methods via preprocessing, feature selection, and SVM/RF/XGBoost ensembles.
AI.motivation: The need for accurate, timely cardiovascular risk stratification using continuous physiological data from Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices, addressing data quality and diagnostic precision by integrating traditional ML and deep learning within scalable infrastructure.
AI.method: Collect real-time IoMT data (ECG, heart rate, blood pressure); apply preprocessing (noise reduction, normalization, missing value imputation); perform feature selection; train and combine classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost) in an ensemble; deploy on cloud infrastructure for real-time processing and scalability; evaluate on real-world cardiovascular datasets.
AI.result: Higher diagnostic accuracy, reduced false positives, and improved consistency compared with conventional methods; effective in early-stage risk assessment and clinical decision support; validated on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the feasibility and potential of integrating ML and DL paradigms with IoMT-enabled data in a cloud-based framework to enable proactive cardiovascular care and scalable clinical decision support.

title: The Mirror Agent Model: a Bayesian Architecture for Interpretable Agent Behavior
comment: Accepted at the International Workshop on Explainable, Transparent Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems, 2022
summary: In this paper we illustrate a novel architecture generating interpretable behavior and explanations. We refer to this architecture as the Mirror Agent Model because it defines the observer model, that is the target of explicit and implicit communications, as a mirror of the agent's. With the goal of providing a general understanding of this work, we firstly show prior relevant results addressing the informative communication of agents intentions and the production of legible behavior. In the second part of the paper we furnish the architecture with novel capabilities for explanations through off-the-shelf saliency methods, followed by preliminary qualitative results.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Mirror Agent Model, a framework where the observer is a mirror of the agent to generate interpretable behavior and explanations, integrating prior results on informative communication with saliency-based explanations and presenting preliminary qualitative results.
AI.motivation: To achieve interpretable agent behavior and explanations by aligning the observer's perspective with the agent's communications; to improve legibility of agent intentions and actions for humans or other agents.
AI.method: Proposes the Mirror Agent Model architecture that defines the observer (target of communication) as a mirror of the agent. The paper surveys prior work on informative communication of intentions and legible behavior, then extends the architecture with explanations using off-the-shelf saliency methods, reporting preliminary qualitative results.
AI.result: Qualitative evidence that the architecture can generate interpretable behavior and provide explanations via saliency, with initial demonstrations of the proposed explanatory capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The Mirror Agent Model offers a general framework for interpretable agent behavior and explanations by tying information transfer to a mirrored observer model, with early qualitative results supporting its feasibility and potential for broader applicability.

title: What Matters in On-Policy Distillation? A Perspective on Data Efficiency and Data Selection
summary: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a widely adopted post-training paradigm for enhancing large language models in reasoning domains. However, the data-centric mechanisms in OPD remain relatively underexplored. This paper presents a empirical study of data efficiency and data selection in OPD. We begin by investigating an extreme setting: training OPD on only one example, namely 1-shot OPD. Surprisingly, we find that 1-shot OPD is consistently effective across all sampled training examples and harder examples often yield superior performance gain. We next investigate what actually drives the student model's improvement in the training data. Our analysis reveals that the improvement is not driven by high token entropy, but the longer CoT paths which hard problems naturally generate. Training on longer CoT can help maintain closer alignment with the teacher over a long reasoning horizon, and learn critical thinking patterns usually missing in short CoTs, such as reflection (e.g., ``Alternatively''). Based on these insights, we propose a simple data selection method that selects only hard examples for training, where even ``unsolvable'' examples that completely exceed the teacher's capability can be successfully used. Our experiments conducted on four models ranging from 1.5B to 7B show that training the student model on only 8 selected hard examples matches the performance of the 17K dataset baseline.

AI.tldr: One-shot OPD is surprisingly effective across training examples; harder examples often yield bigger gains. The driver of improvement is longer chain-of-thought (CoT) paths rather than high token entropy. A data-selection method using only hard examples (even 'unsolvable' ones) achieves the 17K baseline with just 8 examples.
AI.motivation: To understand data-centric mechanisms in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) and evaluate data efficiency and selection strategies for reasoning-heavy LLM training.
AI.method: Empirical study across four models (1.5B–7B). Examine 1-shot OPD performance, analyze what drives improvement (entropy vs. CoT length), and propose a hard-example data-selection strategy that uses a small set of hard, including unsolvable, examples. Compare against baseline trained on a large 17K-example dataset.
AI.result: 1-shot OPD consistently yields gains across sampled examples; hard examples often provide larger performance improvements; longer CoT paths help maintain alignment with the teacher over extended reasoning; the proposed hard-example data selection with only 8 examples matches the 17K-example baseline across models.
AI.conclusion: Data-centric tuning that prioritizes hard CoT-based reasoning samples can achieve strong data efficiency in OPD; training with a minimal set of strategically chosen hard examples can rival large-scale data baselines, highlighting the value of reasoning-depth and difficulty-aware data selection.

title: CABAL: Multi-Agent Simulacra for Tracing the Effects of Collusive Bidding in Peer Review
summary: Recent reports during the AAAI-27 review cycle highlight the risk of reviewers coordinating bids for reciprocal assignment advantage. Prior work treats bidding, reviewer assignment, and review manipulation as separate stages, leaving the lifecycle effects of collusive bidding unclear. Real-world analysis is further constrained by typically unobservable collusive intent and the lack of counterfactuals for the same conference. Motivated by this gap, we introduce \alg, an end-to-end multi-agent simulacra framework for studying reviewer assignment integrity by holding the conference environment fixed and configuring LLM-driven reviewer agents with honest or collusive policies. We further develop an affinity-guided collusive bidding strategy that uses mutual reviewer-paper affinities to construct collusion rings and select target papers, producing expertise-consistent rather than arbitrarily targeted attacks. Controlled experiments show that collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture and that assigned colluders score target papers about two points higher than honest co-reviewers, while conference-wide effects remain comparatively modest. Evaluated bid-phase detectors provide only limited evidence of collusion: in a fixed-triplet detector stress test, native positive-bid graphs are confounded by benign affinity, while a Very-High-only diagnostic view enables precise but low-coverage local recovery.

AI.tldr: Proposes an end-to-end multi-agent simulacra framework ('alg') to study reviewer assignment integrity using LLM-driven reviewer agents with honest or collusive policies; introduces affinity-guided collusive bidding to form collusion rings; finds colluders can double target-paper capture and improve scores by ~2 points; detectors for collusion show limited efficacy; highlights confounds due to reviewer-paper affinity and low-coverage detection.
AI.motivation: Address the lifecycle effects of collusive bidding in conference peer review, which are difficult to observe in real settings due to unobservable intent and lack of counterfactuals; develop an end-to-end simulation to isolate and study these dynamics while keeping the conference environment fixed.
AI.method: Build an end-to-end simulacra framework ('alg') with fixed conference environment; configure LLM-driven reviewer agents with honest or collusive policies; develop an affinity-guided collusive bidding strategy leveraging mutual reviewer-paper affinities to form collusion rings and select target papers; evaluate using collusion-target capture metrics and review scores; assess detection performance via bid-phase detectors (fixed-triplet, Very-High-only views).
AI.result: Controlled experiments show collusive bidding more than doubles target-paper capture; colluders' target papers score ~2 points higher than honest co-reviewers; conference-wide effects remain modest; bid-phase detectors provide limited evidence; a fixed-triplet detector is confounded by benign affinity, while a Very-High-only diagnostic view yields precise but low-coverage local recovery.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven, end-to-end simulations reveal lifecycle effects of collusive bidding and show that affinity-guided collusion can be effective, yet existing detectors have limited reliability; results underscore the need for robust, counterfactual-aware detection and system-level defenses in conference review.

title: ACE: Adaptive Calibration-Free Expert Skipping for MoE-based LLMs
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures provide an efficient paradigm for scaling large language models (LLMs), yet fixed top-k routing activates the same number of expert slots for every token, causing substantial redundant computation. Existing expert-skipping methods often rely on router confidence, calibration data, or additional training, and therefore cannot reliably estimate the actual contribution of routed experts. To this end, we propose ACE, a training-free, calibration-free, and checkpoint-preserving framework for token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE-based LLMs. ACE contains two complementary components: 1) Global Spectral Proxy (GSP), which estimates global transformation capacity from the coupled gate, up, and down projections together with RMSNorm scaling; and 2) Router-Conditioned Refinement (RCR), which constructs expert-specific direction prototypes from centered router weights and evaluates expert responses along routing-preferred directions. During inference, ACE combines both estimates with runtime router gates and skips an expert slot only when both views identify it as low-contribution, while always retaining the top-1 expert. All expert statistics are computed offline, leaving only table lookups and lightweight scalar operations online. Extensive experiments across three MoE-based LLMs and eight benchmarks demonstrate that ACE consistently outperforms existing static and dynamic baselines, with increasingly pronounced advantages under aggressive expert skipping. For instance, at a 50% skipping ratio on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ACE reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 7.96% and improves average downstream accuracy by 4.15 percentage points over the strongest competing method.

AI.tldr: A training-free, calibration-free framework ACE enables token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE-based LLMs by combining a Global Spectral Proxy and Router-Conditioned Refinement to prune low-contribution experts at inference, while preserving the top-1 expert.
AI.motivation: Existing fixed top-k MoE routing causes redundant computation; prior expert-skipping methods rely on router confidence, calibration data, or training, which are unreliable or costly. A training-free, calibration-free, checkpoint-preserving solution is needed.
AI.method: ACE comprises two components. Global Spectral Proxy (GSP) estimates global transformation capacity from the coupled gate, up, and down projections together with RMSNorm scaling. Router-Conditioned Refinement (RCR) constructs expert-specific direction prototypes from centered router weights and evaluates expert responses along routing-preferred directions. During inference, ACE fuses both estimates with runtime router gates and skips an expert slot only when both views indicate low contribution, always retaining the top-1. All expert statistics are computed offline; online only table lookups and lightweight scalar operations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across three MoE-based LLMs and eight benchmarks show ACE consistently outperforms static and dynamic baselines, with stronger advantages under aggressive skipping. For example, at 50% skipping on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, ACE reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 7.96% and improves average downstream accuracy by 4.15 percentage points over the strongest competing method.
AI.conclusion: ACE provides a training-free, calibration-free, checkpoint-preserving mechanism for token-adaptive expert skipping in MoE LLMs. By combining a global transformation capacity proxy with router-conditioned refinement, ACE achieves reliable reductions in computation while maintaining or improving accuracy across diverse benchmarks.

title: Substrate-Aware AI Agents: Execution Context as a First-Class Input
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Reproducibility artifacts and source-linked evaluation code: https://github.com/manu2/Context-Aware-Agent-Experiment
summary: Autonomous AI agents increasingly select actions in environments whose memory, execution-time, runtime, compute, and operational constraints determine what counts as a suitable plan. We call the absence of this execution context from an agent's planning state substrate blindness. We test this general proposition through numerical code generation, where selected implementation choices and operational consequences are directly observable. Three frontier model configurations--Anthropic Claude Opus 5, OpenAI GPT-5.6-Sol, and Google Gemini 3.7 Flash--generate code for a high-dimensional pairwise Euclidean-distance task either from the task alone or with a 128 MB RAM and 10.0 s wall-time contract. Contract disclosure reduced measured peak process memory in 13 of 14 executable index-aligned task-only versus contract-disclosed comparisons and reduced mean wall time in all three cohorts, making execution up to 3.1x faster. Across the audited corpus, disclosure produced structural code changes including bounded blocking, float32 retention, upper-triangle traversal, and in-place or memory-mapped buffers. At a tighter 96 MB contract, independently sampled contract-disclosed cohorts achieved correct-and-within-budget outcomes of 4/5 for Claude Opus 5, 5/5 for GPT-5.6-Sol, and 3/5 for Gemini 3.7 Flash, compared with task-only outcomes of 0/5, 1/5, and 0/5; cohort mean MaxRSS and wall time were 49-74% and 35-64% lower than their task-only references. These results establish a controlled proof of concept for substrate-aware agent planning: a minimal execution contract induces proactive structural adaptation in generated programs, shifting computation away from unconstrained allocations and substantially improving observed resource-time profiles before execution.

AI.tldr: Substrate-aware planning: execution contracts shape code-generation under constraints, improving resource usage and success rates.
AI.motivation: Address 'execution-context blindness' in planning by testing whether explicit memory/time constraints alter generated programs to respect budgets.
AI.method: Generate code for a high-dimensional Euclidean-distance task using three frontier models (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini 3.7 Flash) under task-only and memory/time contracts (128 MB, 10.0 s; also 96 MB). Compare peak memory, wall-time, and structural code changes; evaluate correctness within budget.
AI.result: Contract-disclosed code show reduced peak memory (13/14 task-only comparisons) and reduced mean wall-time across cohorts (up to 3.1x faster). Observed structural shifts: bounded blocking, retention of float32, upper-triangle traversal, and use of in-place or memory-mapped buffers. At 96 MB, correctness-within-budget outcomes: Claude 4/5, GPT-5.6-Sol 5/5, Gemini 3.7 Flash 3/5 (vs 0/5, 1/5, 0/5 with task-only). Cohort means: MaxRSS and wall-time 49-74% and 35-64% lower than task-only.
AI.conclusion: A minimal execution contract can induce proactive, substrate-aware adaptations in generated programs, steering computation toward constrained resources and yielding substantial pre-execution resource-time efficiency gains.

title: Uncensored Open-weight Models: Redistribution as the Persistence Layer
summary: A rapidly expanding ecosystem of actors is removing built-in safety guardrails from open-weight AI models. We profile this ecosystem by identifying key producers, downstream reproductions, and emerging applications. Between January 2024 and March 2026, we identified 3,471 original uncensored models on HuggingFace, each repackaged an average of 2.4 times; three actors account for 52% of all 8,164 compressed redistributions. Once quantized and mirrored across separate accounts, formats, and registries such as Ollama, these models persist regardless of upstream removal and become easier to deploy downstream. Of the 1,643 identified GitHub applications integrating uncensored large language models (ULLMs), 25% were classified as explicitly malicious.

AI.tldr: A rapid, centralized ecosystem rapidly uncensors and redistributes large-language models, with heavy repackaging, persistence across formats/registries, and a notable share of malicious GitHub apps.
AI.motivation: Quantify the growth, structure, and risk of uncensored LLMs to inform mitigation strategies and policy.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of uncensored models and deployments: tracking 3,471 original uncensored HuggingFace models (Jan 2024–Mar 2026) with an average of 2.4 repackagings, identifying top actors accounting for >50% of 8,164 compressed redistributions, and cataloging 1,643 GitHub apps integrating ULLMs with a 25% malicious rate; includes downstream mirroring across formats/registries like Ollama.
AI.result: Key findings include (1) 3,471 original uncensored models on HuggingFace, repackaged an average of 2.4 times; (2) three actors account for 52% of 8,164 redistributions; (3) repackaged models persist after quantization and are mirrored across separate accounts/registries, complicating takedown; (4) among 1,643 GitHub apps integrating ULLMs, 25% are explicitly malicious.
AI.conclusion: The ecosystem is highly centralized, resilient to upstream removals, and poses significant downstream safety risks; comprehensive mitigation requires coordinated platform governance, provenance tracking, and stronger enforcement across distributions.

title: Do LLMs Exhibit Coherent Knowledge Structures in Mathematical Reasoning? A Perspective from Knowledge Space Theory
summary: Human knowledge is inherently structured and interdependent: mastery of a concept requires prior mastery of its prerequisites, a principle formalized by Knowledge Space Theory (KST). While LLMs achieve strong performance on complex reasoning tasks, it remains unclear whether they exhibit coherent, human-like knowledge structure. We introduce a KST-grounded framework for evaluating LLM knowledge structure in mathematical reasoning, using it as a normative framework to analyze whether LLM behavior adheres to principled knowledge dependencies. Evaluating eight open- and closed-source LLMs against real human learners, we find that (1) LLMs do not adhere to human knowledge structure -- they frequently violate knowledge dependencies and fail to leverage related knowledge provided in context to improve performance on dependent questions; (2) LLMs do not share a consistent knowledge structure among themselves, as reflected by low overlap in their knowledge distributions. Furthermore, these structural deficiencies remain largely invisible to accuracy-based and LLM-as-judge evaluations. Together, our results provide behavioral evidence that current LLMs knowledge does not follow a human-like structure.

AI.tldr: KST-based evaluation shows current LLMs lack human-like knowledge structure: they violate prerequisite dependencies, don’t consistently leverage related context, and differ across models; accuracy metrics miss these structural deficiencies.
AI.motivation: Assess whether LLM reasoning exhibits coherent, human-like knowledge structure as formalized by Knowledge Space Theory (KST).
AI.method: Apply a KST-grounded framework to eight open-/closed-source LLMs, compare against real human learners on mathematical reasoning, evaluate adherence to knowledge dependencies, use of contextual prior knowledge, and overlap of knowledge distributions among models.
AI.result: LLMs frequently violate knowledge dependencies, fail to utilize context to bolster dependent items, and show low cross-model overlap in knowledge distributions; these structural issues are largely invisible to standard accuracy-based or LLM-as-judge evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM knowledge does not exhibit human-like structured knowledge per KST; the framework reveals structural deficiencies not captured by accuracy alone, highlighting a need for KST-informed evaluation and training approaches.

title: A Unified Physics-Aware Quantum Machine Learning Framework across Power GaN HEMTs and Logic Nanowire FETs: Predicting Unseen Process Splits and Held-Out Geometry Combinations with Lower Error and Tighter Split-to-Split Variability
summary: We present a unified reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that discovers compact parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) for data-scarce device modeling. A graph neural network (GNN) policy optimized by proximal policy optimization (PPO) searches circuit architectures using leave-one-group-out cross-validation (LOGOCV) error on held-out process or geometry groups as the reward. The framework achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all 11 targets versus six classical baselines, with 59% lower error (Ioff) and 81% tighter fold variability (VTH) for HEMTs and 84% lower error (VTH, SS, Ioff) and 82% tighter fold variability (Ioff) for NWFETs. These results demonstrate the potential of RL-selected, classically simulated PQCs as compact surrogates with low OOD error and improved physical consistency, despite imposing no explicit physical constraints, penalty terms, or device-specific equations, on the two evaluated device datasets.

AI.tldr: RL framework discovers compact PQCs for data-scarce device modeling, achieving state-of-the-art MAE across 11 targets via LOGOCV-guided PPO on a GNN policy, outperforming six baselines with substantial robustness gains on HEMTs and NWFETs.
AI.motivation: Tackle data scarcity in device modeling by learning compact, physically coherent quantum circuit surrogates that generalize beyond the training data without enforcing explicit physics constraints.
AI.method: A graph neural network policy optimized with proximal policy optimization searches circuit architectures. The reward is LOGOCV error computed on held-out process or geometry groups. Evaluated on 11 targets against six classical baselines.
AI.result: Achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on all 11 targets. 59% lower error (Ioff) and 81% tighter fold variability (VTH) for HEMTs; 84% lower error (Ioff, V TH, SS) and 82% tighter fold variability (Ioff) for NWFETs. Indicates RL-selected, classically simulated PQCs act as compact surrogates with low OOD error and improved physical consistency, without explicit physics constraints or device-specific equations.
AI.conclusion: RL-informed PQCs can serve as compact, generalizable surrogates for data-scarce device modeling, achieving superior accuracy and stability across multiple device types without hard-coding physics, suggesting potential for broader adoption in quantum-classical hybrid surrogates.

title: Commonsense Reasoning in Computer Vision: Foundations, Recent Advancements, and Future Directions
summary: Commonsense reasoning in computer vision encompasses integrating visual data and contextual knowledge, crucial for enhancing AI's understanding of everyday scenarios. This understanding not only improves machine learning models but also enhances their ability to interact meaningfully with humans and the environment. Unlike CNN-based conventional vision models, which are designed to identify objects within a specific image, incorporating commonsense knowledge enables models to interpret scenes in a more holistic manner, thereby improving their spatial ability to reason about relationships among objects and actions. This integration not only enhances object recognition but also facilitates a deeper understanding of the contextual factors, ultimately leading to more precise predictions and interactions in real-world applications. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of recent developments that integrate commonsense knowledge into computer vision tasks. We systematically review approaches based on knowledge graphs, scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-augmented transformers. We also outline current limitations related to dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, and integration challenges. Finally, we highlight prospective research trajectories in cross-modal reasoning, scalable commonsense knowledge injection, and neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures to develop truly intelligent visual systems.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of integrating commonsense knowledge into computer vision, reviewing knowledge graphs, scene graphs, neuro-symbolic models, and commonsense-augmented transformers; identifies limitations (dataset bias, knowledge incompleteness, integration challenges) and outlines future directions (cross-modal reasoning, scalable knowledge injection, neuro-symbolic hybrids).
AI.motivation: To move beyond traditional object-centric CV models by embedding contextual and commonsense knowledge, enabling holistic scene understanding, improved relational reasoning, and more natural interactions with humans and environments.
AI.method: Systematic literature review and taxonomy of approaches that inject commonsense into CV, categorized by knowledge representations (knowledge graphs, scene graphs), model paradigms (neuro-symbolic, transformer-based), and cross-modal reasoning frameworks; analysis of dataset biases and integration challenges.
AI.result: Synthesis of current approaches, showing that incorporating commonsense improves relational and contextual reasoning in CV but remains hampered by incomplete knowledge and biased datasets; no standardized benchmarks yet for fair cross-study comparisons; evidence suggests hybrid neuro-symbolic and transformer methods are promising.
AI.conclusion: The survey highlights future directions including scalable commonsense knowledge injection, robust cross-modal reasoning, and neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures, along with the need for standardized benchmarks and datasets to evaluate progress toward truly intelligent visual systems.

title: Trace2Tower: Transition-Aware EigenTrace Induction of Multi-Level Skills for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on execution traces to master complex interactive tasks. However, current paradigms are bottlenecked by shallow trajectory retrieval and flat skill summarization, fundamentally ignoring the temporal dependencies and outcome-conditioned topology of agent behavior.
